x: In the temple precinct of Eanna at Uruk, scribes pressed reed styluses into clay to keep the accounts of grain, cattle, and labor. Their pictographs grew within centuries into cuneiform, the script of Sumerians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Hittites, and Persians, and history in the strict sense, the written record of the past, begins here.

The first kings of united Egypt, Hor-Aha, Djer, Den, and their successors, were laid in brick-lined tombs in the desert behind Abydos, ringed by the graves of servants who followed them in death. Later Egyptians believed the tomb of Djer to be the grave of Osiris himself, and pilgrims brought offerings there for two thousand years.

On the plain above Hangzhou Bay the Liangzhu people raised a walled city of some three hundred hectares, guarded against mountain floods by a great system of earthen dams. Their lords went to the grave with cong tubes and bi discs of carved jade, the finest of the age, and the city stands among the earliest states of East Asia.

At the northern tip of Honshu the hunters and fishers of the Jōmon age kept a great settlement for some seventeen centuries, with long halls, raised storehouses, and a tower set on six chestnut posts a metre thick. Heirs to one of the oldest pottery traditions in the world, they buried their dead in rows along the road that led into the village.

At Susa and on the Iranian plateau, scribes of the land later called Elam kept accounts in a script of their own, borrowed in idea from Uruk but not in signs. The proto-Elamite tablets, found as far east as Tepe Yahya, are the oldest writing of Iran, and they remain undeciphered.

At Shuruppak excavators found a layer of river silt laid down about 2900 B.C. by a great flood of the Euphrates. The Sumerian King List divides its history at the Flood, after which kingship came down from heaven to Kish, and Ziusudra of Shuruppak, saved from it in a great boat, lived on under other names in the Epic of Gilgamesh.

On the banks of the vanished Ghaggar river the farmers of Kalibangan scored their field in a criss-cross of furrows, among the oldest ploughed fields ever uncovered. Their walled town of mud brick, older than the great Indus cities, was later rebuilt on a grid of streets with a citadel and rows of fire altars, as the Harappan order took hold.

Gilgamesh, fifth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk in the Sumerian King List, was remembered as the builder of the great wall of Uruk, nearly six miles around, and as the hero who sought the plant of life and lost it to a serpent. His rival in the old tales, Aga of Kish, was the son of Enmebaragesi, the oldest king of Sumer whose own inscriptions survive.

For King Djoser of the Third Dynasty, his minister Imhotep raised six stepped terraces of dressed limestone above the necropolis of Memphis, the first colossal building of cut stone in the world. Imhotep, architect, priest, and sage, was honored by later Egyptians as a god of wisdom and healing, and the Greeks likened him to Asclepius.

In the dry valley of the Supe, some fourteen miles from the Pacific, a people without pottery or writing raised platform mounds and sunken circular plazas, the oldest known city of the Americas, in the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Fed by irrigated fields of squash and beans and by anchovies traded from the coast, they grew cotton for fishing nets and kept their accounts, it seems, in knotted cords.

In the death pits of Ur, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s, lay the lady Puabi beneath a cloak of beads and a headdress of golden leaves, with dozens of attendants, soldiers, and musicians who had gone with her into the grave. Lyres with bulls' heads of gold and lapis, and the Standard of Ur, show the wealth of the Sumerian cities.

At Harappa and its sister cities carvers cut thousands of small square seals of steatite, each bearing a beast, most often a one-horned bull, beneath a line of signs. Some four hundred distinct signs are known, written for the most part from right to left, yet no one has read them, and the tongue of the Indus people remains silent.

t: Sneferu Builds the First True Pyramid
x: Sneferu, father of Khufu, raised three pyramids. At Dahshur the Bent Pyramid changed its angle halfway up, probably for fear of collapse, and beside it the Red Pyramid rose at a gentle slope to become the first true smooth-sided pyramid, the model for Giza.

t: Mesalim Fixes the Border of Lagash
x: Mesalim, king of Kish and overlord of Sumer, judged the quarrel of Lagash and Umma over the rich plain of the Gu-edina and set up a boundary stone between them. The border did not hold: the two cities fought over that field for more than a century, the first war that can be followed in written record.

Beside the causeway to Khafre's pyramid, a ridge of limestone was carved into a lion with the head of a king, some seventy meters long. Half buried in sand for most of its history, the Great Sphinx was the guardian of the Giza plateau and became the emblem of Egypt itself.

On Salisbury Plain the builders of Stonehenge raised a ring of sarsen stones, each weighing some twenty-five tons, capped with lintels joined like timber, around a horseshoe of great trilithons. Smaller bluestones were dragged from the Preseli hills of Wales, and the axis is set on the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset.

Above the Third Cataract the Nubians built Kerma, the first great city of Africa beyond Egypt, with a towering temple of mud brick, the western deffufa, at its heart. Its kings, whom the Egyptians called rulers of Kush, grew rich on gold, ivory, and cattle, and in time were buried beneath vast mounds with hundreds of sacrificed retainers.

t: Ur-Nanshe and the Ships of Dilmun
x: Ur-Nanshe founded the first dynasty of Lagash, dug canals, and built temples to the city's gods. His inscriptions boast that the ships of Dilmun brought him timber from foreign lands as tribute, early witness to the sea trade that linked Sumer with the Gulf, Magan, and the cities of the Indus.

Eannatum of Lagash crushed the men of Umma in the war over the Gu-edina, made their ruler swear by the great gods to respect the boundary, and raised a stele of victory. On it the god Ningirsu holds the enemy in a great net while vultures carry off the heads of the slain. Its fragments are in the Louvre.

On an island in the salt Rann of Kutch the builders of Dholavira cut great stone reservoirs and channels to catch every monsoon stream, for the land around them was nearly desert. By the northern gate lay a signboard of ten large Indus signs inlaid in white gypsum, perhaps the city's name, the longest public inscription the Harappans left.

In 1873 Heinrich Schliemann dug from the burned second city of Troy a hoard of gold diadems, earrings, cups, and silver vessels and called it the Treasure of Priam. In truth it was a thousand years older than any Trojan War, the wealth of a lord of the early Bronze Age who held the straits.

In the burial chamber of Unas, last king of the Fifth Dynasty, spells were carved in columns of blue-painted hieroglyphs to guide the dead king to the stars and the company of Ra. They are the oldest religious writings of Egypt, and the source of the later Coffin Texts and Book of the Dead.

Urukagina of Lagash curbed the officials and priests who had seized the people's fields, cut the fees for burial and divorce, and swore to the god Ningirsu that the widow and the orphan would not be given over to the powerful. His decree, the oldest known reform of law, first uses the word amargi, freedom.

Lugalzagesi of Umma sacked Lagash, took Uruk, and ruled from it as king of all Sumer, claiming dominion from the Lower Sea to the Upper. His triumph lasted until Sargon of Akkad defeated him, took him captive, and led him in a neck stock to the gate of Enlil at Nippur.

Sargon of Akkad boasted that ships of Meluhha, Magan, and Dilmun moored at the quay of his capital. Meluhha was the Indus country: its carnelian beads, ivory, and timber reached Mesopotamia, and Indus seals turn up at Ur. At Lothal, on the Gulf of Khambhat, a great brick basin beside the warehouses has been read as a dockyard for this trade.

When the royal palace of Ebla burned, the fire baked some seventeen thousand clay tablets and fragments in its archive rooms, preserving the records of a Syrian kingdom that traded textiles and metals from Anatolia to Mesopotamia. Found by Paolo Matthiae's Italian expedition in the 1970s, they revealed a great power known before only from a few boasts of the kings of Akkad.

t: The Walls and Observatory of Taosi
x: In the Fen valley of southern Shanxi rose a walled town of nearly three hundred hectares, with palaces, granaries, and a semicircular platform whose pillars framed the sunrise at the solstices. Many have seen in it the seat of the sage-king Yao of tradition, and its painted dragon basins show a lordly class long before the Shang.

In the mountains of Oman the people of Magan built round stone towers and great communal tombs, mined and smelted copper, and shipped it with diorite to Sumer. Sargon boasted that the ships of Magan moored at the quay of Akkad, and Naram-Sin claimed to have defeated Manium, the lord of Magan.

In the heart of the Hattian land the lords of Alaca were laid in stone-lined graves with gold vessels, diadems, and the bronze standards of sun disks and stags that were carried before them. The tombs show a rich Anatolian kingdom long before the Hittites.

A man buried near Stonehenge with arrowheads, wrist guards, copper knives, and the oldest gold ornaments found in Britain had grown up, the chemistry of his teeth shows, in the Alpine lands. He belonged to the Beaker folk who brought metalworking to Britain.

t: Enheduanna, Priestess of the Moon God
x: Sargon made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of Nanna, the moon god of Ur, binding the old Sumerian cult to the new Akkadian throne. Her hymns to Inanna and to the temples of Sumer, copied by scribes for centuries after, make her the first author in history known by name.

Harkhuf of Elephantine led donkey caravans deep into Nubia to the land of Yam. On his fourth journey he brought back a pygmy who danced for the gods, and the boy king Pepi II wrote urging him to guard the dancer night and day. Harkhuf had the letter carved on his tomb.

t: Naram-Sin, King of the Four Quarters
x: Naram-Sin, grandson of Sargon, carried the arms of Akkad from the Persian Gulf to the Taurus and styled himself king of the four quarters of the world and a god. His victory stele, showing him climbing a mountain over the slain Lullubi, was carried off a thousand years later by the Elamites to Susa, where French excavators found it in 1898.

To hold the Khabur plains and the roads to the north, Naram-Sin of Akkad raised a massive fortified storehouse at Nagar, its bricks stamped with his name. Its massive walls were the grip of the first empire on a land of Hurrian princes.

Seafaring farmers from Taiwan crossed the Luzon Strait and settled the valley of the Cagayan, bringing red-slipped pottery, polished stone adzes, and the Austronesian tongue. From these first villages, at sites such as Nagsabaran, their descendants spread through the Philippines and Indonesia, and at last across the Pacific and the Indian Ocean as far as Easter Island and Madagascar.

In the oases of Margiana and Bactria a Bronze Age people built fortified compounds of mud brick with towers, palaces, and temples, as at Gonur Depe in the old delta of the Murghab. Their seals, bronze axes, and fine stone vessels travelled to the Indus and to Elam. The archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi named their world the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex.

After the death of Shar-kali-sharri the empire of Sargon dissolved. The Sumerian King List asks, 'Who was king? Who was not king?' The Gutians came down from the Zagros, the cities of Sumer went their own way, and the fall of Akkad passed into legend as the curse of the gods upon Naram-Sin's house.

Pepi II, who came to the throne as a child and was said to have reigned for some ninety years, outlived his heirs, and after him the power of Memphis crumbled. Provincial governors ruled as princes, low Nile floods brought famine, and for more than a century rival kings at Herakleopolis and Thebes contended for the Two Lands.

Gudea, ruler of Lagash in the Gutian years, rebuilt the Eninnu, the temple of Ningirsu, after the god commanded it in a dream. He brought cedar from the Amanus and diorite from Magan, and dozens of his statues in hard black stone, hands folded in prayer, survive.

Utu-hengal of Uruk called Sumer to arms against the Gutians, 'the fanged serpent of the mountains,' and defeated their king Tirigan, who fled and was handed over to him in chains. The victory restored the kingship to Sumer and prepared the way for Ur-Nammu.

t: Ur-Nammu Founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
x: Ur-Nammu, once governor of Ur, made himself king of Sumer and Akkad, raised the great ziggurat of the moon god Nanna, and issued the oldest law code yet found, setting fines in silver for injuries. His son Shulgi ruled for forty-eight years over a state whose scribes counted every sheep, every measure of barley, and every day of labor.

The oldest law code to survive was issued at Ur by Ur-Nammu or his son Shulgi. Its prologue promises that the orphan will not be given to the rich nor the widow to the powerful, and its laws set fines in silver for injuries where later codes would demand an eye for an eye.

As Akkad faded, Puzur-Inshushinak, king of Awan, made himself master of Susa and the lands of Elam and carried his arms into the Diyala and Akkad. He set up inscriptions in Akkadian and in Linear Elamite, a script of his own country, before Ur-Nammu and Shulgi drove Elam back.

Ur-Nammu began, and Shulgi finished, a stepped temple mountain for Nanna, the moon god of Ur: a mud brick core faced with baked brick set in bitumen. Restored by Nabonidus fifteen centuries later and dug out by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s, it still stands above the plain.

t: Yu the Great Founds the Xia
x: The Chinese histories tell that Yu the Great tamed the floods of the Yellow River by digging channels to the sea, labouring thirteen years without entering his own gate, and that the throne passed to his son, founding the Xia, the first dynasty in which rule passed from father to son.

Shulgi founded Puzrish-Dagan near Nippur as the receiving yard for the sheep, goats, and cattle that every province of his kingdom owed the crown and the temples. Tens of thousands of its tablets, recording each animal received and issued, show the most exacting bureaucracy of the ancient world.

Mentuhotep II, prince of Thebes, overcame the kings of Herakleopolis and joined the Two Lands again, opening the Middle Kingdom. He built his terraced mortuary temple in the bay of cliffs at Deir el-Bahari, and in a tomb nearby were found some sixty of his soldiers, slain in battle and buried with honor.

Shu-Sin of Ur built a long wall across the north of his kingdom and named it 'the one that keeps away the Tidnum,' to hold back the Amorite herdsmen pressing in from the Syrian steppe. It failed: within a generation Amorite chiefs ruled the cities of the land.

Ishbi-Erra of Mari, sent by Ibbi-Sin of Ur to buy grain, kept the grain and the city of Isin and made himself king there. When the Elamites sacked Ur he drove their garrison out and claimed the inheritance of the Third Dynasty, the kingship of Sumer and Akkad.

Weakened by famine and by Amorite tribes pressing in from the west, the empire of Ur fell to an army from Elam and Shimashki, which stormed the city and led King Ibbi-Sin away in chains to Anshan. The Lament for Ur mourned the dead lying in the streets and the abandoned temple of Nanna.

From the hill country between the Cross River and the Cameroon Grassfields, farmers speaking the ancestral Bantu tongue began a slow advance south and east. Over the following two and a half thousand years their descendants, carrying the yam, the hoe, and in time the forge, peopled the Congo forest, the Great Lakes, and the lands beyond the Zambezi, until one family of languages covered nearly half the continent.

On the steppe east of the southern Urals, men of the Sintashta culture built walled towns of bronze-smiths and buried their chiefs with horses and two-wheeled chariots with spoked wheels, the oldest known. Within a few centuries the war chariot had spread to the Near East, India, and China.

Dilmun, the land of the rising sun and of paradise in Sumerian song, grew rich as the market between Mesopotamia, Magan, and the Indus. On Bahrain its people raised the temples of Barbar and tens of thousands of burial mounds, great and small, which still cover the island's center.

t: Amenemhat I Founds the Twelfth Dynasty
x: Amenemhat, vizier of the last Mentuhotep, took the throne, founded the Twelfth Dynasty, and built a new capital, Itjtawy, Seizer of the Two Lands, near the mouth of the Faiyum. Murdered in a palace plot after thirty years, he was made to counsel his son Senusret I from beyond the grave in a famous Instruction, and the Tale of Sinuhe opens with his death.

When Amenemhat I was murdered in his palace, the courtier Sinuhe fled in panic to Retenu, in Canaan, where he married a chief's daughter, grew rich, and slew a champion in single combat. Old and homesick, he begged leave to return and be buried in Egypt. His story was the favorite classic of Egyptian schools.

Senusret I carried Egypt's border south to the second cataract and built the fortress of Buhen, with walls of mud brick, towers, and a dry ditch, to command the river and the gold of Wawat. A chain of such forts made Lower Nubia an Egyptian province for nearly three centuries.

Lipit-Ishtar, king of Isin, issued laws in Sumerian on inheritance, slaves, hired oxen, and orchards, set between a prologue and an epilogue that call down the gods' curses on any who erase them. They are the model Hammurabi followed nearly two centuries later.

At the word of the Lord, Abram left Haran with Sarai his wife and Lot his nephew and came into the land of Canaan, to the oak of Moreh at Shechem, where God promised the land to his offspring and Abram built an altar. Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike call him father in faith.

On Crete the Minoans raised palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia, sprawling courts of storerooms, shrines, and painted halls without walls of defense, the seats of the first civilization of Europe. Their ships carried oil, wine, and fine pottery to Egypt and the Levant, and their scribes wrote in hieroglyphs and in the still unread Linear A.

After seven centuries of order the great Indus cities emptied. Rivers shifted their beds, the Ghaggar-Hakra dwindled to a seasonal stream, and the Mesopotamian trade fell away. Mohenjo-daro's drains choked and its fine houses were cut up into hovels; the script and the standard weights passed out of use, and the people scattered into villages eastward and south into Gujarat.

Merchant families of Assur kept a trading colony beside the Anatolian city of Kanesh, sending tin and fine textiles by donkey caravan across the Taurus and taking home silver and gold. More than twenty thousand of their letters and contracts, found at Kültepe, make up the oldest great business archive in the world.

t: Sumu-abum Founds the Dynasty of Babylon
x: Sumu-abum, an Amorite chieftain, made the small town of Babylon on the Euphrates the seat of his house. His line would hold it for three centuries, and under his descendant Hammurabi the obscure town became the capital of Mesopotamia and the holy city of Marduk.

t: Senusret III Sets the Border at Semna
x: Senusret III fixed Egypt's southern frontier at Semna, above the second cataract, with fortresses on both banks and a boundary stele forbidding any Nubian to pass north except to trade. A later stele mocks the Nubians as cowards and warns his sons to hold the line.

Canaanite workers at the Egyptian turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim wrote their own tongue with a few dozen signs borrowed from hieroglyphs, each standing for the first sound of the word it pictured. From this alphabet came the Phoenician, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and Arabic letters.

Amenemhat III, who completed the reclamation of the Faiyum, built his pyramid at Hawara with a vast temple beside it, a maze of courts and chambers. Herodotus, who saw it thirteen centuries later, called it the Labyrinth and judged it greater than the pyramids.

Shamshi-Adad, an Amorite adventurer, seized Ashur and built a kingdom across upper Mesopotamia, ruling from Shubat-Enlil while his sons held Ekallatum and Mari. He took the title king of the universe, and his letters scold the idle younger son at Mari like any exasperated father.

In the desert of the Tarim, on a dune bristling with tall wooden posts, a herding people buried their dead in boat-shaped coffins wrapped in cowhide. The dry sands preserved them whole, felt caps, woollen cloaks, and baskets of grain beside them, and they are among the oldest witnesses of human life in the Tarim Basin.

A scribe, probably at Larsa, ruled a clay tablet into columns and filled it with right-angled triangles whose sides are whole numbers, set out in base sixty. Plimpton 322, now at Columbia University, shows Babylonian mathematicians at home with such triples a thousand years before Pythagoras.

Rim-Sin I of Larsa captured Isin and ended its dynasty, making himself master of all Sumer. So great was the victory that his scribes dated every year by it for the rest of his reign, three decades in all, until Hammurabi of Babylon took Larsa in its turn.

Sobekneferu, daughter of Amenemhat III, ruled Egypt as king after the death of Amenemhat IV, the first woman known with certainty to have taken the full titles of a pharaoh. Her short reign closed the Twelfth Dynasty, the classic age of the Middle Kingdom.

On the death of Shamshi-Adad, Zimri-Lim recovered his father's throne at Mari. His palace of some three hundred rooms, with its painted courts, held an archive of about twenty thousand tablets whose letters on war, diplomacy, prophecy, and river trade light up the age of Hammurabi.

A letter at Mari reckons the powers of the age: ten or fifteen kings follow Hammurabi of Babylon, as many follow Rim-Sin of Larsa, but twenty kings follow Yarim-Lim of Yamhad. From Halab, the city of the storm god Hadad, his house ruled northern Syria for two centuries.

The sukkalmah of Elam, greatest of the kings to the east, took Eshnunna and tried to set Babylon and Larsa against each other. Hammurabi joined with Zimri-Lim of Mari and drove the Elamites back across the Tigris, the first step in his conquest of all Mesopotamia.

After a long siege Hammurabi of Babylon took Larsa and the aged Rim-Sin, and with it all of Sumer. Within two years Eshnunna and Mari had fallen too, and the Amorite king of a small city ruled from the Gulf to the middle Euphrates.

Zimri-Lim of Mari had been Hammurabi's ally, but the king of Babylon turned on him, took the city, and two years later pulled down its walls. The great palace of some three hundred rooms burned, preserving about twenty thousand tablets of royal correspondence, the richest record of politics and diplomacy in the age of Hammurabi.

On the Luo River near Luoyang rose the first palace city of China, with halls of rammed earth inside a walled enclosure, a bronze foundry, and a turquoise workshop. Here were cast the earliest ritual bronze vessels, and here a dragon of some two thousand turquoise pieces lay upon a buried lord. Many scholars take it for a capital of the Xia.

At Kerma, capital of Kush, the kings raised a temple of solid mud brick, the Western Deffufa, nearly twenty meters high. Their burial mounds held beds, bronze daggers, and hundreds of retainers sacrificed to follow them, the wealth of the strongest power on the Nile south of Egypt.

t: Hazor, Head of All Those Kingdoms
x: Hazor, above the Sea of Galilee, was the largest city of Canaan, its lower town spread over some eighty hectares behind earthen ramparts. Its kings corresponded with Mari, and the Book of Joshua remembers it as 'the head of all those kingdoms.'

Anitta, king of Kussara and Kanesh, took Hattusa by night, razed it, sowed weeds on its site, and cursed any king who would settle there again. His account is the oldest text in the Hittite language, and within a century Hattusa rose again as the Hittite capital.

When the cities of the south rose under a second Rim-Sin, Hammurabi's son Samsu-iluna put them down and tore down the walls of Ur and Uruk. Within a generation the oldest cities of Sumer stood half empty, and the marshes of the far south passed to the kings of the Sealand.

Iluma-ilum made himself king in the marshes and the old cities of the far south, beyond the reach of Babylon. His line, the First Dynasty of the Sealand, held the land of Sumer for some two and a half centuries and kept its learning alive, until the Kassites took it.

t: The Princess of Khok Phanom Di
x: At Khok Phanom Di, a village of potters near the old shore of the Gulf of Thailand, a woman was laid in her grave beneath some 120,000 shell beads, with a great shell disc on her breast and a clay anvil at her side. Her burial, among generations of rice-growing fishers, is the richest of the Neolithic age of mainland Southeast Asia.

Above the floodplain of the lower Mississippi, hunters and fishers heaped up six concentric ridges of earth three quarters of a mile across and a great mound beside them, carrying the soil in baskets. Their trade drew copper from the Great Lakes and soapstone from the Appalachians, making Poverty Point the hub of the widest exchange network of its age in North America.

In the palace of Phaistos a clay disc was stamped on both sides with a spiral of signs, forty-five different stamps in all, among them heads with crested headdresses, ships, and shields. Found in 1908, it is the oldest printed text, and no one has read it.

West Semitic rulers from Canaan, whom the Egyptians called heqau khasut, rulers of foreign lands, took power in the eastern Delta and made Avaris their capital. Their Fifteenth Dynasty held Lower Egypt for a century and took tribute from Thebes, and in their time the horse-drawn chariot and the composite bow came to the Nile.

Labarna, who took the name Hattusili, rebuilt Hattusa in defiance of Anitta's curse and made it the seat of the Hittite kingdom. He led his chariots over the Taurus against Yamhad and the cities of Syria, and his grandson Mursili I would carry the war to Babylon.

In the reign of Ammi-saduqa the astronomers of Babylon recorded the first and last appearances of Venus over twenty-one years. Copied into later omen collections, the Venus Tablet is still used to fix the dates of Hammurabi's dynasty and so of the whole Bronze Age Near East.

The volcano of Thera blew apart in one of the greatest eruptions of human history, burying the Minoan town of Akrotiri under ash and pumice and casting tephra across the Aegean and beyond. Its people had fled in time; their houses, with frescoes of boxing boys, swallows, and fleets, lay beneath the ash until Spyridon Marinatos began to excavate them in 1967.

Tradition holds that Tang, lord of Shang, rose against Jie, the last and most wicked king of Xia, routed him at Mingtiao, and founded a house that ruled the Yellow River plain for more than five centuries. A walled Shang city built soon afterward stands only a few kilometres from the old palaces of Erlitou.

Within a ring of upright slabs on the hill of Mycenae, warrior lords were buried with gold death masks, inlaid daggers, and cups of gold. Heinrich Schliemann opened them in 1876 and believed he had found Agamemnon; they were three centuries older, the first great lords of Mycenaean Greece.

A bronze disc inlaid with gold, showing the sun or full moon, a crescent, and stars among them a cluster like the Pleiades, was buried on a hill near Nebra. Recovered from looters in 2002, it is the oldest known picture of the heavens and may have served to reckon the farming year.

The Hittite king Mursili I marched down the Euphrates, took Babylon, and ended the dynasty of Hammurabi under its last king, Samsu-ditana. He carried off the statue of Marduk and went home with his plunder, leaving the land to the Kassites, who would rule Babylonia for more than four centuries.

In the years of Egypt's division, a great army of Kush, with Medjay and men of Punt, swept north into Upper Egypt. An inscription in the tomb of Sobeknakht, governor of Elkab, found in 2003, records how he beat them back, a glimpse of how near Kerma came to ruling Thebes.

Seqenenre Tao of Thebes took up the struggle against the Hyksos king Apepi. His mummy, found in 1881, shows the wounds that killed him: blows of axe and spear to the head, of the kind dealt by Hyksos weapons. His sons Kamose and Ahmose carried on the war.

Kamose of Thebes would not share Egypt with an Asiatic in Avaris and a Nubian in Kush. He sailed north, sacked the towns of the Hyksos' allies, and reached the walls of Avaris, and on the desert road he caught a messenger carrying Apepi's letter asking the king of Kush to attack Thebes from the south.

The Shang kings built at Zhengzhou a city enclosed by walls of rammed earth nearly seven kilometers around, with palaces, bronze foundries, and bone workshops beyond them. Its great bronze cauldrons show the casting skill of the early Shang state.

Seqenenre Tao of Thebes died in battle with the Hyksos, his skull split by their axes, and Kamose carried the war north to the walls of Avaris. It was Ahmose, his successor, who took the city, pursued the enemy into Canaan, and besieged Sharuhen for three years, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom.

After two generations in which Hittite kings and princes murdered one another for the throne, Telipinu laid down the order of succession and ordered the council of nobles to judge any prince who shed royal blood. His edict recalls the reigns before him as a warning to his heirs.

Herding tribes speaking an Indo-Aryan tongue came over the passes into the land of seven rivers and there composed the Rigveda: 1,028 hymns to Indra, Agni, Varuna, and Soma, in a Sanskrit kin to Greek and Latin. Learned by heart and handed down by priestly families with flawless exactness for three thousand years, the hymns are the oldest scripture still in use.

Thutmose I sailed beyond the Third Cataract, slew the ruler of Kush, and hung his body head downward from the prow of the royal ship on the way home. His boundary inscription at Kurgus, upstream of the Fourth Cataract, marked the farthest reach of Egypt, and within a generation Kerma lay in ruins and Nubia was ruled by an Egyptian viceroy, the King's Son of Kush.

Seafarers from the islands to the north brought the dingo, a half-tamed dog of Asian descent, to the Australian continent, where it spread from coast to coast and became the companion and hunting partner of the Aboriginal peoples. The oldest dingo bones yet found, at Madura Cave on the Nullarbor Plain, are some three thousand two hundred years old.

t: The Stone Villages of Dhar Tichitt
x: Along the sandstone cliffs of Dhar Tichitt, at the edge of a Sahara that was slowly drying, herders and millet farmers raised hundreds of dry-stone compounds, some villages holding thousands of souls. They are the oldest known stone-built settlements of West Africa, and their builders, probable ancestors of the Soninke, foreshadowed the towns of ancient Ghana.

Thutmose I led the first Egyptian army to the Euphrates and set up a stele on its bank. His soldiers marveled at a river that seemed to run backward, flowing south where the Nile flows north. Egypt was now a power in Asia as well as Africa.

Hatshepsut, widow of Thutmose II and regent for the young Thutmose III, had herself crowned king and ruled some fifteen years. She built the terraced temple of Deir el-Bahari beneath the cliffs of Thebes and sent a fleet to Punt for incense trees, carved on its walls.

Idrimi, a prince of Halab driven into exile, lived seven years among the Habiru, then sailed with them to take Alalakh and swore fealty to Parattarna, king of Mitanni. He told his life on his own statue, found in 1939 and now in the British Museum, a rare royal autobiography.

The Kassite kings of Babylon conquered the Sealand, and its last king, Ea-gamil, fled to Elam. For the first time since Hammurabi's sons the whole of Babylonia, from the Diyala to the Gulf, obeyed one throne, and the Kassites would hold it for nearly three centuries more.

Against the advice of his officers, Thutmose III led his army in single file through the narrow Aruna pass and fell on the coalition of the king of Kadesh before Megiddo. The enemy fled into the city, hauled up over the walls by their clothing, and surrendered after a siege of seven months. It is the first battle recorded in detail.

The palaces of Crete burned, and Greek-speaking lords from the mainland took Knossos. Their scribes adapted the Minoan script into Linear B to write early Greek, a script Michael Ventris deciphered in 1952. From this time the Aegean belonged to the Mycenaeans.

t: The Exodus and the Law at Sinai
x: Four hundred and eighty years before Solomon began the Temple, by the reckoning of the First Book of Kings, Moses led the children of Israel out of Egypt after the plagues and the first Passover. They crossed the sea on dry ground, and at Mount Sinai God gave them the Law and the Ten Commandments.

Twenty-two lands of western Anatolia, among them Wilusiya and Taruisa, leagued together as Assuwa against the Hittites. Tudhaliya I crushed them and carried off thousands of captives. A bronze sword of Aegean make, inscribed as an offering after this victory, was found at Hattusa in 1991.

The scribes of Ugarit pressed an alphabet of thirty wedge-shaped letters into clay and wrote with it the myths of Baal and El, the epics of Kirta and Aqhat, letters, and accounts. Tablets for schoolboys set the letters in nearly the order of the later Hebrew alphabet.

Kikkuli of Mitanni, master horse trainer, wrote out for the Hittite court a seven-month course for chariot horses: grazing, trotting, bathing in the river, and gallops measured by the day. His technical words and numbers come from an Indo-Aryan tongue, the language of Mitanni's charioteer class.

The Kassite king Kurigalzu I founded a new royal city on the edge of the Babylonian plain and named it for himself. Its ziggurat, layered with reed mats and bitumen, still rises above the desert west of Baghdad, so tall that travelers once took it for the Tower of Babel.

Ashur-uballit I threw off the overlordship of Mitanni, wrote to Pharaoh as a great king and a brother, and married his daughter to the Kassite king of Babylon. From his reign Assyria was a great power, and the city state of merchants became the kingdom that would one day rule the Near East.

t: The Lapita Potters of the Bismarck Sea
x: In the Bismarck Archipelago appeared a people who stamped their pottery with fine toothed patterns of faces and geometric bands, raised houses on stilts over the lagoons, and sailed outrigger canoes. These were the Lapita folk, Austronesians from Island Southeast Asia, and within a few centuries their voyages would carry them into the empty ocean beyond the Solomons.

The archive of Amarna, found in 1887, holds the letters that the kings of Babylon, Assyria, Mitanni, Hatti, and Alashiya wrote to Amenhotep III and Akhenaten in Akkadian, as brothers and equals, along with the pleas of Canaanite vassals such as Rib-Hadda of Byblos against the Habiru and Amurru.

When the Hittites set Shattiwaza on the throne of Mitanni, the treaty called its gods to witness: Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Nasatya twins, gods of the Rigveda. The Mitanni kings bore Indo-Aryan names and their charioteers Indo-Aryan words, though their people spoke Hurrian.

Amenhotep IV turned from Amun and the old gods to the sole worship of the sun disk, the Aten, took the name Akhenaten, and built a new capital, Akhetaten, on virgin ground halfway between Thebes and Memphis. In its ruins were found the Amarna letters, cuneiform tablets of the pharaoh's correspondence with Babylon, Mitanni, Assyria, and the princes of Canaan.

The Hittite king Suppiluliuma I crossed the Euphrates, sacked the Mitannian capital Washukanni, and stripped King Tushratta of his Syrian vassals. When Tushratta was murdered by one of his sons, Suppiluliuma set the fugitive prince Shattiwaza on a vassal throne, and the Hittites stood supreme from central Anatolia to the Euphrates.

The boy king Tutankhamun, raised under Akhenaten, abandoned Amarna, reopened the temples of Amun and the old gods, and proclaimed the restoration on a stele at Karnak. He died young, and his small tomb in the Valley of the Kings, found nearly intact by Howard Carter in 1922, made him the most famous pharaoh.

Prisoners brought back from a war against Egypt carried a plague that ravaged the Hittite land for twenty years and killed Suppiluliuma I and his son. Mursili II searched the old tablets, confessed his father's broken oath, and in long prayers begged the gods to lift their anger.

Mursili II marched on Arzawa, the great kingdom of the west, whose king had defied his father. Arzawa's capital Apasa, later Ephesus, fell; its king fled across the sea; tens of thousands of captives were led to Hatti; and the west was divided into vassal kingdoms sworn to the Hittite king.

A merchant ship sank off the Lycian coast carrying ten tons of Cypriot copper and a ton of tin, the makings of eleven tons of bronze, with glass ingots, ebony, ivory, amber, Canaanite jars, and a gold scarab of Nefertiti. Found by a sponge diver in 1982, it is the richest cargo of the Bronze Age.

Seti I built at Abydos a temple of finely carved limestone to Osiris and the gods. In one corridor he and his son Ramesses offer to a list of seventy-six kings of Egypt from Menes onward, the King List of Abydos, which leaves out Hatshepsut and the kings of Amarna.

Ramesses II made his family's seat in the eastern Delta, beside the ruins of Avaris, into a great capital, Pi-Ramesses, 'House of Ramesses, Great of Victories,' with palaces, temples, and chariot barracks facing Asia. Its stones were later carried off to build Tanis.

t: Abu Simbel Cut from the Cliff
x: In Nubia, Ramesses II had a temple cut deep into a sandstone cliff, fronted by four seated colossi of himself twenty meters high. Twice a year the rising sun lights the gods in its inmost sanctuary. In the 1960s the whole temple was cut apart and raised above the waters of Lake Nasser.

Shalmaneser I of Assyria defeated Shattuara II, last king of Hanigalbat, the remnant of Mitanni, and his Hittite and Aramean allies. He annexed the Khabur and the Balikh, set Assyrian governors in the old Hurrian cities, and carried the frontier to the Euphrates opposite the Hittites.

t: Ramesses II Makes Peace with the Hittites
x: Fifteen years after Kadesh, Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III swore an alliance of mutual defense, extradition of fugitives, and brotherhood between their houses, recorded in hieroglyphs at Karnak and in Akkadian on clay tablets at Hattusa. It is the oldest peace treaty whose text survives from both sides, and Ramesses later married Hattusili's daughter.

At Yin, the last Shang capital, the diviners of King Wu Ding heated ox shoulder blades and turtle shells until they cracked, and carved the king's questions upon them: of harvests, wars, childbirth, and the will of the ancestors. Some 150,000 fragments survive, the oldest body of Chinese writing, and their script is the direct ancestor of the characters still in use.

Untash-Napirisha, king of Anshan and Susa, built a new holy city southeast of Susa around a ziggurat dedicated to Inshushinak, the god of Susa, its bricks stamped with his inscriptions in Elamite and Akkadian. It is the best preserved ziggurat in the world; sacked by Ashurbanipal in the seventh century B.C., it lay buried until its excavation in the 1950s.

A Hittite king wrote to the king of Ahhiyawa as a brother and a great king, complaining of raids out of Millawanda, later Miletus, and of quarrels over Wilusa. Most scholars take Ahhiyawa for the land of the Achaeans, Homer's name for the Greeks who fought at Troy.

The kings of Mycenae ringed their citadel with walls of stones so huge that later Greeks believed the Cyclopes had laid them, and over the main gate two lions face each other across a column, the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe. Nearby rose the tholos tomb called the Treasury of Atreus.

On a hill above the bay of Navarino stood the palace of the kings of Pylos, Homer's sandy Pylos of Nestor, with a painted throne room and a clay bathtub. When it burned about 1180 B.C. the fire baked its archive of Linear B tablets: lists of land, flocks, smiths, and rowers for the fleet.

In the Tollense valley of northern Germany, several thousand warriors fought at a river crossing. The bones of more than a hundred men, struck by bronze and flint arrowheads and wooden clubs, lie in the riverbed with those of their horses. It is the largest battlefield of the Bronze Age yet found in Europe.

In a rock sanctuary outside Hattusa, Tudhaliya IV had the gods of Hatti carved in two processions meeting at the storm god Teshub and the goddess Hebat. The great king himself stands in the embrace of his protecting god, the culmination of the Hittite marriage of Anatolian and Hurrian faiths.

Tukulti-Ninurta I built a new royal city across the Tigris from Ashur, with a palace, a ziggurat, and a temple of the god Ashur, and named it after himself. It was the first of the great new capitals that Assyrian kings would raise for their own glory.

Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria defeated the Kassite king Kashtiliash IV, led him to Ashur in chains, and carried off the statue of Marduk. For some seven years Assyria ruled Babylon through its governors, and an Assyrian epic celebrated the triumph, until the Babylonian nobles rose and the Assyrian king was murdered by his own son.

Merneptah, son of Ramesses II, defeated the Libyans and their allies of the Sea Peoples who invaded the western Delta. His victory stele, found at Thebes in 1896, lists the conquered of Canaan and declares 'Israel is laid waste,' the oldest mention of Israel outside the Bible.

In the Chengdu plain a kingdom unknown to the written record buried its treasures in sacrificial pits: bronze heads with faces of gold foil, masks with eyes thrust out on stalks, a standing figure taller than a man, and a bronze tree nearly four metres high. Its art is unlike anything of the Shang, and it shows how many peoples made ancient China.

t: The Colossal Heads of San Lorenzo
x: On a plateau above the Coatzacoalcos River, the Olmec, earliest of the great peoples of Mesoamerica, built their first capital and carved from basalt hauled out of the Tuxtla Mountains colossal portrait heads of their rulers, some weighing more than twenty tons. Their were-jaguar gods, their rubber ball game, and their rites passed down to every later people of Mexico and Central America.

Fu Hao, a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, led armies against the Qiang and other enemies and presided over sacrifices. Her tomb at Anyang, found intact in 1976, held hundreds of bronzes, jades, and ivories, and the oracle bones record the king's anxious questions about her health.

Ugarit, the rich port of northern Syria, was stormed and burned and never rebuilt. Among the ruins lay tablets in its own cuneiform alphabet of thirty signs, the epics of Baal and Keret, and a letter from its last king, Ammurapi, telling the king of Alashiya that enemy ships were burning his towns while his army was away in the Hittite land.

In the reign of Suppiluliuma II the Hittite empire, worn by famine, revolt, and the troubles that shook the whole eastern Mediterranean, came apart. The court abandoned Hattusa, which was later burned, and the name of the Hittites lived on only in the Neo-Hittite kingdoms of Syria and the Taurus, such as Carchemish and Melid.

Fire destroyed the palace at Pylos, and with it baked hard the Linear B tablets of its last year, which record rowers summoned to the coast and watchers posted against an enemy from the sea. One by one the Mycenaean palaces fell, writing was lost in Greece for four centuries, and the age of heroes passed into the memory of the epic poets.

t: Ramesses III Repels the Sea Peoples
x: In his eighth year Ramesses III met a confederacy of the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, Tjekker, Shekelesh, Denyen, and Weshesh, who had come down through Syria by land and sea. He crushed them on the borders of Egypt and in the river mouths of the Delta, and carved the sea battle on the walls of his temple at Medinet Habu.

The Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte swept through Babylonia, broke Kassite power, and carried home to Susa the greatest monuments of Mesopotamia: the law stele of Hammurabi, the victory stele of Naram-Sin, and the obelisk of Manishtushu. He had his own name carved upon some of them as trophies, and there French archaeologists found them between 1898 and 1902.

Tiglath-Pileser I of Assyria fought the Aramean tribes across the Euphrates, by his own count twenty-eight times, and marched to the Mediterranean, where Byblos, Sidon, and Arvad paid him tribute. Off Arvad he put out to sea and killed a nahiru, a great sea creature, and in Syria he hunted elephants and lions, as his annals proudly record.

t: The Regency of the Duke of Zhou
x: When King Wu died soon after the conquest of Shang, his brother Dan, the Duke of Zhou, governed for the boy King Cheng. He crushed the rising of the Three Guards and the Shang prince Wugeng, planted the conquered nobles in a new eastern capital at Luoyi, and enfeoffed kinsmen across the plain. Confucius revered him as the model of a loyal minister.

At Byblos the sarcophagus of King Ahiram bears an inscription in twenty-two letters, each standing for a consonant, the script the Phoenicians carried in their ships to every shore of the Mediterranean. From it came the Aramaic and Hebrew letters, and through the Greeks, who added vowels, the Etruscan and Latin alphabets in which most of the world now writes.

David, son of Jesse of Bethlehem, who had fought the Philistines in the service of King Saul, was anointed king over Judah and then over all Israel. He took the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem, made it the City of David, and brought into it the Ark of the Covenant, making it the royal and holy center of his people for all time.

As iron came into use the Vedic tribes pushed east into the plain between the Yamuna and the Ganges. There the Kuru kings united the clans, fixed the great sacrifices in their solemn order, and gathered the hymns into the collections of the Vedas. Hastinapura, remembered in the Mahabharata as the Kuru capital, lay at the heart of this first true Vedic kingdom.

Across the Mongolian steppe the herders of the Bronze Age raised tall stones carved with leaping stags, their antlers swept back like wings, and with belts, daggers, and bows. Set beside great burial mounds ringed with the skulls of horses, the deer stones mark the rise of the horse-breeding peoples who would shape the history of the east for three thousand years.

On the Khorat Plateau the villagers of Ban Chiang were casting bronze bracelets, spearheads, and bells in clay moulds and burying them with their dead; their later graves hold the painted red-on-buff pots for which the site is famed. Found by chance in 1966, Ban Chiang opened the Bronze Age of mainland Southeast Asia to the learned world.

Lapita voyagers crossed a stretch of open sea wider than any their forebears had braved and settled Efate, the first men in these islands. At Teouma they buried their dead headless, the skulls taken away for rites of ancestor worship; three skulls were laid upon the chest of one man. It is the oldest cemetery yet found in Remote Oceania.

Solomon, son of David, built the Temple of the Lord on Mount Moriah with cedar from Lebanon and craftsmen sent by Hiram, king of Tyre, and set the Ark of the Covenant in its inner sanctuary. His reign, remembered for its wisdom, its wealth, and the fleets sent to Ophir, marked the height of the united kingdom of Israel.

Beneath a long apsidal hall at Lefkandi in Euboea, built about 950 B.C. and the largest building of its age in Greece, a warrior's ashes lay in a bronze urn beside a woman richly adorned with gold, while four horses were buried in a shaft alongside. The find shows that wealth and seafaring to the Levant survived the darkest Greek centuries.

High in the Andes where two rivers meet, the priests of Chavín de Huántar built a temple of stone galleries in which, amid the roar of water rushing through hidden channels, pilgrims were brought before the Lanzón, a carved granite blade bearing a fanged god. Its feline and serpent imagery spread along the coast and the highlands, the first style shared across the Andes.

Sailing east from Fiji, Lapita canoes reached Tongatapu and founded a village at Nukuleka on the lagoon shore, held to be the first settlement in Polynesia. In Tonga and Samoa the newcomers, cut off from their kin to the west, slowly became the Polynesians, and there they lingered for nearly two thousand years before the great voyages to the east.

Ashurnasirpal II, who boasted of flaying rebels and walling up their bodies, rebuilt Kalhu on the Tigris as his capital. To open his palace, lined with carved reliefs and guarded by winged human-headed bulls, he feasted 69,574 guests for ten days, as his banquet stele records, and the Assyrian war machine began its march to the west.

Shalmaneser III met a coalition of twelve kings at Qarqar on the Orontes, led by Hadadezer of Damascus and Irhuleni of Hamath, with Ahab of Israel bringing 2,000 chariots and an Arab chieftain named Gindibu 1,000 camels, the first Arabs named in history. Shalmaneser boasted of a great victory, but the allies held him back from Syria for years.

t: The People Drive Out King Li
x: King Li of Zhou, greedy and quick to silence his critics, was driven from Haojing by a rising of the people of the capital and fled to Zhi. For fourteen years the realm was governed under the Gonghe regency, and from this year the Chinese record runs in an unbroken count of years, the oldest certain date in Chinese history.

By the tradition the Greeks and Romans told, Elissa, whom Virgil called Dido, fled Tyre after her brother King Pygmalion murdered her husband, and founded Qart-hadasht, the New City, on a peninsula of the Gulf of Tunis. Her colony, placed where the sea lanes of the western Mediterranean narrow, grew into the queen of the Phoenician west.

In the Alpine valley of Hallstatt, miners dug salt from deep galleries and grew rich by its trade, and the warrior chiefs buried in the cemetery above the lake took iron swords, bronze vessels, and amber with them to the grave. The Hallstatt culture of the early Iron Age spread across central Europe and was the cradle of the Celtic world.

In a cave of the Lipuun headland on Palawan the bones of the dead were gathered into great earthen jars. The lid of one, the Manunggul Jar, bears two seated figures in a boat, a steersman and a soul with arms crossed upon its breast, sailing to the afterworld. Found by Robert Fox in 1964, it is a treasure of the Philippines.

After San Lorenzo declined, the center of Olmec power moved to La Venta, an island amid the swamps of Tabasco, where a fluted pyramid of clay rose more than thirty metres. Beneath its plazas the Olmec buried massive offerings of serpentine blocks, mosaic pavements shaped like jaguar masks, and caches of polished jade, never meant to be seen again.

Argishti I, king of Urartu, built the fortress of Erebuni on a hill above the Ararat plain and settled it with 6,600 captives from his wars, as a cuneiform inscription found on the spot in 1950 records. The Urartians, rivals of Assyria in the highlands around Lake Van, were masters of irrigation and fortification; Erebuni is the seed of modern Yerevan.

At the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia, by the reckoning of later Greek scholars, Koroibos of Elis won the footrace in 776 B.C., the first victor on the lists of the Olympic Games. Every four years the Greeks gathered there under a sacred truce, and they came to count the years of their history in Olympiads.

King You of Zhou put aside his queen and heir for the concubine Bao Si, and the queen's father, the Marquis of Shen, called in the Quanrong. They sacked Haojing and slew the king at the foot of Mount Li; no lords came, the tale says, for he had lit the beacons too often in jest. The next year King Ping moved the court east to Luoyi.

Corinthian settlers under Archias landed on the island of Ortygia, with its spring of Arethusa and its fine harbor, and founded Syracuse, which grew into the greatest Greek city of the west. It was one of a wave of colonies, Naxos, Leontini, Megara Hyblaea, and others, that made Sicily and southern Italy a new Greece.

Piye, king of Kush, ruling from Napata beneath the holy mountain of Jebel Barkal, came north to save Egypt from the Libyan chiefs who had divided it. He took Hermopolis, stormed Memphis, and received the submission of the Delta princes, chiding King Nimlot on his victory stela for letting his horses go hungry. His Twenty-fifth Dynasty ruled Egypt for some sixty years.

Hoshea of Israel withheld his tribute and sought help from Egypt, and Shalmaneser V laid siege to Samaria for three years. The city fell, and Sargon II, by his own boast, deported some twenty-seven thousand of its people to Assyria and Media and settled foreigners in their place. The northern kingdom was no more, and its ten tribes passed out of history.

From Gordion on the Sangarius ruled Midas, whom the Assyrians called Mita of Mushki and the Greeks remembered for the touch that turned all to gold. He was the first foreign king, Herodotus says, to send an offering to Delphi, a royal throne; beneath a great mound at Gordion, opened in 1957, lay a king of his house with bronze bowls and the remains of a funeral feast.

When Hezekiah of Judah rebelled, Sennacherib took forty-six of his walled towns and stormed Lachish, a siege his sculptors carved on the walls of his palace at Nineveh. Hezekiah, shut up 'like a bird in a cage' in Jerusalem, paid a heavy tribute, but the city was not taken, and the Bible tells how the angel of the Lord struck the Assyrian camp.

At the court of Janaka, king of Videha, the sage Yajnavalkya disputed with the Brahmins and with the learned woman Gargi on the nature of the self. Their teachings, set down in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, held that the inmost self, atman, is one with brahman, the ground of all being. On this rock rose the philosophy of later Hinduism.

Through the first millennium B.C. the rice farmers of the Mumun age raised great stone tombs across the Korean peninsula, which holds perhaps two in five of all the dolmens in the world. At Gochang more than four hundred lie along a single range of hills, their capstones weighing up to three hundred tonnes, raised for the chiefs of a society growing in rank and power.

Karib'il Watar, ruler of Saba, recorded on a great inscription at Sirwah the campaigns that made the Sabaeans masters of the incense kingdoms of southern Arabia, and an inscription of Sennacherib names a Sabaean Karibilu who sent him precious stones and spices. Marib, watered by its great dam across the Wadi Dhana, was the richest city of Arabia.

When Tantamani, the last Kushite pharaoh, marched north to retake Egypt, the army of Ashurbanipal drove him back and sacked Thebes, the city of Amun, carrying off two obelisks sheathed in electrum to Nineveh. The fall of hundred-gated Thebes echoed through the ancient world, and the prophet Nahum warned Nineveh that it was no better than No-Amon.

After years of war with Elam, Ashurbanipal took Susa, plundered its temples, smashed the tombs of its kings, and carried their bones to Assyria so that their spirits would know no rest. He boasted that he had sown the fields with salt and made the land a haunt of wild asses; Elam never recovered its power.

t: Duke Wen of Jin at Chengpu
x: Duke Wen of Jin, who had wandered nineteen years in exile before winning his throne, met the army of Chu at Chengpu. Keeping an old promise to the King of Chu, he drew back three days' march before giving battle, then broke both Chu wings. The victory made him hegemon of the central states and checked Chu's advance into the north for a generation.

Driven by famine and the bidding of the Delphic oracle, settlers from the island of Thera under Battus founded Cyrene on a high terrace above the Libyan coast, where, the Libyans told them, there was a hole in the sky. Rich in grain, horses, and the healing plant silphium, Cyrene became the greatest Greek city of Africa before Alexandria.

The kings of Lydia, rich in the electrum washed down by the river Pactolus, began to stamp lumps of the metal with the head of a lion as a warrant of weight and value. Croesus later struck the first coins of pure gold and silver, and the invention passed quickly to the Greek cities and around the world.

The Medes under Cyaxares and the Babylonians under Nabopolassar besieged Nineveh, the greatest city in the world, and stormed it after three months; King Sinsharishkun perished in the sack. The palaces of Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal burned, and the Hebrew prophet Nahum exulted over the bloody city. A remnant of Assyria fled to Harran, which fell in 610.

The crown prince Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon destroyed the Egyptian army of Necho II and the last of the Assyrians at Carchemish on the Euphrates, pursuing the survivors to Hamath. The victory gave Babylon all of Syria and Palestine, and within weeks Nebuchadnezzar hurried home across the desert to take the throne of his dead father.

Buddhist scripture names sixteen mahajanapadas, great realms, spread across northern India from Gandhara to Anga: kingdoms such as Kosala, Magadha, Avanti, and Vatsa, and republics of clans such as the Vajji league and the Mallas. Walled and moated cities rose along the Ganges, and silver punch-marked coins began to pass from hand to hand between them.

Greek seafarers from Phocaea in Ionia founded Massalia at a sheltered inlet east of the Rhone delta; legend says their leader Protis married the daughter of the local Celtic king, who chose him at her wedding feast. The colony carried wine, olives, and coinage up the Rhone into the Celtic world and became the oldest city of France.

Chosen archon to end the strife between rich and poor, Solon cancelled debts, forbade enslavement for debt, and freed Athenians sold abroad. He divided the citizens into classes by wealth, opened the assembly and the courts to all, and replaced the harsh laws of Draco, then left Athens for ten years so that no one could make him change them.

Psamtik II sent an army of Egyptians and Greek and Carian mercenaries deep into Kush, where they sacked Napata and broke the statues of the Kushite kings; on the march some of them carved their names on the colossi of Abu Simbel. The Kushite court thereafter looked ever more to the south, toward Meroë.

After King Zedekiah rebelled, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem for eighteen months, broke through its walls, and burned the Temple of Solomon. Zedekiah's sons were killed before his eyes, he was blinded and taken to Babylon in fetters, and much of the people of Judah followed him into the Babylonian captivity mourned in the Psalms.

Nabonidus, last king of Babylon and devotee of the moon god Sin, left the city in the charge of his son Belshazzar and lived for ten years at the oasis of Tayma in northern Arabia, subduing the oases as far as Yathrib. His absence halted the New Year festival of Babylon and alienated the priests of Marduk on the eve of the Persian conquest.

Cyrus, king of Anshan in Persis, rose against his overlord Astyages of Media, whose army mutinied and handed its king over to him. Cyrus took Ecbatana with its treasures and made the Medes partners in a new Persian empire; within twelve years he ruled from the Aegean to Central Asia.

Croesus of Lydia, richest of kings, crossed the Halys after the Delphic oracle told him that he would destroy a great empire. Cyrus fought him to a standstill, followed him home in winter, routed his horsemen by setting camels against them, and took Sardis after a siege of fourteen days. The empire Croesus destroyed was his own, and the Ionian Greeks passed under Persia.

From Rajagriha, ringed by five hills and a wall of rough stone some forty kilometres long, King Bimbisara of the Haryanka line made Magadha the rising power of the Ganges. He annexed Anga and its port of Champa, bound Kosala and the Licchavis to him by marriage, and welcomed both the Buddha and Mahavira to his city.

After defeating the Babylonian army at Opis, the troops of Cyrus entered Babylon without a battle, and Cyrus came as a liberator who restored the gods carried off by Nabonidus, as his clay cylinder proclaims. He let the exiles of Judah go home to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and the whole Fertile Crescent was united in the Persian empire, the largest the world had yet seen.

Siddhartha Gautama, a prince of the Shakya clan who had left his home to seek release from suffering, sat beneath a pipal tree on the bank of the Niranjana and there attained enlightenment. As the Buddha he preached his first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath, setting forth the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Way. His teaching would spread across Asia.

Vardhamana, a prince of the Jnatrika clan near Vaishali, had renounced his station, wandered for twelve years in naked austerity, and won the title Mahavira, the Great Hero. As the twenty-fourth Tirthankara he taught non-violence toward every living thing, truth, and the giving up of possessions. He died at Pava in the year Jain tradition reckons as 527 B.C.

Cambyses, son of Cyrus, crossed the Sinai with water supplied by Arab allies, defeated the young pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium, and took Memphis. Egypt became a satrapy of Persia; Psamtik was later put to death for plotting revolt, and Herodotus, three generations afterward, saw the bones of the fallen still lying on the field.

Darius I, who seized the throne in 522 by killing the man he named the Magian impostor Gaumata, and then crushed nine rebel kings in a single year, had his deeds carved on a cliff above the road to Ecbatana in Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian. Copied by Henry Rawlinson at the risk of his life, it became the key to cuneiform.

Darius the Great carried Persian rule over Gandhara and down the Indus, sending Scylax of Caryanda to sail the river to the sea. Hindush, the Indus country, became the richest province of the empire: Herodotus says it paid 360 talents of gold dust a year, nearly a third of all the empire's tribute. Indian archers in cotton later marched with Xerxes into Greece.

Darius bridged the Bosporus and the Danube and led a great army into the steppe north of the Black Sea. The Scythians under King Idanthyrsus would not give battle; they retreated before him, burned the grass, and stopped the wells, and Darius, his army hungry and harried, turned back to the Danube bridge, which the Ionian Greeks had kept for him.

After the rape of the virtuous Lucretia by the king's son, Lucius Junius Brutus led the Romans in driving out Tarquin the Proud and all his house. They swore never again to suffer a king, and in his place elected two consuls for a year at a time. In the same year, tradition says, the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol was dedicated.

When the tyrant's family had been expelled and the Spartan king Cleomenes tried to set up an oligarchy, the Athenian people rose and recalled Cleisthenes. He broke the power of the old clans by dividing the citizens into ten new tribes drawn from the city, the coast, and the inland, and founded the council of five hundred: the government of the people, demokratia, was born.

t: Wu Takes the Capital of Chu
x: King Helü of Wu, served by the exile Wu Zixu and, by tradition, by Sun Wu, author of the Art of War, struck deep into Chu, won five battles, and took the capital at Ying. Wu Zixu, whose father and brother the Chu king had murdered, dug up King Ping's corpse and flogged it three hundred times. Only the arrival of an army from Qin saved Chu.

t: The Bronze Drums of Dong Son
x: On the Ma River the lords of the Dong Son culture cast great bronze drums, their faces ringed with flying herons, feathered warriors, and long boats about a central star. Traded and treasured from Yunnan to the Moluccas, the drums are the emblem of the first rice-growing chiefdoms of the Red River country, which the Vietnamese remember as the realm of the Hung kings.

On the Jos Plateau a people known to us only by the village where tin miners first turned up their work modeled life-sized heads in fired clay, with pierced eyes and elaborate coiffures. At sites such as Taruga they were smelting iron by the fourth century before Christ, among the earliest ironworkers of Africa south of the Sahara.

The Zapotec lords of the Valley of Oaxaca leveled the summit of a mountain four hundred metres above the valley floor and built there a capital of plazas, temples, and ballcourts that endured for more than a thousand years. On the slabs of its gallery of Danzantes they carved hundreds of slain or captive enemies, beside some of the earliest hieroglyphic writing of the Americas.

t: The Jar Burials of Sa Huynh
x: Along the central coast of Vietnam an iron-working people buried the ashes of their dead in tall jars with lids, together with earrings of jade and glass carved as double-headed beasts. Ornaments of the same make have been found in Palawan, Borneo, and Taiwan, proof of a busy commerce across the South China Sea; the Sa Huynh folk are held to be forebears of the Cham.

Crushed by debt and harsh levies, the common people of Rome marched out of the city to the Sacred Mount and refused to fight or work. Menenius Agrippa won them back with his fable of the belly and the limbs, and the patricians granted them tribunes of their own, sacrosanct officers who could forbid the acts of any magistrate.

Darius sent Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean to punish Athens. On the plain of Marathon some 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans under Miltiades charged at a run, broke the Persian wings, and drove the invaders to their ships, losing 192 men against 6,400 Persians. The runner Pheidippides had gone to Sparta for help, which came too late.

King Fuchai of Wu, eager to carry his armies north against Qi, built the walled town of Han and cut a canal from the Yangtze to the Huai. The Hangou was the first stretch of what would become the Grand Canal, and the town at its head became Yangzhou, for two thousand years a crossroads of the empire's grain and salt.

On the same day as Salamis, it was said, Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas destroyed a huge Carthaginian army under Hamilcar at Himera. Hamilcar was killed or cast himself into the sacrificial fire, and the captives were set to build the temples of Akragas. The victory kept Sicily Greek for generations.

Ajatashatru, who had seized the throne of Magadha and starved his father Bimbisara in prison, waged a long war on the Vajji league of republics north of the Ganges. Jain texts tell of a great stone-hurling engine and a chariot fitted with whirling maces. To guard the river crossing he built a fort at the village of Pataligrama, seed of Pataliputra.

Kong Qiu, Master Kong, died in Lu at seventy-three, never having found a prince who would put his teaching into practice. He taught that order rested on ritual, filial duty, and the cultivation of humane virtue in rulers and ministers alike. His disciples set down his sayings in the Analects, and his teaching became the moral foundation of China, Korea, Vietnam, and Japan.

The Spartan regent Pausanias led the largest Greek army ever assembled, nearly 40,000 hoplites, against the Persian general Mardonius below Mount Cithaeron. The Spartans and Tegeans broke the Persian charge, Mardonius fell, and the camp was taken. On the same day, tradition says, the Greeks burned the Persian fleet at Mycale, and the invasions of Greece were over.

Twenty years after his defeat and his humbling service at the Wu court, King Goujian of Yue, who by legend slept on brushwood and tasted gall to keep his hatred alive, took Gusu and destroyed Wu. King Fuchai, refused the mercy he had once shown Goujian, took his own life, covering his face so as not to meet Wu Zixu in the world below.

Zhi Bo, strongest of the ministers who ruled Jin, besieged Zhao Xiangzi in Jinyang and flooded the city until frogs bred in the cooking pots. But the Han and Wei clans secretly turned against him, broke the dikes onto his own camp, and with Zhao destroyed him. The three families divided Jin among themselves, and the age of the Warring States began.

To end the patricians' hold on unwritten law, the Romans suspended the consuls and chose ten men, the decemvirs, to write the law down. Their Twelve Tables, set up in bronze in the Forum, governed debt, family, property, and crime, and Roman boys learned them by heart for centuries: the root of the civil law of Europe.

At La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel the Celts cast swords, spears, shields, and brooches into the water as offerings, and from them the second Celtic Iron Age takes its name. Its art of swirling tendrils and fantastic beasts spread from the Marne and the Rhine to Bohemia and Ireland, as the Celts began their great migrations.

At Olbia, the Milesian colony at the mouth of the Bug and the Dnieper, Herodotus gathered the lore of the Scythians: their royal burials with strangled servants and horses, their steam baths of hemp, and the tale of King Scyles, who was put to death by his own people for joining in Greek rites at Olbia.

At the urging of Pericles, and paid in part with the tribute of the Delian League, the architects Ictinus and Callicrates began a new temple of Athena on the Acropolis, with Phidias directing its sculpture and making its statue of the goddess in gold and ivory. Finished in 432, the Parthenon remains the standard of classical architecture.

At Panticapaeum on the straits of Kerch, Spartocus, perhaps a Thracian, took power over the Greek cities of the Cimmerian Bosporus and founded a dynasty that lasted more than three centuries. Its kings sold the wheat of the Scythian steppe to Athens, which honored them with gold crowns, and buried their dead in rich barrows.

In the spring of 431 three hundred Thebans slipped into Plataea by night, and the long-dreaded war between Athens and Sparta broke out. King Archidamus invaded Attica, while Pericles brought the country people inside the Long Walls and trusted to the fleet. Thucydides, an Athenian, began his history of the war at once, believing it the greatest ever fought.

The great armada that Athens sent against Syracuse in 415 was trapped in the Great Harbor after the Spartan Gylippus came to the city's aid. Its fleet broken, the army tried to escape inland, and Demosthenes and then Nicias surrendered on the march. The survivors were penned in the stone quarries, where many died; some, it is said, were freed for reciting Euripides.

The Spartan admiral Lysander, paid with Persian gold, caught the Athenian fleet drawn up on the beach at Aegospotami in the Hellespont while its crews were scattered for food, and took some 170 ships. Cut off from the grain of the Black Sea, Athens surrendered in 404, pulled down its Long Walls to the music of flutes, and submitted to the Thirty Tyrants.

Panini of Gandhara compressed the whole grammar of Sanskrit into nearly four thousand terse rules, the Ashtadhyayi. With its roots, suffixes, and laws of sound ordered like an algebra, it fixed the classical language for two thousand years and stands as the most complete grammar of any tongue made before modern times. Later Indian learning everywhere bore its stamp.

Socrates, the philosopher who had spent his life questioning the Athenians in the marketplace, was accused of impiety and of corrupting the young. A jury of 501 citizens condemned him, and he refused to flee, drinking the hemlock among his friends. His disciple Plato made his last days the subject of the Apology, the Crito, and the Phaedo.

After a siege that legend stretched to ten years like that of Troy, the dictator Marcus Furius Camillus took Veii, the great Etruscan city twelve miles from Rome, by a tunnel driven under its citadel, the story went. Its land doubled the territory of Rome, and its goddess Juno was invited to a new temple on the Aventine.

The Senones under Brennus routed the Roman army at the river Allia and entered an undefended Rome. The Capitol held out, saved, the story went, by the sacred geese of Juno, whose cackling woke Marcus Manlius against a night assault. When the Romans haggled over a ransom of a thousand pounds of gold, Brennus threw his sword on the scales and cried, 'Woe to the vanquished.'

The Theban general Epaminondas massed his left wing fifty shields deep, led by Pelopidas and the Sacred Band, and smashed the Spartan right where King Cleombrotus stood. The king and some four hundred Spartiates fell. The legend of Spartan invincibility was broken, and Epaminondas went on to free Messenia from its long servitude.

Lord Shang, a minister from Wey in the service of Duke Xiao of Qin, broke the old nobility, bound the people in groups of five and ten sworn to inform on one another, and granted rank for heads taken in battle. Farming and war became the only roads to honour. His enemies tore his body apart with chariots after his patron died, but his laws made Qin the strongest state in China.

Mahapadma, a man of low birth whom the Puranas call the destroyer of all the Kshatriyas, overthrew the Shishunaga line and made Magadha an empire from the Punjab to Kalinga. The Nandas filled their treasuries with heavy taxes; Greek writers heard that their king beyond the Hyphasis commanded 200,000 foot, 20,000 horse, 2,000 chariots, and thousands of elephants.

After two failed attempts, Artaxerxes III led a great army into Egypt, overcame the frontier forts of Pelusium, and drove out Nectanebo II, who fled to Upper Egypt and then, it was said, to Nubia. He was the last native Egyptian to rule all Egypt for more than two thousand years, and the Persians held Egypt again until Alexander came.

Ateas, king of the Scythians, who had pushed across the lower Danube into the Dobruja, quarreled with his former ally Philip II. The Macedonians killed the old king, said to be past ninety, in battle and carried off twenty thousand women and children and as many fine mares; on the way home Philip was wounded by the Triballi.

Philip II met the allied armies of Athens and Thebes, roused by the speeches of Demosthenes, at Chaeronea. The eighteen-year-old Alexander led the cavalry that broke the Theban line, and the Sacred Band died where it stood, buried beneath a stone lion still on the field. Greek liberty ended, and Philip bound the cities to him in the League of Corinth.

Alexander crossed the Hellespont with some 35,000 men, cast a spear into the soil of Asia, and honored the tomb of Achilles at Troy. At the river Granicus he charged at the head of his Companion cavalry across the stream against the Persian satraps, was nearly killed until Cleitus the Black cut down his attacker, and won the first of his great victories.

Darius III came down behind Alexander with the royal army and met him on the narrow coastal plain of Issus. Alexander's cavalry broke the Persian left and drove at the king, who fled in his chariot, leaving behind his mother, his wife, and his daughters, whom Alexander treated with courtesy. The road to Syria and Egypt lay open.

Welcomed in Egypt as a deliverer from the Persians, Alexander chose a site between Lake Mareotis and the sea opposite the island of Pharos and marked out a city, tracing its streets with barley meal. He went on to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, which hailed him as the son of the god. Alexandria became the greatest Greek city in the world.

While Alexander built a city on the Jaxartes, the Sogdian lord Spitamenes rose behind him, besieged the garrison of Maracanda, and destroyed a Macedonian column on the Polytimetus river. For two years he harried the invaders from the steppe, until in 328 B.C. the Massagetae, by Arrian's account wearied of the war, cut off his head and sent it to Alexander.

With the river swollen by rain and melting snows, Alexander slipped across the Hydaspes by night and fell upon King Porus, whose line was anchored by some two hundred elephants. The beasts trampled friend and foe alike before the phalanx prevailed. Porus, a giant of a man, was brought in wounded and asked how he would be treated: as a king, he answered.

t: The Army Turns Back at the Hyphasis
x: On the banks of the Hyphasis, with the Ganges plain and the Nanda empire before them, Alexander's veterans refused to march further. Eight years from Macedon, worn by monsoon rains and battle, they heard his pleading in silence, and Coenus spoke for them. Alexander raised twelve great altars to the gods and turned back toward the Indus and the sea.

Planning a voyage around Arabia, Alexander fell into a fever after a night of drinking and died in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar on 10 or 11 June, not yet thirty-three. Asked to whom he left his empire, he was said to answer, 'To the strongest.' His generals divided it in a generation of wars, and Ptolemy carried off his body to Egypt.

With the counsel of the Brahmin Chanakya, the young Chandragupta Maurya raised an army, cleared the Macedonian garrisons from the Punjab, and overthrew Dhana Nanda at Pataliputra. From that city he ruled the first empire to embrace nearly all of northern India, governed through a great standing army, a host of salaried officials, and a corps of spies.

The Samnite general Gaius Pontius trapped two consular armies in a narrow wooded pass near Caudium. The Romans surrendered and were sent under a yoke of spears, stripped to their tunics, while six hundred knights were held as hostages. Rome repudiated the peace, rebuilt its legions, and learned to fight in the looser maniples fit for the mountains.

The Qin general Sima Cuo, overriding those who urged a blow at the Zhou heartland, marched over the Qinling passes into the Sichuan basin and conquered the kingdoms of Shu and Ba. The rich plain of Chengdu gave Qin a granary beyond the reach of its rivals and an upstream base from which to fall upon Chu.

Antigonus the One-Eyed sent his officer Athenaeus against the Nabataeans, who seized their rock stronghold while the men were away at a fair and carried off women, children, frankincense, and myrrh. The Nabataeans overtook and destroyed his force. Diodorus describes them as nomads who drank no wine and built no houses; within three centuries they had carved the tombs of Petra from its cliffs.

t: Appius Claudius Builds the Appian Way
x: The censor Appius Claudius Caecus began a paved military road from Rome to Capua, and an aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, the first to bring water to the city. Extended in time to Brundisium, the Queen of Roads carried the legions south, and along it the Romans buried their dead, so that its tombs line it still.
