t: King Wuling Takes Up the Bow
x: King Wuling of Zhao ordered his warriors to put on the trousers and short tunics of the northern horsemen and to fight as mounted archers, overruling ministers who held it shameful to dress as barbarians. His new cavalry conquered the Linhu and Loufan and swallowed the state of Zhongshan, and the horseman entered Chinese warfare for good.

Seleucus Nicator crossed the Indus to win back Alexander's Indian provinces, but met Chandragupta and came to terms. He ceded Arachosia, Gedrosia, and the Paropamisadae, received five hundred war elephants, and sealed the peace with a marriage alliance. The elephants helped win the battle of Ipsus in 301 B.C., and Seleucus sent Megasthenes as his envoy to Pataliputra.

The Greek envoy Megasthenes found Pataliputra stretched along the Ganges for some fifteen kilometres, girdled by a timber palisade with 570 towers and 64 gates. In his Indica he described the king's palace, the vast army, and seven classes of Indian society, and marvelled that no Indian was a slave. Fragments of his book shaped the Western picture of India for centuries.

Old Antigonus the One-Eyed, who hoped to reunite Alexander's empire, met the combined armies of Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Cassander at Ipsus. Seleucus's war elephants from India, some four hundred, held back Demetrius's cavalry, and Antigonus, past eighty, fell under a shower of javelins. The empire was divided for good among the Successors.

Deep in the forests of the Petén, the Preclassic Maya of El Mirador raised La Danta, among the most massive pyramids in the world, upon platforms rising some seventy metres, and joined their city to its neighbors by raised causeways of white plaster. El Mirador flourished centuries before Tikal and Calakmul and was abandoned about the second century after Christ.

Jain tradition holds that Chandragupta, in a time of great famine, gave up his throne, followed the sage Bhadrabahu south into the Deccan, and fasted to death on the hill of Chandragiri at Shravanabelagola. The hill bears his name and a temple to his memory, and the Jains of Karnataka trace the planting of their faith in the south to that migration.

t: The Museum and Library of Alexandria
x: Ptolemy I, on the advice of Demetrius of Phalerum, founded the Museum, a shrine of the Muses where scholars lived at royal expense, and a library that grew under his son to hundreds of thousands of scrolls. There Euclid wrote his Elements, Eratosthenes measured the earth, and the Pharos lighthouse rose over the harbor.

Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, called in by Tarentum against Rome, beat the legions at Heraclea in 280 and again at Asculum with his phalanx and war elephants, but lost so many of his best men that he said another such victory would ruin him. A Pyrrhic victory has meant ever since a triumph bought at ruinous cost.

Celtic hosts burst into Macedonia and killed King Ptolemy Keraunos, and another Brennus led a great army south on the treasures of Delphi. The Aetolians and Phocians drove them back in snow and earthquake, the Greeks said with the help of Apollo. Three of their tribes crossed into Asia Minor in 278 and settled the land called Galatia.

t: Qu Yuan and the Fall of Ying
x: The Qin general Bai Qi took Ying, the old capital of Chu, burned the tombs of its kings, and drove the court east to Chen. Qu Yuan, the banished poet and minister who had warned against trusting Qin, clasped a stone and drowned himself in the Miluo River. The dragon boats of the Duanwu festival are said to race in search of him still.

At a Greek city on the Oxus, far beyond the Hindu Kush, a philosopher named Clearchus set up the maxims of Delphi at the shrine of the city's founder Kineas: in childhood be well behaved, in youth self-controlled, in middle age just, in old age wise, at death without grief. The city had a gymnasium, a theatre for some six thousand, and a great palace.

t: The Kings of Kush Move to Meroë
x: The kings of Kush, long buried in the royal cemeteries near Napata, began to raise their steep pyramids beside Meroë, their city on the Nile between the Atbara and the Sixth Cataract. Rich in iron, cattle, and the caravan trade, Meroë developed its own script and its own gods, among them the lion-headed Apedemak.

The Mamertines, Campanian mercenaries who had seized Messana, appealed to Rome against Hiero of Syracuse and Carthage. The consul Appius Claudius Caudex crossed the strait, and Rome for the first time sent an army out of Italy. The First Punic War had begun, a struggle of twenty-three years for Sicily and the sea.

Eight years after his consecration, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga on the eastern coast. His own edict counts 150,000 carried away, 100,000 slain, and many times that number dead. Struck by remorse, he turned to the Buddha's teaching and proclaimed a rule of dhamma, carving his edicts on rocks and pillars across the empire and sending envoys to the Greek kings.

After long deadlock Zhao replaced its cautious general Lian Po with young Zhao Kuo, who knew the books of war by heart. Bai Qi of Qin feigned retreat, cut off his army, and starved it for forty-six days. When Zhao Kuo fell, the Qin buried the surrendered men alive, by the old count four hundred thousand, and Zhao never recovered.

On a rock at Old Kandahar, Ashoka had his message of piety cut in Greek and Aramaic for the Greek and Iranian subjects at the western edge of his empire. The Greek text tells how the king, ten years after his consecration, showed piety to men, and how the royal hunters and fishermen ceased their killing. It is the westernmost of all his inscriptions.

t: An Duong Vuong Builds Co Loa
x: Thuc Phan, a prince from the hill country to the north, overthrew the last Hung king, took the name An Duong Vuong, and founded the kingdom of Au Lac. At Co Loa he raised a citadel of three spiraling earthen ramparts, the largest fortress of ancient Southeast Asia; a hoard of ten thousand bronze arrowheads was dug from its ground in 1959.

t: Li Bing Tames the Min River
x: Li Bing, the Qin governor of Shu, split the Min River with an artificial island shaped like a fish's mouth and cut a channel through the mountain to carry its waters onto the Chengdu plain. Without a single dam, the work ended the floods and watered a plain that became the Land of Abundance, and it waters that plain to this day.

t: Mahinda Brings the Dhamma to Lanka
x: Ashoka's son Mahinda, a monk, met King Devanampiya Tissa on the hill of Mihintale while the king was hunting deer, and converted him to the Buddha's teaching. Mahinda's sister Sanghamitta followed with a cutting of the Bodhi tree, planted at Anuradhapura, where its descendant grows still. Theravada Buddhism has been the faith of the Sinhalese ever since.

Diodotus, satrap of Bactria, threw off allegiance to the Seleucid king and founded a Greek kingdom between the Hindu Kush and the Oxus, rich in irrigated grain and the caravan trade. Justin calls it the land of a thousand cities. Its kings struck some of the finest coins of the Hellenistic world, portraits of startling realism above Zeus hurling the thunderbolt.

On a mound in the floodplain of the Bani, a tributary of the Niger, settlers founded the town that grew into Jenne-jeno, ancient Djenné. By about A.D. 800 it was a walled town of many thousands, trading iron, copper, grain, and fish along the river, and rich long before the first Arab caravan crossed the desert.

At Sarnath, where the Buddha first preached, Ashoka raised a polished sandstone column crowned by four lions standing back to back above a drum carved with wheels of the law and running beasts. Shaped with a skill unmatched in India before it, the capital was dug up in 1905 and became the state emblem of the Republic of India in 1950.

t: The Battle of the Aegates Islands
x: With the treasury empty, wealthy Romans paid for a new fleet of two hundred ships, and the consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus caught the Carthaginian relief fleet, heavy with grain, off the Aegates Islands. Carthage sued for peace, gave up Sicily, and paid an indemnity of 3,200 talents; Sicily became Rome's first province.

Arsaces, chief of the Parni, a nomad people of the steppe east of the Caspian, rode into the Seleucid province of Parthia, killed its rebel satrap Andragoras, and made himself king. His successors, the Arsacids, took the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids and ruled for nearly five centuries as the great rival of Rome in the East.

t: Jing Ke and the King of Qin
x: Prince Dan of Yan sent the swordsman Jing Ke to Xianyang bearing the head of the renegade Qin general Fan Yuqi and a map of Yan's best land, with a poisoned dagger rolled inside. As the map unrolled Jing Ke seized the king's sleeve and struck, but King Zheng tore free and ran about a pillar until he could draw his long sword. Jing Ke died, and Yan fell five years later.

Hannibal led an army of Spaniards and Africans, with thirty-seven elephants, over the Pyrenees and the Rhone and in late autumn across the Alps, fighting mountain tribes and snow. He came down into the plain of the Po with some 26,000 men, beat the Romans at the Trebia in December, and won the Gauls of the north to his side.

In a morning mist Hannibal trapped the consul Gaius Flaminius and his army on the narrow shore of Lake Trasimene, attacking from the hills above. Some fifteen thousand Romans died, the consul among them, and Rome named Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator; his strategy of delay won him the name Cunctator.

t: Meng Tian and the Long Wall
x: The general Meng Tian, with three hundred thousand men, drove the Xiongnu from the Ordos loop of the Yellow River and joined the walls of Qin, Zhao, and Yan into a single rampart running ten thousand li from Lintao to Liaodong. A straight road was cut from the capital to the frontier, and the toil of the conscripts on the wall became a byword for suffering.

On the advice of the chancellor Li Si, the First Emperor ordered the burning of the histories of the conquered states and of private copies of the Odes and the Documents, sparing only works on medicine, divination, and farming. The next year, tradition says, some 460 scholars were buried alive. Later Confucians remembered Qin chiefly for this assault on learning.

t: The First Emperor Dies at Shaqiu
x: Seeking the elixir of immortality on a tour of the east, the First Emperor died at Shaqiu. The eunuch Zhao Gao and the chancellor Li Si hid his death, carting salted fish beside his litter to cover the stench, and forged an edict ordering the heir Fusu to kill himself. The younger son Huhai took the throne as Second Emperor, and the dynasty began its swift collapse.

Beside the First Emperor's mound at Mount Li were buried some eight thousand soldiers of fired clay, each with his own face, drawn up in battle order with real bronze weapons, chariots, and horses. Sima Qian wrote that 700,000 convicts built the tomb, with rivers of mercury and crossbows set to shoot robbers. Peasants digging a well found the army in 1974.

Two conscript leaders, Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, held up by rain on the road to the frontier, knew that lateness meant death under the laws of Qin. They killed their officers and raised the cry: are kings and nobles a breed apart? Their rising lasted barely six months, but it set the whole empire ablaze.

Modu, son of the Xiongnu chanyu Touman, trained his horsemen to shoot wherever his whistling arrow flew, testing them on his own horse and wife and killing those who held back. On a hunt he loosed an arrow at his father, and his men cut Touman down. Modu then crushed the Donghu, drove back the Yuezhi, and built the first great empire of the steppe.

To relieve the rebel kingdom of Zhao, besieged in Julu by the Qin generals Zhang Han and Wang Li, Xiang Yu of Chu crossed the Zhang River, sank his boats, smashed the cooking pots, and gave his men three days' rations. In nine fights his army broke the besiegers while the other rebel lords watched from their ramparts; afterwards they came into his tent on their knees.

Liu Bang reached the Qin capital first and took the surrender of Ziying, but yielded it to the stronger Xiang Yu, escaping with his life from the feast at Hong Gate. Xiang Yu killed Ziying, burned the palaces, which smouldered, it is said, for three months, and carved the empire into eighteen kingdoms, taking for himself the title Hegemon-King of Western Chu.

As Qin collapsed, Zhao Tuo, a Qin officer from the north, sealed the passes through the southern mountains, seized the commanderies of the far south, and proclaimed himself King of Nanyue at Panyu, the later Canton. He adopted the customs of the Yue, ruled for nearly seventy years, and for a time styled himself emperor in defiance of Han.

Publius Cornelius Scipio, who had conquered Spain, carried the war to Africa and allied himself with the Numidian prince Masinissa. At Zama he let Hannibal's elephants pass through lanes in his lines, and the Numidian and Roman horse, returning from the pursuit, fell on the Carthaginian rear. Carthage gave up its fleet and its empire, and Scipio was named Africanus.

t: Gaixia and the Founding of Han
x: Surrounded at Gaixia, Xiang Yu heard the songs of Chu rising from the Han camps on every side and knew his homeland had gone over to the enemy. He broke out with eight hundred horsemen, made his last stand at the Wu River, and cut his own throat. Liu Bang, once a village constable, was proclaimed emperor, founder of the dynasty that gave the Han Chinese their name.

In the dry heart of Burma the Pyu raised Beikthano, the City of Vishnu, ringed by a wall of brick, with a monastery and stupas among its earliest buildings. With Halin and Sri Ksetra after it, Beikthano was among the first cities of Burma, where a Tibeto-Burman people took up Indian letters and the Buddhist faith.

The priests of Egypt met at Memphis to honor the boy king Ptolemy V at his coronation, and their decree was cut on stone in hieroglyphs, demotic, and Greek. A slab of it, found by French soldiers at Rosetta in 1799, passed to the British, and with its help Jean-François Champollion deciphered the hieroglyphs in 1822.

Wiman, a refugee captain from the Han kingdom of Yan, came east with a thousand followers and was given land on the frontier by King Jun of Joseon. He then marched on the capital at Wanggeom, drove the king south to the lands of the Han peoples, and founded a kingdom that grew rich on the trade between China and the peoples of the peninsula.

Antiochus III the Great, with Hannibal among his counselors, faced the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio at Magnesia, while his brother Africanus lay sick at Elaea. His scythed chariots panicked, his elephants broke his own phalanx, and the cavalry of Eumenes of Pergamon finished the work. By the Peace of Apamea Antiochus gave up all of Asia Minor beyond the Taurus.

Pushyamitra Shunga, commander of the Mauryan army, struck down King Brihadratha as he reviewed the troops, and took the throne. The empire had already shrunk to the Ganges heartland. Pushyamitra revived the Vedic horse sacrifice, fought off the Greeks from the northwest, and founded the Shunga line, which ruled from Pataliputra and Vidisha for more than a century.

Demetrius, son of Euthydemus, led the Bactrian Greeks over the Hindu Kush into Arachosia, Gandhara, and the Punjab, opening two centuries of Greek rule in India. His coins show him wearing an elephant scalp in the manner of Alexander. The kingdom he founded passed through many hands, its Greek kings striking coins in Greek and Kharoshthi for their Indian subjects.

In a letter to the Han court Modu boasted that his Wise King of the Right had crushed the Yuezhi, masters of the grasslands of Gansu. Some years later the chanyu Laoshang killed their king and made his skull into a drinking cup. The Yuezhi fled west to the Ili and then to Bactria, setting off a chain of migrations felt as far as India.

Eucratides overthrew the house of Euthydemus. Justin tells that, besieged by Demetrius with sixty thousand men, he broke out with three hundred and won. He struck the largest gold coin of the ancient world, a twenty-stater piece now in Paris. Returning in triumph from India, he was murdered by his own son, who drove his chariot through his father's blood.

Lucius Aemilius Paullus met Perseus, last king of Macedon, at Pydna after an eclipse of the moon the night before had dismayed the Macedonians. On broken ground the phalanx lost its order, and the legionaries cut into its gaps; twenty thousand Macedonians fell. Perseus walked in Paullus's triumph, and the kingdom of Alexander was divided into four republics.

When Antiochus IV forbade the Jewish law and set up an altar to Olympian Zeus in the Temple, the priest Mattathias killed a royal officer at Modein and fled to the hills with his five sons. His son Judas Maccabeus beat the Seleucid generals and in 164 cleansed and rededicated the Temple, a deliverance still kept at Hanukkah.

Dutugemunu, prince of Ruhuna in the south of Lanka, marched north against Elara, a Chola from the mainland who had ruled at Anuradhapura for forty-four years. The chronicle tells that the two kings met in single combat on their elephants beneath the city's walls and Elara fell. Dutugemunu honoured his foe with a monument and raised the great Ruwanwelisaya stupa.

Menander, greatest of the Indo-Greek kings, ruled from Sagala in the Punjab and pressed his arms toward the Ganges. The Pali book Milindapanha preserves his dialogues with the monk Nagasena on the self, rebirth, and the chariot that is nothing but its parts. Plutarch says that when he died the cities quarrelled over his ashes and shared them among themselves.

On the brow of a cave at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar, King Kharavela of Kalinga had the deeds of his reign carved year by year: a canal extended, a capital rebuilt, campaigns against Magadha and the north, and the recovery of an image of a Jina that a Nanda king had carried off. A devout Jain, he hollowed caves in the hills for the monks.

When the Achaean League defied Rome, the consul Lucius Mummius defeated its army at the Isthmus and destroyed Corinth, killing its men, selling its women and children, and shipping its statues and paintings to Rome, warning the shippers, it was said, that any masterpiece they lost they must replace with a new one. In the same year Carthage fell, and Greece passed under Roman rule.

The Greek city on the Oxus was sacked and burned in the last years of Eucratides. Nomads from the north, Sakas with the Yuezhi pressing behind them, swept over Bactria; the palace treasury was plundered, and the greatest Greek outpost of Central Asia never rose again. Its ruins lay forgotten until a Corinthian capital found there was shown to the king of Afghanistan in 1961.

Mithridates I of Parthia, having taken Media from the Seleucids, entered Seleucia on the Tigris, and the scribes of Babylon began to date their tablets by his reign. Three years later his generals captured the Seleucid king Demetrius II, and Parthia was master of the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia; its kings made Ctesiphon, across the river, their winter capital.

Emperor Wu sent the courtier Zhang Qian to find the Yuezhi and win them to an alliance against the Xiongnu. Captured on the way, he lived ten years among the Xiongnu and took a wife, then escaped and reached Ferghana and Bactria. He came home in 126 B.C. with news of blood-sweating horses, vines, and unknown kingdoms, and opened the road later called the Silk Road.

The tribune Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, grandson of Scipio Africanus, passed a law to share out the public land among the poor and, when blocked, had a fellow tribune deposed. Seeking a second term, he was clubbed to death on the Capitol with some three hundred of his followers by senators led by the chief pontiff Scipio Nasica: the first blood of the strife that ended the Republic.

The Celtiberian hill town of Numantia had defied Roman armies for twenty years. Scipio Aemilianus, the destroyer of Carthage, ringed it with a wall nearly six miles around and seven camps and starved it for months; many of the defenders killed themselves rather than surrender, and the few survivors were sold into slavery.

The Han envoy Zhang Qian, after ten years a captive of the Xiongnu, reached the Yuezhi, who had driven the Sakas from the Ili and now ruled north of the Oxus over the Greek cities of Bactria. He failed to win them as allies, but in the markets of Bactria he saw Chinese bamboo and cloth brought by way of India, and his report opened the Silk Road.

On the proposal of the chancellor Gongsun Hong, Emperor Wu founded the Imperial Academy at Chang'an, where fifty students studied under the masters of the Five Classics. Office was opened to men trained in the Confucian books, and the scholar-official, chosen for learning rather than birth, began his two-thousand-year reign over Chinese government.

Wei Qing and Huo Qubing crossed the Gobi with fifty thousand horsemen each. Wei Qing broke the chanyu Yizhixie in a sandstorm, while Huo Qubing drove two thousand li beyond the desert and sacrificed to Heaven on Mount Langjuxu. The Xiongnu court withdrew far to the north, though fewer than thirty thousand of the 140,000 Han horses came home.

t: Heliodorus Raises a Pillar to Vasudeva
x: Heliodorus of Taxila, envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to King Bhagabhadra at Vidisha, set up a stone column crowned with a Garuda in honour of Vasudeva, god of gods. Its inscription calls him a Bhagavata, a devotee of Vishnu, and names three precepts that lead to heaven: self-restraint, generosity, and vigilance. A Greek had embraced an Indian god.

t: The Han Annex the Red River Delta
x: After the armies of Emperor Wu destroyed Nanyue, the Han divided its southern lands into commanderies: Jiaozhi on the Red River, Jiuzhen, and Rinan beyond. So began more than a thousand years of Chinese rule, broken by revolts, in which the Vietnamese took Chinese letters, Confucian learning, and Buddhism, yet kept their own speech and spirit.

Emperor Wu sent armies by land and sea against Ugeo, grandson of Wiman, who had barred the southern states from trading with Han. Wanggeom held out for a year until its ministers murdered the king and opened the gates. Four commanderies were set up, and Lelang, near later Pyongyang, carried Chinese writing, lacquer, and law into Korea for four centuries.

The Cimbri and Teutones, Germanic wanderers from the shores of the North Sea, had destroyed Roman armies at Arausio and elsewhere. Gaius Marius, consul again and again, remade the legions, enrolled the landless poor, and made each soldier carry his own pack; at Aquae Sextiae he annihilated the Teutones, and the next year the Cimbri at Vercellae. He was hailed the third founder of Rome.

The Han emperor Wu coveted the heavenly horses of Dayuan in the Fergana valley, and when its king refused to sell them and his men slew a Chinese envoy, he sent the general Li Guangli across the deserts. The second expedition besieged the capital and cut off its water; the nobles killed their king, Mugua, and gave up three thousand horses.

When the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus, who proposed to give the Italians citizenship, was murdered, the Marsi, the Samnites, and other allies rose in arms and set up a state of their own, Italia, with its capital at Corfinium. Rome won the war, but only by granting all Italians south of the Po the citizenship it had refused them.

t: The Records of the Grand Historian
x: Castrated for defending the general Li Ling, who had surrendered to the Xiongnu, the court astrologer Sima Qian chose disgrace over suicide so that he might finish the history his father had begun. His Records of the Grand Historian, in 130 chapters, run from the Yellow Emperor to his own day and set the model for every later dynastic history.

When the tribune Sulpicius, at the bidding of Marius, took the command against Mithridates from the consul Lucius Cornelius Sulla, Sulla led his six legions on the city, the first Roman to take Rome by force. In 82, back from the East, he won the battle of the Colline Gate, posted lists of the proscribed, and ruled as dictator.

Mithridates VI of Pontus overran the Roman province of Asia and sent secret orders to its cities to kill every Roman and Italian on a single day. Some eighty thousand men, women, and children were murdered, even at the altars where they had fled for refuge, and Athens and much of Greece went over to the king.

Maues, a Saka chief whose people had been driven south by the Yuezhi, broke the Greek hold on Gandhara and took Taxila, styling himself on his coins Great King of Kings. The Indo-Scythians who followed him, Azes and his successors, ruled the Punjab for generations and left the era of Azes by which the Kharoshthi inscriptions of Gandhara are dated.

In a time of famine and war, when it was feared that the teaching might perish with the monks who carried it in memory, the monks of Lanka assembled in the rock caves of Aluvihara in the reign of Vattagamani Abhaya and wrote the Buddha's words on palm leaves. The Tipitaka in Pali, the scripture of Theravada Buddhism, was thus first set in writing.

Seventy-odd gladiators led by Spartacus, a Thracian, broke out of their training school at Capua with kitchen knives and spits, took refuge on Vesuvius, and raised an army of runaway slaves that beat several Roman armies. Marcus Licinius Crassus crushed them in 71, and six thousand captives were crucified along the Appian Way.

Pursuing Mithridates, Pompey defeated King Artoces of Iberia and the Albanians under Oroezes, and marched toward the Caspian until, Plutarch says, he turned back three days short of it for fear of the deadly serpents. Iberia and Albania became clients of Rome, and the Romans first learned the lands beyond the Caucasus.

Called in to settle the war between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, Pompey besieged the Temple Mount for three months and took it, entering the Holy of Holies, which he found empty of any image. He left the treasury untouched but made Judea tributary to Rome and set Hyrcanus over it as high priest.

By the reckoning of the old Korean chronicles, the six villages of the Saro plain chose as their king the boy Bak Hyeokgeose, born, the legend says, from a great egg found beside a well. From this small state in the southeast, ruled in turn by the Bak, Seok, and Kim clans, grew the kingdom of Silla, which lasted nearly a thousand years.

The calendar still used across northern and western India counts its years from 57 B.C. Early inscriptions call it the Krita or Malava era; from the ninth century it bore the name of Vikramaditya, the legendary king of Ujjain said to have driven out the Sakas. In Nepal, where it is the official reckoning, the year 2081 began in April 2024.

Marcus Licinius Crassus, seeking glory to match Caesar and Pompey, marched into Mesopotamia and was met on the open plain by the Parthian general Surena with mounted archers and armored lancers, supplied with arrows by a train of camels. Crassus's son died with his cavalry, Crassus himself was killed at a parley, and some twenty thousand Romans fell and ten thousand were taken.

Vercingetorix, chief of the Arverni, united the Gauls in a last great revolt. Caesar shut him up in the hill town of Alesia behind eleven miles of works and beat off from an outer ring a vast army of relief. Vercingetorix rode out and laid his arms at Caesar's feet, and Gaul was Roman.

Ordered by the Senate to give up his army, Caesar stood on the bank of the Rubicon, the little stream that marked the border of his province and of Italy, and crossed with a single legion, saying, 'The die is cast.' Pompey and most of the Senate fled Rome, and the civil war that would end the Roman Republic had begun.

Pompey, with twice Caesar's infantry and seven times his horse, gave battle at Pharsalus. Caesar posted a fourth line of picked cohorts, who stopped Pompey's cavalry by thrusting their javelins at the riders' faces, and the senatorial army broke. Pompey fled to Egypt, where the ministers of the boy king Ptolemy XIII had him stabbed as he stepped ashore.

The Roman calendar of lunar months had drifted so far from the seasons that harvest festivals fell in spring. On the advice of the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria, Caesar stretched the year 46 B.C. to 445 days and introduced a year of 365 days with a leap day every fourth year. With Pope Gregory's correction of 1582, it is the calendar of the world.

Caesar, named dictator for life, was stabbed twenty-three times on the Ides of March at a meeting of the Senate in the hall beside the Theater of Pompey by some sixty conspirators led by Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius. He fell at the foot of Pompey's statue. The conspirators cried liberty, but the people mourned Caesar, and Antony turned them against the assassins.

In two battles on the plain of Philippi in October, Antony and Octavian defeated the armies of the Liberators. Cassius, believing all lost, killed himself after the first; Brutus after the second, saying that he had found no man who was not true to him. With them died the last army of the Republic.

By the account of the Samguk Sagi, Jumong, a prince of Buyeo famed as an archer, fled his jealous brothers across a river where fish and turtles rose to make him a bridge, and founded a kingdom at Jolbon in the mountains of the middle Yalu. His Goguryeo grew into the most warlike power of the northeast and ruled Manchuria and northern Korea for seven centuries.

A year after Actium, Octavian entered Alexandria. Antony fell on his sword and died in Cleopatra's arms, and the queen, the last of the Ptolemies, took her own life rather than be led in triumph, by the bite of an asp as the story goes. Caesarion, her son by Caesar, was put to death, and Egypt became the private province of the conqueror.

In January Octavian laid down his extraordinary powers before the Senate, which returned to him command of the frontier provinces and their legions and voted him the name Augustus, the revered. Calling himself only princeps, first citizen, he governed for forty years, ended the civil wars, and founded a monarchy that would rule the Mediterranean for five centuries.

While the prefect of Egypt was away in Arabia, the one-eyed Kushite queen Amanirenas sent her army north, took Syene and Philae, and threw down the statues of Augustus; a bronze head of the emperor was buried beneath the steps of a temple at Meroë. Petronius struck back as far as Napata, but peace was made on terms generous to Kush.

Strabo records that an embassy from King Pandion of southern India, or as some said from Porus, reached Augustus, bearing a letter in Greek, great snakes, and an armless boy who could draw a bow with his feet. With it travelled an Indian ascetic who, at Athens, mounted a pyre and burned himself alive before the astonished crowd.

Nero Claudius Drusus, stepson of Augustus, led the legions in four campaigns from the Rhine into Germany, cutting a canal to the North Sea and reaching the Elbe. There, the story went, a woman of more than human size warned him to turn back; he died on the way home after a fall from his horse and was given the name Germanicus.

In the last years of King Herod, Jesus was born at Bethlehem, the city of David, to Mary, betrothed to Joseph the carpenter of Nazareth, who had come there for a Roman census. The Gospels tell of the shepherds, the star, and the wise men from the East who came to worship the newborn King of the Jews, and of the flight into Egypt from Herod's wrath.

Wang Mang, nephew of a dowager empress and regent for a child, hailed by Confucian scholars as a new Duke of Zhou, took the throne himself and named his dynasty Xin, the New. He declared the land the property of the state, forbade the sale of slaves, and minted bewildering new coins, and his reforms ended in ruin when the Yellow River broke its banks and famine spread.

Rebel armies of the Red Eyebrows and the Green Woods rose across the starving east. At Kunyang the Han prince Liu Xiu, with a few thousand men, routed a vast imperial host in a thunderstorm, and that autumn the rebels broke into Chang'an. Wang Mang was cut down in his palace; two years later Liu Xiu restored the Han at Luoyang as Emperor Guangwu.

On a low hill near Sheberghan in northern Afghanistan, six nomad princes and princesses were laid in their graves dressed in some twenty thousand ornaments of gold: a folding crown of hammered leaf, daggers set with turquoise, and Greek, Indian, and steppe motifs blended. A gold coin of the Roman emperor Tiberius lay in one grave. The hoard was found in 1978.

In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, John the Baptist preached repentance by the Jordan, and Jesus of Nazareth came to be baptized by him. Jesus then went about Galilee, making Capernaum on its lake his home, calling the fishermen Simon Peter, Andrew, James, and John, preaching the Kingdom of God, and healing the sick, as the four Gospels record.

At the Passover Jesus entered Jerusalem, shared a last supper with his disciples, and was arrested in the garden of Gethsemane. Jesus was handed over to Pontius Pilate by the high priest Caiaphas and the Temple authorities, and Pilate ordered him crucified. He died on the cross at Golgotha outside the walls; on the third day the tomb was found empty, and the risen Christ appeared to his disciples.

Fifty days after the Passover, as the Acts of the Apostles records, the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples gathered in Jerusalem like tongues of fire, and they spoke in the languages of pilgrims from every nation. Peter preached the risen Christ to the crowd, about three thousand were baptized that day, and the Church began.

Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Kushan clan, one of five Yuezhi tribes holding Bactria, overthrew the other four and made himself king. The Chinese annals tell that he went on to take the Kabul valley and Gandhara from the Parthians, founding the Kushan Empire. He lived past eighty, and his early coins copied the head of the Greek king Hermaeus.

t: The Revolt of the Trung Sisters
x: When the Han governor Su Ding put to death the husband of Trung Trac, she and her sister Trung Nhi raised the Lac lords against Chinese rule and took sixty-five citadels. Trung Trac reigned as queen at Me Linh until the general Ma Yuan marched south; defeated in A.D. 43, the sisters perished, and Vietnam honors them still as its first heroines.

Aulus Plautius landed in Kent with four legions and forced the crossing of the Medway against Caratacus and the Catuvellauni. The emperor Claudius came over with elephants for the final advance and entered Camulodunum, the British capital, staying sixteen days; eleven kings submitted, and Britain became a Roman province for nearly four centuries.

At Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians, the church laid hands on Barnabas and Paul and sent them to Cyprus and Asia Minor. On this and later journeys Paul founded churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus and wrote them the letters that stand in the New Testament, carrying the Gospel from the synagogues to the Gentiles.

Greek pilots had learned to ride the southwest monsoon straight across the Arabian Sea, and each summer ships from Roman Egypt reached Muziris on the Malabar coast for pepper, pearls, and fine cloth. Pliny grumbled that India drained the empire of fifty million sesterces a year, and hoards of Roman gold and silver coins are still turned up in southern India.

A Greek merchant's handbook, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes Adulis on the Red Sea as the port of the Axumites, eight days' journey from their city, shipping ivory, tortoiseshell, and rhinoceros horn. Its king, Zoskales, was grasping in his dealings, the author says, but upright and well read in Greek letters.

The Apostle Thomas, as the Christians of Malabar have always held, landed at Muziris in A.D. 52, preached the Gospel along the coast, and founded seven churches. He was martyred at Mylapore near Madras in A.D. 72, and his tomb there drew pilgrims for centuries; Marco Polo saw it. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala honour him as their father in the faith.

Envoys from Na, a small state of the Wa people in northern Kyushu, reached Luoyang, and Emperor Guangwu granted their king a seal. In 1784 a farmer on the island of Shikanoshima turned up a seal of solid gold with a coiled snake for a handle, inscribed King of Na of the Wa of Han, one of the oldest written witnesses to Japan.

While the governor Suetonius Paulinus was storming the druid stronghold of Mona, Boudica, queen of the Iceni, raised the tribes of eastern Britain after Roman officials seized her late husband's kingdom and outraged her family. Her host burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium, killing tens of thousands of citizens and allies. Paulinus, with some ten thousand men, broke her vast army in a single battle; Boudica took poison, and the province was saved.

t: The Great Fire and Nero's Persecution
x: Fire broke out by the Circus Maximus and burned for six days, leaving only four of Rome's fourteen districts untouched. Rumor blamed Nero, who built his Golden House on the ruins, and he turned the blame on the Christians, who were torn by dogs and burned as torches in his gardens. In these years, by ancient tradition, Peter and Paul died as martyrs in Rome.

To end the long war over Armenia, the Parthian prince Tiridates journeyed overland to Rome with three thousand horsemen and knelt before Nero in the Forum, receiving the diadem of Armenia from his hands. The Armenian throne was henceforth held by Arsacids under Roman investiture, and the doors of the temple of Janus were closed.

Emperor Ming, the story goes, dreamed of a golden man flying before his palace and sent envoys west to seek him. They returned with the Indian monks Kasyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna and sutras carried on a white horse, and the emperor built for them outside Luoyang the White Horse Temple, by tradition the first Buddhist temple in China.

Four years into the Jewish revolt, Titus, son of Vespasian, besieged Jerusalem with four legions, starved it, and stormed it after five months. The Temple was burned in August, the city destroyed, and its treasures, the seven-branched lampstand among them, carried in the triumph shown on the Arch of Titus. Judaism endured, without its Temple, in the schools of the rabbis.

Vesuvius, long thought extinct, erupted and buried Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Stabiae under ash and pumice. Pliny the Elder, admiral of the fleet at Misenum, sailed to the rescue and died on the shore; his nephew, Pliny the Younger, described the cloud shaped like a pine. The buried towns, uncovered since the eighteenth century, show the daily life of a Roman city as no book can.

Titus dedicated the Flavian Amphitheater, built by his father Vespasian on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House, with a hundred days of games in which some nine thousand animals were killed. Holding perhaps fifty thousand spectators beneath its awnings, it was the greatest arena of the Roman world.

Gnaeus Julius Agricola, governor of Britain, led his legions and auxiliaries into the far north and defeated the Caledonians under Calgacus at Mons Graupius, probably in the hills of Aberdeenshire. His fleet then sailed round the north of the island and proved Britain an island, and his son-in-law Tacitus recorded the campaign. Agricola was recalled soon after, and Rome drew its frontier farther south.

t: Dou Xian Carves His Victory on Yanran
x: The general Dou Xian, with Southern Xiongnu allies, crushed the Northern Xiongnu at Mount Jiluo and pursued them far into the steppe. On Mount Yanran the historian Ban Gu composed an inscription in praise of the victory, cut into the cliff; in 2017 Mongolian and Chinese scholars found it in the Delgerkhangai hills. Two years later the Northern Xiongnu were driven west.

t: Ban Chao in the Western Regions
x: Ban Chao, brother of the historian Ban Gu, had gone west with thirty-six men and by daring and diplomacy brought the Tarim states back under Han. In 91 he was made Protector General at Kucha; he had already turned back a Kushan army, and in 97 he sent his envoy Gan Ying toward Rome, who halted at the shore of a great western sea.

Earlier artists had shown the Buddha only by signs: a footprint, an empty throne, a tree. Under the Kushans the sculptors of Gandhara, schooled in Greek and Roman forms, carved him as a serene young man in a robe of heavy folds with waving hair, while the workshops of Mathura shaped him in red sandstone after the Indian manner. Both images travelled with the faith to China.

In the valleys of the Ohio and its tributaries, the farming peoples called Hopewell built geometric enclosures of earth, circles and octagons aligned to the risings of the moon, and buried their dead with ornaments of Great Lakes copper, Rocky Mountain obsidian, Gulf Coast shell, and mica from the Carolinas. The earthworks at Newark spread over some four square miles.

Cai Lun, a eunuch in charge of the imperial workshops, presented to Emperor He a writing sheet made from tree bark, hemp ends, rags, and old fishing nets, beaten to pulp and dried on a screen. Cruder papers had existed before, but his method made paper cheap and good, and over the next thousand years it carried learning across Asia and into Europe.

In two hard wars Trajan bridged the Danube at Drobeta and broke the Dacian kingdom of Decebalus, who killed himself rather than be taken; his head was brought to Rome. The gold of Dacia paid for Trajan's Forum and the great column whose spiral reliefs tell the story, and Roman settlers gave the land its Latin speech.

On the death of Rabbel II, last king of the Nabataeans, Trajan's legate Cornelius Palma annexed the kingdom of Petra as the province of Arabia, with its capital at Bostra. The legionaries built a new road from Bostra to the Red Sea at Aila, and the caravan trade in incense and spices passed under Roman control.

Hadrian, who spent half his reign touring the frontiers, came to Britain and ordered a wall built from the Tyne to the Solway, eighty Roman miles, to separate the Romans from the barbarians. Of stone and turf, with milecastles, turrets, and forts like Housesteads, it marked the limit of the empire for nearly three centuries.

Gautamiputra Satakarni, king of the Satavahanas of the Deccan, overthrew the Saka satrap Nahapana and restored his house's power from the Narmada to the Krishna. In the Jogalthembi hoard thousands of Nahapana's silver coins were found restruck with Gautamiputra's name. His mother Gautami Balashri praised him in a cave inscription at Nashik as destroyer of Sakas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas.

Hadrian rebuilt Agrippa's temple to all the gods with a dome of concrete 142 feet across, lightened with pumice toward the top and open to the sky at its center. Consecrated as a church in 609, it is the best preserved building of ancient Rome, and its dome was the largest in the world for thirteen centuries.

Kanishka, greatest of the Kushan emperors, ruled from the Oxus to the Ganges with his winter capital at Purushapura. His Rabatak inscription tells that he issued his edicts in the Bactrian tongue and that his rule reached Pataliputra and Champa. Buddhists remember him as a second Ashoka: he raised a towering stupa at Purushapura, and his coins bear one of the first images of the Buddha.

Hadrian's plan to refound Jerusalem as the Roman colony of Aelia Capitolina provoked a second Jewish revolt under Simon bar Kokhba, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as the star out of Jacob. After three years the last stronghold, Betar, fell; Dio says more than half a million died, and Jews were forbidden to enter Jerusalem.

On the same boulder at Junagadh that bears an edict of Ashoka, the Saka satrap Rudradaman recorded in A.D. 150 how he had rebuilt the dam of the Sudarshana lake, burst by a storm, without forced labour or new taxes. Written in polished Sanskrit, it is the first long royal inscription in that tongue, and it boasts that he twice defeated Satakarni, lord of the Deccan.

Oc Eo, the port of Funan on the Gulf of Thailand, was joined by canals to the inland capital and traded with India, China, and the Mediterranean. Among the beads, seals, and Indian jewels dug from its mounds by Louis Malleret in 1944 was a gold medallion of Antoninus Pius struck in A.D. 152, carried there by the long chain of the monsoon trade.

Tanshihuai, chosen by the Xianbei tribes for his courage and justice, set his court at Mount Danhan, beat back the Fuyu in the east and the Wusun in the west, and filled the steppe the Xiongnu had abandoned. He raided the Han frontier year after year and refused the title of king that Han offered him. His confederacy broke apart at his death in 181.

In the Parthian war of Lucius Verus, Avidius Cassius sacked Seleucia on the Tigris, and the legions carried home a pestilence, probably smallpox, that spread through the empire for twenty years. The physician Galen described its fevers and black pustules; it may have killed a tenth of the people of the empire.

While the empire was weakened by plague, the Marcomanni and Quadi broke across the Danube, destroyed a Roman army, and besieged Aquileia, the first barbarian invasion of Italy since the Cimbri. Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher emperor, spent most of his last decade fighting them on the Danube, writing his Meditations in camp.

Zhang Jue, a faith healer whose Way of Great Peace had won hundreds of thousands of followers, proclaimed that the blue heaven was dead and the yellow heaven would rise in the new cycle. His followers, wearing yellow headcloths, rose in eight provinces at once. The rising was crushed within the year, but the generals who crushed it became the warlords who tore Han apart.

As the Han dynasty sank into civil war, Khu Lien, son of a local official in the southern district of Xianglin, slew the magistrate and made himself king. His realm, which the Chinese called Linyi, grew into the Cham kingdom known in its own inscriptions as Champa, a seafaring Hindu state that held the coast of central Vietnam for more than twelve centuries.

Nagarjuna, a monk of the Andhra country in the days of the later Satavahanas, taught that all things are empty of fixed being, arising only in dependence upon one another. His Madhyamaka, the philosophy of the Middle Way, became a foundation of Mahayana thought in Tibet, China, and Japan. In the same land the great stupa of Amaravati was sheathed in carved limestone slabs.

In the northeast of the Valley of Mexico, the builders of Teotihuacan completed the Pyramid of the Sun beside their Avenue of the Dead, in a city laid out on a grid that would house perhaps a hundred thousand people, the greatest of the Americas. Its merchants and soldiers carried the cult of the Feathered Serpent and the storm god as far as the Maya lowlands; its true name and tongue are lost.

t: Judah the Prince Compiles the Mishnah
x: Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, patriarch of the Jews under Roman rule, who lived at Beit Shearim and Sepphoris in Galilee, gathered the oral law of generations of sages into the six orders of the Mishnah. With the commentaries of later rabbis it formed the Talmud, the foundation of Jewish life and learning ever since.

On the desert plateau between the Ingenio and Nazca valleys, the Nazca people scraped away the dark surface stones to draw lines miles long, great trapezoids, and giant figures of a monkey, a hummingbird, and a spider, whole only when seen from the air. Masters of painted pottery and underground aqueducts, they seem to have walked the lines in rites for water in one of the driest lands on earth.

After a battle in eastern Jutland, the victors sank the arms of a defeated army from across the sea, swords, spears, shields, horse gear, and belts, in a lake as an offering to their gods. Excavated from the bog of Illerup since 1950, they reveal a warrior society of the Roman Iron Age, with Roman blades and early runic inscriptions.

Cao Cao, master of the north, came down the Yangtze with a great army to finish Sun Quan and Liu Bei. At the Red Cliffs, Huang Gai sent fire ships loaded with oil and dry reeds into the crowded enemy fleet, and as a southeast wind spread the blaze Cao Cao's host fled north through the marshes, wasted by fever. China would stay divided for seventy years.

By the Constitutio Antoniniana the emperor Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. Dio says he did it to make more men liable to the inheritance tax; but henceforth the peoples of the Mediterranean, from Britain to Syria, called themselves Romans, and the name endured in the East for a thousand years.

Months after the death of Cao Cao, his son Cao Pi had the puppet Emperor Xian yield the throne to him on a platform near Xu, and proclaimed the Wei dynasty. Liu Bei answered by declaring himself emperor of Han at Chengdu, and Sun Quan later took the imperial title in the south. The four centuries of Han were over, and the Three Kingdoms began.

Ardashir, a prince of Persis, overthrew and killed the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, on the plain of Hormozgan and was crowned King of Kings of Iran at Ctesiphon. His Sasanian dynasty made Zoroastrianism the faith of the realm, laid claim to the old Achaemenid lands, and fought Rome for four centuries.

t: The Queen of Wa Sends Envoys
x: Himiko, a priestess queen who ruled the Wa from her palace at Yamatai, unseen by her people and served by a thousand women, sent envoys by way of Daifang to the Wei court. Wei named her Queen of Wa, Friend of Wei, and sent her a gold seal, a hundred bronze mirrors, and silks. Whether Yamatai lay in Kyushu or in the Yamato plain is still disputed.

The Sasanian kings Ardashir I and Shapur I carried Persian arms over the Kushan lands of Bactria and the Kabul valley; Shapur's inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam names Kushanshahr as far as Peshawar among his provinces. Sasanian princes ruled there as Kushanshahs, striking coins in the Kushan manner, while the old Kushan line lingered in the Punjab and at Mathura.

t: Kang Tai and Zhu Ying in Funan
x: The Wu kingdom sent the envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying to Funan, whose king Fan Xun ruled from a walled city on the lower Mekong. Kang Tai wrote of a people who kept books and archives in a script like that of India, and of the founding legend: the stranger Kaundinya, who came by sea, shot an arrow into the boat of the queen Liuye and took her to wife.

In a mud-brick platform of the Lambayeque valley, the Moche of Peru's north coast laid a warrior-priest to rest in a plank coffin with ornaments of gold and silver, crescent headdresses, and necklaces of golden beads shaped like peanuts, attended by sacrificed retainers and a dog. Found intact in 1987, his tomb revealed the splendor of the Moche lords, masters of irrigation, adobe pyramids, and portrait pottery.

The emperor Decius, who had ordered every citizen to sacrifice to the gods and so begun the first empire-wide persecution of Christians, pursued the Gothic king Cniva into the marshes near Abritus. The Goths cut down the legions in the mud, and Decius and his son Herennius became the first Roman emperors to die in battle against a foreign foe.

Near Edessa the emperor Valerian, his army weakened by plague, was taken prisoner by Shapur I, the first Roman emperor ever taken captive by a foreign enemy. Shapur carved his triumph in the rock at Naqsh-e Rostam, with one emperor kneeling before his horse and Valerian held captive by the wrist, and Roman prisoners built his dams and cities.

Zenobia, widow of Odaenathus, had made Palmyra the seat of an eastern empire reaching from Egypt to Ancyra, proclaiming her son Vaballathus Augustus. Aurelian defeated her armies at Immae and Emesa and besieged Palmyra; the queen fled on a camel toward the Euphrates and was taken. She walked in golden chains in his triumph.

Antony, a young Christian of Middle Egypt, gave away his inheritance on hearing the Gospel's words to sell all and give to the poor, and withdrew into the desert to fight the demons in solitude, at last on the inner mountain near the Red Sea. Disciples gathered round him, and the Life of Antony by Athanasius spread the ideal of the monk through the whole Christian world.

Diocletian, a Dalmatian soldier who had ended half a century of chaos, divided the burden of empire among four rulers: himself and Maximian as Augusti, Galerius and Constantius as Caesars. He doubled the provinces, separated civil from military command, fixed prices by edict, and ruled from Nicomedia with the ceremony of an Eastern court.

King Mahasena of Lanka, who favoured the monks of the Abhayagiri over the orthodox Mahavihara, raised the Jetavanaramaya at Anuradhapura, a brick stupa some 122 metres high, then the tallest building in the world after two of the pyramids of Giza. He also built sixteen great reservoirs, and the peasants of the dry zone worshipped him as a god of the tanks.

Gregory the Illuminator, after years in a pit at Khor Virap, cured King Tiridates III of a madness and baptized him with his court; Armenian tradition sets this in 301. Armenia became the first kingdom to adopt Christianity, and Gregory built the cathedral of Etchmiadzin at Vagharshapat.

On the feast of the Terminalia Diocletian and Galerius had the church at Nicomedia pulled down and issued edicts ordering the scriptures burned, the churches destroyed, and the clergy imprisoned, and at last that all must sacrifice. In the East the persecution raged for eight years, the fiercest the Church ever suffered, until Galerius on his deathbed granted toleration in 311.

The Xiongnu state of Han Zhao, founded by Liu Yuan amid the War of the Eight Princes, sent its armies against the Jin capital. Luoyang was stormed and burned, tens of thousands were slaughtered, and Emperor Huai was carried off to pour wine at the banquets of Liu Cong before his execution. The northern plain passed to the non-Chinese peoples for nearly three centuries.

Constantine and Licinius, meeting at Milan to marry Licinius to Constantine's sister, agreed to grant Christians and all others freedom to follow the religion of their choice and to restore the property taken from the churches. The persecutions were over, and the Church, endowed by Constantine with the Lateran and great basilicas, entered the public life of the empire.

After the capture of Emperor Min at Chang'an, Sima Rui, Prince of Langya, took the title King of Jin at Jiankang, and the next year the throne of the Eastern Jin. With the great families of the north fleeing south behind him, the Yangtze became the frontier of Chinese civilization, and the lands of the south were opened and peopled as never before.

t: Chandragupta I Founds the Gupta Era
x: Chandragupta, a chief of Magadha, married the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi, took the title of Great King of Kings, and began an era reckoned from A.D. 319 to 320. His gold coins show king and queen together, for the Licchavi alliance brought him power and prestige. From this beginning the Guptas built the empire of India's classical age.

Constantine summoned some three hundred bishops to Nicaea to settle the dispute raised by Arius, a priest of Alexandria who taught that the Son of God was a created being. The council declared the Son of one substance with the Father, fixed the common reckoning of Easter, and gave the Church its creed, recited ever since in the form enlarged at Constantinople in 381: the first council of the whole Church.

On 11 May Constantine dedicated New Rome on the site of Byzantium, a city of seven hills commanding the Bosporus and the roads between Europe and Asia, with a senate, a hippodrome, and a grain dole like the old capital. Constantinople was to be the capital of the Christian Roman Empire for eleven centuries and the bulwark of Christendom against the East.

Nino, a captive woman from Cappadocia, healed the queen of Iberia, and King Mirian III, the Georgian chronicles say, accepted Christianity after he was saved from darkness on a hunt by calling on her God. Rufinus, who heard the story from an Iberian prince, recorded it within a lifetime; Iberia became one of the oldest Christian kingdoms.

t: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre
x: Constantine had the temple of Venus that Hadrian built over Golgotha torn down, and beneath it was found the rock-cut tomb venerated as the Sepulchre of Christ. His mother Helena, who journeyed through the Holy Land, was credited with finding the True Cross. The basilica and rotunda, dedicated in 335, made Jerusalem the goal of Christian pilgrims.

t: Ezana of Axum Turns to Christ
x: Frumentius, a Syrian youth shipwrecked on the Red Sea coast and taken to the court of Axum, rose to be tutor of the young king Ezana, was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, and led him to the faith. Ezana's coins replaced the crescent and disc with the cross, among the first in the world to bear it.

Mayurasharma, a Brahmin student insulted by a Pallava horseman at Kanchi, so the Talagunda inscription tells, laid down his books, took up the sword, and carved out a kingdom in the forests of the western Deccan. From Banavasi his Kadamba line ruled for two centuries, the first native dynasty of Karnataka and the first to use Kannada in its records.

Samudragupta's court poet Harisena carved a eulogy of his master on an Ashokan pillar: he uprooted nine kings of the north, defeated twelve kings of the south from Kosala to Kanchi and then restored them, and took tribute from the frontier peoples. A player of the vina as well as a conqueror, Samudragupta performed the horse sacrifice and was hailed as without rival on earth.

Wulfila, a Goth of Cappadocian descent, consecrated bishop of the Goths, led his converts across the Danube to settle near Nicopolis, and translated the Bible into Gothic in an alphabet he devised, leaving out the Books of Kings as too warlike for his people. Through his Arian teaching the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards became Arian Christians.

Ezana of Axum recorded on a stone at his capital how he marched to the confluence of the Nile and the Atbara against the Noba, who had seized the cities of Kush, burned their towns, and set up a throne of victory. The kingdom of Meroë, already in decline, came to its end, and the Nubian kingdoms rose in its place.

Julian, now emperor, who had renounced Christianity to restore the old gods, invaded Persia and reached Ctesiphon but could not take it. Retreating up the Tigris, he was struck by a spear in a skirmish and died that night. His successor Jovian bought the army's escape by ceding Nisibis and five provinces beyond the Tigris.

The monk Lezun, seeing a light like a thousand Buddhas over the cliff of Mingsha near Dunhuang, cut the first meditation cave. Over a thousand years monks and donors carved nearly five hundred painted caves, and a sealed library opened in 1900 yielded tens of thousands of manuscripts in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Sogdian, and Uyghur.

Driven by the Huns, who had come out of the steppes and destroyed the realm of Ermanaric, tens of thousands of Tervingi under Fritigern begged leave to cross the Danube into the empire. Valens agreed, but corrupt officers starved them and sold their children into slavery for dog meat, and the Goths rose in revolt.

Without waiting for his nephew Gratian, Valens attacked the Gothic wagon laager near Adrianople on a hot August afternoon. The returning Gothic cavalry fell on the Roman flank, the infantry was hemmed in so tightly that men could not raise their swords, and two-thirds of the army perished with the emperor himself. The Goths were inside the empire to stay.

In January 378 a warlord named Siyaj K'ak', 'Fire Is Born,' arrived at Tikal from the direction of Teotihuacan, and the Tikal king Chak Tok Ich'aak died that same day. A new dynasty with Teotihuacan ties was installed under Yax Nuun Ayiin I, and Tikal rose to dominate the central Maya lowlands for nearly two centuries.

Theodosius I, a Spanish general made emperor of the East after Adrianople, decreed with Gratian and Valentinian II that all their peoples should hold the faith of Nicaea taught by the bishops of Rome and Alexandria. Catholic Christianity became the religion of the Roman state, and in 391 and 392 the old sacrifices were forbidden.

t: The Battle of the Fei River
x: Fu Jian of Former Qin, master of all the north, marched south with a host said to number near a million to finish the Eastern Jin. On the Fei River Xie Xuan asked the Qin to draw back so both armies could fight on open ground; the withdrawal turned to panic, and the fleeing Qin heard Jin soldiers in every gust of wind. Former Qin fell apart within two years.

Jerome, the most learned Latin scholar of his age, had revised the Gospels at Rome for Pope Damasus and then settled in a monastery at Bethlehem near the cave of the Nativity. There, learning Hebrew from Jewish teachers, he translated the Old Testament from the original tongue; his Vulgate became the Bible of the Latin West for a thousand years.

Theodosius marched west against the usurper Eugenius and his Frankish general Arbogast, who had raised the images of Jupiter and Hercules over their army. On the second day a fierce wind, the bora, blew dust into the faces of the Western army, and Theodosius won; it was the last stand of the old religion in arms.

Theodosius died at Milan in January, the last emperor to rule both halves of the Roman world. The East passed to his elder son Arcadius at Constantinople, the West to the ten-year-old Honorius under the half-Vandal general Stilicho. The division, meant as a partnership, proved permanent.

Chandragupta II, called Vikramaditya, overthrew the last Saka satrap of Gujarat and Malwa, ending three centuries of Saka rule in the west and opening the Gupta realm to the ports of the Arabian Sea. He married his daughter Prabhavatigupta to the Vakataka king of the Deccan. His reign is remembered as the high noon of classical Indian civilization, the age of the poet Kalidasa.

On the Mahakam River in eastern Borneo, King Mulavarman, grandson of Kundunga, raised stone sacrificial posts and inscribed them in Sanskrit to record his gift of twenty thousand cows to the Brahmans. These seven yupa are the oldest inscriptions in the Indonesian islands, and show Indian kingship, rites, and letters already rooted far from India by the end of the fourth century.

Bhadravarman, king of Champa, dedicated in a green valley below the Cat's Tooth Mountain a wooden sanctuary to Shiva under the name Bhadreshvara. Rebuilt in brick by later kings, My Son became the holy city of the Cham, where for nine centuries they raised more than seventy towers carved with gods, dancers, and lions.

t: Shelun Takes the Title of Khagan
x: Yujiulü Shelun, chief of the Rouran, a people who had once paid tribute to the Tuoba, gathered the tribes north of the Gobi and took the title of khagan, the first steppe sovereign to make it an imperial title. For a century and a half his successors raided the Wei frontier, until the Türks, their own ironsmiths, overthrew them.

t: Mesrop Mashtots Creates the Armenian Letters
x: With the support of King Vramshapuh and the patriarch Sahak, the monk Mesrop Mashtots devised an alphabet of thirty-six letters for the Armenian tongue, so that his people could read the Scriptures in their own speech. The first sentence written in it was from the Book of Proverbs: to know wisdom and instruction.

The Chinese monk Faxian walked from Chang'an across Central Asia to find complete books of monastic discipline, and spent three years at Pataliputra copying texts. He found the Gupta realm peaceful and mild: the king ruled without the death penalty, fining most offenders, and respectable people killed no living creature. He returned home by sea by way of Lanka.

On the last day of the year, by the traditional date, hosts of Vandals, Alans, and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mogontiacum, overwhelmed the Franks who stood as Roman allies, and spread across Gaul. Within three years they had passed the Pyrenees into Spain; the Roman West never again held the Rhine.

After the execution of Stilicho left Italy without a defender, Alaric and the Visigoths besieged Rome three times, and on 24 August slaves opened the Salarian Gate. For three days the Goths plundered the city, though they spared the churches and those who fled to them. Rome had not fallen to a foreign enemy for eight hundred years, and the shock moved Augustine to write the City of God.

t: Augustine Writes the City of God
x: Augustine, bishop of Hippo, once a teacher of rhetoric whose Confessions told of his conversion in a Milan garden, began his answer to the pagans who blamed the sack of Rome on the Christians. In twenty-two books he set the earthly city of self-love against the City of God; he died in 430 as the Vandals besieged Hippo.

King Jangsu raised a stone more than six metres tall at Gungnae to his father Gwanggaeto the Great, who had pushed Goguryeo's frontiers deep into Manchuria, humbled Baekje, and driven Wa raiders out of Silla. Its eighteen hundred characters, found again in the 1880s, are the oldest long history written in Korea, and scholars of three nations have quarrelled over their reading.

After fighting Rome's enemies in Spain, the Visigoths under Wallia were settled by treaty as federates in the valley of the Garonne, with Toulouse as their seat. Under Theodoric I and his sons the settlement grew into the first Germanic kingdom on Roman soil, which ruled from the Loire to the Strait of Gibraltar.

t: Yax K'uk' Mo' Founds Copán's Dynasty
x: K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', a lord whose bones show he grew up far from the valley and whose portraits wear the goggles of Teotihuacan warriors, took power at Copán in 426 and founded a line of sixteen kings. His heirs buried his tomb beneath a succession of temples and carved all sixteen kings around Altar Q, each seated upon his own name glyph.

Under Kumaragupta I a Buddhist monastery rose at Nalanda, near Rajagriha, and grew under later kings into the greatest seat of learning in Asia. Its brick halls and temples housed thousands of monks studying logic, grammar, medicine, and the Mahayana scriptures, and Xuanzang studied there for five years. Its libraries perished in the Turkish conquest about 1200.

Patrick, a Briton seized by Irish raiders as a boy and enslaved for six years as a herdsman, escaped home and later returned to Ireland as a bishop. He baptized thousands, ordained clergy, and set up his church, by later tradition, at Armagh. His Confession is the oldest document of Irish history, and the island became a land of saints and scholars.

Genseric, the lame and ruthless king who had led the Vandals and Alans across the Strait of Gibraltar ten years before, broke his treaty with Rome, seized Carthage by surprise in October, and made it his capital. Catholic bishops were exiled and their churches given to the Arians, and from Carthage the Vandal ships raided Sicily, Italy, and Greece.

t: Hengist and Horsa Land in Britain
x: According to Bede and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the British king Vortigern invited the Saxon brothers Hengist and Horsa to fight the Picts, and they landed at Ebbsfleet in Thanet with three ships. They soon turned on their hosts, and Angles, Saxons, and Jutes poured in to make the land that would be called England.

Purnavarman, king of Taruma in western Java, had his footprints carved on a river boulder at Ciaruteun beside a Sanskrit verse likening them to the feet of Vishnu. Another of his stones, found near Jakarta, records a canal more than six thousand bows long dug in twenty-one days to tame the floods of the coastal plain.

t: The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
x: Attila invaded Gaul with Huns, Ostrogoths, Gepids, and other subject peoples. The Roman general Aetius, allied with the Visigoths of Theodoric I, the Franks, and the Burgundians, met him on the plains between Troyes and Châlons in one of the bloodiest battles of antiquity. Theodoric fell, but Attila withdrew behind his wagons and then out of Gaul.

Some five hundred bishops, the largest council of antiquity, met at Chalcedon across the Bosporus and, guided by the Tome of Pope Leo, defined that Christ is one person in two natures, truly God and truly man. The definition became the faith of Rome and Constantinople, but Egypt, much of Syria, and Armenia in time rejected it.

When Yazdegerd II ordered the Armenians to return to the fire worship of Persia, Vardan Mamikonian led them against a far larger Persian army with war elephants. Vardan and his captains fell, but the Armenians fought on, and in 484 Persia recognized their right to the Christian faith; the Armenian Church honors Vardan as a saint.

Attila crossed the Julian Alps, razed Aquileia after a long siege, and sacked Milan and the cities of the Po. Near the Mincio he was met by an embassy from Valentinian III led by Pope Leo I, and he turned back from Italy, whether from awe, from plague in his army, or from fear of an Eastern army behind him. He died the next year.

After the murder of Valentinian III, Genseric sailed from Carthage and took Rome without resistance. At the plea of Pope Leo he spared the people from slaughter and the city from fire, but for fourteen days the Vandals stripped it of its treasures, among them the spoils of the Temple of Jerusalem, and carried off the empress Eudoxia and her daughters.

Skandagupta, coming to the throne in a season of peril, drove back the Hunas who had poured into India from the northwest. His pillar at Bhitari tells that the earth shook when he closed with them in battle, and that he passed a night sleeping on the bare ground to restore his family's shaken fortune. The empire held, but its treasury was drained.

After a savage persecution under Emperor Taiwu, the Northern Wei court made amends to Buddhism. At the monk Tanyao's request five great caves were cut into the sandstone cliff west of Pingcheng, each holding a colossal Buddha, the tallest nearly seventeen metres high, said to stand for the emperors of the dynasty. Tens of thousands of images followed.

Manadeva, king of the Licchavis of the Kathmandu valley, raised a pillar before the temple of Vishnu at Changu Narayan and recorded in Sanskrit how he had subdued rebellious vassals to the east and west. Dated by the Shaka era to A.D. 464, it is the oldest dated inscription found in Nepal, and the temple still crowns its hill above the valley.

In the reign of the Vakataka emperor Harishena, ministers and vassals carved monasteries and halls of worship into a horseshoe cliff above the Waghora river. Their walls were painted with the lives of the Buddha and tales of his former births, crowded with princes, dancers, and beasts, the finest painting to survive from ancient India. Abandoned soon after, they lay hidden in jungle for thirteen centuries.

Kashyapa, who had seized the throne of Lanka and walled his father Dhatusena up alive, feared his brother's vengeance and built a palace on the summit of a sheer rock nearly two hundred metres high, entered through the paws of a colossal lion. Painted maidens still float on its face. When his brother Moggallana returned with an army from India in 495, Kashyapa took his own life on the field.

Peroz, king of kings of Persia, had once been taken prisoner by the Hephthalites and ransomed. Seeking revenge, he marched against their king Akhshunwar in 484; the Hephthalites lured his army into a concealed trench, and Peroz perished with much of the Persian nobility. For a generation Persia paid tribute to the White Huns, whose power stretched from the Oxus into India.

Peroz I, King of Kings, who had once been captured by the Hephthalite Huns and ransomed, marched against them a third time and rode with his army into a great concealed trench. He and most of his sons perished; Persia paid tribute to the Hephthalites for years, and his successors were for a time their vassals.

Clovis, the twenty-year-old king of the Salian Franks of Tournai, defeated Syagrius, the last Roman ruler in northern Gaul, at Soissons. Syagrius fled to the Visigoths, who handed him over to be killed. Clovis took his realm between the Somme and the Loire, the foundation of the Frankish kingdom of France.

Sent by the emperor Zeno to wrest Italy from Odoacer, Theodoric led the Ostrogoths over the Julian Alps in 489, won three battles, and besieged Ravenna for nearly three years. He agreed to share power with Odoacer, then killed him with his own hand at a banquet, and ruled Italy for thirty-three years as king of the Goths and viceroy for the emperor.

Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei led his court from the frontier capital Pingcheng to Luoyang, pretending at first to march against the south. He then forbade Xianbei dress and speech at court, changed the royal surname from Tuoba to Yuan, and married his princes into Chinese families. In the same years the first Buddhas were carved at Longmen.

Clovis, hard pressed by the Alamanni in battle, vowed to believe in the God of his Catholic wife Clotilde if he won. Victorious, he was baptized at Reims by Bishop Remigius with three thousand of his warriors: 'Bow your head, proud Sicambrian; adore what you have burned, burn what you have adored.' Unlike the Arian kings of the Goths, Vandals, and Burgundians, he took the Catholic faith.

At Kusumapura the astronomer Aryabhata completed the Aryabhatiya at the age of twenty-three. In 121 verses he gave the value of pi as 3.1416, taught that the earth turns daily on its axis, explained eclipses by the shadows of the earth and moon, and set out a table of sines. Indian and Islamic astronomers studied his rules for a thousand years.

At Uppsala the kings of the Svear were burned with their weapons and treasures and covered with great mounds, three of which still rise above the plain. Here, Adam of Bremen later wrote, stood a temple of Thor, Odin, and Frey where men and beasts were sacrificed every nine years, and the Ynglings, the royal house of legend, traced their descent from Frey.

Iron Age farmers, who had carried Bantu speech and the craft of the forge south of the Limpopo, shaped seven hollow terracotta heads ringed with incised bands, probably for rites of initiation. Turned up by a schoolboy in the 1950s and dated to about the sixth century, they are among the oldest known sculptures of southern Africa.

Clovis, saying it grieved him that Arians held the best part of Gaul, led the Franks against the Visigoths and killed their king Alaric II with his own hand at Vouillé near Poitiers. The Visigoths lost Aquitaine and Toulouse and kept only Septimania north of the Pyrenees, and the emperor Anastasius sent Clovis the insignia of a consul.

A Danish or Geatish king whom Gregory of Tours calls Chlochilaicus raided the Frankish lands on the lower Rhine and was killed by Theudebert, son of King Theuderic, as he was returning to his ships. He is the Hygelac of Beowulf, whose fall in Frisia the poem recalls, the one figure of that epic fixed in history by a Frankish chronicle.

Yusuf Asar Yathar, called Dhu Nuwas, a Jewish king of Himyar, besieged the Christian city of Najran in southern Arabia and, when it surrendered, put many of its people to death for refusing to renounce Christ, among them their leader Harith. Survivors carried the news to Constantinople and Axum, which resolved to avenge them.

Kaleb, king of Axum, with ships furnished by the emperor Justin, crossed the Red Sea to avenge the martyrs of Najran, defeated and killed Dhu Nuwas, and set a Christian king over Himyar. A few years later the Aksumite general Abraha seized power in Yemen and built a great cathedral at Sana'a to rival the shrine of Mecca.

The Alchon Huns under Toramana had torn Malwa from the Guptas, and his son Mihirakula, ruling the Punjab from Sagala, was remembered by Buddhists as a destroyer of monasteries. Yashodharman, a king of Malwa, boasted on victory pillars at Mandasor that he had made Mihirakula bow at his feet, a lord whose head had never bent except to Shiva.

Justinian charged Tribonian and a commission of jurists with gathering the whole of Roman law: the Code of imperial statutes, issued in 529 and revised in 534, the Digest of the writings of the classical jurists, and the Institutes for students. The Corpus Juris Civilis, rediscovered at Bologna in the eleventh century, became the foundation of the law of continental Europe.

Benedict of Nursia, who had fled the vices of Rome to live as a hermit at Subiaco, led his monks to the mountain above Cassino, threw down the altar of Apollo there, and built a monastery. His Rule, ordering a life of prayer and work under an abbot, became the pattern of monastic life in the West, and his monks kept learning alive through the dark centuries.

At al-Hira on the edge of the Euphrates ruled the Lakhmid kings, Arab clients of Persia, whose court drew poets from all Arabia. Al-Mundhir III, who reigned for half a century, raided Roman Syria to the walls of Antioch and sacrificed a captured son of his Ghassanid rival, al-Harith, to the goddess al-Uzza.

The Frankish kings Theuderic and Chlothar, with Saxon allies, routed the Thuringians on the Unstrut and stormed their stronghold. King Hermanafrid fled and was later killed at Zülpich, pushed from the walls while under Frankish safe conduct. His niece Radegund, taken captive, married Chlothar and later founded a convent at Poitiers.

The Blue and Green factions of the Hippodrome united against Justinian's ministers, crying 'Nika,' conquer, burned much of the city and the church of Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed a new emperor. Justinian was ready to flee, but the empress Theodora declared that royalty is a good burial shroud; Belisarius and Mundus trapped the rioters in the Hippodrome and slew some thirty thousand.

On the ruins of the church burned in the Nika riots, Justinian's architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus raised in under six years a church crowned by a dome that seemed to hang from heaven on a chain of gold. At its dedication Justinian was said to cry, 'Solomon, I have surpassed you.'

King Seong of Baekje, seeking allies against Silla, sent the Yamato court a gilt bronze image of the Buddha and sutras, in 538 by one account and 552 by the Nihon Shoki. The Soga clan took up the new faith while the Mononobe and Nakatomi opposed it, and the quarrel ended in 587, when Soga no Umako destroyed the Mononobe in battle.

Belisarius, who had landed in Sicily in 535 and held Rome through a year's siege by the Goths, blockaded Ravenna until the starving Ostrogoths offered to make him emperor of the West. He feigned assent, entered the city, and took King Witiges captive to Constantinople. The Gothic war was not over: under Totila it would rage for twelve more years.

Khosrow I broke the Eternal Peace while Justinian's armies were in Italy, took Antioch, the great city of the East, plundered and burned it, and bathed in the Mediterranean. He carried its people to Mesopotamia and built for them a new city near Ctesiphon, Khosrow's Better Antioch, with baths and a hippodrome.

Bubonic plague appeared at Pelusium in Egypt and spread along the sea lanes to Constantinople, where in the spring of 542, Procopius says, it killed up to ten thousand a day, and Justinian himself fell sick.
