It returned again and again for two centuries, emptying cities and armies from Persia to Ireland.

The empress Theodora sent the priest Julian to the Nobadian kingdom on the Nile, outstripping a rival mission favored by Justinian, and its king and nobles were baptized into the Miaphysite faith. Within a generation the Nubian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria, and Alodia were Christian, and they would hold the faith for nearly a thousand years.

Pulakeshin I, founder of the Chalukya power, fortified the red sandstone heights of Vatapi and, as an inscription carved on its cliff records, performed the horse sacrifice in 543. From this stronghold above its lake his descendants ruled the Deccan for two centuries and cut cave temples to Vishnu, Shiva, and the Jain saints into the living rock.

Ly Bi, a landowner of mixed Chinese and native descent, drove the Liang governor out of Jiaozhou and in 544 proclaimed himself Emperor Ly Nam De of Van Xuan, the Kingdom of Ten Thousand Springs. Liang armies under Chen Baxian broke him within two years, but his heirs held out in the marshes and hills until the Sui came in 602.

Chenla, a vassal kingdom of Khmer speakers on the middle Mekong, turned on its overlord. Under Bhavavarman and his kinsman Chitrasena its armies pressed south and took the old royal hill of Ba Phnom, and the Funan court withdrew toward the coast. Chinese annals record that Chenla swallowed Funan, and with it the delta plains and the Indian learning of its court.

The Türks, ironworkers in the service of the Rouran, were refused a royal bride by the khagan Anagui, who called their chief Bumin a mere blacksmith slave. Bumin allied with Western Wei, routed the Rouran, drove Anagui to suicide, and took the title Il Qaghan. Within a generation his people ruled from Manchuria to the Black Sea.

The eunuch general Narses, with a great army of Lombards, Heruls, and Romans, met the Gothic king Totila on the plain of Busta Gallorum near Taginae. Totila rode between the armies in golden armor, performing feats with his lance to gain time, but his cavalry charge broke against Narses's archers, and he died of his wounds in flight.

t: The Turks and Persians Destroy the Hephthalites
x: Khosrow I of Persia allied with Istami, yabghu of the newly risen Turks, and the two powers closed on the Hephthalites from south and north. Near Bukhara the Turks shattered the Hephthalite host under its king Ghadfar, and the realm of the White Huns was divided between the victors along the Oxus. Sogdia passed under the overlordship of the Turkic khaganate.

Sky Witness, king of the Kaan, or Snake, dynasty, which later ruled from Calakmul, and his ally Lord Water of Caracol overthrew Tikal in a 'star war' in 562, and the Tikal king Wak Chan K'awiil was probably sacrificed. Tikal raised no monuments for more than a century, while the Snake kings built a hegemony of vassal cities across the Maya lowlands.

Columba, an Irish prince and monk of the Uí Néill, sailed with twelve companions to the island of Iona off the coast of Dál Riata and founded a monastery. From it he and his followers preached to the Picts, and Iona's monks later carried the faith to Northumbria and wrote and painted the great Gospel books of the North.

Alboin, king of the Lombards, who had destroyed the Gepids with the Avars and made a drinking cup of the skull of their king Cunimund, led his people, with Saxons and others, out of Pannonia over the Julian Alps. Italy, exhausted by the Gothic war and plague, fell piece by piece, and the Lombard kingdom ruled from Pavia for two centuries.

Abraha, the Aksumite ruler of Yemen, marched on Mecca, it was said, to destroy the Kaaba and make his own cathedral at Sana'a the goal of Arab pilgrimage, bringing with him an elephant. His army was turned back, and Muslim tradition holds that in that year Muhammad was born to the clan of Hashim of the tribe of Quraysh.

At the appeal of the Himyarite prince Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, Khosrow I sent a small force of Persians by sea under the general Wahriz, which defeated the Aksumites and restored Himyarite rule under Persian protection. Within a few years Yemen was a Persian province, governed from Sana'a until its governor accepted Islam.

Bayan, khagan of the Avars, mounted nomads who had fled the Turks and settled in the Hungarian plain, besieged Sirmium, once an imperial capital, for two years after bridging the Sava. The starving city surrendered, its people were allowed to leave with a single garment each, and the Avars and their Slav subjects began to pour into the Balkans.

Reccared, son of Leovigild, who had renounced Arianism two years before, presided at the Third Council of Toledo, where he, the queen, and the Gothic nobles and bishops professed the Catholic faith. Goths and Hispano-Romans became one people in religion, and the council's creed carried the clause that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Yang Jian, who had taken the Northern Zhou throne as Emperor Wen of Sui, sent half a million men under his son Yang Guang across the Yangtze. Jiankang fell almost without a fight, and Chen Shubao, the poet emperor of Chen, was found hiding in a well with two of his consorts. After nearly three centuries of division, China was one again.

Gregory, a former prefect of Rome turned monk, was elected pope while plague raged in the city, and led a procession of penitence through its streets. He fed Rome from the papal estates, bargained with the Lombards, reformed the liturgy and its chant, and called himself the servant of the servants of God; the medieval papacy begins with him.

Khosrow II, driven from his throne by the general Bahram Chobin, fled to the Romans, and the emperor Maurice gave him an army in return for Armenia and the frontier fortresses. Near Ganzak the Romans and loyal Persians routed Bahram, and Khosrow regained Ctesiphon; the murder of Maurice in 602 would give him the pretext for the last great Persian war.

Pope Gregory, who had seen fair-haired English boys for sale in the slave market of Rome, sent the monk Augustine with forty companions to the English. Æthelberht of Kent, whose Frankish queen Bertha was a Christian, received them, was baptized, and gave them a church at Canterbury, where Augustine became the first archbishop.

t: Seafarers from the East Settle Madagascar
x: Seafarers from the islands of the Indonesian archipelago, speaking a tongue whose nearest kin is still spoken in southern Borneo, crossed the breadth of the Indian Ocean to settle the great island of Madagascar, joined in later centuries by Bantu peoples from the mainland. Their descendants, the Malagasy, kept the rice terraces, outrigger canoes, and language of their Austronesian forebears.

Near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, nearly four thousand metres above the sea, Tiwanaku raised its terraced Akapana pyramid and the monolithic Gateway of the Sun, fed by raised fields that defied the frosts of the altiplano. To the north, the Wari of the Ayacucho basin built the first empire of the Andes, bound by roads and administrative centers that the Inca would one day imitate.

In a valley of the Hindu Kush on the road between Bactria and India, monks and patrons carved two colossal standing Buddhas into the cliff, the taller fifty-three metres high, painted and gilded. Xuanzang saw them glittering with gold in 630 and counted ten monasteries with a thousand monks. They stood for some fourteen centuries above the valley.

Ordered to winter beyond the Danube among the Slavs, the army mutinied and raised the centurion Phocas on a shield. Maurice fled the capital, was taken, and at Chalcedon watched his five sons butchered before his own head fell. Khosrow II of Persia, whom Maurice had restored to his throne, took the murder as cause for a war that lasted twenty-six years.

Prince Shōtoku, regent for his aunt Empress Suiko, issued seventeen articles of instruction for the court, commanding harmony, reverence for the Buddha, his teaching, and his monks, and obedience to imperial commands. With the twelve cap ranks of merit and the embassies he sent to Sui, they mark the beginning of a Japanese state built on the Chinese model.

Emperor Yang of Sui set more than a million labourers to dig the Tongji Canal from Luoyang to the Huai, and then the Yongji Canal to the north, joining them with older works into a waterway from the Yangtze to the frontier near Beijing. Grain from the rich south could now feed the capitals and armies of the north, and the emperor sailed to Jiangdu in dragon boats.

When his elder brother Rajyavardhana was treacherously slain by Shashanka of Gauda, the sixteen-year-old Harsha took the throne of Thanesar and vowed to rid the earth of his enemies. He rescued his widowed sister Rajyashri as she was about to mount the pyre, made Kannauj his capital, and built the last great native empire of northern India. His era begins in 606.

t: The First Revelation on Mount Hira
x: In a cave on Mount Hira above Mecca, Muhammad ibn Abdallah, a merchant of the Quraysh some forty years of age, began to receive the revelations that became the Quran, opening with the command "Recite in the name of thy Lord." For a dozen years he preached the one God in Mecca, gathering a small following that the city's chiefs mocked and persecuted.

Emperor Yang of Sui led one of the largest armies of its age, over a million men, against Goguryeo. A picked force of three hundred thousand pushed toward Pyongyang, but the general Eulji Mundeok lured it on, starved it, and fell upon it as it crossed the Salsu River; only 2,700 men are said to have returned. The Sui never recovered.

K'inich Janaab Pakal took the throne of Palenque at the age of twelve and reigned for sixty-eight years, raising a city of graceful palaces and temples on a shelf above the lowland plain. In 1952 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz found his tomb deep beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, the king laid in a jade mask under a sarcophagus lid carved with his descent into the underworld.

Ishanavarman I, king of Chenla, ruled from Ishanapura on the Stung Sen, where more than a hundred brick towers rose within moated enclosures, some carved with the flying palaces of the gods. The Chinese knew him as lord of thirty walled towns of several thousand households each; his city, now Sambor Prei Kuk, was the greatest of Cambodia before Angkor.

t: Tang Rises from the Ruin of Sui
x: With rebellion everywhere, Emperor Yang was strangled by his own guards at Jiangdu, and Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, who had marched from Taiyuan and taken Chang'an, proclaimed himself emperor. His son Li Shimin then beat the rival warlords one by one. The Tang, with its open and cosmopolitan court, became the golden age long remembered in East Asia.

Harsha, master of the north, marched on the Deccan, but the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II met him on the Narmada and threw him back. The Aihole inscription of 634 boasts that Harsha's joy melted away with fear when he saw his elephants fall in battle. The Narmada became the frontier between the two empires, and Pulakeshin took the title Lord of the South.

Warned of a plot against his life, Muhammad slipped out of Mecca with Abu Bakr and reached the oasis of Yathrib, thereafter Medina, the City of the Prophet, in September 622. There he became lawgiver, judge, and war leader of a community bound by faith rather than blood. The Muslim calendar counts its years from this emigration.

At the wells of Badr, some 313 Muslims fell upon a Meccan force about three times their number that had come out to guard a rich caravan led by Abu Sufyan. Abu Jahl and other chiefs of the Quraysh were slain. The victory, won in the month of Ramadan, was taken by the believers as a sign of divine favor and made Medina a power in Arabia.

t: The Ship Grave at Sutton Hoo
x: On a bluff above the river Deben the East Angles hauled a ship nearly ninety feet long up from the water and buried in it a great lord, most likely King Raedwald, overlord of the southern English. With him went a crested helmet, a great gold buckle, silver from Byzantium, and coins of Frankish Gaul: the treasure of a king who, Bede says, kept an altar to Christ beside his pagan shrine.

t: The Avars and Persians Before Constantinople
x: In the summer of 626, while Heraclius campaigned far off in the Caucasus, the Avar khagan and his Slav subjects invested the Theodosian Walls, and the Persian general Shahrbaraz watched from Chalcedon across the Bosporus. Patriarch Sergius carried the icon of the Virgin along the ramparts; the imperial fleet sank the Slav canoes in the Golden Horn, and the khagan burned his engines and withdrew.

Allied with the Western Turks, Heraclius struck south from the Caucasus into the heart of the Persian empire. On 12 December 627 he broke the army of Rhahzadh among the ruins of Nineveh, by tradition slaying the general with his own hand. Khosrow II was deposed and put to death by his own nobles, and Persia gave back the lost provinces of the East and the True Cross.

Ten thousand Meccans and their allies besieged Medina, but a trench dug at the counsel of Salman the Persian halted their horse, and after some weeks of cold and dissension they withdrew. Muhammad then turned on the Jewish tribe of Banu Qurayza, accused of treating with the besiegers; their men, several hundred in number, were beheaded and their women and children enslaved.

At Bhillamala in Rajasthan the astronomer Brahmagupta completed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, the first book to treat zero as a number in its own right, with rules for adding, subtracting, and multiplying by it, and for reckoning with negative numbers as debts. Carried to Baghdad and rendered into Arabic, the Indian numerals with their place value and zero passed to Europe as the Arabic figures.

After the Quraysh broke the truce of Hudaybiyya, Muhammad marched on Mecca with ten thousand men. The city yielded with little bloodshed, and Abu Sufyan made his submission. The idols about the Kaaba, some 360 by tradition, were cast down, and the shrine that Muslims hold was raised by Abraham was given over to the worship of the one God.

In a winter campaign the general Li Jing fell upon the camp of the Eastern Turkic Illig Qaghan near the Yin Mountains, and the qaghan was soon taken and brought to Chang'an. The chiefs of the steppe hailed Emperor Taizong as Tengri Qaghan, Heavenly Khan, and for half a century the Tang emperor reigned as sovereign both of China and of the nomads.

Samo, a Frankish merchant who had led the Wends in revolt against the Avars, was raised to be their king. When Dagobert I sent armies against him, the Slavs met the Austrasians at the fortress of Wogastisburg, whose site is still sought, and routed them after three days of fighting. Samo reigned thirty-five years and, as the chronicler Fredegar relates, left twenty-two sons.

Muhammad died at Medina in June 632, leaving no undisputed successor. In the hall of the Banu Sa'ida the leading companions acclaimed his oldest friend and father-in-law, Abu Bakr, as khalifa, the successor. The partisans of Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, held that the office was his by right, and the seed of the great schism of Islam was sown.

In August 636 the great army Heraclius had gathered to recover Syria met the Arabs under Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda in the gorges of the Yarmouk. After six days of battle the imperial host was broken and driven into the ravines. Heraclius left Syria, by tradition with the words "Farewell, Syria, my fair province." Syria was lost to the empire.

Near al-Hira on the edge of the desert, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas met the Persian army of Rustam Farrokhzad, with its war elephants, in a struggle of several days. Rustam was slain, the jeweled banner of the Sasanian kings was taken, and the rich alluvial plain of Iraq lay open to the Arabs. The conquest of Persia had begun.

Yazdegerd III fled his capital on the Tigris, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas entered the White Palace of the Sasanian kings. The spoil was beyond the reckoning of desert men; the great carpet of Khosrow, worked in gold and jewels as a garden in spring, was cut up and shared among the conquerors. The Persians made their next stand at Jalula and lost again.

After a long siege the Patriarch Sophronius agreed to surrender the Holy City, but only to the caliph in person. Umar ibn al-Khattab came from Medina, granted the Christians safety for their persons and churches in return for tribute, and by tradition declined to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre lest his followers make it a mosque. Jerusalem passed under Muslim rule for 462 years.

An Arab army struck north from Mesopotamia into Armenia and stormed Dvin, the seat of the Catholicos, in October 640. The Armenian chronicler Sebeos records that 12,000 were slain and 35,000 led away into slavery. It was the first of many such raids that would bring the Christian princes of the Caucasus to pay tribute to the caliphs.

Songtsen Gampo, who had united the Tibetan plateau and alarmed the Tang frontier, won a Tang princess as his bride. Princess Wencheng, a kinswoman of Taizong, made the long journey to Lhasa, and Tibetan tradition credits her and the Nepalese princess Bhrikuti with bringing the images of the Buddha honoured in the Jokhang and Ramoche temples.

By a treaty made with the Patriarch Cyrus, the Roman garrison sailed away from Alexandria in September 642, and the second city of the empire, founded by Alexander nearly a thousand years before, passed to the Arabs. Egypt, the granary of Constantinople, now fed Medina. The Coptic Christians, long at odds with the imperial church, paid the poll tax to new masters.

In the Zagros mountains the last great army of the Sasanian kings met the Arabs under al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin, who fell in the battle as the Persians were routed. The Muslims named it the Victory of Victories, for after Nahavand no Persian host could again take the field, and the provinces of the Iranian plateau fell to the invaders one by one.

The Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, avenging his father's defeats, sent his army deep into the Deccan with his ally, the Sinhalese prince Manavamma. They stormed the Chalukya capital of Vatapi, and Pulakeshin II perished. Narasimhavarman took the title Vatapikonda, conqueror of Vatapi, and had the victory recorded on a rock at Badami itself.

t: Xuanzang at the Assembly of Kannauj
x: The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who had crossed the deserts and the Hindu Kush and studied for years at Nalanda, was summoned by Harsha to a great assembly at Kannauj. Before the kings of eighteen realms and thousands of monks and Brahmins he expounded the Mahayana for eighteen days, and none could answer him. He carried 657 books of scripture home to Chang'an.

Prince Naka no Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamatari cut down Soga no Iruka before the empress in the Itabuki palace, and his father Emishi burned himself in his mansion. The Soga ascendancy ended, and the Taika reforms that followed declared all land and people subject to the throne and began to remake Japan in the image of the Tang state.

The monk Xuanzang, who had slipped across the frontier against the emperor's ban in 629, returned after sixteen years in Central Asia and India with 657 Buddhist texts. Taizong welcomed him and bade him write an account of the western lands, and Xuanzang spent the rest of his life translating, beside the Great Wild Goose Pagoda raised to house his books.

At the port of Mamallapuram, named for Narasimhavarman I, Pallava sculptors carved a granite cliff into the relief called the Descent of the Ganges or Arjuna's Penance: gods, sages, elephants, and serpent spirits crowd toward a cleft down which the sacred river falls. Nearby they hewed five shrines, the rathas, each from a single outcrop of stone.

In the plain of the lower Chao Phraya the Mon kings of Dvaravati ruled moated cities such as Nakhon Pathom and U Thong, struck silver coins proclaiming the meritorious works of the lord of Dvaravati, and set up great stone Wheels of the Law. Through them Theravada Buddhism took root in the land that would become Siam.

A fugitive in his own empire, Yazdegerd III, King of Kings, came at last to Merv, whose governor would not stand by him. He was murdered there by a miller, says the tale, for the sake of his rich garments, and with him ended the dynasty of Ardashir after four centuries. Arab garrisons at Merv soon looked out across the Oxus toward Transoxiana.

When the Arab conquerors of Egypt marched up the Nile under Abdallah ibn Sa'd, the bowmen of Christian Makuria, whom the Arabs called 'the pupil-smiters,' met them before Dongola. A catapult struck the cathedral, but the Nubians held, and the Baqt treaty that followed, an annual tribute of 360 slaves exchanged for grain, wine, and cloth, kept Christian Nubia free for six centuries.

Abdallah ibn Sa'd besieged Dongola, capital of Christian Makuria, and his catapults broke its cathedral, but the Nubian archers, called the pupil-smiters, held the walls. The Arabs made terms. By the Baqt the Nubians were bound to deliver 360 slaves a year to Egypt in return for grain and cloth, and Christian Nubia held the middle Nile for six more centuries.

Rebels from Egypt and Iraq, aggrieved by the favor the aged caliph showed his Umayyad kinsmen, besieged Uthman ibn Affan in his house at Medina and cut him down as he read the Quran, his blood falling upon its pages. Ali ibn Abi Talib was acclaimed caliph in the confusion, and the first civil war of Islam, the fitna, began.

On the plain of Siffin by the Euphrates, Ali faced Mu'awiya, governor of Syria and avenger of his kinsman Uthman. When the Syrians were near defeat they raised leaves of the Quran upon their lances and called for arbitration. Ali consented, and a part of his army, crying that judgment belonged to God alone, departed from him. These were the Kharijites, the first sect of Islam.

A Tang fleet under Su Dingfang landed at the mouth of the Geum River while the Silla general Kim Yu-sin marched from the east. At Hwangsanbeol the Baekje general Gyebaek, who had killed his own family rather than see them enslaved, fell with his five thousand. Sabi was taken, King Uija was led captive to Chang'an, and Baekje was no more.

In his palace at Samarkand the Sogdian king Varkhuman had the walls painted with a procession of envoys: Chinese bearing silk, Koreans with feathered caps, and men of Chaganian and Chach. A Sogdian inscription records an embassy received, and Chinese records name Varkhuman a vassal of the Tang. The murals show the Sogdians at the height of their glory as merchants of the Silk Road.

As he entered the mosque of Kufa for the dawn prayer in January 661, Ali was struck with a poisoned sword by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam, and he died two days later. His son Hasan soon gave up the caliphate to Mu'awiya, who ruled from Damascus as the first caliph of the house of Umayya. The Shi'a, the party of Ali, venerate his tomb at Najaf.

Yamato sent fleets and tens of thousands of men to restore Baekje. At the mouth of the Baekgang the Tang navy, though fewer, caught the Japanese ships in the narrows and burned four hundred of them. Japan withdrew from the peninsula and began to build fortresses at home against a Tang invasion that never came.

At the abbey of the abbess Hilda, King Oswiu of Northumbria heard the Irish party of Bishop Colman and the Roman party of Wilfrid dispute the reckoning of Easter and the form of the tonsure. When Wilfrid declared that Peter held the keys of heaven, the king chose Rome, and the English Church was bound thenceforth to the Roman order rather than to the customs of Iona.

After the death of the dictator Yeon Gaesomun his sons fell to quarrelling, and the eldest went over to Tang. The armies of Li Ji and of Silla closed on Pyongyang, which fell after a month's siege, and King Bojang was carried to Chang'an. Goguryeo had lasted seven centuries; within eight years Silla had driven the Tang from the peninsula south of the Taedong.

Uqba ibn Nafi planted a fortified camp in the Tunisian plain, out of reach of the Roman fleet, as a base for the conquest of the Maghreb. He called it al-Qayrawan, the camp, and laid out its Great Mosque. Kairouan became the capital of Ifriqiya, a seat of learning, and in the eyes of the Maghreb the holiest city after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem.

For several summers the fleets of the Caliph Mu'awiya pressed upon Constantinople from a base at Cyzicus. Against them Constantine IV turned a new weapon, the liquid fire of Kallinikos, an architect who had fled from Syria, pumped through bronze siphons onto the enemy ships. The Arabs withdrew with heavy loss, and the caliph bought a thirty-year peace with tribute.

Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, set out from Mecca to lead the Kufans against the new caliph Yazid. On the plain of Karbala, cut off from the Euphrates, his band of some seventy men was surrounded by the governor's troops and slain on the tenth of Muharram, October 680. His head was carried to Damascus. The Shi'a have kept that day of Ashura in mourning ever since.

Driven west by the Khazars, Khan Asparukh led his Bulgars over the Danube and in 680 routed the army of Constantine IV in the marshes of the delta. The next year the emperor bought peace with tribute and yielded the land between the Balkan range and the river. There the Bulgars ruled the Slav tribes from Pliska, and a new state stood on Byzantium's doorstep.

An Old Malay inscription found on the Tatang River records that in 682 Dapunta Hyang Jayanasa set out by boat with twenty thousand men on a sacred expedition and founded a settlement, bringing victory and prosperity to Srivijaya. It is the oldest record of the maritime empire that would rule the Straits of Malacca and Sunda for three centuries and more.

Uqba ibn Nafi led his horsemen across the whole Maghreb and at the Atlantic shore rode into the waves, calling God to witness that no land remained before him to conquer. On his return the Berber chief Kusayla, whom he had humiliated, ambushed him at Tahuda near Biskra in 683 and slew him with three hundred of his men. His tomb at Sidi Okba is venerated still.

On 20 May 685 King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, against the counsel of his friends, led his host deep into Pictland. Bridei son of Beli feigned flight, drew him among the hills about Dun Nechtain, and slew him with the greater part of his army. Bede marks that day as the moment from which the hopes and strength of the Northumbrian kingdom began to ebb.

Pepin of Herstal, mayor of the palace of Austrasia, defeated Berchar, mayor of Neustria, and the Neustrian king Theuderic III at Tertry. Thenceforth the Merovingian kings reigned in name while Pepin's house governed the whole Frankish realm, the first step toward the crown his grandson Pepin the Short would take in 751.

Wu Zhao, a concubine of Taizong who became the empress of Gaozong and then ruled through her sons, set aside the last of them and proclaimed herself emperor of a new Zhou dynasty, the only woman ever to rule China in her own name. She favoured Buddhism, made Luoyang her Divine Capital, and widened the examinations, ruling by informers until she was forced from the throne in 705.

On the Temple Mount the caliph Abd al-Malik raised an octagonal shrine over the rock from which Muslims hold that Muhammad ascended to heaven, completing it in 691 or 692. Its golden dome and mosaics, the work of craftsmen trained in the Byzantine manner, rivaled the churches of Christendom, and its inscriptions rebuked the Christian doctrine of the Trinity. It is the oldest surviving great monument of Islam.

Hassan ibn al-Nu'man first stormed Carthage, the last great Roman city of Africa, in 695; a Roman fleet retook it, but in 698 it fell again and for good. The Arabs razed it and built their port at Tunis instead. The Berber resistance under the prophetess the Arabs called al-Kahina was broken soon after, and her sons went over to the conquerors.

Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo officer, led Goguryeo exiles and Mohe tribesmen out of Tang control, beat a pursuing Tang army at Tianmenling, and built a fortress on Dongmo Mountain. His kingdom of Balhae, which Tang soon recognized, ruled Manchuria and northern Korea for over two centuries and was called the Flourishing Land in the East.

t: The Burning of the Armenian Princes
x: After an Armenian rising, the Umayyad commanders in the Caucasus summoned the Armenian nobles to Nakhchivan in 705 with promises of reconciliation, then shut them in the church there and in the church of Khram on the Araxes and burned them alive. With its princely houses thus cut down, Armenia was held firmly under the governors of the caliph as the province of Arminiya.

Empress Genmei moved the court to Heijō-kyō, a new capital laid out on the grid of Chang'an, with a great avenue running north to the palace. Through the Nara age the city held perhaps a hundred thousand people, and its temples grew so mighty that the court later moved away to escape them.

Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber freedman in the service of the governor Musa ibn Nusayr, crossed the strait with some seven thousand men in April 711 and landed beneath the rock that bears his name, Jabal Tariq. In July he destroyed the army of the Visigothic king Roderic by the Guadalete, and Roderic was never seen again. Toledo fell within months, and nearly all Spain within seven years.

Qutayba ibn Muslim, Umayyad governor of Khorasan, had already reduced Bukhara when in 712 he forced the surrender of Samarkand, the richest city of Sogdia. Its prince Ghurak agreed to tribute, the idols of its temples were burned, and a mosque was built and garrisoned. Within a generation the Sogdian merchant cities of the Silk Road had passed into the world of Islam.

Sent by the governor al-Hajjaj, the young Arab general Muhammad bin Qasim brought siege engines by sea and stormed the port of Debal, where his troops slew its people for three days. Marching up the Indus, he killed Raja Dahir in battle near Aror in 712, took Brahmanabad and Multan, and sent Dahir's head, a fifth of the plunder, and thousands of captives to Iraq.

t: The Great Arab Siege of Constantinople
x: In August 717 Maslama, brother of the Caliph Sulayman, invested Constantinople with a vast army while a great fleet sought to close the straits. Leo III, emperor for barely five months, burned the ships with Greek fire. A winter of deep snow, famine, and Bulgar attacks wasted the besiegers, and in August 718 the remnant withdrew. Europe's eastern gate had held.

Al-Samh, governor of al-Andalus, crossed the Pyrenees, took Narbonne, and laid siege to Toulouse. After three months Duke Odo of Aquitaine fell upon the besiegers on 9 June 721 and broke them; al-Samh died of his wounds. It was the first great check to the Muslim advance beyond the Pyrenees, eleven years before Charles Martel's victory near Tours.

Below a cave shrine of the Virgin in the Asturian mountains, Pelayo, a Visigothic noble, and a band of followers turned on a Muslim column sent to crush them and drove it back down the valley. The fight, magnified by the chroniclers into a miracle, gave birth to the kingdom of Asturias, and Spaniards would reckon the Reconquista from that day.

Divashtich, lord of Panjikent, who had styled himself king of Sogdia, rose against the Arabs and fled into the mountains with his archive to a fortress on Mount Mug. The governor Sa'id al-Harashi besieged and took him, and though promised his life, Divashtich was crucified. His letters, written in Sogdian on leather and wood, were found at Mount Mug in 1933.

After a volcanic eruption in the Aegean, which he took for a sign of divine anger, Leo III by the traditional account had the image of Christ taken down from the Chalke Gate of the palace, and the women of the city killed the officer who did it. So began more than a century of Iconoclasm, which set emperors against monks and popes and divided the empire to its roots.

In the monastery of Jarrow the monk Bede finished the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, tracing the coming of the faith from Augustine's mission to his own day with a scholar's care for his sources. Through it and his treatises on time, the reckoning of years from the Incarnation, Anno Domini, passed into common use across Christian Europe.

Bilge Qaghan of the Second Turkic Khaganate raised a stone in the Orkhon valley to his brother Kül Tigin, the warrior who had restored their power. In the runic letters of the Old Turkic script he warned his people against the silks and honeyed words of the Chinese, which had once led them into bondage. With the stones of Tonyukuk and of Bilge himself, it is among the oldest long texts in any Turkic tongue.

Arab armies from Sind, the Tajikas of Indian inscriptions, raided deep into Gujarat and Rajasthan, destroying, as a copper plate of 739 relates, the Saindhavas, the Chavotakas, and other kingdoms of the west. At Navsari the Chalukya prince Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin turned them back, and in the north the Pratihara Nagabhata I drove them off. The caliphate's advance into India stopped for nearly three centuries.

Taxed as unbelievers though they had embraced Islam, and their daughters seized for the harems of Damascus, the Berbers of the far Maghreb rose under the water-seller Maysara in 740, preaching the levelling creed of the Kharijites. They took Tangier and destroyed the flower of the Arab aristocracy at the Battle of the Nobles. The far west was lost to the caliphs forever.

Lalitaditya Muktapida, the warrior king of Kashmir who campaigned against the Tibetans and the kings of the plains, raised a great temple to the Sun at Martand on a plateau above the valley of the Jhelum, its colonnaded court of grey limestone looking toward the snows. Sultan Sikandar of Kashmir had it torn down in the fifteenth century; its broken walls still stand.

In the villages around Merv a freedman of obscure origin named Abu Muslim unfurled the black banners in June 747, calling for a caliph from the family of the Prophet. Persian converts, long held second-class by their Arab masters, and discontented Arab settlers alike flocked to him. Within a year Merv was his, and his armies were moving west upon Iraq.

On the Great Zab the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, was routed by the Abbasid army in January 750. He fled to Egypt and was slain there. Abu al-Abbas, called al-Saffah, the shedder of blood, was proclaimed caliph at Kufa, and at a banquet near Jaffa his uncle Abdallah had some eighty princes of the fallen house clubbed to death. One youth escaped to Spain.

After a century of anarchy that the Bengalis called the law of the fishes, when the strong devoured the weak, the chiefs of Bengal chose a man named Gopala as their king. His son Dharmapala recorded the election on a copper plate. The Pala dynasty he founded ruled Bengal and Bihar for four centuries and became the last great royal patrons of Buddhism in India.

Pope Zacharias having ruled that he who held the power should bear the title, Pepin the Short had the last Merovingian, Childeric III, shorn and sent to a monastery. The Franks chose Pepin king at Soissons in November 751, and the bishops anointed him with holy oil, the first such anointing of a Frankish king. The Carolingian dynasty had begun.

Near the Talas river, Ziyad ibn Salih, general of the new Abbasid caliph, met a Tang Chinese army under the Korean-born Gao Xianzhi in July 751. The defection of the Karluk Turks in mid-battle turned the day for the Muslims. China never again pushed west of the Tian Shan, and Transoxiana remained within Islam. Tradition holds that captured Chinese craftsmen taught papermaking at Samarkand.

Xianyu Zhongtong, the Tang governor of Jiannan, marched with eighty thousand men against Geluofeng, King of Nanzhao, who had risen after insults from a Tang official. By the shores of Lake Erhai the Tang host was cut to pieces, and a second army sent in 754 fared no better. Nanzhao turned to Tibet and became the strongest power of the southwest.

Emperor Shōmu, hoping to shield the realm from plague and rebellion, had a bronze Buddha of Vairocana some fifteen metres high cast at Tōdai-ji, using most of the copper in Japan. At the eye-opening ceremony the Indian monk Bodhisena painted in the pupils before priests from across Asia. The hall, rebuilt, is still among the largest wooden buildings in the world.

Winfrid of Wessex, called Boniface, had felled the oak of the thunder god at Geismar, organized the Church of Germany, and set bishops over sees from Salzburg to Würzburg. Nearly eighty, he went back to preach among the Frisians, and on 5 June 754 a band of heathen fell on his camp at Dokkum and slew him with his companions. Germans honor him as their apostle.

An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic blood who commanded three frontier armies, rose at Fanyang, took Luoyang, and proclaimed himself emperor of Yan. Emperor Xuanzong fled Chang'an, and his mutinous guards forced him to have his beloved Yang Guifei strangled at Mawei. Eight years of war followed, and the Tang census fell from over fifty million to under seventeen.

Twice summoned by Pope Stephen II against the Lombards, Pepin crossed the Alps, besieged King Aistulf in Pavia, and gave the cities he surrendered, the old Exarchate of Ravenna, to St. Peter. The abbot Fulrad laid their keys on the apostle's tomb. Thus were born the Papal States, which would endure for eleven centuries.

Abd al-Rahman, grandson of the caliph Hisham, escaped the slaughter of his house and wandered five years through Africa before crossing to Spain. In May 756 he defeated the governor Yusuf al-Fihri on the banks of the Guadalquivir and was proclaimed emir at Córdoba. His dynasty ruled al-Andalus for nearly three centuries, owing nothing to Baghdad.

Under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I, masons cut a whole temple to Shiva downward out of the basalt hillside at Ellora, removing some two hundred thousand tonnes of rock to free a shrine, a hall, and a gateway in a single piece. Carved to stand for Mount Kailasa, the god's Himalayan home, it is the greatest of all rock-cut temples.

The caliph al-Mansur chose a site on the Tigris where the canals from the Euphrates came nearest, and in 762 began his City of Peace: a perfect circle of brick walls, four gates facing the quarters of his empire, and at the center his green-domed palace and mosque. Within fifty years Baghdad was the greatest city west of China.

t: The Uyghur Qaghan Turns to Mani
x: The Uyghur Bögü Qaghan, who had helped the Tang retake Luoyang from the rebels, brought four Manichaean priests home from the city and made their faith the religion of his court, the only state ever to do so. Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon grew into a walled city of palaces and markets, and Uyghur merchants grew rich on horses traded for Tang silk.

Answering the appeal of Pope Hadrian I, Charlemagne besieged Pavia through the winter until King Desiderius surrendered in June 774. Desiderius ended his days in a Frankish cloister, and Charlemagne took the Lombard crown himself, styling himself King of the Franks and the Lombards. The kingdom the Lombards had held for two centuries passed into the Frankish realm.

t: Raiders from the Sea Burn Po Nagar
x: Men described in a Cham inscription as black, thin, and terrible as death came in ships, burned the temple of the goddess at Po Nagar, and carried off its linga; King Satyavarman pursued and beat them at sea. In 787 raiders called the armies of Java burned another temple near Phan Rang, proof of how far the sea lords of the archipelago could strike.

Returning from a fruitless campaign before Zaragoza, Charlemagne razed the walls of Pamplona. On 15 August 778 Basques fell upon his rearguard in the Pyrenean passes and slew it to a man, among them Roland, prefect of the Breton March. Three centuries later the disaster was sung, with Saracens in place of Basques, as the Song of Roland.

King Trisong Detsen, with the Indian masters Śāntarakṣita and Padmasambhava, completed Samye, the first Buddhist monastery in Tibet, laid out as a mandala of the universe, and saw the first Tibetans ordained as monks. A great debate held there between Indian and Chinese teachers ended, by Tibetan tradition, in favour of the Indian school.

After the Saxons under Widukind destroyed a Frankish army in the Süntel hills, Charlemagne returned in fury. At Verden on the Aller, the Royal Frankish Annals record, he had 4,500 Saxons who had joined the revolt beheaded in a single day. Widukind held out until 785, when he submitted and was baptized with Charlemagne as his godfather.

Summoned by the Empress Irene in the name of her young son Constantine VI, some three hundred bishops met in the church of Hagia Sophia at Nicaea and restored the veneration of icons, distinguishing the honor paid to holy images from the worship due to God alone. It was the seventh and last council that the Orthodox and Catholic Churches both hold ecumenical.

Idris ibn Abdallah, a great-grandson of Hasan and descendant of the Prophet, fled the Abbasids after the Alid rising crushed at Fakhkh and found refuge among the Awraba Berbers at Volubilis. Proclaimed imam, he founded Fez on the river of that name in 789. He was poisoned, it was said by an agent of Harun al-Rashid, but his son Idris II made Fez the capital of the first Moroccan state.

The Pala king Dharmapala founded the monastery of Vikramashila on a hill above the Ganges in Bihar, and the great Somapura monastery at Paharpur in Bengal, the greatest Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas. Vikramashila became the chief school of Tantric Buddhism, and its teachers carried their learning over the mountains to Tibet.

On 8 June 793 heathen raiders from the sea fell on Lindisfarne, the holy island of Aidan and Cuthbert, slew monks, drowned others, and carried off the treasures of the church. 'Never before has such terror appeared in Britain,' wrote Alcuin from the court of Charlemagne. The Viking Age had begun.

Emperor Kanmu, leaving behind the overbearing temples of Nara and an ill-omened capital at Nagaoka, founded Heian-kyō, the Capital of Peace and Tranquillity, on a grid of streets copied from Chang'an. It remained the seat of the emperors for more than a thousand years, until the court moved to Tokyo in 1869.

In the Porphyra, the purple chamber where he had been born, the Empress Irene had her son Constantine VI blinded, and she reigned alone, the first woman to rule the empire in her own name. To the West a woman on the throne of the Caesars meant the throne was empty, and three years later Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in Rome.

Shankara, a Brahmin of Kerala who renounced the world in boyhood, wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras teaching that the self and brahman are one and the world of many things an appearance. Tradition holds that he walked the length of India in debate, founded monasteries at Sringeri and at the other quarters of the land, and died young.

For two centuries three empires fought for Kannauj, the imperial city of the Ganges plain: the Palas of Bengal, the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Rajasthan, and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan. Dharmapala set his nominee on its throne; the Rashtrakutas Dhruva and Govinda III swept north and beat both rivals; and about 816 Nagabhata II took the city for the Pratiharas.

Jayavarman II, a prince returned, as the inscriptions say, from Java, had the Brahman Hiranyadama perform on the Kulen hills a rite to make him chakravartin, universal monarch, so that Cambodia would no longer be subject to Java. The ceremony, recorded in the Sdok Kak Thom inscription of 1052, marks the founding of the Khmer Empire of Angkor.

Nikephoros I marched into Bulgaria with a great army, burned Khan Krum's capital at Pliska, and spurned his pleas for peace. On 26 July 811 the Bulgars trapped the Byzantines in a mountain pass behind palisades and slaughtered them. The emperor fell, the first since Valens to die in battle with barbarians, and Krum had his skull lined with silver for a drinking cup.

In the House of Wisdom of the caliph al-Ma'mun, where the works of Aristotle, Galen, and Ptolemy were turned into Arabic, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote his book on restoring and balancing, al-jabr, from which algebra takes its name. His treatise on the Indian numerals carried the decimal place system to the West, and his own name survives in the word algorithm.

t: The Tomb of St. James Found
x: In the reign of Alfonso II of Asturias, tradition tells, Bishop Theodemir of Iria Flavia, led by a light shining over a wood, found the tomb of the Apostle James. The king raised a church above it, and Santiago de Compostela grew into the greatest shrine of the Christian West after Rome, its pilgrim road thronged from every land of Europe.

t: Borobudur Rises on the Kedu Plain
x: Under the Sailendra king Samaratungga the builders finished Borobudur, a stepped mountain of some two million blocks of andesite wrapped about a hill. Pilgrims climbed its nine terraces past 2,672 relief panels telling the life of the Buddha and the quest of the youth Sudhana, to 72 latticed stupas below the summit: the greatest Buddhist monument in the world.

Invited by the rebel admiral Euphemius, an Aghlabid army of some ten thousand foot and seven hundred horse under the aged jurist Asad ibn al-Furat crossed from Africa and landed at Mazara in June 827. The conquest of the island took three-quarters of a century of sieges, massacres, and enslavements; Syracuse fell in 878 and Taormina in 902.

Jang Bogo, a Silla commoner who had risen as an officer in Tang service, was given ten thousand men by King Heungdeok to stamp out the pirates who carried Koreans off to be sold as slaves in China. From his garrison at Cheonghae on Wando island he made himself master of the Yellow Sea trade between Silla, Tang, and Japan.

The Pyu, a Buddhist people whose walled cities of brick had ruled the dry zone of the Irrawaddy for centuries, fell prey to Nanzhao in Yunnan. In 832 its armies sacked a Pyu capital and drove three thousand captives north to the shores of the lake of Kunming. From the wreck of the Pyu rose the Burmans, who soon built their own city at Pagan.

In his last year al-Ma'mun required judges and scholars to profess that the Quran was created, not eternal. Those who refused were imprisoned, and the traditionist Ahmad ibn Hanbal was flogged under al-Mu'tasim rather than yield. The inquisition was abandoned under al-Mutawakkil, and the scholars, not the caliphs, emerged as the guardians of the faith.

Weary of the brawls between the Baghdad populace and his Turkish slave soldiers, al-Mu'tasim built a new capital some eighty miles up the Tigris at Samarra in 836. For over fifty years the caliphs ruled from its palaces, which stretched for miles along the river, and al-Mutawakkil raised there the largest mosque in the world, with its spiral minaret. The Turkish guards soon became masters of the caliphs.

For twenty years Babak and his red-clad Khurramite sectaries held the mountains of Azerbaijan against the armies of the caliphs. In 837 the general Afshin stormed his fortress of Bazz; Babak fled to an Armenian prince, who handed him over to the Muslims. At Samarra in 838 he was paraded on an elephant, his hands and feet were cut off, and he was gibbeted.

t: The Kyrgyz Destroy the Uyghur Khaganate
x: In a year of famine, plague, and heavy snows, a rebel Uyghur minister opened the steppe to the Yenisei Kyrgyz, who stormed Ordu-Baliq, killed the qaghan, and burned the city. The Uyghurs scattered: some fled to the Tang frontier, others to the oases of Turfan and Gansu, where they founded kingdoms that lasted for centuries.

Norse raiders who had harried Ireland for half a century built a longphort, a fortified ship camp, beside the black pool, Dubh Linn, where the Poddle met the Liffey. It grew into the first true town of Ireland, a great port and a market for slaves taken in raids across the Irish Sea and beyond, and the seat of Norse kings for three centuries.

Langdarma, remembered in Buddhist history as a persecutor of the faith, was shot dead with an arrow by the monk Lhalung Palgyi Dorje, who by tradition escaped on a horse blackened with soot that the river washed white. The succession was disputed between two infant princes, the empire broke apart, and Tibet entered a long age of fragmentation.

After three years of civil war, the bloody field of Fontenoy, and the Oaths of Strasbourg, the three surviving sons of Louis the Pious divided Charlemagne's empire. Lothair kept the imperial title and a middle kingdom from Frisia to Italy; Louis the German took the lands east of the Rhine, Charles the Bald the west. The lines drawn at Verdun foreshadowed France and Germany.

t: Kenneth MacAlpin, King of the Picts
x: Kenneth son of Alpin, king of the Scots of Dál Riata, made himself master of the Picts, whose nobility the Vikings had lately slaughtered in battle. From his seat at Forteviot he ruled both peoples; within two generations the Picts and their tongue had passed from history, and the kingdom of Alba, the root of Scotland, had taken their place.

Emperor Wuzong, a devotee of Taoist alchemy, decreed the closing of the Buddhist monasteries. Some 4,600 were destroyed and over 260,000 monks and nuns returned to lay life, their lands and bronze seized for the treasury; Nestorian Christians, Manichaeans, and Zoroastrians were swept away with them. Chinese Buddhism never again held such wealth.

A Viking fleet of 120 ships under a chief the annals call Reginherus rowed up the Seine and plundered Paris at Easter 845. Charles the Bald, his army divided, bought their departure with 7,000 pounds of silver, the first of many such payments that taught the Northmen the kingdom of the West Franks would pay.

In August 846 an Arab fleet from Africa sailed into the mouth of the Tiber, and its raiders, finding the great basilicas outside the walls undefended, stripped the shrines of St. Peter and St. Paul of their gold and silver and plundered the apostles' tombs. Pope Leo IV answered by enclosing the Vatican hill within the Leonine Wall, and in 849 his league destroyed a Saracen fleet off Ostia.

Between 850 and 859 some forty-eight Christians of Córdoba were beheaded under the emirs Abd al-Rahman II and Muhammad I, most for denouncing the Prophet in public or for holding to the faith of their fathers when the law reckoned them Muslims. The priest Eulogius, who recorded their deaths, was himself executed in 859. Their witness shows the strain on the Mozarabs as Arabic culture drew their young away.

The Arab merchant Sulaiman, writing in 851, counted the Balhara, as the Arabs called the Rashtrakuta king, among the four great sovereigns of the world with the caliph, the emperor of China, and the emperor of the Romans, and praised his friendship toward the Arabs. Amoghavarsha I ruled from his new capital at Manyakheta, and the Kannada treatise on poetics, Kavirajamarga, is ascribed to his court.

Rakai Pikatan, the Shaivite king who had married the Sailendra princess Pramodhawardhani, consecrated the temple of Shiva at Prambanan, as the Shivagrha inscription of 856 records. Its central tower, forty-seven meters high, rose among more than two hundred lesser shrines, and its Ramayana reliefs answered Borobudur, a day's journey to the west.

Fatima al-Fihri, daughter of a wealthy merchant who had come to Fez from Kairouan, spent her inheritance on a mosque for her quarter of the city in 859. Al-Qarawiyyin grew into the greatest mosque of the Maghreb and a seat of learning whose masters taught law, grammar, and astronomy, and it is reckoned among the oldest continuing places of study in the world.

The Primary Chronicle tells how the Slav and Finnic tribes of the north, weary of strife among themselves, sent across the sea to the Varangian Rus': 'Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come and rule over us.' Rurik and his brothers came, and Rurik's house would rule in Rus' and Muscovy until 1598.

At the request of Prince Rastislav, who wished for teachers in his people's own tongue, Michael III sent two brothers from Thessalonica, Constantine, called Cyril, and Methodius. For the Slavs they devised the Glagolitic alphabet and rendered the Gospels and the liturgy into Slavonic, laying the foundation of the written culture of the Orthodox Slavs.

Khan Boris, pressed by a Byzantine army and a famine, accepted baptism from Constantinople, taking the name Michael after his godfather the emperor. He crushed a revolt of boyars who clung to the old gods, played Rome against Constantinople to win a church of his own, and welcomed the disciples of Methodius, who made Bulgaria the cradle of Slavonic letters.

A host of Danes, which the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle called the great army, landed in East Anglia in 865, led, tradition says, by the sons of Ragnar Lodbrok, Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan. Within five years they had taken York, slain the kings of Northumbria and King Edmund of East Anglia, and broken both kingdoms; of the English realms only Wessex would stand.

On a scroll five metres long, a man named Wang Jie had the Diamond Sutra printed from carved wooden blocks for free distribution, on behalf of his parents. Found in the sealed library cave at Dunhuang, it is the oldest printed book that bears a date. Under the Song, printing spread to the classics, the histories, and paper money, and transformed learning in East Asia.

Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, a coppersmith of Sistan who had made himself master of eastern Iran, marched through Bost and Zabulistan to Kabul and Bamiyan, overthrowing their Buddhist and Hindu lords. He sent their idols as trophies to the caliph in Baghdad. Islam had won its first lasting foothold in the valleys below the Hindu Kush.

On the salt flats below Basra, East African slaves toiled in gangs to clear the soil for the planters. In 869 a pretender named Ali ibn Muhammad roused them to revolt, and in September 871 the Zanj stormed and burned Basra and slaughtered its people. Their marsh state endured fourteen years, until the regent al-Muwaffaq stormed their capital, al-Mukhtara, in 883.

In the fjord near Stavanger, Harald Fairhair defeated a league of chieftains of the west coast in a great sea battle and became the first king over most of Norway. The sagas say he had sworn not to cut his hair until he ruled the whole land; many of the chiefs who would not bow to him sailed west to the isles and to Iceland.

Ingolf Arnarson, a Norwegian chieftain, cast the pillars of his high seat overboard as he neared Iceland and vowed to settle wherever they came ashore. His thralls found them at a bay he named Reykjavik, the bay of smoke, for the steam of its hot springs. Within sixty years, the Book of Settlements records, every habitable shore had been taken by Norse families and their Irish slaves.

Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish soldier sent from Samarra to govern Egypt in 868, made himself its master, raised an army of slaves, and annexed Syria. At his new capital of al-Qata'i he built between 876 and 879 a great mosque of brick and stucco, with a spiral minaret after the model of Samarra. It stands today, the oldest mosque of Cairo preserved in its original form.

Surprised at Chippenham in midwinter by Guthrum's Danes, Alfred of Wessex took refuge in the marshes of Athelney. In May 878 he gathered the men of Somerset, Wiltshire, and Hampshire and routed the Danes at Edington. Guthrum accepted baptism with Alfred as his godfather, and England was soon divided between Wessex and the Danelaw.

Huang Chao, a salt smuggler who had failed the examinations, led a rebel host the length of China, massacring the foreign merchants of Canton in 879, and entered Chang'an in triumph. He proclaimed himself emperor of Qi, but his men pillaged the city and slaughtered its officials. The Tang outlived his defeat only as a shell, ruled by its generals.

Oleg, kinsman and successor of Rurik, came down the Dnieper from Novgorod, lured the Varangian lords Askold and Dir out of Kiev by a ruse, and slew them. Making Kiev his seat, 'the mother of the cities of Rus',' he joined north and south along the great river road from the Varangians to the Greeks, and the Kievan state was born.

After two centuries of Arab governors, the caliph al-Mu'tamid sent a crown to the presiding prince Ashot Bagratuni, and the Byzantine emperor Basil I soon sent another. Crowned at Bagaran in 885, Ashot I restored the kingdom of Armenia, and his Bagratid house ruled from Shirakavan, Kars, and at last Ani, the city of a thousand and one churches.

Yasovarman I, crowned in 889, left Hariharalaya and laid out a new capital, Yasodharapura, about the hill of Phnom Bakheng, whose summit he crowned with a temple-mountain of 108 towers. East of it he dug a reservoir seven kilometers long. The city that grew here, called Angkor by later ages, remained the seat of the Khmer kings for more than five hundred years.

Driven from the Pontic steppe by the Pechenegs, the seven tribes of the Magyars under Árpád crossed the Carpathian passes into the plain of the Danube and the Tisza. They broke Great Moravia, and for half a century their horsemen rode out to plunder Germany, Italy, and France, until the Lechfeld taught them to settle as a Christian people.

Yahya ibn al-Husayn, a descendant of Hasan from the Hijaz, was invited to arbitrate among the warring tribes of northern Yemen and established himself at Sa'da in 897 as imam with the title al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq. The Zaydi imamate he founded endured, through long eclipses, for over a thousand years, until the revolution of 1962.

East of the lower Niger, the smiths of an Igbo priest-kingdom cast by the lost-wax method bronzes of a delicacy unmatched in their age: shell-shaped bowls, ornate pendants, and a ceremonial pot wrapped in a cast rope. Beside them lay a dignitary buried seated, among more than a hundred thousand beads, many of them glass brought across the Sahara from distant lands.

Near Balkh in 900 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad of Bukhara defeated and captured Amr ibn al-Layth, brother of the coppersmith Ya'qub and master of the Saffarid realm. The caliph rewarded Isma'il with Khorasan, and the Samanids, Persian lords of Transoxiana, made Bukhara a capital of Persian letters, nursery of the poet Rudaki and the young Avicenna.

Zhu Wen, once a lieutenant of Huang Chao and now the strongest general in the north, forced the last Tang boy emperor to abdicate and proclaimed his own Later Liang dynasty at Kaifeng. He had already razed Chang'an and murdered the Tang court officials. China broke into the Five Dynasties of the north and the Ten Kingdoms of the south.

On 4 July 907 a Bavarian army under Margrave Luitpold marched down the Danube to crush the Magyars and was itself annihilated at Brezalauspurc, most likely Pressburg. The margrave, Archbishop Theotmar of Salzburg, two bishops, and a host of counts fell. The East Frankish frontier fell back to the Enns, and the Carpathian basin was left to the Magyars.

The Isma'ili missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, preaching among the Kutama Berbers, overthrew the Aghlabids and drove the last emir from Raqqada in 909. He fetched his hidden master Ubayd Allah from Sijilmasa, and in January 910 proclaimed him caliph with the name al-Mahdi. A Shi'ite caliphate, descended by its own reckoning from Fatima, now challenged Baghdad for the rule of Islam.

At Toniná in the Chiapas highlands, a small monument carved in January 909 bears the last known date in the Maya Long Count. Through the ninth century the great cities of the southern lowlands, Copán, Palenque, Tikal, and Calakmul, had ceased one by one to raise monuments and emptied of people, worn down by war, drought, and the exhaustion of their land.

Duke William of Aquitaine gave his hunting estate at Cluny to Abbot Berno and his monks and placed the house under the protection of the apostles Peter and Paul, free of any lord or bishop. Under its great abbots Cluny led a reform of monastic life across Europe; by the twelfth century it ruled hundreds of priories, and its abbey church was the largest in Christendom.

At Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, by tradition, Charles the Simple granted the Viking chief Rollo the lands about Rouen on condition that he defend the Seine against other Northmen and receive baptism. Rollo's Norsemen became Normans, and within a century and a half his descendants would conquer England and southern Italy.

Yelü Abaoji, who had made himself khagan of the eight Khitan tribes by setting aside their custom of electing a new chief every three years, proclaimed himself emperor in the Chinese manner and soon built a walled Supreme Capital on the steppe. His state, named Liao in 947, ruled nomads by tribal custom and farmers by Chinese law, and gave the West its old name for China, Cathay.

Simeon of Bulgaria, schooled at Constantinople and called half-Greek, sought the imperial crown itself. On 20 August 917 his army fell on the Byzantine host of Leo Phokas by the river Achelous near Anchialos and destroyed it in one of the bloodiest battles of the age. For a decade Simeon was master of the Balkans, styling himself emperor of the Bulgarians and the Romans.

The officers of the tyrant Gung Ye, who called himself a living Maitreya and had murdered his own wife and sons, overthrew him and raised the general Wang Geon as king. Wang named his kingdom Goryeo after old Goguryeo, the name from which Korea comes, and set his capital at his home of Songak, later Kaesong. In 935 Silla yielded to him, and in 936 he united the peninsula.

An embassy from the caliph al-Muqtadir reached the Bulgar king Almış on the middle Volga in May 922, bringing a teacher of the law and a builder of mosques. The king embraced Islam and had the caliph's name recited at the Friday prayer. Ibn Fadlan, the embassy's secretary, left a vivid account of the journey, with his famed description of a Rus chieftain's ship burial.

t: Abd al-Rahman III Takes the Caliph's Title
x: In January 929 the emir Abd al-Rahman III, who had brought rebellious al-Andalus to heel, proclaimed himself caliph and Commander of the Faithful in answer to the Fatimids across the strait. Under him and his son al-Hakam II Córdoba became the richest city of the West, with a library said to hold 400,000 volumes and embassies from Constantinople and from the German king Otto I.

t: Mpu Sindok Moves to East Java
x: King Mpu Sindok removed the court of Mataram from Central Java to the valley of the Brantas in the east, whether after an eruption of Merapi or for the sea trade of the river mouth the records do not say. Borobudur and Prambanan were left to the forest and the ash, and for six centuries the heart of Javanese power lay in East Java.

t: The Qarmatians Carry Off the Black Stone
x: Abu Tahir al-Jannabi, ruler of the Qarmatian state of Bahrain in eastern Arabia, fell upon Mecca during the pilgrimage of 930. His men slaughtered thousands of pilgrims, threw their bodies into the well of Zamzam, and tore the Black Stone from the Kaaba. They kept it at al-Ahsa for over twenty years before returning it in 951.

The chieftains of Iceland, a land without a king, met for the first time at Thingvellir, the assembly plains, to make laws and settle feuds. Each summer the lawspeaker recited a third of the law from the Law Rock. The Althing governed a commonwealth of free farmers that endured until the Icelanders submitted to the King of Norway in 1262.

Wenceslaus, Duke of Bohemia, a devout Christian who had made peace with Henry the Fowler, was cut down at the door of the church of Stará Boleslav on the morning after a feast, by followers of his brother Boleslaus. Venerated at once as a martyr, he became the patron saint and eternal prince of the Czech lands.

Shi Jingtang, a Shatuo general rebelling against Later Tang, bought the help of the Khitan emperor Yelü Deguang by calling himself his son and ceding sixteen prefectures south of the mountains, among them Youzhou, the later Beijing, and Yunzhou, the later Datong. With them went the passes that guarded the North China plain, which no Chinese dynasty held again for over four centuries.

Below the Sierra Morena, five miles west of Córdoba, Abd al-Rahman III began in 936 a palace city named for al-Zahra, the radiant one. Its halls of marble and gold, its terraced gardens, its mint and workshops housed the caliph's court and treasury. In the civil wars that tore the caliphate apart it was sacked by Berber soldiers in 1010 and left in ruins.

Athelstan of Wessex, first king to rule all the English, met a grand alliance of Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin, Constantine II of the Scots, and Owain of Strathclyde. In the greatest slaughter yet seen on the island, the Chronicle sang, the invaders were broken. The field is still disputed, perhaps on the Wirral, but the victory confirmed the making of England.

t: Ngo Quyen at the Bach Dang River
x: Ngo Quyen planted iron-tipped stakes in the bed of the Bach Dang and, when the tide ran in, lured the war junks of the Southern Han upstream. As the water fell the fleet was impaled and broken, and the Han prince Liu Hongcao was slain. The victory ended a thousand years of Chinese rule, and Ngo Quyen made himself king at Co Loa.

Abd al-Rahman III led a great army north, which his chroniclers called the Campaign of Omnipotence, against Ramiro II of León. Before Simancas on the Duero in August 939 the Leonese and their allies routed it, and the caliph, who barely escaped, never again led an army in person. The Christians resettled the valley of the Duero.

Ahmad ibn Buya, one of three Daylamite brothers from the mountains south of the Caspian, entered Baghdad in December 945. The caliph al-Mustakfi gave him the title Mu'izz al-Dawla and was blinded and deposed within weeks. For a hundred and ten years the Shi'ite Buyid amirs ruled Iraq and western Persia, keeping the Sunni caliphs as revered prisoners in their own palace.

The Rashtrakuta emperor Krishna III, with his Western Ganga ally Butuga II, crushed the Chola army at Takkolam. The Chola crown prince Rajaditya was slain on his elephant by an arrow from Butuga. Krishna III occupied the country about Kanchi, styling himself conqueror of Kanchi and Tanjore, and the Cholas did not recover their strength for a generation.

On a ridge above the Tula River, the Toltecs built Tollan, a city of perhaps sixty thousand, whose temple roof was borne by colossal stone warriors with butterfly breastplates and spear-throwers. Later peoples remembered the Toltecs as masters of all the arts and their priest-king Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl as a god; the Aztec kings claimed descent from them.

t: Otto the Great at the Lechfeld
x: On 10 August 955 a Magyar host besieging Augsburg met Otto I and the levies of every German duchy, marching beneath the Holy Lance. The Magyars were routed and hunted down at the river crossings, and their leaders were hanged at Regensburg. Their raids on the West ended forever, and Otto's victory won him the renown that carried him to Rome.

Marching north against the Khitan, the officers of the Later Zhou palace army halted at Chenqiao, wrapped their commander Zhao Kuangyin in a yellow robe, and hailed him emperor. He returned to Kaifeng, received the throne from the boy emperor, and founded the Song. Later, over wine, he persuaded his generals to retire to rich estates, and the soldier was made servant to the scholar for a thousand years.

Ethiopian tradition remembers Gudit, a queen from the south, who sacked Aksum, burned its churches, and slaughtered the royal house; the Arab traveler Ibn Hawqal heard in the tenth century of a queen who had slain the king of the Abyssinians and ruled in his place. Out of the ruin of old Aksum the Zagwe kings would rise.

On 2 February 962 Pope John XII crowned Otto, King of the Germans and of Italy, as emperor in St. Peter's, and the imperial dignity, vacant in the West for nearly forty years, passed to the German kings. The empire later called Holy and Roman would endure until 1806.

Sviatoslav of Kiev, who sent his enemies the warning 'I come against you,' fell upon the Khazar khaganate, which had taken tribute from the eastern Slavs. He stormed the fortress of Sarkel on the Don, which the Rus' renamed the White Tower, and ravaged Atil on the Volga. The Jewish khaganate never recovered, and the steppe lay open to the Pechenegs.

t: Harald Bluetooth Raises the Jelling Stone
x: Beside the mounds of his parents Gorm and Thyra, King Harald Bluetooth set up a great runestone carved with the figure of Christ, recording that he had won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian. Danes call it their kingdom's baptismal certificate.

Mieszko I of the Polans, who had married the Christian princess Dobrawa of Bohemia, received baptism at Easter 966 with his court. By taking the faith from Bohemia and Rome rather than at the point of German swords, he set his realm among the Christian states of Latin Europe, and within two years Poland had its first bishop at Poznań.

t: Dinh Bo Linh Unites Dai Co Viet
x: After Ngo rule dissolved into the anarchy of the Twelve Warlords, Dinh Bo Linh, a buffalo boy turned captain, subdued them one by one and took the title of emperor. He named his realm Dai Co Viet and fixed his capital among the limestone crags of Hoa Lu, where a cauldron and a caged tiger in his courtyard awaited those who broke his laws.

The Fatimid general Jawhar, a slave of Greek or Slav birth in the service of the caliph al-Mu'izz, took Egypt in July 969 almost without a fight and laid out a walled palace city north of Fustat. It was named al-Qahira, the Victorious. In 973 al-Mu'izz moved his court there from Ifriqiya, and Cairo became the capital of a Shi'ite empire reaching from Sicily to the Hijaz.

Sviatoslav of Kiev, who had overrun Bulgaria and meant to make his capital on the Danube, was shut up in Dorostolon by John I Tzimiskes. After three months of sallies and duels the Rus' sued for terms and departed; on the homeward road the Pechenegs slew Sviatoslav at the Dnieper rapids and made a drinking cup of his skull.

When the Paramaras of Malwa sacked the Rashtrakuta capital of Manyakheta in 972, the Chalukya vassal Tailapa II rose against his weakened overlord and in 973 overthrew Karka II, proclaiming the return of the Chalukya house. The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, as they came to be called, ruled the Deccan for two centuries and warred endlessly with the Cholas.

Exiled from Iceland for manslaughter, Erik the Red explored the southwest coast of a great ice-bound land and named it Greenland, for men would be drawn there, he said, if it had a good name. He returned with twenty-five ships, of which fourteen arrived, and founded the Eastern Settlement at Brattahlíð; the Norse colony endured some four and a half centuries.

When Louis V, last Carolingian king of the West Franks, died in a hunting fall, the magnates passed over his uncle Charles of Lorraine and chose Hugh Capet, Duke of the Franks. Crowned on 3 July 987, Hugh had his son Robert crowned within the year to secure the succession. His direct heirs ruled France until 1328, and his house until 1848.

Vladimir of Kiev, having sent envoys to weigh the faiths of his neighbors, chose the Christianity of Constantinople, whose liturgy in Hagia Sophia had seemed to his men like heaven upon earth. Baptized, he married Anna, sister of Basil II, cast the idol of Perun into the Dnieper, and had the people of Kiev baptized in its waters. The Orthodox civilization of Russia begins here.

Rajaraja Chola sent his fleet across the strait and conquered the north of Lanka, sacking Anuradhapura, which had been the royal city for more than twelve centuries. The Cholas made Polonnaruwa the seat of their new province. In 1017 his son Rajendra completed the conquest and carried King Mahinda V captive to India, where he died.

Almanzor, the all-powerful chamberlain of the Córdoban caliph, led one of his fifty-odd raids against the Christian north to the shrine of St. James at Compostela in August 997. The town was razed, though the apostle's tomb was spared. The bells of the church were carried to Córdoba on the shoulders of Christian captives to hang as lamps in the Great Mosque.

The Turkish Karakhanids rode down from the steppe and entered Bukhara in 999 unopposed, its clergy having told the people that the quarrel was only between princes. The Samanid house that had ruled Transoxiana for over a century fell, and the land beyond the Oxus passed for good under Turkish lords. South of the river, Mahmud of Ghazni took Khorasan.

Vajk, son of the Árpád prince Géza, baptized Stephen, crushed his pagan kinsman Koppány and was crowned at Esztergom at Christmas 1000 with a crown sent, by tradition, by Pope Sylvester II. He founded bishoprics, counties, and royal castles, and the nomad confederation of the Magyars became a Christian kingdom of the Latin West.

Leif, son of Erik the Red, sailed west from Greenland and wintered on a coast he called Vinland for the wild grapes his men found there. The sagas tell of later voyages and of fights with the natives, and the Norse turf halls found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland bear them out: Europeans had reached America five centuries before Columbus.

After two thousand years in Tonga and Samoa, Polynesian navigators sailed east in double-hulled canoes laden with taro, breadfruit, pigs, dogs, and fowls, and found the Society Islands and the Marquesas. Steering by stars, swells, and the flight of birds, their children reached within three centuries the farthest corners of the Polynesian triangle: Hawaii, Rapa Nui, and Aotearoa.

On the dry limestone plain of northern Yucatán, Chichen Itza rose to be the greatest Maya city after the southern collapse, with the Castillo pyramid of Kukulcan, the Feathered Serpent, the largest ballcourt in Mesoamerica, and the Sacred Cenote, into which pilgrims cast jade, gold, and human victims. Its Temple of the Warriors recalls Tula, more than a thousand kilometres away.

Mahmud of Ghazni, son of the Turkish slave-commander Sabuktigin, met the Hindu Shahi king Jayapala near Peshawar and routed his army; Jayapala was taken with fifteen of his kin and ransomed. Shamed by defeat, he gave up the throne to his son Anandapala and burned himself on a pyre. It was the first great battle of the seventeen invasions of India that tradition ascribes to Mahmud.

When the Liao empress dowager Xiao Chuo and Emperor Shengzong drove deep into Song territory, Emperor Zhenzong was persuaded by his minister Kou Zhun to go to the front at Chanyuan. The armies stood deadlocked and made peace: Song would pay 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk each year, and the two emperors would call each other brothers. The peace held for over a century.

After a long war the Kara-Khanid prince Yusuf Qadir Khan took Khotan, the ancient Buddhist kingdom of jade and silk on the southern rim of the Tarim. Turkic verses preserved by Mahmud al-Kashgari tell of temples thrown down and images defiled. The oases of the western Tarim passed from Buddhism to Islam, which they have kept to this day.

Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting to the empress Shōshi, daughter of the all-powerful regent Fujiwara no Michinaga, was at work on a long tale of the loves of Prince Genji, which her diary mentions in 1008. Its fifty-four chapters, rich in poetry and the sadness of passing things, are often called the first novel, and they are the crown of Heian court culture.

The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, whose edicts against Christians and Jews grew wilder with the years, ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem torn down to its foundations in 1009. The rock-cut tomb of Christ was hacked away nearly to the bedrock. The church was rebuilt by agreement with Byzantium some decades later, but the outrage was long remembered in the West.

After some thirty years of labor, the poet Abu'l-Qasim Ferdowsi of Tus completed in 1010 the Book of Kings, some fifty thousand couplets of Persian verse telling the history of Iran from the creation of the world to the Arab conquest. He presented it to Mahmud of Ghazni, who paid him poorly. The Shahnameh preserved the Persian tongue and the memory of its heroes for all the centuries after.

Rajaraja I dedicated the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur in 1010, its granite tower rising sixty-six metres above the shrine, the tallest in India in its day. Its walls carry his inscriptions listing lands, gifts of gold and jewels, and the four hundred temple women assigned to its service. It stands as the noblest monument of the Chola age.

Ly Cong Uan, a palace commander raised in a Buddhist pagoda, founded the Ly dynasty in 1009 and the next year moved the court from cramped Hoa Lu to the old Chinese citadel of Dai La on the Red River. Legend says a golden dragon rose there before his boat, and he named the place Thang Long, the city that is now Hanoi.

On 29 July 1014 Basil II turned the Bulgarian stockade in the pass of Kleidion and captured the army of Tsar Samuel. He had the prisoners blinded, by the chroniclers' count fifteen thousand, leaving one man in each hundred a single eye to lead the rest home. Samuel, the story goes, died of grief at the sight, and by 1018 Bulgaria was a Byzantine province.

On Good Friday 1014 Brian Boru, High King of Ireland, met the men of Leinster and the Norse of Dublin with their allies from Orkney and Man. The Norse were driven into the sea, but Brian, past seventy, was cut down in his tent by the fleeing Viking Brodir. The victory broke Norse power in Ireland, but Brian's high kingship died with him.

After a year of hard fighting the Danish prince Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside at Assandun in October 1016, and when Edmund died weeks later the English accepted Cnut as king. Adding Denmark in 1018 and Norway in 1028, he ruled an empire of the northern seas, and governed England by English law through English and Danish earls.

Mahmud's army crossed the Ganges plain and sacked Mathura, whose temples the sultan wrote could not be built again in two hundred years, before burning them and carrying off their idols of gold. Kannauj, the old imperial city, fell almost without a blow. Al-Utbi writes that the captives were so many that they sold in Ghazni for two to ten dirhams apiece.

Xiao Paiya led a Liao army of a hundred thousand in the third Khitan invasion of Goryeo. The old commander Gang Gam-chan dammed a stream with cowhides and loosed the flood upon them, harried them on their march, and at Gwiju destroyed them; by the Korean chronicle only a few thousand escaped. The Liao made peace, and Goryeo kept its independence.

Some twenty years after Leif Eriksson, son of Erik the Red, sailed from Greenland to a land of grapes and timber he called Vinland, Norsemen at L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland felled trees with iron axes; the tree rings date their cutting to 1021. Their turf halls, found in 1960, are the only proven Norse settlement in the Americas outside Greenland, nearly five centuries before Columbus.

Rajendra I sent his armies north through Kalinga to the Ganges, where they defeated the Pala king Mahipala. Waters of the holy river were carried south in vessels to fill a great tank at his new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the city of the Chola who took the Ganges, crowned with a temple rivalling his father's at Thanjavur.
