Rajendra I, the Chola emperor of south India, sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal that fell on the ports of Srivijaya, Palembang, Malaiyur, Tamralinga, and Kadaram among them, as his inscriptions boast. King Sangrama Vijayottungavarman was taken with his treasures and the jeweled gate of his city. Srivijaya never wholly recovered its grip on the Straits.

In midwinter Mahmud of Ghazni crossed the Thar desert with thirty thousand horse to Somnath on the coast of Gujarat, the most celebrated temple of Shiva in India. Its defenders fought on the walls for two days; tens of thousands, the chroniclers say, were slain. Mahmud had the lingam broken and its pieces laid at the steps of the mosque of Ghazni to be trodden underfoot.

Al-Biruni of Khwarazm, carried to Ghazni in Mahmud's train, learned Sanskrit and wrote his Kitab al-Hind, a sober account of Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy, and custom without equal in medieval literature. He noted coolly that Mahmud's raids had utterly ruined the prosperity of the country and left the Hindus cherishing the most inveterate aversion toward all Muslims.

Olaf Haraldsson, who had forced Christianity on Norway with fire and sword, returned from exile in Russia to win back his kingdom from Cnut. On 29 July 1030 an army of farmers and chieftains met him at Stiklestad and slew him. Within a year his body was found uncorrupted, and St. Olaf became Norway's eternal king and the patron saint of the North.

The Chandela kings of Bundelkhand raised some eighty-five temples at their royal seat of Khajuraho, of which about twenty-five survive. The Kandariya Mahadeva, built under King Vidyadhara, who had stood against Mahmud, lifts its spire through a mounting cluster of lesser peaks like the Himalaya, its walls alive with gods, dancers, warriors, and lovers.

t: The Great Houses of Chaco Canyon
x: In a dry canyon of the San Juan basin, the Ancestral Pueblo people raised great houses of fitted sandstone, Pueblo Bonito alone holding some seven hundred rooms and dozens of round kivas, and drove straight roads across the desert to outlying towns. Turquoise worked at Chaco went south toward Mexico for macaws and cacao; drought in the twelfth century emptied the canyon.

After two decades of civil war, in which Berber and Slav soldiers set up and pulled down caliphs and sacked Córdoba and Madinat al-Zahra, the notables of Córdoba deposed Hisham III in 1031 and declared the caliphate at an end. Al-Andalus broke into some two dozen taifa kingdoms, rich in poets and palaces and weak in arms, which soon paid tribute to the Christian kings.

t: Li Yuanhao Proclaims the Great Xia
x: Li Yuanhao, chief of the Tangut people of the Ordos and Gansu, threw off his Song titles, ordered his subjects to shave their crowns, had a script of his own devised for the Tangut tongue, and proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Xia at Xingqing. His armies beat the Song three times in as many years, and the Western Xia endured for nearly two centuries.

Tughril and Chaghri, grandsons of the Oghuz chief Seljuk, had led their Turkmen herdsmen across the Oxus into Khorasan. Near the fort of Dandanaqan between Merv and Sarakhs, in May 1040, their horsemen wore down the heavier army of the Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud in the waterless desert and routed it. Khorasan was theirs, and the road to Persia and Baghdad lay open.

Atisha Dipankara, a Bengali prince turned monk and the chief teacher at Vikramashila, accepted the invitation of the kings of western Tibet and set out across the Himalaya, reaching their court in 1042. His teaching revived Buddhism in Tibet after a century of decline, and his disciples founded the Kadampa order, forerunner of the Gelug school of the Dalai Lamas.

The kings of Guge in western Tibet, heirs of the old royal line, had long sought a great teacher to renew the faith. In 1042 the Bengali master Atisha, a famous scholar of the monastery of Vikramashila, arrived at Tholing; his Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment and his disciple Dromtön, founder of the Kadam order, opened the second spreading of Buddhism in Tibet.

The Complete Essentials for the Military Classics, compiled for Emperor Renzong by Zeng Gongliang and Ding Du, set down the earliest known recipes for gunpowder, mixing saltpetre, sulphur, and charcoal for fire arrows, smoke balls, and bombs hurled by catapult. Over the next three centuries the invention passed to the Mongols, the Islamic world, and Europe, and it overturned the castles and armies of the earth.

t: Anawrahta Takes the Throne of Pagan
x: Anawrahta slew his kinsman Sokkate, the chronicles say in single combat, and became king of Pagan. In thirty-three years he made the little city on the Irrawaddy the head of the first empire of Burma, building irrigation works around Kyaukse, beating back his neighbors, and setting a chain of forty-three fortified towns along the eastern hills.

Across the Mississippi from the site of St. Louis, the Mississippian people of Cahokia, growing maize on the rich bottomlands, built within a few generations a town of perhaps fifteen thousand around Monks Mound, a platform of earth a hundred feet high and broader at its base than the Great Pyramid of Giza. Its lords, buried with sacrificed retainers and thousands of shell beads, ruled the largest town north of Mexico.

On 16 July 1054 Cardinal Humbert, legate of Pope Leo IX, strode into Hagia Sophia at the hour of the liturgy and laid on the altar a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The patriarch answered with anathemas of his own. Quarrels over the authority of Rome, the Filioque, and unleavened bread hardened into a rupture between the Latin and Greek Churches that has never healed.

Invited by the caliph al-Qa'im to deliver him from the Buyids, the Seljuk Tughril Beg entered Baghdad in December 1055 and was hailed as sultan; the caliph later styled him King of East and West. The last Buyid amir was sent into captivity. The Seljuks, fierce champions of the Sunna, took up the sword of the caliphate, and the age of the Turkish sultans in the heartlands of Islam began.

When the Zirid emir al-Mu'izz broke with Cairo, the Fatimids loosed upon Ifriqiya the Bedouin tribes of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym, long camped in Upper Egypt. They overran the countryside like locusts, and in 1057 Kairouan was abandoned and plundered. Ibn Khaldun wrote that wherever these Arabs conquered, ruin followed; the Maghreb took their speech for good.

Urged by the Mon monk Shin Arahan to seek the pure scriptures, Anawrahta marched on the Mon city of Thaton when its king Manuha refused to share them. After a long siege he carried Manuha, his court, his artisans, and the Pali scriptures back to Pagan. Theravada Buddhism became the faith of the Burmans, and Mon art and letters shaped their kingdom.

The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan besieged Ani, the Armenian capital lately annexed by Byzantium, and stormed it in August 1064 after twenty-five days. The chronicler Ibn al-Athir says the streets were so choked with the dead that one could not pass. The fall of the city of a thousand and one churches opened Armenia to the Turks and hastened the Armenian migration into Cilicia.

Harald Hardrada of Norway, the most famous warrior of the North and once a captain of the Varangian Guard, landed in Yorkshire with Tostig, the English king's brother. On 25 September 1066 Harold Godwinson, marching north from London in four days, fell on them at Stamford Bridge and slew both. Three days later William of Normandy landed in Sussex.

Joseph ibn Naghrela, the Jewish vizier of the Zirid king of Granada and son of the poet and general Samuel ha-Nagid, was dragged from the palace by a mob and crucified on 30 December 1066, after a preacher had stirred the Berbers against Jewish power. The rioters fell upon the Jewish quarter and killed a great part of its people, by some accounts four thousand.

Writing at Cordoba from the reports of merchants, the geographer al-Bakri described the capital of Ghana as two towns six miles apart, one of stone for the Muslim traders with twelve mosques, the other for the king, Tunka Manin, who gave audience in a domed pavilion among horses caparisoned in gold and could put 200,000 warriors in the field. His wealth rested on gold from the south and salt from the desert.

t: The New Policies of Wang Anshi
x: Emperor Shenzong raised Wang Anshi to power to save a treasury drained by armies and tribute. Wang lent seed money to farmers at state interest, replaced labour service with a tax, reorganized the village militia, and set the state up as a trader. Sima Guang and the conservatives fought him bitterly, and the feud between reformers and their enemies divided the Song court until its fall.

Vijayabahu I, a prince of Ruhuna, waged war on the Chola occupiers for years and in 1070 drove them from Lanka, while the Chola realm was torn by a disputed succession. He kept Polonnaruwa as his capital, restored the Buddhist order by bringing monks from Burma to renew the ordination, and reigned in all for more than half a century.

On 26 August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan met Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes near Manzikert, north of Lake Van. Feigned flight drew the Roman host apart, the rearguard under Andronikos Doukas deserted, and the emperor was taken prisoner, the first to fall into a Muslim ruler's hands. Alp Arslan released him on easy terms, but Turkmen bands poured into Anatolia, and Asia Minor began its long change into Turkey.

On 16 April 1071, after a siege of nearly three years by land and sea, Robert Guiscard took Bari, the capital of Byzantine Italy. Five centuries of imperial rule in the peninsula, reaching back to Justinian's reconquest, came to an end; that same summer the emperor Romanos IV was taken prisoner by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert.

Excommunicated by Gregory VII and deserted by his princes, the German king Henry IV crossed the Alps in midwinter and stood three days in the snow, barefoot and in penitent's garb, before the castle of Countess Matilda of Tuscany, where the pope had taken refuge. Gregory lifted the ban, but the image of a king humbled before a pope outlived them both.

t: Ly Thuong Kiet on the Nhu Nguyet
x: Having struck first into Song China in 1075 and razed Yongzhou, the eunuch general Ly Thuong Kiet awaited the Song counterblow behind the Nhu Nguyet River. Tradition says that at night a voice from a riverside shrine recited the poem of the Mountains and Rivers of the Southern Land, declaring that the south belongs to its own emperor; the Song army, wasted by fever, fell back and made peace.

On 25 May 1085 Alfonso VI of León and Castile entered Toledo, the ancient capital of the Visigoths, after years of pressure on its taifa king. Christian Spain now held the line of the Tagus and the heart of the peninsula, and Toledo's scholars, Christian, Muslim, and Jewish, would turn the Arabic learning of Aristotle and Ptolemy into Latin.

t: A King of Kanem Turns to Islam
x: Hummay, founder of the Sayfawa line, became the first Muslim king of Kanem, northeast of Lake Chad, according to the dynasty's own chronicle, the Diwan. His house would rule Kanem and then Bornu for more than seven and a half centuries, one of the longest-lived royal lines in the history of the world, until the last of them fell in 1846.

Frightened by Alfonso VI's capture of Toledo, the taifa kings of al-Andalus summoned Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the veiled Saharan emir of the Almoravids. On 23 October 1086, at Sagrajas, called by the Arabs al-Zallaqa, his Berber and Black African troops broke the Castilian army, and Alfonso fled wounded. Yusuf soon deposed the taifa kings themselves and made al-Andalus a province of his Moroccan empire.

At his Christmas court at Gloucester in 1085 William the Conqueror ordered a survey of his kingdom, and through 1086 his commissioners recorded the holder, value, and stock of every manor, down to the last ox and pig. Kept in the treasury at Winchester, the returns became the Domesday Book, the most complete record of any realm of medieval Europe.

Retired to his garden of Mengxi at Runzhou, the statesman and scholar Shen Kuo wrote his Dream Pool Essays. Among notes on fossils, tides, and calendars he gave the first clear account of the magnetic needle and its deviation from true south, and described how the commoner Bi Sheng had printed with movable type of baked clay some forty years before.

The Isma'ili missionary Hasan-i Sabbah won over the garrison of the eagle's nest castle of Alamut in the Elburz mountains in 1090. From it he led the Nizari Isma'ilis, called by their enemies hashishiyya, whence our word assassin, in a long war against the Seljuks waged with daggers rather than armies. Their castles held out until Hulagu's Mongols reduced them in 1256.

Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, the Cid, a Castilian lord exiled by Alfonso VI who had fought for Christian and Muslim masters alike, starved Valencia into surrender in June 1094 and held it as his own principality. He broke the Almoravids before its walls, and his widow Jimena kept the city until 1102. The Poem of the Cid made him the hero of Spain.

On 27 November 1095, in a field outside Clermont, Pope Urban II called upon the knights of France to go to the aid of the Christians of the East and free Jerusalem from the Turks, promising remission of sins to all who died on the way. The crowd answered, 'God wills it.' Within a year tens of thousands had sewn the cross upon their garments.

Bands gathering for the crusade under Count Emicho of Leiningen turned first on the Jews of the Rhine. Despite the efforts of some bishops to shield them, the communities of Worms and Mainz were slaughtered in May 1096, and many chose death by their own hands rather than forced baptism. The massacres scarred the memory of the Jews of Germany for centuries.

After a siege of eight months, Bohemond of Taranto bribed Firuz, the commander of a tower, and the crusaders poured into Antioch on 3 June 1098. Days later they were themselves besieged by Kerbogha of Mosul. Starving, heartened by the finding of the Holy Lance, they sallied out on 28 June and routed the Turkish host. The road to Jerusalem lay open.

Robert of Molesme and a band of monks seeking to keep the Rule of St. Benedict to the letter settled in the marshy forest of Cîteaux. Bernard of Clairvaux joined them in 1113 with some thirty companions, and the Cistercians, the white monks, spread to more than three hundred abbeys within his lifetime, clearing forests and draining marshes across Europe.

After the native line of Croatian kings died out and the last claimant, Petar, fell fighting the Hungarians, King Coloman of Hungary was crowned King of Croatia and Dalmatia at Biograd on the sea. Croatia was joined to the Hungarian crown in a union that, in one form or another, lasted until 1918.

Suryavarman II, who seized the throne in 1113, raised Angkor Wat to Vishnu: a temple-mountain of five lotus towers within a moat nearly two hundred meters wide, its galleries carved with the churning of the ocean of milk and the marching armies of the king. Facing west, toward the realm of the dead, it served also as his tomb, and is the largest religious monument on earth.

Wanyan Aguda, chief of the Jurchen tribes of the Manchurian forests, who had refused to dance for the Liao emperor at a fishing feast, rose against his Khitan overlords and beat a far larger Liao army at Hubudagang. He proclaimed the Jin, the Golden dynasty, and within ten years the Jurchen had taken all five Liao capitals and captured the last Liao emperor.

The Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana, who by tradition had turned from the Jain faith to the worship of Vishnu under the teacher Ramanuja, raised the Chennakeshava temple at Belur in 1117 to celebrate his victory over the Cholas. Its soapstone walls and brackets of dancing maidens carry some of the most intricate carving of the medieval Deccan.

Hugh de Payens and a handful of companions vowed to guard pilgrims on the roads of the Holy Land, and King Baldwin II housed them in the Aqsa mosque, held to be the Temple of Solomon. Endorsed by Bernard of Clairvaux and given a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129, the warrior monks grew into the richest order in Christendom and the bankers of kings.

King David IV of Georgia, who had rebuilt his army around some forty thousand Kipchak warriors settled with their families in his realm, met a great coalition of Seljuk emirs under Ilghazi at Didgori on 12 August 1121 and routed it. The next year he took Tbilisi, held by Muslim emirs for four centuries, and made it his capital. Georgia's golden age had begun.

The Song had allied with the Jurchen against the Liao, then broken faith with them. The Jin armies besieged Kaifeng twice, and in the spring of 1127 carried off the retired emperor Huizong, painter and collector, his son Emperor Qinzong, and some three thousand of the imperial clan and court to the forests of Manchuria. A surviving prince, Zhao Gou, restored the Song in the south.

t: Roger II Crowned King of Sicily
x: On Christmas Day 1130 Roger II, son of the Norman conqueror of Sicily, was crowned in Palermo king of Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia. From his palace he ruled Greeks, Arabs, Lombards, and Normans with an even hand, and his court, where the geographer al-Idrisi drew his great map of the world, was among the most brilliant of the age.

In 1136 the townsmen of Novgorod, gathered in their assembly, the veche, seized Prince Vsevolod Mstislavich, held him seven weeks, and drove him out for cowardice and neglect. Thenceforth Novgorod chose and dismissed its own princes, and Lord Novgorod the Great, mistress of the fur trade from the Baltic to the Urals, governed itself as a republic for three and a half centuries.

Ramiro II of Aragon, a monk drawn from the cloister to keep his dynasty alive, betrothed his infant daughter Petronilla to Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona at Barbastro and went back to his monastery. The union of the kingdom and the county created the Crown of Aragon, which would build a Mediterranean empire from the Balearics to Sicily and Athens.

On the Qatwan steppe north of Samarkand, the heathen Kara-Khitai, Khitan exiles from northern China under their gurkhan Yelü Dashi, destroyed the army of the Seljuk sultan Sanjar in September 1141. Transoxiana passed under infidel overlords. Garbled news of a great king of the East who had smitten the Muslims reached Europe and fed the legend of Prester John.

Yue Fei, the general whose back by legend bore the tattooed words Serve the Country with Utmost Loyalty, had driven the Jin from the middle Yangtze and beaten their cavalry at Yancheng. But Emperor Gaozong and his chancellor Qin Hui wanted peace; they recalled him with twelve gold tablets and had him put to death in prison. The Song accepted the Huai River frontier and paid the Jin a yearly tribute.

On 11 June 1144 Abbot Suger consecrated the new choir of the royal abbey of Saint-Denis before Louis VII and a crowd of bishops. Its pointed arches and ribbed vaults, and walls opened into windows of colored glass that flooded the sanctuary with light, announced the Gothic style in which the cathedrals of Europe would rise.

Imad al-Din Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, struck while Count Joscelin II was away and took Edessa, the first of the Crusader states, on Christmas Eve 1144 after a siege of four weeks. The Franks of the town were slain, though the native Christians were for the most part spared. The news shocked Christendom and called forth the Second Crusade.

Ibn Tumart, a Masmuda Berber scholar who preached the absolute unity of God and proclaimed himself the Mahdi in the High Atlas, had died about 1130, leaving his disciple Abd al-Mu'min to lead the Almohads. In 1147 Abd al-Mu'min stormed Marrakesh, slaughtered the last of the Almoravid house, and made the city his capital. By 1160 he ruled from the Atlantic to Tripoli.

English, Flemish, and German crusaders sailing for the Holy Land put in at Porto and were persuaded to help Afonso Henriques, first king of Portugal, besiege Lisbon. After seventeen weeks the city surrendered on 24 October 1147. It was the one lasting gain of the Second Crusade, and Lisbon would become the capital of the young kingdom.

In 1147 Yuri Dolgoruky, Prince of Suzdal, sent to his ally Sviatoslav of Novgorod-Seversky: 'Come to me, brother, to Moscow.' So the chronicle first names a small estate on the Moskva river, where Yuri gave his guest a mighty feast. Nine years later he ringed it with wooden walls; its rise to empire lay centuries ahead.

Famine and Bedouin raids had brought the Zirid emirs low, and in June 1148 the fleet of King Roger II of Sicily under the admiral George of Antioch sailed into Mahdia, whose prince al-Hasan fled. With Tripoli, Sfax, and Gabès it formed the Norman Kingdom of Africa, which the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min swept away in 1160.

The Kashmiri poet Kalhana, son of a royal minister, completed the Rajatarangini, the River of Kings, about 1149: nearly eight thousand Sanskrit verses tracing the kings of Kashmir from legend to his own troubled day. Weighing inscriptions, land grants, and older chronicles with a critical eye, he wrote the nearest thing to history in the Western sense that old India produced.

Ala al-Din Husayn of Ghur, avenging the execution of his brothers by the Ghaznavid sultan Bahram Shah, stormed Ghazni and gave it to the flames for seven days. The palaces and tombs of the Ghaznavid sultans, all but a few, were destroyed, and he earned the name Jahan-suz, the World-Burner. The house of Mahmud never recovered its old seat.

Parakramabahu I made himself master of all Lanka and from Polonnaruwa ruled for thirty-three years, building the Parakrama Samudra, a reservoir so vast the chronicle calls it a sea, and decreeing that not one drop of rain should flow to the ocean without first serving man. He reformed the Buddhist order and sent his fleets against Burma and the Pandyas.

t: Henry II and the Angevin Empire
x: On 19 December 1154 Henry of Anjou was crowned at Westminster, ending the long anarchy of Stephen's reign. Through his father he held Anjou and Normandy, and through his wife Eleanor, lately divorced from Louis VII, the vast duchy of Aquitaine. He ruled from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, a greater domain in France than the French king's own.

Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, rebuilt the burned town of Lübeck on the Trave and invited the merchants of Gotland, Russia, and Scandinavia to trade there in peace. Lübeck became the queen of the Hanseatic League, whose merchant towns would rule the commerce of the Baltic and the North Sea for three centuries.

Basava, minister to the Kalachuri usurper Bijjala at Kalyani, preached devotion to Shiva alone in Kannada verse and rejected caste, temple ritual, and the authority of the Brahmins. His followers, the Lingayats or Virashaivas, wore the lingam on their bodies and gathered in a hall of experience open to all. They remain a great community of Karnataka.

Thomas Becket, Henry II's chancellor turned champion of the Church's liberties as Archbishop of Canterbury, was cut down in his own cathedral on 29 December 1170 by four knights who had heard the king's angry words. Canonized within three years, Becket drew pilgrims to Canterbury for three and a half centuries, and Henry did penance at his tomb.

Cambro-Norman knights called in by Diarmait Mac Murchada, the exiled king of Leinster, had taken Wexford, Waterford, and Dublin, and their leader Strongbow had married Diarmait's daughter. Lest they found a rival kingdom, Henry II landed at Waterford in October 1171 with a great army and received the submission of most of the Irish kings: the beginning of English lordship in Ireland.

Saladin, the Kurdish nephew of Shirkuh, had become vizier to the last Fatimid caliph, al-Adid, in 1169 as officer of the Sunni Nur al-Din. In September 1171 he had the Friday prayer said in Cairo for the Abbasid caliph of Baghdad; days later al-Adid died. Two centuries of Shi'ite rule over Egypt ended without a blow, and Saladin became master of the Nile.

Saladin sent his elder brother Turanshah with an army to Yemen in 1174, and Zabid, Aden, and Ta'izz were soon taken from the petty dynasties of the south. Yemen, with its port of Aden on the Indian trade, was held by Ayyubid princes until 1229, when their deputy Nur al-Din Umar ibn Rasul made himself independent and founded the Rasulid dynasty.

On 29 May 1176 the foot soldiers of Milan and the Lombard cities, rallied round their carroccio, the great ox-drawn standard wagon, withstood the charge of Frederick Barbarossa's knights until their own horsemen returned to rout the Germans. The emperor was unhorsed and thought dead. He made peace with Pope Alexander III at Venice, and the cities kept their liberties.

Jaya Indravarman IV, king of Champa, sent a war fleet up the Mekong and across the Great Lake to Yasodharapura. The Khmer usurper Tribhuvanadityavarman was slain and the city plundered. The shame was avenged by a Khmer prince, Jayavarman, who drove the Cham out in a battle on the lake that the reliefs of the Bayon still show in grim detail.

t: The Stone City of Nan Madol
x: Off the reef of Pohnpei in the Carolines the Saudeleur kings were building Nan Madol, nearly a hundred artificial islets walled with prismatic basalt columns stacked crosswise like the logs of a cabin, where the lords dwelt and their dead were entombed. The Saudeleur dynasty ruled all Pohnpei until the hero Isokelekel overthrew it in the early seventeenth century.

Crowned after his war against the Cham, Jayavarman VII made Mahayana Buddhism the faith of the court and built as no Khmer king before him. He walled Angkor Thom with a moat and five gates crowned by great faces, set the Bayon with its fifty-odd face towers at its heart, and lined the royal roads with 121 rest houses and 102 hospitals.

In the strait of Shimonoseki the Minamoto fleet under Minamoto no Yoshitsune met the last ships of the Taira. When the tide turned against them the Taira were destroyed, and the grandmother of the boy Emperor Antoku took him in her arms and leapt into the sea with the sacred sword. The Genpei War was over, and the warriors ruled Japan.

Refused a fief by Isaac II Angelos, the brothers Peter and Asen, Vlach and Bulgarian lords of the Balkan range, raised their people in revolt at the new church of St. Demetrius in Tarnovo. Within a few years they had restored a Bulgarian empire, which under their younger brother Kaloyan would capture a Latin emperor.

Saladin drew the whole army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, some twenty thousand men under King Guy of Lusignan, away from the springs of Sepphoris into the waterless hills above Tiberias. On 4 July 1187, parched and choked by the smoke of brush fires, they were cut down on the Horns of Hattin. The True Cross was taken, Guy captured, and Reynald of Châtillon slain by Saladin's own hand.

Balian of Ibelin held Jerusalem against Saladin until, threatening to destroy the Dome of the Rock and every Muslim within, he won terms. The city surrendered on 2 October 1187. Its Latin inhabitants might ransom themselves for ten dinars a man, five a woman, and one a child; some fifteen thousand who could not pay were led away into slavery. The great cross atop the Dome was torn down.

The young Alfonso IX, newly king of León, summoned to the cloister of San Isidoro not only bishops and nobles but chosen citizens of the towns, and swore to make no war or peace without their counsel. It is held to be the first assembly in Europe in which townsmen sat beside the clergy and nobility to advise their king.

The siege of Acre had dragged on for two years when Philip Augustus and Richard I of England arrived. The city surrendered on 12 July 1191; when Saladin delayed the terms, Richard had some 2,700 Muslim prisoners put to death. He marched down the coast, routed Saladin at Arsuf, and twice came within a day's march of Jerusalem, but never took it.

Prithviraj Chauhan of Ajmer, the hero of Rajput ballad, met Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghur at Tarain, north of Delhi, and routed his army; the sultan himself was wounded by a lance and barely carried from the field by a Khalji soldier. Prithviraj let the beaten Turks retire and spent the year besieging their garrison at Bathinda.

A year later Mu'izz al-Din returned with some 120,000 horsemen. Feigning retreat through the day and wheeling his mounted archers in relays against the Rajput host, he broke it at dusk with a charge of twelve thousand picked horsemen. Prithviraj was taken in flight and put to death. The road to Delhi lay open, and Muslim rule over northern India began.

Minamoto no Yoritomo, victor of the Genpei War, received from the court the title of sei-i taishōgun, barbarian-subduing generalissimo. From his headquarters at Kamakura, far from the imperial court at Kyoto, he ruled through stewards and constables planted across the provinces, and for nearly seven centuries shoguns, not emperors, governed Japan.

Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Turkish adventurer, rode into Bihar and stormed the walled monastery of Odantapuri, which he took for a fortress. Minhaj records that its inmates, shaven-headed men he took for Brahmins, were all slain, and that none was left alive who could read its books. Nalanda and Vikramashila were laid waste in the same years, and Buddhism all but vanished from the land of its birth.

Gebre Meskel Lalibela, king of the Zagwe dynasty, had eleven churches hewn downward into the living red rock of Roha, among them the cross-shaped Bete Giyorgis. Ethiopian tradition holds that he meant to raise a New Jerusalem in the highlands after Saladin's capture of the Holy City in 1187 made the pilgrimage perilous; the town has borne his name ever since.

The Tui Tonga Tuitatui raised on Tongatapu the Haamonga a Maui, a gate of three coral limestone blocks each weighing some thirty to forty tons. The sacred kings of Tonga, who traced their descent from the sky god Tangaloa, built a maritime power whose great canoes carried tribute and brides between Tonga, Samoa, Uvea, and Fiji.

Polynesian voyagers, remembered in tradition as the company of the chief Hotu Matua, landed at Anakena on the most isolated inhabited island on earth. Their descendants carved nearly a thousand moai from the volcanic tuff of Rano Raraku and moved them, standing, to stone platforms along the shore, and they left tablets of rongorongo glyphs that no one now can read.

Albert of Buxhoeveden, Bishop of Livonia, moved his see to a new town at the mouth of the Daugava and the next year founded the Sword Brothers, a crusading order to subdue the heathen Livs and Letts. German merchants, knights, and priests made Riga the capital of a crusader land on the Baltic that would last until the sixteenth century.

Diverted to Constantinople to restore a pretender, the Fourth Crusade quarreled with the Greeks and on 12 April 1204 stormed the city from the Golden Horn. For three days knights and Venetians pillaged the treasures of nine centuries, stripping churches and melting statues. A Latin empire was set up, and the Roman East was broken into fragments that never wholly reunited.

Riding ahead of his army with only eighteen horsemen, so Minhaj tells, Bakhtiyar Khalji passed the gates of Nadia, taken by the guards for horse dealers, and burst upon the palace of the aged Sena king Lakshmana Sena as he sat at his meal. The king fled barefoot by a back door to eastern Bengal, and the Turks made Lakhnauti their capital.

On 14 April 1205 the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan, with his Cuman horsemen, lured the knights of the new Latin Empire into a reckless pursuit before Adrianople and cut them to pieces. Emperor Baldwin I was taken and died a captive in Tarnovo; Count Louis of Blois fell on the field. The Latin conquest of the Greek lands was checked within a year of its birth.

When Mu'izz al-Din was murdered on the Jhelum in 1206, his Turkish slave-general Qutb al-Din Aibak took power over the Indian conquests at Lahore. Thus began the Delhi Sultanate, ruled at first by former slaves. Aibak had begun the Quwwat ul-Islam mosque at Delhi from the pillars of demolished temples and the Qutb Minar beside it, but died in 1210 when his horse fell on him at polo.

After the murder of his legate, Pope Innocent III proclaimed a crusade against the Cathar heretics of Languedoc. On 22 July 1209 the crusading army burst into Béziers and massacred its people, Catholics and Cathars alike, in the church of La Madeleine and in the streets. Twenty years of war delivered the south to the northern barons and the French crown.

Under a crusade bull of Innocent III, Alfonso VIII of Castile, Peter II of Aragon, and Sancho VII of Navarre crossed the Sierra Morena by a shepherd's path and on 16 July 1212 fell on the great army of the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir. Sancho's men broke through the chained guard about the caliph's tent. Almohad power in Spain never recovered.

On 27 July 1214 Philip Augustus met the coalition of the emperor Otto IV, the Count of Flanders, and the English, paid for by King John. The French knights and the militias of the towns broke them; Otto fled, and Count Ferrand was led captive to Paris. The victory secured Philip's conquests, ruined Otto, and sent John home to face his barons.

In the meadow at Runnymede beside the Thames, King John, beaten in France and confronted by rebel barons who held London, set his seal to the Great Charter in June 1215. Annulled within weeks by the pope, it was reissued under his son, and its promise that no free man be imprisoned or dispossessed save by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land became a cornerstone of English liberty.

Genghis Khan had broken the Jin field armies at Badger's Mouth in 1211 and besieged their capital. When Emperor Xuanzong fled south to Kaifeng, the Mongols stormed Zhongdu, sacked it, and left it burning for a month. Among those who passed into Mongol service was the Khitan scholar Yelü Chucai, whose counsel later persuaded the khans to tax the farmers of China rather than slaughter them.

Stefan Nemanjić, grand prince of Serbia, received a royal crown from Pope Honorius III in 1217, and two years later his brother Sava, a monk of Mount Athos, won from the patriarch at Nicaea an independent Serbian Church, with himself as archbishop at Žiča. Serbia now stood as a kingdom with its own church, poised between Rome and Constantinople.

A caravan of some four hundred and fifty Muslim merchants sent by Genghis Khan reached Otrar on the Syr Darya in 1218. The governor Inalchuq, kinsman of the Khwarazm-shah Muhammad II, accused them of spying and put them to death, and the shah then slew one of the khan's envoys sent to demand justice. Genghis turned the whole might of the Mongols against Khwarazm.

Valdemar II of Denmark landed in northern Estonia on crusade and began a castle at Lyndanisse. On 15 June 1219 the Estonians surprised his camp, and, the legend goes, a red banner with a white cross fell from heaven to rally the Danes to victory: the Dannebrog. The town that grew beneath the castle was Tallinn, the Danish town.

Where the Limpopo meets the Shashe, a cattle-keeping people grown rich on ivory and gold traded to the coast set their ruler apart on a sandstone hill above his subjects, the first kingdom of southern Africa. In the royal graves lay a little rhinoceros of gold foil over a wooden core. By about 1290 the hill was abandoned, and power passed north to Great Zimbabwe.

Tolui, youngest son of Genghis Khan, took Merv by false promises in February 1221 and had its people driven onto the plain and divided among his soldiers for slaughter, the artisans alone excepted. The chroniclers counted the dead at seven hundred thousand or more, a number beyond belief, yet the queen of Khorasan's cities was left a desolation. Nishapur suffered the like in April.

A Mongol force under Jebe and Subutai, pursuing the Cumans onto the Pontic steppe, met the princes of Rus' and the Cuman khan Köten. On 31 May 1223 by the river Kalka the allies, divided and quarreling, were destroyed piecemeal. The captured princes were crushed beneath the boards on which the victors feasted. Rus' would hear from the Mongols again.

t: The End of the Western Xia
x: Genghis Khan returned from the west to punish the Tangut, who had refused him troops. He died in the summer of 1227 during the campaign, by some accounts after a fall from his horse; his death was kept secret, and when the Tangut capital at Xingqing surrendered soon after, its people were put to the sword. The khan was carried home to a hidden grave.

Sukaphaa, a Tai prince from the hills of upper Burma, crossed the Patkai range with some nine thousand followers in 1228 and settled in the Brahmaputra valley, founding the Ahom kingdom. His heirs ruled Assam for six centuries, gave the land its name, and kept court chronicles called buranjis, the finest historical writing of medieval northeast India.

With Mongol armies overrunning the peninsula, the military dictator Choe U carried the Goryeo court to Ganghwa Island, guarded from the horsemen by a narrow strait of racing tides. For nearly forty years the court ruled from the island while the Mongols wasted the mainland in campaign after campaign, until the kings made peace and returned to Kaesong in 1270.

Driven from Kaifeng, the last Jin emperor Aizong held out at Caizhou against the Mongols and their new Song allies. As the walls fell he passed the throne to his kinsman Wanyan Chenglin and hanged himself; Chenglin was killed in the street fighting the same day. The Song, who shared the spoils, now faced the Mongols alone.

Sundiata Keita, the lame prince of the Malinke whose story the griots still sing, gathered the clans of the upper Niger against Sumanguru Kante, the smith-king of Sosso, who had overrun the remnants of Ghana. At Kirina Sumanguru was broken, and Sundiata, hailed as mansa, founded the empire of Mali, whose laws, the griots say, were proclaimed at Kurukan Fuga.

Iltutmish named his daughter Razia his heir over his sons, and in 1236 the people of Delhi raised her to the throne. She put off the veil, rode an elephant before her troops, and held court in a man's coat and cap. The Turkish nobles would not bear her favour to the Abyssinian Yaqut; they rose against her, and in 1240 she was killed in flight.

On 29 June 1236, feast of St. Peter and St. Paul, Ferdinand III of Castile entered Córdoba, once the capital of the caliphs and the greatest city of Western Europe. The cross was raised over the Great Mosque, consecrated as a cathedral, and the bells Almanzor had carried off from Santiago were sent back on the shoulders of Muslim captives.

Two Tai chiefs, Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao and Pho Khun Pha Mueang, expelled the Khmer governor of Sukhothai, and Bang Klang Hao reigned there as Si Inthrathit. Thai tradition honors his kingdom as the first Thai state, where Theravada Buddhism, free trade, and a fatherly kingship joined to form the model of later Siam.

Batu's Mongols, having burned Ryazan and Vladimir, stormed Kiev, the mother of Russian cities, on 6 December 1240 after battering down its walls. The last defenders died around the Church of the Tithes, which collapsed beneath the crowd sheltering on its vaults. Six years later the papal envoy John of Plano Carpini found scarcely two hundred houses standing.

t: Batu Crushes the Hungarians at Mohi
x: Two days after another Mongol army destroyed the Silesian and Polish knights at Liegnitz, Batu and Subutai forced the bridge over the Sajó and surrounded the camp of Béla IV on the plain of Mohi on 11 April 1241, leaving a gap through which the fleeing Hungarians were cut down by the thousand. Hungary was ravaged for a year, until news of the Great Khan's death drew the Mongols back east.

On 5 April 1242 Prince Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod met the knights of the Livonian Order and the bishop of Dorpat's men on the frozen lake between Pskov and Estonia. Their wedge of horsemen broke against the Novgorod foot and was driven back across the ice. The Order's drive into Russian lands was ended, and the border of Latin and Orthodox Christendom was fixed for centuries.

The Mongol general Baiju, pressing west from Persia, met the army of the Seljuk sultan of Rum, Kaykhusraw II, at Köse Dağ east of Sivas on 26 June 1243. The Seljuk host, swollen with Georgian, Greek, and Latin mercenaries, broke at the first onset. Rum became a Mongol tributary, and in its decay the Turkish frontier beyliks, the Ottomans among them, would rise.

Summoned by Köten, grandson of Genghis Khan, the abbot Sakya Pandita made the long journey to Liangzhou, where he agreed to the submission of Tibet, cured the prince of an illness, and was made his agent over Central Tibet. His nephew Phagpa became the teacher of Kublai, and the bond of lama and patron between Tibet and the Mongol khans began.

After a siege of fifteen months, in which the Castilian fleet under Ramón Bonifaz broke the bridge of boats that fed the city, Seville surrendered to Ferdinand III on 23 November 1248. Its Muslim people departed for Granada and Africa. Of al-Andalus there remained only the emirate of Granada, a vassal of Castile, which would hold out for nearly two and a half centuries.

King Louis IX of France took Damietta in 1249, but in February 1250 his brother Robert of Artois charged into the streets of Mansura and was slain by the Bahri Mamluks, the slave guards of the late sultan al-Salih Ayyub. Louis was captured in the retreat and ransomed. In May the Mamluks murdered the new sultan Turanshah, and Egypt passed into the hands of its slave soldiers.

Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, who had carried the war against the Muslims of Bengal into their own land, built at Konark on the Orissa coast a temple to the Sun in the form of the god's chariot, drawn by seven stone horses on twenty-four carved wheels. Its great tower, a landmark for sailors who called it the Black Pagoda, fell in later centuries.

Praying for deliverance from the Mongols, the Goryeo court had the whole Buddhist canon carved anew on more than eighty thousand wooden blocks, the earlier set having burned in the invasions. Finished in 1251, it is the most complete and accurate canon in Chinese characters, and the blocks stand in their halls at Haeinsa to this day.

Sent by his brother Möngke to outflank the Song, Kublai led his army through the mountains of western Sichuan, crossed the Jinsha River on rafts of inflated hides, and came down on the kingdom of Dali. The capital surrendered, Kublai forbade a massacre, and King Duan Xingzhi was kept as a vassal. Yunnan passed under the rule of China for good.

Hulagu, brother of the Great Khan Möngke, having reduced the Assassin castles, summoned the caliph al-Musta'sim to submit. When he temporized, the Mongols stormed Baghdad in February 1258 and sacked it for a week; the dead were reckoned in the hundreds of thousands. The last Abbasid caliph of Baghdad was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses, and the Tigris, it was said, ran black with the ink of its libraries.

The Great Khan Möngke led the Mongol armies into Sichuan in person and laid siege to the mountain fortress of Diaoyu, above the meeting of three rivers at Hechuan. Its Song garrison held out for months, and the khan died in his camp, of sickness or, by Chinese accounts, of a wound. The Mongol armies in Syria and China turned back for the succession, and the Song gained twenty years.

When the death of the Great Khan drew Hulagu east with most of his army, the Mamluk sultan Qutuz marched out of Egypt against the force left in Syria under Kitbuqa. On 3 September 1260, at the Spring of Goliath in the valley of Jezreel, the Mamluks drew the Mongols into an ambush and destroyed them; Kitbuqa was slain. The westward tide of the Mongol conquest was turned for good.

On 25 July 1261 the Nicaean general Alexios Strategopoulos, passing near the city with a small force while the Venetian fleet was away, slipped into Constantinople by an unguarded gate. The Latin emperor Baldwin II fled, and on 15 August Michael VIII Palaiologos entered the city on foot behind the icon of the Virgin. His dynasty ruled until the end.

On 18 May 1268 the Mamluk sultan Baybars stormed Antioch, held by the Franks for 170 years. The gates were shut that none might escape; the men were put to the sword and the women and children sold, so many that the price of a captive fell to a few dirhams. Baybars wrote to the absent prince Bohemond VI to describe the slaughter. The great city never recovered.

Conradin, sixteen-year-old grandson of Frederick II and last of the Hohenstaufen, crossed the Alps to win back his inheritance from Charles of Anjou. Beaten at Tagliacozzo and betrayed in flight, he was beheaded in the market square of Naples on 29 October 1268. The great house of the Staufer emperors ended on the block.

The Banu Marin, Zenata nomads who had come up from the desert fringes as the Almohads weakened after Las Navas, took Fez in 1248. In September 1269 Abu Yusuf Ya'qub entered Marrakesh, and the last Almohad caliph was slain in flight. The Marinids ruled Morocco from Fez, raised there a new royal city and splendid madrasas, and crossed often into Spain to aid Granada.

Louis IX of France, hoping, it was said, to convert the Hafsid sultan al-Mustansir, turned his second crusade against Tunis and landed at the ruins of Carthage in July 1270. Dysentery swept the camp in the African heat; the king died on 25 August, murmuring the name of Jerusalem. His brother Charles of Anjou made terms with the sultan and sailed home.

Yekuno Amlak, an Amhara noble who traced his descent to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through Menelik I, overthrew the last Zagwe king with the support of the monks of Lake Hayq and Shewa, and took the throne of Ethiopia. His Solomonic dynasty, whose title the Kebra Nagast, set down soon after, would enshrine, reigned with few interruptions until 1974.

Kublai, who had won a four-year succession war against his brother Ariq Böke, named his dynasty Yuan, the Origin, from the Book of Changes, and was raising a new capital, Dadu, the Khanbaliq of the Turks and of Marco Polo, beside the ruins of Zhongdu. He ruled China as emperor and the Mongols as Great Khan, though the western khanates went their own way.

Jalal al-Din Rumi, born in Balkh and brought west as a boy ahead of the Mongols, died at Konya, capital of the Seljuks of Rum, on 17 December 1273. His Masnavi, some twenty-five thousand couplets of Persian verse, was called the Quran in Persian. His disciples formed the Mevlevi order, whose whirling dervishes keep his tomb under its green dome.

For five years the twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng on the Han River held out against the Mongols, fed by Song boats that ran the blockade. In the end Kublai sent for two Muslim engineers from the Ilkhanate, whose counterweight trebuchets hurled stones that shook the walls, and the commander Lü Wenhuan surrendered. The road down the Han to the Yangtze lay open.

The Venetian merchants Niccolò and Maffeo Polo returned to Kublai's court with Niccolò's son Marco, who by his own account reached the summer capital at Shangdu in 1275 and served the khan for seventeen years. His book told of paper money, black stones that burned like logs, and cities greater than any in Europe, and set the West dreaming of Cathay.

Kertanegara of Singhasari, a Tantric Buddhist king of vast ambition, sent an army to Malayu on the Batang Hari to bring Sumatra under Java. In 1286 he sent a statue of Amoghapasa to Dharmasraya as a gift to its ruler Tribhuwanaraja, and in 1289 he defied Kublai Khan by marking the face of the Mongol envoy Meng Qi.

t: Rudolf of Habsburg on the Marchfeld
x: Ottokar II of Bohemia, the iron and golden king whose lands stretched from the Bohemian forests to the Adriatic, refused to yield Austria to the new German king, Rudolf of Habsburg. On 26 August 1278 at Dürnkrut on the Marchfeld, Rudolf's reserve, held back against the customs of chivalry, struck the Bohemian flank, and Ottokar was slain. Austria was the Habsburgs' for 640 years.

The last Song loyalists made their stand with a great fleet in the bay of Yamen near Canton. When the Yuan admiral Zhang Hongfan broke their lines, the minister Lu Xiufu took the boy emperor Zhao Bing on his back and leapt into the sea. The Song dynasty perished, and all China passed for the first time under a conquering people of the steppe.

Voyaging canoes from eastern Polynesia, remembered in Maori tradition by names such as Aotea, Tainui, and Te Arawa, reached the last great land on earth to be settled by man. At Wairau Bar the first settlers buried their dead with drilled moa eggs and necklaces of moa-bone reels; within two centuries the giant moa were hunted to extinction, and the newcomers had become the Maori.

Seven years after a first landing at Hakata had been driven off, Kublai sent two fleets, said to carry 140,000 men, against Japan. The samurai held the stone wall built along Hakata Bay, and in the summer a typhoon wrecked the Yuan ships gathered off Takashima. The Japanese called it the kamikaze, the divine wind, and the invasion was never tried again.

At the hour of vespers on Easter Monday 1282, outside the church of the Holy Spirit at Palermo, a French soldier insulted a Sicilian wife, and the crowd killed him. The rising spread through the island, and some thousands of Frenchmen were massacred. The Sicilians offered their crown to Peter III of Aragon, and Charles of Anjou lost the island forever.

King Narathihapate, who had refused tribute to Kublai Khan, fled south before the Mongols, earning the name Tayokpyemin, the king who ran from the Chinese, and was poisoned by his son at Prome. A Yuan army pressed down the Irrawaddy, and the empire of Anawrahta broke apart among Mon kings at Martaban, Shan lords in the hills, and three brothers in the Kyaukse valley.

t: Tran Hung Dao at the Bach Dang
x: In the third Mongol invasion the Tran prince Tran Hung Dao repeated the stratagem of Ngo Quyen: he drove stakes into the Bach Dang, drew the Yuan fleet in on the high tide, and fell on it as the ebb impaled the ships. Four hundred vessels were taken with the admiral Omar, and Kublai's son Toghon fled north in disgrace.

At the beginning of August 1291, soon after the death of Rudolf of Habsburg, the men of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden swore a perpetual league to aid one another against all who would do them violence. Tradition placed the oath on the Rütli meadow above the Lake of Lucerne. From that league grew the Swiss Confederation.

Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil brought scores of siege engines against Acre, the last capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and stormed it on 18 May 1291 after six weeks. The Templars held their fortress ten days more, until it collapsed on attackers and defenders alike. Tyre, Sidon, Beirut, and Haifa were abandoned within weeks, and two centuries of Frankish rule on the Syrian coast came to an end.

t: Marco Polo in the Land of Maabar
x: Returning from China by sea, Marco Polo landed on the coast the Arabs called Maabar, the realm of the Pandya kings. He described the pearl fishery in the gulf, the king who wore a necklace of 104 pearls and rubies to count his prayers, the warhorses brought yearly from Arabia that died for want of care, and the tomb of the Apostle Thomas at Mylapore.

Kublai Khan sent a fleet to punish Kertanegara, but found him dead, slain by the rebel Jayakatwang of Kediri. Kertanegara's son-in-law Raden Wijaya joined the Mongols to destroy Jayakatwang, then turned on his allies and drove them to their ships. At the village of Majapahit, named for a bitter fruit, he founded the greatest of the Javanese empires.

Ghazan, great-grandson of Hulagu, professed Islam in June 1295 to win the support of the emir Nawruz and the Muslim Mongols, and that autumn he seized the throne of the Ilkhanate. At his accession Nawruz had the churches, synagogues, and Buddhist temples of Tabriz pulled down. With his vizier Rashid al-Din, Ghazan reformed the taxes, and the Mongols of Persia became Muslims in faith.

Mangrai, Tai king of Ngoen Yang, having taken the old Mon city of Haripunjaya by stratagem, laid out a new capital on the Ping River, consulting, the chronicle says, with his allies Ram Khamhaeng of Sukhothai and Ngam Mueang of Phayao. Chiang Mai, the New City, became the seat of Lan Na, the kingdom of a million rice fields.

Alauddin Khalji, governor of Kara, crossed the Vindhyas without his uncle the sultan's leave and fell upon Devagiri, capital of the Yadavas, with a few thousand horse. King Ramachandra bought peace with a huge ransom of gold, pearls, and elephants. With this treasure Alauddin returned north, had his uncle Jalal al-Din murdered on the Ganges, and took the throne of Delhi.

t: The Tomb of Sultan Malik al-Saleh
x: At Samudra on the north coast of Sumatra died Malik al-Saleh, first Muslim ruler of Pasai, whose gravestone of 1297 is the oldest dated record of a Muslim kingdom in Southeast Asia. Marco Polo, passing in 1292, had found the people of nearby Perlak converted by Saracen merchants; from these ports of pepper and gold Islam would spread along the trade routes of the archipelago.

On a granite hill near the Mutirikwi River, the Shona kings of the Zimbabwe plateau raised enclosures of fitted stone without mortar; the outer wall of the Great Enclosure runs some 250 metres and rises to eleven. From here they taxed the gold of the plateau and traded it through Sofala and Kilwa for Persian bowls and Chinese porcelain, ruling a town of perhaps ten thousand or more.

In Ife, holy city of the Yoruba, where Oduduwa was said to have let down the first earth upon the waters, court artists cast heads of copper and brass of a serene and lifelike beauty, probably portraits of the onis and their court. The first of them, unearthed in 1910, astonished Europe; Ife remained the sacred source from which the Yoruba kings drew their crowns.

t: Osman Defeats the Byzantines at Bapheus
x: Osman, son of Ertuğrul, a Turkmen chief whose frontier lands lay on the Sakarya facing Byzantium, met and routed a Byzantine force under the general Mouzalon at Bapheus near Nicomedia in July 1302. The victory brought warriors flocking to his banner from all Anatolia. From his name came that of the Ottomans, who would rule for six centuries.

t: The Battle of the Golden Spurs
x: On 11 July 1302 the weavers and burghers of Flanders, armed with pikes and the spiked club they called goedendag, stood behind ditches at Courtrai and slaughtered the charging chivalry of Philip IV. Hundreds of gilded spurs taken from the dead knights were hung in the church of Our Lady. Townsmen on foot had beaten the knighthood of France.

When the Black Guelfs seized Florence with the backing of Pope Boniface VIII, the poet Dante Alighieri, a White Guelf and former prior, was condemned in his absence and then sentenced to be burned should he return. He never saw his city again; in exile he wrote the Divine Comedy, which made the Tuscan tongue the speech of Italy.

After a siege of some eight months Alauddin Khalji took the great Rajput fortress of Chittor from Ratnasimha of Mewar. His court poet Amir Khusrau, who was present, wrote that thirty thousand Hindus were put to the sword in a single day. The tale that the sultan coveted Ratnasimha's queen Padmini comes from a Sufi poem written by Malik Muhammad Jayasi in 1540.

At dawn on Friday 13 October 1307 the officers of Philip IV seized every Templar in France on charges of heresy and blasphemy, and torture produced confessions. Pope Clement V suppressed the order at the Council of Vienne in 1312, and in March 1314 the Grand Master Jacques de Molay, retracting his confession, was burned on an island in the Seine.

Clement V, a Gascon pope elected under the shadow of the French king, settled in 1309 at Avignon on the Rhône, beside the papal Comtat Venaissin. For nearly seventy years his successors ruled the Church from its great palace there, an age Petrarch called the Babylonian Captivity, until Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377.

Malik Kafur, a slave bought for a thousand dinars and raised to command Alauddin's armies, swept through the south: he humbled the Kakatiyas of Warangal, sacked the Hoysala capital of Dwarasamudra, and pressed on into the Pandya country during a war between royal brothers, plundering Madurai and the temples of the Kaveri. He returned to Delhi with elephants and treasure beyond any earlier hoard.

t: Özbeg Khan Brings Islam to the Horde
x: Özbeg, khan of the Golden Horde from 1313, embraced Islam and made it the faith of the house of Jochi. In his reign of nearly thirty years Sarai on the lower Volga was one of the great cities of the world, the clearing house of the trade between the Black Sea, Persia, and the Russian forests, and the princes of Rus came to it to buy their patents of rule.

On 23 and 24 June 1314 Robert the Bruce met the far larger army of Edward II marching to relieve Stirling Castle. Bruce slew Henry de Bohun with his axe in single combat before the hosts, and on the second day the Scottish spearmen drove the English knights into the Bannock burn. Scotland's freedom was won in fact, and in 1328 by treaty.

t: The Throne Hall of Dongola Becomes a Mosque
x: After decades of Mamluk invasions and puppet kings, Sayf al-Din Abdallah Barshambu, a Muslim prince of the Nubian royal house installed by the sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, turned the two-storied throne hall of the Christian kings of Makuria into a mosque; a stone dated 1317 records the change. Christian Makuria lingered a few decades more before it dissolved.

On his pilgrimage to Mecca, Mansa Musa of Mali reached Cairo with a train of thousands and spent and gave away gold so freely that its value in the city was depressed for years, as al-Umari recorded a dozen years later. Returning, he built mosques at Gao and Timbuktu; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him enthroned, holding a nugget of gold.

The Mexica, latecomers to the Valley of Mexico who had served its lords as mercenaries, settled on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco where, their priests said, they saw the sign promised by their god Huitzilopochtli: an eagle perched upon a cactus growing from a rock. There they built Tenochtitlan, which within two centuries was a city of perhaps two hundred thousand.

Prusa, at the foot of Mount Olympus in Bithynia, had been blockaded by Ottoman forts for years when it surrendered in April 1326 to Orhan, son of Osman, who died about that time. As Bursa it became the first Ottoman capital, where Osman and Orhan were buried. Nicaea fell in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337, and the Byzantine hold on Bithynia was ended.

t: Muhammad bin Tughlaq Moves to Daulatabad
x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq, a sultan of vast learning and wild schemes, ordered the people of Delhi to remove to Devagiri, which he renamed Daulatabad, some seven hundred miles to the south, to rule the Deccan from its centre. Many died on the road. Within a few years he let them return, and Ibn Battuta found Delhi, the greatest city of the Muslim east, half empty.

The Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta sailed down the Swahili coast and judged Kilwa one of the most beautiful and best-built towns in the world. Its sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman, called Abu al-Mawahib, 'father of gifts,' for his generosity, grew rich on Zimbabwe gold shipped from Sofala, struck his own coins, and raised the palace of Husuni Kubwa on the cliff above the sea.

The warrior emperor Amda Seyon answered the revolt of Sabr ad-Din, sultan of Ifat, who had vowed to make himself king of all Ethiopia and turn its churches into mosques, with a campaign recorded in one of the first royal chronicles. He broke the Muslim coalition in battle after battle and made the sultanates of the east pay tribute to the Christian crown.

Emperor Go-Daigo escaped from exile in the Oki islands and called the warriors to rise against the Hōjō regents. Ashikaga Takauji, sent against him, changed sides and took Kyoto, while Nitta Yoshisada stormed Kamakura from the beaches; the regent Hōjō Takatoki and hundreds of his house took their own lives in the burning city. Go-Daigo's restoration lasted barely three years.

Harihara and Bukka, two brothers of the Sangama family who had served the kingdom of Kampili, founded a city on the south bank of the Tungabhadra amid fantastic hills of granite boulders. Vijayanagara, the City of Victory, became the bulwark of the Hindu south against the sultanates, and Bukka's heirs ruled from it an empire reaching from sea to sea.

t: The Palapa Oath of Gajah Mada
x: Gajah Mada, who had risen from captain of the royal guard to chief minister of Majapahit, swore before Queen Tribhuwana that he would taste no palapa until the islands were subdued: Gurun, Seram, Tanjungpura, Haru, Pahang, Dompo, Bali, Sunda, Palembang, and Tumasik. For twenty years he waged war to make the oath good.

t: Ibn Battuta and the King of Jaffna
x: Ibn Battuta, cast ashore in Lanka on his way from the Maldives to the Coromandel coast, was received at Puttalam by Arya Chakravarti, the Tamil king of Jaffna and master of the pearl fishery. The king gave him an escort to climb Adam's Peak and see the great footprint on its summit, revered alike by Buddhists, Hindus, and Muslims.

At Easter 1346 in Skopje, Stefan Dušan, conqueror of Macedonia and Albania, had his archbishop raised to patriarch and was crowned by him Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks. His law code of 1349 bound the strongest realm in the Balkans, but on his death in 1355 it fell apart among his lords.

On 26 August 1346 Edward III, marching through northern France, drew up his army on a slope near Crécy. The Genoese crossbowmen were shot down by English and Welsh archers, and the French knights rode again and again into the arrow storm until some fifteen hundred lords and knights lay dead. The blind King John of Bohemia had himself led into the fight to die.

In October 1347 Genoese galleys from the Black Sea put in at Messina with dying men at the oars. The plague they carried, borne along the trade routes by rats and fleas, swept Italy, France, England, and Germany within three years and killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people. Labor grew dear, serfdom loosened, and the faith and art of Europe were shadowed for generations.

The amirs of the Deccan rose against Muhammad bin Tughlaq and crowned one of their number, Hasan Gangu, as Ala al-Din Bahman Shah at Daulatabad. He made Gulbarga his capital, and the Bahmani kingdom he founded ruled the northern Deccan for nearly two centuries, waging almost ceaseless war with Vijayanagara for the rich lands between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra.

Carried by ships from the Black Sea, the plague reached Alexandria in the autumn of 1347 and Cairo the following spring. At its height, the historian al-Maqrizi wrote, the dead of Cairo numbered thousands a day, and corpses were carried to burial on planks and ladders. Egypt and Syria may have lost a third of their people, and the Mamluk lands never wholly recovered.

On 7 April 1348 Charles IV, King of Bohemia and soon emperor, founded at Prague the first university of central Europe, open to students of four nations. He made Prague an imperial capital, laying out the New Town, raising the cathedral of St. Vitus, and later the stone bridge over the Vltava; it became one of the great cities of Christendom.

t: The Burning of the Jews of Strasbourg
x: As the plague drew near, the Jews of the Rhineland were accused of poisoning the wells. At Strasbourg the guilds overthrew the council that sought to protect them, and on 14 February 1349, before the plague had even reached the city, hundreds of Jews were burned on a scaffold in their own cemetery. Across Germany scores of communities were destroyed.

The Yuan conscripted 150,000 labourers to repair the broken dikes of the Yellow River, and among them the White Lotus sect of Han Shantong spread the word that a one-eyed stone man would be dug up to herald the fall of the dynasty. The Red Turban armies rose along the Huai, and within a decade the Yuan had lost the south to rebel warlords.

Prince U Thong, fleeing, the chronicles say, from an epidemic, crossed to an island where three rivers meet and there founded Ayutthaya, taking the name Ramathibodi. Heir to the Khmer arts of government and the Mon and Thai traditions of the Chao Phraya basin, his city ruled Siam for four centuries and became one of the richest ports of Asia.

Shams al-Din Ilyas Shah united the three governorships of Bengal into one independent sultanate and defied an invasion by Firuz Shah Tughlaq from his fortress of Ekdala. His son Sikandar raised at Pandua the Adina mosque, then the largest in India. Bengal kept its independence of Delhi for nearly two centuries, and its sultans patronised Bengali verse.

Fa Ngum, a Lao prince raised in exile at the Khmer court of Angkor, marched up the Mekong with a Khmer army and his wife, a Cambodian princess, and was crowned at Xieng Dong Xieng Thong. He named his realm Lan Xang, the Million Elephants, and Khmer monks brought with them the Theravada faith and, by tradition, the golden image called the Phra Bang.

Orhan's son Süleyman had led Turks into Thrace as allies of John VI Kantakouzenos in his civil war. When an earthquake shook down the walls of Gallipoli on the Dardanelles in March 1354, Süleyman's men occupied the ruins and refused to leave. Settled with Turkish colonists, it was the first lasting Ottoman foothold in Europe, from which they spread across Thrace.

t: The Golden Bull of Charles IV
x: At diets in Nuremberg and Metz, Charles IV issued a law sealed in gold that fixed the election of the King of the Romans in seven electors: the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, and Trier, the King of Bohemia, the Count Palatine, the Duke of Saxony, and the Margrave of Brandenburg. The pope's approval went unmentioned. The bull governed the Empire until 1806.

Chen Youliang of the rebel Han regime came down the Yangtze with towering warships to destroy his rival Zhu Yuanzhang. For over a month the fleets fought on the shallow lake; Zhu sent fire ships into Chen's crowded fleet, and Chen was killed by an arrow as he tried to break out at the lake's mouth. The battle made Zhu master of the Yangtze valley.

Zhu Yuanzhang, an orphan of famine who had begged as a monk and risen through the Red Turban armies, proclaimed the Ming, the Brilliant dynasty, at Nanjing. That summer his general Xu Da marched north and took Dadu without a battle, and the last Yuan emperor, Toghon Temür, fled to the steppe. China was ruled by a Chinese house once more.

Timur, a petty noble of the Barlas tribe lamed by arrows in his youth, besieged his former ally and brother-in-law Amir Husayn in Balkh, and on Husayn's death in April 1370 was proclaimed sovereign of the Chagatai lands. Not being of Genghis Khan's blood, he ruled in the name of puppet khans, taking only the styles of emir and royal son-in-law.

t: Che Bong Nga Burns Thang Long
x: Che Bong Nga, the Red King of Champa, sailed up the Red River, sacked and burned Thang Long, and carried off its women and treasure. In 1377 the Vietnamese emperor Tran Due Tong fell in an ambush before Vijaya, and the Cham raided the north again and again until 1390, when a deserter pointed out Che Bong Nga's ship and Vietnamese gunners shot him down.

The Mamluks had raided the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia for a century when they laid siege to Sis, its capital, in 1375. King Leo V of the house of Lusignan surrendered in April and was led captive to Cairo; he died an exile in Paris. The last independent Armenian kingdom of the Middle Ages was extinguished.

Weary of the courts of North Africa and Granada, the Tunisian scholar and statesman Ibn Khaldun withdrew to the castle of Ibn Salama in the hills of western Algeria, and there in 1377 completed the Muqaddimah, the introduction to his universal history. Its doctrine of asabiyya, the group feeling by which desert peoples conquer cities and are in turn corrupted by them, founded the philosophy of history.

In 1378 the cardinals, under the threats of a Roman mob demanding an Italian pope, elected Urban VI; repelled by his violence, most of them withdrew to Fondi and chose Clement VII, who returned to Avignon. For nearly forty years Christendom had two popes, after 1409 three, until the Council of Constance deposed or accepted the resignation of all and elected Martin V in 1417.

On 8 September 1380 Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow, blessed by St. Sergius of Radonezh, led the princes of Rus' across the Don against Mamai, warlord of the Golden Horde. After a day of slaughter the Tatars broke. Two years later Tokhtamysh burned Moscow, but the spell of Tatar invincibility was broken, and Dmitry was called Donskoy, of the Don.

Tradition holds that Makhdum Karim, an Arab missionary, landed on Simunul in the Sulu archipelago and built there the first mosque in the Philippines. About the middle of the next century Sharif ul-Hashim, a scholar of Arab descent who came by way of Johor, married into the Sulu nobility and founded the sultanate that would rule these islands for four hundred years.

Provoked by a third poll tax, the commons of Essex and Kent rose under Wat Tyler and the priest John Ball, who asked, 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?' They burned the Savoy palace and beheaded the Archbishop of Canterbury. At Smithfield on 15 June 1381 the mayor struck Tyler down, and the boy king Richard II rode forward to lead the leaderless rebels away.

By the act sealed at Krewo on 14 August 1385, Jogaila, pagan grand duke of Lithuania, pledged to accept baptism with his people, join his lands to Poland, and marry the young Queen Jadwiga. Crowned at Kraków in 1386 as Władysław II, he founded the Jagiellonian dynasty, and the last pagan state of Europe entered Latin Christendom.

t: Timur's Towers of Skulls at Isfahan
x: Isfahan had surrendered to Timur and accepted a garrison when its people rose in November 1387 and killed some three thousand of his soldiers. Timur ordered each division of his army to bring in a quota of heads. Contemporaries counted seventy thousand, piled into towers outside the walls, an example that made other Persian cities open their gates.

Ordered by King U and the general Choe Yeong to march on Liaodong against the new Ming, the commander Yi Seong-gye halted his army on Wihwa Island in the flooding Yalu and turned back. He seized Kaesong, exiled Choe Yeong, and deposed the king. Four years later he took the throne himself and founded the Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea for over five centuries.

On St. Vitus' Day, 15 June 1389, Prince Lazar of Serbia and his allies met Sultan Murad I on the Field of Blackbirds. Murad was slain in his tent, by tradition by the knight Miloš Obilić, and Lazar was taken and beheaded. Both armies were shattered, but Serbia could not replace its dead and became an Ottoman vassal; the battle became the heart of Serbian memory.

In a sermon of 1395 Isidore Glabas, metropolitan of Thessalonica, then under Ottoman rule, lamented the seizure of the city's Christian boys by the sultan's officers. His is the earliest witness to the devshirme: the levy of Christian children from Balkan villages, who were taken from their families, made Muslims, and trained as Janissaries or palace servants. The levy continued for three centuries.

Tokhtamysh, whom Timur had once set on the throne of the Golden Horde, turned against his patron. On the Terek in April 1395 Timur crushed him, then swept up the Volga and burned Sarai, Astrakhan, and the Italian colony of Tana. The ruin of the Horde's cities and trade road freed the princes of Moscow from their strongest master.

King Sigismund of Hungary and the chivalry of France and Burgundy under John of Nevers came to drive the Turks from Europe. On 25 September 1396 at Nicopolis on the Danube the French knights charged headlong against Sultan Bayezid I and were destroyed. Bayezid had some thousands of prisoners slaughtered before him; John of Nevers was ransomed for 200,000 florins.

In June 1397 at Kalmar, Queen Margaret, mistress of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, had her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania crowned king of all three realms. The union of the Scandinavian crowns under one monarch, from Greenland to Finland, endured with lapses and Swedish rebellions until 1523.

Timur crossed the Indus and came down on Delhi, ruled by the feeble Tughlaq sultan Nasir al-Din Mahmud. Before the battle he ordered some hundred thousand Hindu captives in his camp put to death lest they rise. He scattered the sultan's army and its war elephants, his troops sacked and slaughtered in the city for days, and he left with masons, artisans, and slaves beyond counting.

Parameswara, a prince of Palembang who had fled Majapahit to Temasek and then been driven out again, settled at the mouth of a little river on the Malay coast, where, the Malay Annals say, a mouse deer turned on his hunting dogs. Seeking the protection of the Ming, whose emperor he visited in 1411, he made Malacca the great emporium of the Straits.

Baghdad defied Timur and was stormed in the heat of July 1401. Each of his soldiers was ordered to bring in heads, and the chroniclers tell of 120 towers of skulls raised about the city. Only the mosques and their keepers were spared. Baghdad, already ruined by Hulagu, did not regain its rank among the cities of Islam for centuries.

Timur invaded Anatolia at the plea of the beys whom Bayezid had dispossessed. On 28 July 1402, near Ankara, the Tatar and Turkmen troops in the Ottoman ranks went over to their old lords, and Bayezid was taken prisoner. He died in captivity the next year. The Ottoman state fell into a decade of civil war among his sons, and Constantinople won half a century of life.

The Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He sailed from the Yangtze with over sixty great treasure ships and some 27,000 men. In seven voyages to 1433 his ships reached Java, Ceylon, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden, and the coast of Africa, bringing home envoys and a giraffe. Then the court turned inward, and the fleets were left to rot.

Ho Quy Ly, who had seized the Tran throne and built the stone citadel of Tay Do, gave the Yongle Emperor his pretext by killing a Tran pretender under Ming escort. Two Ming armies under Zhang Fu and Mu Sheng overran the country, captured Ho Quy Ly and his son, and made Dai Viet the province of Jiaozhi, carrying off its books and craftsmen to China.

In September 1408 Thorstein Olafsson and Sigrid Bjornsdottir were married in the stone church of Hvalsey, the last recorded event of the Norse colony in Greenland, known from letters their Icelandic guests carried home. Cut off as the climate cooled and the Norwegian ships ceased to come, the colony of some two thousand souls vanished in the decades that followed.

The reformer Tsongkhapa, who called the monks of Tibet back to strict discipline and the study of Indian logic, inaugurated the Great Prayer Festival at the Jokhang in Lhasa and founded the monastery of Ganden on a mountain to the east. His followers, the Gelug order, built Drepung and Sera soon after, and in time their leaders, the Dalai Lamas, came to rule Tibet.

On 15 July 1410, in the fields between Grunwald and Tannenberg, Władysław II Jagiełło and his cousin Vytautas, leading Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, and Tatars, broke the army of the Teutonic Order. Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen and most of the Order's officers fell. Marienburg held out, but the Order never recovered its strength.

Ahmad Shah I, sultan of Gujarat, founded a new capital on the east bank of the Sabarmati beside the old town of Ashaval and named it Ahmedabad. Its Jami Masjid of 1424, raised by Gujarati masons on some 260 carved pillars, joined Indian and Islamic forms, and the city grew rich on cotton, silk, and indigo.

Jan Hus, the Prague preacher who followed Wyclif in attacking indulgences and the wealth of the clergy, came to the Council of Constance under a safe conduct from Sigismund. He was imprisoned, condemned as a heretic, and burned on 6 July 1415. Bohemia rose in fury, and for twenty years the Hussite armies defied the Empire and the Church.

On St. Crispin's Day, 25 October 1415, Henry V's sick and hungry army, perhaps 6,000 men and most of them archers, faced a French host several times its size between two woods. The French men-at-arms, floundering in the mud, were shot down and crushed in their own press. Henry went on to conquer Normandy, and by the Treaty of Troyes was made heir to France.

Sigismund's crusading army of many nations, come to crush the Hussites and claim the Bohemian crown, laid siege to Prague. On 14 July 1420 Jan Žižka, the one-eyed captain, threw back its assault on Vítkov hill with a few score peasants and townsmen. Žižka's war wagons, chained together and bristling with handguns, would defeat crusade after crusade.

The Yongle Emperor, who had seized the throne from his nephew in 1402 and left the palace at Nanjing in flames, moved his capital north to Beijing, his old princely seat. There a hundred thousand craftsmen and perhaps a million labourers had raised the Forbidden City, some 980 buildings behind a moat and walls, the home of twenty-four emperors until 1912.

To end the raids of Cypriot corsairs on the Syrian and Egyptian coasts, Sultan Barsbay sent an army to Cyprus that routed the Lusignan king Janus at Khirokitia on 7 July 1426. Nicosia was plundered and Janus led in chains through the streets of Cairo before he was ransomed. Cyprus remained a tributary of the Mamluks until their fall.

t: Le Loi Drives Out the Ming
x: Le Loi, a landowner of Lam Son, rose against the Ming in 1418 and fought a guerrilla war for ten years. In 1427 he destroyed a Ming relief army at the pass of Chi Lang, where its general Liu Sheng was killed, and the Ming withdrew. Crowned as Le Thai To, he proclaimed the victory in Nguyen Trai's Great Proclamation upon the Pacification of the Wu.

Itzcoatl of Tenochtitlan joined Nezahualcoyotl, the exiled poet-prince of Texcoco, and the lord of Tlacopan to overthrow Maxtla and the Tepanec overlords of Azcapotzalco, to whom the Mexica had paid tribute. The victors formed the Triple Alliance that became the Aztec empire, and Itzcoatl had the old painted books burned so that the history of the Mexica could be written anew.

Ulugh Beg, grandson of Timur and governor of Samarkand for his father Shah Rukh, built on a hill outside the city about 1428 an observatory with a great meridian arc sunk into the rock. His tables fixed the places of over a thousand stars and the length of the year with remarkable precision. Two years after he became sovereign, his own son had him murdered in 1449.

Joan, a peasant girl of Domrémy who heard the voices of saints bidding her save France, came to the Dauphin Charles at Chinon and was sent with a convoy to besieged Orléans. Within nine days of her arrival the English forts were taken and the siege raised on 8 May 1429; in July she stood beside Charles at his crowning in Reims. Captured the next year, she was burned at Rouen in 1431.

t: Min Saw Mon Founds Mrauk U
x: Min Saw Mon, king of Arakan, driven out by the Burmans of Ava, spent twenty-four years in exile at the court of Bengal and returned with a Bengali army to win back his throne.
