In 1430 he founded Mrauk U, whose Buddhist kings took Muslim titles and struck coins in Persian, and whose fleets and Portuguese freebooters made it a terror of the Bay of Bengal.

t: The Rise of the Mwene Mutapa
x: As Great Zimbabwe declined, the Shona ruler Nyatsimba Mutota led his warriors north toward the Zambezi and won the praise name Mwene Mutapa, 'lord of the conquered lands.' His successors ruled the gold country between the plateau and the river, trading with the Swahili of Sofala and, in later times, receiving and resisting the Portuguese of Sena and Tete.

King Borommarachathirat II of Ayutthaya besieged Yasodharapura for seven months, took it, and carried off its images, Brahmans, and dancers to Siam. The Khmer court soon abandoned the city for the region of the Four Faces, where the Mekong meets the Tonle Sap; Angkor was left to the monks and the forest, and the age of the god-kings was over.

On 25 March 1436 Pope Eugenius IV consecrated the cathedral of Florence, crowned at last with the great dome Filippo Brunelleschi had raised without wooden centering, ring upon ring of brick laid in herringbone. The largest dome built since antiquity, it was the first triumph of the art of the Renaissance, and Florence its capital.

When the Chanka invaded the valley of Cusco and the old Inca ruler Viracocha fled, his son Cusi Yupanqui stayed to defend the town and, by Inca tradition, saw the very stones rise up as warriors to help him. Victorious, he took the name Pachacuti, 'Earth-shaker,' rebuilt Cusco in fitted stone, and began the conquests that made the Inca masters of the Andes.

Oba Ewuare, remembered in Edo tradition as the Great, seized the throne, rebuilt Benin City with broad avenues and a vast palace, and girdled it with moats and earthen walls. He exalted the oba into a sacred king and carried his armies far and wide; his successors' brass-casters would cover the palace pillars with plaques recording the court in its glory.

George Kastrioti, an Albanian lord's son raised as a hostage at the Ottoman court and called Iskender Bey, deserted the sultan's army after Hunyadi's victory at Niš in November 1443 and seized Krujë. Returning to the faith of his fathers, he held the Albanian mountains against Murad II and Mehmed II for a quarter of a century, and died unconquered in 1468.

Breaking a truce at the urging of the papal legate Cesarini, Władysław III, King of Poland and Hungary, and John Hunyadi marched to the Black Sea. On 10 November 1444 Murad II met them before Varna; the young king charged the sultan's Janissaries and was cut down, and his head was raised on a lance. It was the last great crusade to save Constantinople.

King Sejong, grieved that his people could not write their own tongue in Chinese characters, published the Hunminjeongeum, the Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People: twenty-eight letters whose consonants were drawn, as no other alphabet's were, from the shapes of the mouth and tongue that speak them. Court scholars long scorned it, but it became the national script of Korea.

Urged on by the eunuch Wang Zhen, the young Zhengtong Emperor led a vast army against the Oirat chief Esen. Turning back in disorder, it was caught without water at the post station of Tumu and destroyed; Wang Zhen was killed and the emperor taken prisoner. The minister Yu Qian set the emperor's brother on the throne and saved Beijing, and the Ming thereafter kept behind their walls.

On a saddle between two peaks above the gorge of the Urubamba, Pachacuti's builders raised a royal estate of granite temples, palaces, and terraces, with the Intihuatana stone and the curved Temple of the Sun. Abandoned after the Spanish conquest and never found by the conquerors, it was brought to the notice of the world by Hiram Bingham in 1911.

By the tradition of the Haudenosaunee, the Peacemaker and his spokesman Hiawatha persuaded the warring Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca to bury their weapons beneath a Tree of Peace and join in a league governed by a council of fifty chiefs, its fire kept at Onondaga. The Five Nations became the strongest native power of the northeast; the Tuscarora joined them in the 1720s.

In his workshop at Mainz, Johann Gutenberg, a goldsmith by training, joined movable metal type cast in a hand mould, an oil-based ink, and a screw press to print some 180 copies of the Latin Bible. Within fifty years presses in more than two hundred towns had printed millions of books, and the Reformation, the new science, and the modern state would all be carried by type.

Three years after taking Constantinople, Mehmed II laid siege to Belgrade, the key to Hungary. John Hunyadi broke the Turkish blockade on the Danube, and on 22 July 1456 crusaders roused by the friar John of Capistrano poured from the fortress and stormed the sultan's camp; Mehmed was wounded and withdrew. Hunyadi died of plague within weeks. The noon bells of Catholic Europe still recall the victory.

The bendahara Tun Perak, chief minister to four sultans, beat back the fleets and armies of Ayutthaya from Malacca. Under Sultans Muzaffar Shah and Mansur Shah the city's rulers took the Muslim title of sultan, spread their rule over Pahang, Kampar, and Siak, and made Malacca the center from which Islam and the Malay tongue spread through the archipelago.

Eight years after Constantinople, Mehmed II marched over the Pontic mountains against Trebizond, the last Greek empire, ruled by the Grand Komnenoi since 1204. Emperor David surrendered in August 1461 without a fight and was sent into exile; two years later he and his sons were put to death at Constantinople. Many youths of the city were taken for the sultan's palace and the Janissaries.

Vlad III of Wallachia, called Dracula, son of the Dragon, refused his tribute and raided the Ottoman bank of the Danube. When Mehmed II invaded in June 1462, Vlad burst into his camp by night in a vain attempt to kill him. Advancing on Târgoviște, the sultan's army came upon a forest of stakes bearing, by the chroniclers' count, twenty thousand captives, and turned back in horror.

Muhammad Rumfa, greatest of the kings remembered in the Kano Chronicle, extended the walls of Kano, built the Gidan Rumfa palace that still serves its emirs, and set up a council of nine officers of state. The North African scholar al-Maghili came to his court and wrote for him a treatise on Muslim government, and Kano grew into the chief market of the Hausa cities.

Kerey and Janibek, sultans of the line of Jochi, broke away with their followers from the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr and led them east into the valley of the Chu, where the Chagatai khan gave them pasture. Their people were called Kazakhs, the free wanderers, and after Abu'l-Khayr's death in 1468 their khanate grew to rule the steppe for three and a half centuries.

A quarrel over the succession to the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa set the great lords Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen at war in the streets of Kyoto. For ten years their armies burned the capital quarter by quarter, while the shogun gave himself to painting, poetry, and the tea ceremony. When it ended, power lay with the provincial lords, and the Age of the Warring States had begun.

Sunni Ali, the Songhai king of Gao, a peerless horseman and a sorcerer in the eyes of his people and a tyrant in the eyes of the scholars, drove the Tuareg from Timbuktu and sacked the town, slaying and scattering its learned men. Five years later he starved Djenné into surrender, and Songhai replaced Mali as master of the Niger bend.

On 19 October 1469, in a house in Valladolid, Isabella, half-sister and heir of Henry IV of Castile, married Ferdinand, heir of Aragon, without her brother's consent and on the strength of a forged papal dispensation. Ten years later both were reigning; their union of crowns created Spain.

Afanasy Nikitin, a merchant of Tver, became the first Russian to reach India and spent years in the Bahmani capital of Bidar. In his Journey Beyond Three Seas he wrote of the sultan's splendour, the multitude of the poor, the parades of elephants, and the great vizier Mahmud Gawan, who in 1472 built at Bidar a college three storeys high faced with glazed tiles.

Chimor, the coastal kingdom whose capital Chan Chan was the largest adobe city of the Americas, its royal compounds walled with friezes of carved clay, ruled some six hundred miles of the Peruvian shore. Topa Inca Yupanqui overcame its king Minchancaman, by tradition by cutting the canals that watered its valleys, and carried the goldsmiths of Chan Chan away to Cusco.

Le Thanh Tong, the ablest of the Le emperors, led a host said to number a quarter of a million against Champa, stormed its capital of Vijaya, slew tens of thousands, and carried off thirty thousand captives with King Tra Toan. The northern half of Champa was annexed; what remained in the far south survived only as a shrunken vassal.

Uzun Hasan, the Aq Qoyunlu lord of Persia and Mesopotamia, had sought an alliance with Venice against the Ottomans. At Otlukbeli near Erzincan on 11 August 1473 the cannon and Janissaries of Mehmed II broke his Turkmen horsemen. Uzun Hasan never again troubled the Ottoman east, and Karaman, the Ottomans' old rival in Anatolia, was left without an ally.

On 10 January 1475, in fog in the marshy valley of the Bârlad near Vaslui, Stephen III of Moldavia, with a far smaller army, routed an Ottoman host under Hadım Suleiman Pasha that had come to punish him for withholding tribute. Pope Sixtus IV hailed him as the true champion of the Christian faith, though no Christian prince came to his aid.

t: Charles the Bold Falls at Nancy
x: Beaten twice by the Swiss at Grandson and Murten, Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, laid siege to Nancy in the snow. On 5 January 1477 René of Lorraine and his Swiss pikemen overwhelmed him; his body was found days later frozen in a pond, the head cleft by a halberd. Louis XI seized Burgundy, and Charles's daughter Mary carried the Netherlands to Maximilian of Habsburg.

After crushing Novgorod's army on the Shelon in 1471, Ivan III of Moscow marched on the republic again and in January 1478 forced its surrender. The veche was abolished, its great bell carried off to Moscow, and its leading families deported. Moscow now ruled the north from the Baltic to the Urals, and Ivan styled himself sovereign of all Rus'.

During High Mass in the cathedral of Florence on 26 April 1478, conspirators of the Pazzi family, with the knowledge of Pope Sixtus IV, stabbed Giuliano de' Medici to death; his brother Lorenzo, wounded, escaped into the sacristy. The people rose for the Medici, and Archbishop Salviati of Pisa was hanged from a window of the Palazzo della Signoria. Lorenzo the Magnificent was master of Florence.

Axayacatl, ruler of Tenochtitlan, led some 24,000 warriors west against the Purépecha of Michoacán, whose kings ruled from Tzintzuntzan on Lake Pátzcuaro and whose smiths worked copper and bronze. Near Taximaroa the Tarascans destroyed the Aztec host, and only a remnant escaped; the Aztecs never conquered them, and the two empires faced each other across a fortified frontier.

t: The Great Stand on the Ugra
x: Ivan III having ceased to pay tribute, Khan Akhmat of the Great Horde marched on Moscow in 1480 and found the Russian army waiting across the river Ugra. For weeks the hosts faced each other; as winter came and his Lithuanian allies failed him, Akhmat withdrew. The Tatar yoke, laid on Rus' two and a half centuries before, was ended.

An Ottoman fleet under Gedik Ahmed Pasha landed in Apulia and stormed Otranto on 11 August 1480. The archbishop was slain in his cathedral. Some eight hundred men of the town who refused to renounce Christ were beheaded on a hill outside the walls on 14 August; their bones are kept in the cathedral, and the Church has numbered them among its saints. The Turks left Italy after Mehmed's death.

Diogo de Azambuja landed with some six hundred men and blocks of dressed stone shipped from Portugal, and in a few weeks raised the castle of São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast, the first European fortress in Africa south of the Sahara. Through it the gold of the Akan forest flowed to Lisbon; in later centuries, under the Dutch, its dungeons held slaves for the Atlantic crossing.

On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor, a Lancastrian exile with French backing, met Richard III near Market Bosworth. When the Stanleys turned against the king, Richard charged at Henry and was hacked down, the last English king to die in battle. Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty and, marrying Elizabeth of York, ended the Wars of the Roses.

Driven south out of sight of land by storms, Bartolomeu Dias turned east and found the coast running northeast: he had passed the tip of Africa unawares. He landed at Mossel Bay among Khoikhoi herders, pressed on to the Great Fish River until his crews refused to go farther, and on the voyage home sighted the cape that King John II named Good Hope.

Eight years after Diogo Cão's ships entered the Congo River, a Portuguese embassy of priests and masons reached Mbanza Kongo, and the manikongo Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptized as João I. His son Afonso I, who reigned from 1509 to 1542, made Kongo a Catholic kingdom, sent his son Henrique to study in Lisbon, and saw him made in 1518 the first black African bishop of the Latin Church.

On 2 January 1492, after a war of ten years, Boabdil, last Nasrid emir of Granada, handed the keys of the Alhambra to Ferdinand and Isabella and rode into exile. The silver cross was raised on the Torre de la Vela. Nearly eight centuries after the Muslim conquest, all Spain was Christian, and that same year the queen sent Columbus across the Ocean Sea.

t: The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain
x: By the edict signed at Granada on 31 March 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella commanded every Jew in their kingdoms to accept baptism or leave by the end of July. Many thousands chose exile, to Portugal, Italy, North Africa, and the Ottoman lands, where Sultan Bayezid II welcomed them; the Sephardim carried their Spanish tongue across the Mediterranean for four centuries.

Charles VIII of France, claiming Naples as heir of Anjou, crossed the Alps in 1494 with an army and a train of bronze siege guns that brought down Italian fortresses in hours. He entered Naples unopposed on 22 February 1495. The Italian states leagued against him and he fought his way home at Fornovo, but the Italian Wars had begun, and Italy was the battleground of Europe for sixty years.

Vasco da Gama, having rounded the Cape of Good Hope and found a pilot at Malindi, anchored off Calicut in May 1498, ten months out of Lisbon. Asked what they sought, his men answered: Christians and spices. The Zamorin received him coldly, but the sea road from Europe to India was open, and Portuguese cannon would soon command the Arabian Sea.

After skirmishes at Mozambique and an attempted attack at Mombasa, Vasco da Gama's ships found a friendly sultan at Malindi, the rival of Mombasa, who gave him a pilot skilled in the monsoon. In less than a month the pilot brought the fleet across the Indian Ocean to Calicut, and the sea road from Europe to India lay open.

Nanak, a keeper of the stores of the Lodi governor at Sultanpur, vanished into the river Bein for three days and returned to proclaim that there was no Hindu and no Muslim. He travelled far preaching devotion to one God, the equality of all, and honest labour, and at Kartarpur gathered the first community of Sikhs. Nine Gurus followed him.

Pedro Álvares Cabral, leading thirteen ships to India in Vasco da Gama's wake, swung far west into the Atlantic and on 22 April 1500 sighted a mountain he named Monte Pascoal. He anchored at the bay of Porto Seguro, where on the Sunday after Easter the Franciscan Henrique de Coimbra said the first Mass in the land, and took possession of it for Portugal before sailing on to India.

Ismail, the fourteen-year-old head of the Safavid Sufi order of Ardabil, led his red-capped Qizilbash Turkmen to victory over the Aq Qoyunlu and entered Tabriz in the summer of 1501. Proclaimed shah, he decreed Twelver Shi'ism the faith of his realm and imposed it by the sword on a largely Sunni people. Iran took the religious identity that has set it apart from its neighbors ever since.

Driven from Fergana and Samarkand by the Uzbeks, the young Timurid prince Babur crossed the Hindu Kush with a few hundred ragged followers and took Kabul in 1504. He loved its gardens and melons all his life, ruled it for twenty-two years before he turned on India, and at his wish was buried there in a garden on the hillside.

The Funj, cattle people of the Blue Nile under Amara Dunqas, and the Arab Abdallab under Abdallah Jamma destroyed Soba, capital of Christian Alodia, the last of the Nubian kingdoms. Amara founded his capital at Sennar and his line ruled as Muslim sultans; the churches of the middle Nile, after nearly a thousand years, fell silent.

Two years after laying the foundation stone of a new St. Peter's, Julius II set Michelangelo to paint the vault of the Sistine Chapel. Working through four years, almost alone on his scaffold, the sculptor covered it with the Creation, the Fall, and the Flood, with prophets and sibyls. Unveiled in October 1512, it set a standard for the human figure that no painter could ignore.

Off Diu the viceroy Francisco de Almeida, avenging his son slain by the Mamluk fleet at Chaul the year before, destroyed the combined navies of Mamluk Egypt, the sultan of Gujarat, and the Zamorin of Calicut. Portuguese broadsides decided the day. The victory gave Portugal mastery of the trade of the Indian Ocean for a century.

Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa from the sultan of Bijapur, lost it, and in November 1510 stormed it again, putting its Muslim defenders to the sword. He made it the capital of the Portuguese Estado da India, encouraged his men to marry local women, and from Goa reached out to seize Malacca and Hormuz. Goa remained Portuguese until 1961.

Muhammad Shaybani, the Uzbek khan who had driven the Timurids from Samarkand and Herat, was drawn into battle near Merv by Shah Ismail in December 1510 and slain. Ismail had his skull mounted in gold as a drinking cup and sent his stuffed skin to the Ottoman sultan. The Oxus became the frontier between Shi'ite Iran and the Sunni Uzbeks.

Afonso de Albuquerque came with eighteen ships and some twelve hundred men to avenge the Portuguese seized at Malacca two years before. After two assaults on the bridge over the river he took the city from Sultan Mahmud Shah in August 1511 and built the fortress of A Famosa. Portugal now held the gate between the Indian Ocean and the China Sea.

t: The Portuguese Reach the Spice Islands
x: Francisco Serrao, shipwrecked on the first Portuguese voyage to the Banda Islands, was welcomed at Ternate by Sultan Bayan Sirrullah, who sought allies against Tidore. The Moluccas grew all the world's cloves, and Serrao's letters to his friend Ferdinand Magellan, telling of islands richer than the Indies, set Magellan dreaming of a westward road to them.

Vasco Núñez de Balboa, with some 190 Spaniards and hundreds of native guides and porters, hacked his way over the mountains and through the jungles of the Isthmus of Darién, and on 25 September 1513, from a peak, became the first European to see the Pacific from the shores of the Americas. Four days later he waded into its waters at the Gulf of San Miguel and took possession of it all for Castile.

Selim I, having put to death tens of thousands of suspected Qizilbash sympathizers in Anatolia, marched east against Shah Ismail. On 23 August 1514 at Chaldiran his artillery and Janissary muskets broke the charges of the Persian horse, and Selim briefly occupied Tabriz. Ismail, his aura of invincibility gone, never again led an army in person, and eastern Anatolia was won for the Ottomans.

North of Aleppo on 24 August 1516 Selim I met the aged Mamluk sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri. The Mamluk horsemen, brave beyond measure but scornful of firearms, were shattered by Ottoman cannon and musketry; al-Ghawri fell from his horse and died on the field. Aleppo, Damascus, and all Syria opened their gates to Selim.

Oruç and Hızır, sons of a Turkish soldier of Lesbos, had made themselves the scourge of Christian shipping from Tunisian ports. Called to Algiers in 1516 against the Spaniards, Oruç seized the town and killed its emir. After Oruç fell fighting the Spanish in 1518, Hızır, called Hayreddin Barbarossa, placed Algiers under the Ottoman sultan, and for three centuries it was the chief den of the Barbary corsairs.

On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, Augustinian friar and professor of theology, sent his ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences to the Archbishop of Mainz, and by tradition nailed them to the door of the castle church at Wittenberg. Printed and carried across Germany within weeks, they began the Reformation, which divided Western Christendom forever.

Selim crossed the Sinai and routed the last Mamluk sultan, Tumanbay, at Ridaniya outside Cairo on 22 January 1517. Tumanbay fought on for weeks in the streets and the countryside until he was betrayed, and in April he was hanged at the Bab Zuwayla gate. The sharif of Mecca sent the keys of the holy cities, and the last Abbasid shadow caliph was carried off to Constantinople. The Ottoman sultans became the guardians of Islam's holiest places.

t: Charles I Licenses the African Slave Trade
x: With the Taíno of the Antilles dying of overwork and disease, Charles I licensed the shipment of four thousand African slaves to the Indies, the first great grant of what became the asiento; soon ships sailed direct from Guinea and São Tomé to the islands. In three and a half centuries some twelve and a half million Africans were carried in chains across the Atlantic, and nearly two million died on the way.

Hernán Cortés, who had landed on the Gulf coast with some five hundred soldiers, scuttled his ships, and won the Tlaxcalans to his side, came over the southern causeway into Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519. Moctezuma II received him with gifts and lodged him in the palace of his father Axayacatl; within a week Cortés had made the emperor his prisoner.

Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese sailing for Spain, wintered on the Patagonian coast, crushed a mutiny there, and on 21 October 1520 entered the strait that bears his name. After thirty-eight days among its fjords and squalls three of his ships came out into an ocean so calm he called it the Pacific; one of them, the Victoria, completed the first voyage around the world in 1522.

Christian II of Denmark, crowned king of Sweden after defeating the Sture party, invited the Swedish nobles to his coronation feast and then on 8 and 9 November 1520 had some eighty of them, with two bishops, beheaded in Stockholm's great square as heretics. The massacre roused Sweden to revolt under Gustav Vasa, whose father died in it, and in 1523 Gustav was elected king.

Pressing the chiefs of the islands to submit to his ally Humabon, Ferdinand Magellan waded ashore at Mactan on 27 April 1521 with some fifty men against the warriors of Lapulapu, and was cut down in the shallows. Of his five ships only the Victoria, under Juan Sebastian Elcano, came home to Spain in 1522, completing the first voyage around the world.

t: Luther Before the Diet of Worms
x: Summoned before the young emperor Charles V and the princes of the Empire, Luther refused on 18 April 1521 to recant his writings unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason, and is said to have ended, 'Here I stand; I can do no other.' Outlawed by the Edict of Worms, he was spirited away by his prince to the Wartburg, where he turned the New Testament into German.

t: The First Mass in the Philippines
x: On Easter Sunday, 31 March 1521, the chaplain of Magellan's fleet said Mass on Limasawa before the rajahs Kolambu and Siaui, and a cross was raised on a hill. Two weeks later at Cebu Rajah Humabon and his queen were baptized with some eight hundred of their people, and the queen received the image of the Holy Child that the Spaniards would find again in 1565.

Pedro de Alvarado, the boldest and hardest of Cortés's captains, marched into the Guatemalan highlands with Spanish horsemen and thousands of Tlaxcalan and Mexica allies and defeated the K'iche' Maya near Quetzaltenango, where tradition says their prince Tecun Uman fell. He burned the K'iche' kings at their capital of Q'umarkaj and turned next upon the Tz'utujil of Lake Atitlán.

On 24 February 1525, the emperor's birthday, the army of Charles V, Spanish arquebusiers and German landsknechts, fell on Francis I in the hunting park outside besieged Pavia. The French men-at-arms were shot to pieces, and the king, unhorsed, surrendered. He was carried prisoner to Madrid, writing to his mother that nothing remained to him but honor and his life.

Babur came down from Kabul with some twelve thousand men and met Ibrahim Lodi's army, perhaps eight times larger, at Panipat. Lashing carts together to shelter his matchlockmen and field guns, and sweeping round the flanks with mounted archers, he broke the Afghan host before midday. Ibrahim died on the field, and the Mughal Empire was born.

On the marshy plain of Mohács on 29 August 1526 the Hungarian army of King Louis II, some twenty-five thousand men, charged Suleiman's far greater host and was annihilated in two hours. The king drowned in a stream as he fled, and seven bishops lay among the dead. Suleiman entered Buda, and the kingdom of Hungary was broken into Ottoman, Habsburg, and Transylvanian parts.

t: Afonso of Kongo Protests the Slave Trade
x: King Afonso I, devout Catholic and ally of Portugal, wrote to John III that Portuguese traders were seizing his free subjects, even noblemen and his own kinsmen, to sell abroad, so that the land was being depopulated. He asked that only priests and teachers be sent him, not merchants; the trade went on regardless, feeding the sugar plantations of São Tomé and, in time, of Brazil.

On 6 May 1527 the unpaid army of Charles V, Spanish soldiers and Lutheran landsknechts, stormed Rome after its general, the Constable of Bourbon, was killed on the walls. For weeks they murdered, tortured, and plundered, while Pope Clement VII watched from the Castel Sant'Angelo. The sack ended the High Renaissance in Rome and bound the papacy to the emperor.

t: Babur Defeats Rana Sanga at Khanwa
x: Rana Sanga of Mewar led a great Rajput confederacy against the newcomer. Before battle at Khanwa, Babur poured out his wine, broke his gold and silver cups, and swore off drink to rally his frightened troops for a holy war. His guns and flanking horse broke the Rajputs; Sanga, wounded, escaped but died the next year, and the Mughals were masters of Hindustan.

t: Demak Overthrows the Last of Majapahit
x: The Muslim port kings of the north coast of Java, led by Sultan Trenggana of Demak, crushed the last Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the Majapahit line at Daha in the Brantas valley. Priests and nobles who would not accept Islam fled east to Blambangan and across the strait to Bali, which alone kept the old faith of the Javanese courts.

The Hindu king of Sunda had granted the Portuguese leave in 1522 to build a fort at his pepper port of Sunda Kalapa. Before they could return, the Muslim commander Fatahillah, with forces of Demak and Cirebon, took the port, drove off the Portuguese ships, and renamed it Jayakarta, Complete Victory. Jakarta keeps 22 June 1527 as its birthday.

Suleiman marched up the Danube and laid siege to Vienna in September 1529, but the autumn rains had forced him to leave his heavy guns behind. The garrison under Count Niklas Salm beat back every assault, and on 14 October, with winter coming on, the Ottomans burned their camp and withdrew, slaughtering many of their captives. It was the farthest reach of Ottoman conquest for a century and a half.

In December 1531, on the hill of Tepeyac north of Mexico City, the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego, a Nahua convert, speaking to him in his own tongue and bidding him ask the bishop for a church upon that place. When he opened his cloak before Bishop Juan de Zumárraga, roses fell from it and her image was found upon the cloth; the shrine became the heart of Mexican Catholicism.

Fresh from his victory over his brother Huascar in a civil war that had torn the Inca empire, Atahualpa met Francisco Pizarro's 168 Spaniards in the square of Cajamarca on 16 November 1532. At a signal the Spaniards fell upon his unarmed retinue with guns, horses, and steel, killing thousands, and took him captive; he filled a room with gold for his ransom and was garroted the following July.

When Pope Clement VII would not annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII had Parliament declare him Supreme Head of the Church of England in November 1534. Sir Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher went to the block for refusing the oath, and within six years the king had dissolved the monasteries and seized their lands.

Francisco Pizarro founded Lima on the banks of the Rímac on 18 January 1535, naming it the City of the Kings for the Magi of the Epiphany. Seat of the viceroyalty of Peru from 1544, with the university of San Marcos founded in 1551, its cathedral, and its Inquisition, it was for two centuries the capital of all Spanish South America.

Barbarossa had seized Tunis from its Hafsid sultan in 1534. The next summer the Emperor Charles V sailed against him with some four hundred ships, stormed the fortress of La Goulette, and entered Tunis in July 1535, where thousands of Christian captives broke out of their prisons. The city was sacked, the Hafsid Mawlay Hasan restored as a Spanish vassal, and Barbarossa escaped to Algiers.

Tabinshwehti, the young king of Toungoo, and his general and brother-in-law Bayinnaung overran the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy and made Pegu their capital. Tabinshwehti wore his hair in the Mon fashion and courted Mon loyalty, took Martaban with Portuguese gunners in 1541, and by 1544 ruled the Irrawaddy from the sea to Pagan.

Sher Khan Sur, an Afghan of Bihar, beat Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and again near Kannauj in 1540, driving him into exile in Persia. As Sher Shah he ruled only five years, but he rebuilt the great road from Bengal to the Indus with inns and wells, measured the land for revenue, and struck the silver rupiya that gave India its rupee.

Recalled from exile in Strasbourg in September 1541, the French reformer John Calvin, author of the Institutes of the Christian Religion, made Geneva a city governed by the discipline of its pastors and elders. Its academy trained preachers for France, Scotland, the Netherlands, and Hungary, and Calvinism became the fighting faith of the Reformation.

Francisco de Orellana, sent downriver by Gonzalo Pizarro to find food for an expedition starving east of Quito, never returned: with some fifty men he drifted and fought his way down the whole length of the great river to the Atlantic in eight months. His chaplain Gaspar de Carvajal told of populous towns along the banks and of a battle with women warriors, after whom the river was named for the Amazons.

Nicolaus Copernicus, canon of Frauenburg in Royal Prussia, had long worked out a system with the sun at rest near the center and the earth turning about it. His On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was printed at Nuremberg in 1543, and by tradition the first copy reached him on his deathbed. The same year Vesalius published his great anatomy of the human body.

For fourteen years Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, called Gragn, 'the left-handed,' had led the armies of Adal with Ottoman matchlocks across the Christian highlands, burning churches and monasteries, and forcing Islam upon the conquered. Four hundred Portuguese musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama, Vasco's son, came to Emperor Gelawdewos's aid; Cristóvão was taken and beheaded, but at Wayna Daga in February 1543 Gragn was shot dead and his host scattered.

A Chinese junk driven off course carried the first Portuguese to reach Japan to the island of Tanegashima. The young lord Tanegashima Tokitaka bought two of their arquebuses and set his smiths to copy them, and within a few decades Japanese armies carried tens of thousands of matchlocks, more perhaps than any kingdom of Europe.

Returning from his winter at Toulon with the French, his allies against the emperor, Barbarossa ravaged the coasts of Italy. In July 1544 he battered the island town of Lipari, north of Sicily, into surrender and carried off nearly its whole population, some thousands of souls, to the slave markets of Constantinople. It was among the heaviest single blows of the corsair raids that emptied Mediterranean shores for three centuries.

An Indian herder named Diego Huallpa found silver on the Cerro Rico, the Rich Mountain, more than four thousand metres up in the Andes, and within a few decades Potosí was one of the largest cities in the world. Worked by Andean laborers drafted under the mita, its mines poured out silver that paid for Spain's wars, flowed through Manila to China, and bound the commerce of the world together.

On 13 December 1545 Pope Paul III's council opened at Trent, an imperial city on the road between Italy and Germany. In three periods of sitting over eighteen years it defined Catholic doctrine against the Protestants, upheld the seven sacraments and the Latin Vulgate, ordered seminaries for the training of priests, and set the Catholic Church upon the course it held for four centuries.

The Jesuit Francis Xavier, guided by a Japanese convert named Anjirō, landed at Kagoshima and began to preach the Gospel in Japan, whose people he praised as the best yet discovered. In two years he founded the first Christian communities there, and within half a century Japan counted perhaps three hundred thousand Christians, among them great lords of Kyushu.

Tomé de Sousa, first governor-general of Brazil, arrived on the Bay of All Saints with a thousand soldiers, settlers, and convicts, and with the first Jesuits under Manuel da Nóbrega, and founded the city of Salvador as the capital of the colony. Ringed by sugar mills worked first by Indians and then by slaves from Africa, it remained the capital of Brazil until 1763.

The corsair admiral Turgut Reis, beaten off from Malta in July 1551, fell on the neighboring island of Gozo and forced its citadel to surrender. Nearly the whole population, some five thousand people, were carried into slavery. Turgut sailed on and in August took Tripoli from the Knights of St. John, making it a corsair base under the sultan.

Ivan IV, crowned in 1547 as the first Tsar of all Russia, laid siege to Kazan with a great army and sappers who mined its walls. On 2 October 1552 the mines blew breaches and the Russians stormed the city, slaughtering its defenders and freeing the Russian captives held there as slaves. Astrakhan fell four years later, the Volga became a Russian river, and St. Basil's rose on Red Square.

Lautaro, a young Mapuche who had served Pedro de Valdivia as a groom and learned the ways of Spanish horses and war, returned to his people and led them against the fort of Tucapel on Christmas Day 1553. Valdivia, conqueror of Chile and founder of Santiago, was taken and killed; for more than three centuries the Mapuche held the land south of the Biobío against Spain and Chile.

Exhausted by war, the princes of the Empire and King Ferdinand, acting for his brother Charles V, agreed at Augsburg on 25 September 1555 that each ruler should choose between the Catholic and the Lutheran faith for his own land, a rule later summed up as cuius regio, eius religio. Calvinists were left outside the peace, and Charles abdicated within the year.

Hemu, a Hindu merchant who had risen to command the armies of the Sur Afghans, took Delhi and crowned himself Raja Vikramaditya. At Panipat he was winning against the Mughals of the fourteen-year-old Akbar when an arrow struck him in the eye. His leaderless army fled; Hemu was brought before Akbar and beheaded, and the Mughal Empire was restored for good.

Before dawn on a winter night an earthquake struck the Wei valley near Huazhou. The loess cliffs, in which great numbers of peasants lived in cave dwellings, collapsed upon them, and the official histories reckoned some 830,000 dead across the provinces of the north, the deadliest earthquake in the human record.

Threatened by the armies of Bayinnaung, King Setthathirath moved the capital of Lan Xang down the Mekong to Vientiane, leaving the Phra Bang at the old capital, which took its name as Luang Prabang. At Vientiane he housed the Emerald Buddha, brought from Chiang Mai, and in 1566 raised the great golden stupa of That Luang.

At the urging of Francis Xavier, who had come to Goa as a Jesuit missionary in 1542, the Inquisition was established there in 1560 to guard the faith of the new converts. It tried New Christians suspected of Jewish practice and converts who kept Hindu rites, and the Hindu temples of Portuguese territory were pulled down. The tribunal was abolished in 1812.

From May to September 1565 Grand Master Jean de Valette, with some six hundred knights and a few thousand Maltese and Spanish soldiers, held the harbor forts of Malta against Suleiman's armada. Fort St. Elmo fell after a month; Birgu and Senglea held through repeated assaults until a Spanish relief force landed and the Turks sailed away. Valletta, the new capital, bears the Grand Master's name.

The sultans of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar buried their quarrels and met the army of Vijayanagara under the aged regent Aliya Rama Raya near Talikota. Rama Raya was captured and beheaded, and his host broke. The victors spent months sacking the City of Victory, burning, levering apart, and hacking at its temples and palaces until it was a ruin.

Miguel Lopez de Legazpi, sent from New Spain by Philip II, after whom the islands had been named, landed at Cebu and founded the first Spanish town in Asia. A soldier found in a burned hut the image of the Holy Child left by Magellan's men, and the Augustinian Andres de Urdaneta sailed north to find the westerly winds that would carry the galleons home to Acapulco.

Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, sent by Philip II to drive the French Huguenots from Fort Caroline, founded St. Augustine on the Florida coast on 8 September 1565, then marched north, took the French fort, and put most of its defenders and their leader Jean Ribault to the sword at the inlet still called Matanzas, 'slaughters.' St. Augustine is the oldest continuously inhabited European town in the continental United States.

Count Nikola Zrinski, former Ban of Croatia, with some 2,300 men held Szigetvár for a month against the last campaign of Suleiman the Magnificent. On 7 September 1566, the fortress in flames, he led the survivors out in a final charge to their deaths. The aged sultan had died in his tent days before, his death concealed from the army, and the Ottoman host turned for home.

On 1 July 1569, under pressure of the long war with Muscovy, the Polish and Lithuanian nobles sealed at Lublin a lasting union of their states into one Commonwealth of Both Nations, with a common king elected by all the nobility and a common Diet. Lithuania's Ukrainian lands passed to the Polish crown, and the Commonwealth was among the largest states of Europe.

Bayinnaung, who styled himself king of kings, took Ayutthaya after a siege of ten months and set Maha Thammarachathirat on its throne as his vassal. His empire, the largest Southeast Asia had ever seen, stretched from Manipur to Lan Xang; yet when he died in 1581 it was held together by little more than his own will.

Having driven Rajah Sulayman from his stockade on the Pasig, Legazpi proclaimed Manila the capital of the Spanish Philippines on 24 June 1571. From 1573 the Manila galleons carried Chinese silk and porcelain to Acapulco and returned with Mexican silver: for the first time the trade of the Americas, Asia, and Europe was joined in one ring around the globe.

In thanksgiving for the birth of a son foretold by the Sufi Shaikh Salim Chishti, Akbar built a red sandstone city on the ridge at Sikri and, after conquering Gujarat, named it Fatehpur, City of Victory. In its House of Worship he heard Muslim divines, Brahmins, Jains, Zoroastrians, and Jesuit fathers dispute. He left it within fifteen years.

Selim II sent an army to take Venetian Cyprus in 1570. Nicosia was stormed and sacked, and Famagusta held out for eleven months under Marcantonio Bragadin until it surrendered on terms in August 1571. Lala Mustafa Pasha broke the terms, slew the Venetian officers, cut off Bragadin's ears, and some days later had him flayed alive. Two months later came Lepanto.

Days after the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to the king's sister, on the night of 23 to 24 August 1572, the court of Charles IX and Catherine de' Medici had the Huguenot leader Admiral Coligny murdered, and the Catholic mob of Paris turned on the Huguenots gathered for the wedding. Some three thousand died in Paris and thousands more in the provinces.

t: Altan Khan Builds the Blue City
x: Altan Khan of the Tümed, who had burned the suburbs of Beijing in 1550, made peace with the Ming in 1571 and was named Prince Shunyi, with horse markets opened along the wall. On the plain below the Yin Mountains he began a walled city, Kökeqota, the Blue City, settled with Chinese farmers and craftsmen, which grew into Hohhot.

The viceroy Francisco de Toledo sent an army into the forests of Vilcabamba, where Inca kings had held out since 1537, captured Tupac Amaru, the last of them, and brought him in chains to Cusco. On 24 September 1572, before a weeping multitude in the great square, the young Inca was beheaded; Toledo then remade the Andes with forced resettlements and the mita labor draft.

In 1570 the Portuguese captain of Ternate had Sultan Hairun stabbed to death when he came to parley in the fortress. His son Babullah swore vengeance, besieged the Portuguese for five years, and starved them out in 1575. Lord of seventy-two islands, Babullah made Ternate the strongest Muslim power of eastern Indonesia, and in 1579 welcomed Francis Drake.

Rana Pratap of Mewar, who alone among the great Rajput princes refused to bow to Akbar, met a Mughal army under the Rajput Man Singh of Amber in the narrow pass of Haldighati. Pratap was driven from the field, his horse Chetak, by legend, dying beneath him, but he fought on from the hills for twenty years and won back much of Mewar.

t: The Battle of the Three Kings
x: King Sebastian of Portugal landed in Morocco to restore the deposed Saadi sultan al-Mutawakkil against his uncle Abd al-Malik. On 4 August 1578 near Ksar el-Kebir the Portuguese army was enveloped and destroyed; all three kings died, Sebastian vanishing in the melee. Abd al-Malik's brother Ahmad al-Mansur grew rich on the ransoms of Portuguese nobles, and Portugal soon passed to Philip II of Spain.

Altan Khan met Sonam Gyatso, head of the Gelug order, in the Kokonor country and gave him the title Dalai Lama, Ocean of Wisdom, while the lama hailed Altan as a reincarnation of Kublai. The title was carried back to his two predecessors, so that Sonam Gyatso became the Third Dalai Lama. The Mongols turned to the Gelug faith, and their swords would one day make it master of Tibet.

Thirteen years after the Iconoclastic Fury and the coming of Alba's Spanish army, Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, and other northern provinces bound themselves at Utrecht on 23 January 1579 in a perpetual union against Philip II, sharing defense and taxes while keeping their own liberties. Two years later they abjured the king, and the union became the Dutch Republic.

Oda Nobunaga, who had seized Kyoto, burned the monastery fortress of Mount Hiei, and broken the Takeda horsemen with massed musketry at Nagashino, lay at the temple of Honnō-ji with a small guard when his general Akechi Mitsuhide turned on him. Nobunaga died in the burning temple. Eleven days later his lieutenant Toyotomi Hideyoshi destroyed Mitsuhide at Yamazaki.

By the bull Inter gravissimas, Pope Gregory XIII reformed the calendar of Julius Caesar, which had drifted ten days from the seasons. In Catholic lands Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October, and the leap day was dropped in three centuries out of four. Protestant countries followed slowly, Britain only in 1752, Russia in 1918.

The Cossack chief Yermak Timofeyevich, hired by the Stroganov merchants with some eight hundred men, crossed the Urals and on the Irtysh defeated the Siberian khan Kuchum, a Shaybanid of the blood of Genghis Khan. In October 1582 he entered the khan's capital, Qashliq. Yermak drowned in the Irtysh in 1585, but Russia's march across Siberia had begun.

Philip II sent some 130 ships under the Duke of Medina Sidonia up the Channel to carry Parma's army to England. Driven from their anchorage at Calais by fireships on the night of 7 August 1588, the Spaniards were mauled off Gravelines by Howard and Drake. Storms wrecked dozens more on the coasts of Scotland and Ireland, and barely half came home.

Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco, coveting the gold of the Sudan, sent some four thousand men, many of them Spanish renegades and Andalusian exiles armed with arquebuses, across the Sahara under the eunuch Judar Pasha. At Tondibi in March 1591 their gunfire scattered the far larger host of Askia Ishaq II; Gao and Timbuktu fell, and the Songhai empire, last of the three great empires of the western Sahel, broke apart.

Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, sultan of Golconda and a poet in the Deccani tongue, founded Hyderabad on the Musi river below his crowded fortress and raised at its heart the Charminar, a triumphal gateway of four minarets. The diamond mines of the Golconda country made it one of the richest cities of Asia.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi, master of all Japan, sent some 150,000 men into Korea on the road, he boasted, to the conquest of Ming China; they took Busan and Hanseong within three weeks. At sea it went otherwise: Admiral Yi Sun-sin lured the Japanese fleet out of the Gyeonnaeryang strait off Hansan Island and destroyed it in a crane-wing formation, cutting the invaders' supply by sea.

Naresuan, the Siamese prince who had grown up a hostage at Pegu and in 1584 renounced allegiance to Burma, met the Burmese crown prince Mingyi Swa at Nong Sarai near Suphan Buri. The two princes fought from the backs of war elephants, and Naresuan cut down his rival with his blade. Siam was free, and Naresuan carried the war into Burma and Cambodia.

Cornelis de Houtman's four ships, after a voyage on which scurvy and fever carried off many of their men, reached the pepper port of Banten in June 1596. Houtman quarreled with the Bantenese and bombarded towns along the coast of Java, and fewer than ninety of his 249 men came home; yet the profit set off a rush of Dutch companies, merged in 1602 into the East India Company.

Hideyoshi, fearing that the missionaries prepared the way for Spanish conquest, had twenty-six Christians, Franciscan friars, Japanese Jesuits, and laymen, three of them boys, marched in winter from Kyoto to Nagasaki. On the hill of Nishizaka they were crucified and pierced with lances, singing psalms. The Church honours them as saints, and their deaths opened half a century of persecution.

Henry IV, the Huguenot king who had turned Catholic to win Paris, ended thirty-six years of religious war with the edict signed at Nantes in April 1598. The Huguenots received freedom of conscience, public worship in named places, equal right to offices, and some hundred fortified towns as surety. The settlement held for nearly ninety years.

t: Shah Abbas Makes Isfahan His Capital
x: Abbas I, who had won back Khorasan from the Uzbeks and remade his army around a corps of slave soldiers taken from Georgia and Armenia, moved his capital to Isfahan in 1598. Around a vast square, the Naqsh-e Jahan, he raised the royal mosque, the mosque of Shaykh Lutfallah, the Ali Qapu palace, and the royal bazaar. Persians said that Isfahan was half the world.

With Hideyoshi dead, the Japanese armies sought to withdraw from Korea. Admiral Yi Sun-sin and the Ming admiral Chen Lin caught the fleet of Shimazu Yoshihiro in the Noryang strait by night and destroyed some two hundred ships. At the height of the fight Yi was struck by a bullet, and with his last breath forbade that his death be announced until the battle was won.

Two years after Hideyoshi's death the great lords divided between Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Western Army raised by Ishida Mitsunari in the name of Hideyoshi's son. In the fog of an autumn morning at Sekigahara the treachery of Kobayakawa Hideaki decided the day for Ieyasu. Three years later he was named shogun, and his house ruled Japan in peace for two and a half centuries.

In the Nine Years' War Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, had beaten the English at the Yellow Ford. When a Spanish army landed at Kinsale, O'Neill and O'Donnell marched the length of Ireland to join it, only to be routed by Lord Mountjoy on Christmas Eve 1601. The Gaelic order of Ulster was broken, and in 1607 its earls sailed into exile.

The Jesuit Matteo Ricci, who had mastered the classics and dressed as a Confucian scholar, was admitted to Beijing with gifts of chiming clocks for the Wanli Emperor. He won converts among the learned, above all the official Xu Guangqi, with whom he translated Euclid into Chinese, and his map of the world showed the Chinese a globe on which China was not the whole.

t: James VI Takes the English Crown
x: When Elizabeth I died childless on 24 March 1603, the crown passed to her cousin James VI of Scotland, great-grandson of Henry VII's daughter Margaret. He rode south to London as James I, and the two kingdoms, enemies for three centuries, shared one king; a century later they would share one Parliament.

Retreating before an Ottoman army in 1604, Shah Abbas laid waste the Armenian borderlands and drove their people south across the Araxes; thousands drowned or died on the march. The merchants of Julfa, famed in the silk trade, were settled at New Julfa outside Isfahan, where they prospered under royal protection and built the Vank Cathedral; their old town was razed.

Guru Arjan, fifth of the Sikh Gurus, completed the Harmandir Sahib in the midst of the pool of Amritsar, open on all four sides to men of every caste, and in 1604 installed there the Adi Granth, the hymns of the Gurus with those of Kabir and other saints. Two years later Jahangir had him put to death at Lahore, the faith's first martyrdom.

In January 1605 the Madrid printer Juan de la Cuesta brought out the first part of The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha, by Miguel de Cervantes, a veteran maimed at Lepanto and for five years a slave of the corsairs in Algiers. The knight of the sorrowful countenance and his squire Sancho Panza rode at once into the affection of all Europe.

Willem Janszoon, sent from Banten in the little ship Duyfken to seek gold in New Guinea, coasted the western shore of Cape York in March 1606, believing it part of New Guinea. His men, the first Europeans known to set foot in Australia, fought with the Aboriginal people, and Janszoon named the farthest point he reached Cape Keerweer, Cape Turnabout.

One hundred and four men and boys of the Virginia Company landed on a marshy peninsula of the James River on 14 May 1607 and built a fort they named for King James. Disease and hunger killed most of them, and the 'starving time' of 1609 and 1610 nearly ended the venture, but John Rolfe's tobacco, first shipped in 1614, gave Virginia its fortune and England its first lasting colony in America.

Samuel de Champlain built a fortified habitation of timber beneath the cliffs where the St. Lawrence narrows, at the place the Algonquins called kebec. Of the twenty-eight men who wintered there only eight survived the scurvy, but Champlain held on, allied himself with the Huron and Algonquin against the Iroquois, and made Quebec the capital of New France.

Turning a telescope of his own making on the heavens from Padua, Galileo Galilei saw the mountains of the moon, the countless stars of the Milky Way, and four moons circling Jupiter, and published them in March 1610 in the Sidereus Nuncius. His later defense of the motion of the earth brought him before the Roman Inquisition in 1633, where he abjured it.

In the Time of Troubles a Polish army had routed the Russians at Klushino in 1610 and occupied the Kremlin. Kuzma Minin, a meat trader of Nizhny Novgorod, raised money and men, and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky led the people's levy to Moscow. In November 1612 the starving Polish garrison surrendered, and the next year an assembly of the land chose Michael Romanov as tsar.

Jesuits driven from Japan opened a mission at Faifo, the port of the Nguyen lords where Japanese and Chinese merchants kept their own quarters. Among those who followed was Alexandre de Rhodes, whose dictionary printed in Rome in 1651 fixed the Latin letters for Vietnamese, the script that the whole nation writes today.

Ngawang Namgyal, a prince-abbot of the Drukpa school, fled Tibet in 1616 after a disputed succession and came south into the valleys of Bhutan. As the Zhabdrung he united the warring valleys, beat back Tibetan invasions, built fortress-monasteries such as Punakha, and gave the land its dual rule of religious and civil chiefs.

On 23 May 1618 Protestant nobles of Bohemia, enraged at breaches of the royal charter of religious liberty, threw two Catholic regents of the emperor and their secretary from a window of Prague Castle. All three survived the fall of some seventy feet. The estates chose the Calvinist Frederick of the Palatinate as king, and the Thirty Years' War began.

Jan Pieterszoon Coen, governor-general of the Dutch East India Company, stormed Jayakarta on 30 May 1619, burned the town, and on its ashes built Batavia, a walled city of canals on the Dutch model. 'Despair not, spare not your enemies,' he wrote; from Batavia the Company would rule the trade of the Indies, and in time the islands themselves, for nearly two hundred years.

Nurhaci, who had united the Jurchen tribes and in 1616 proclaimed the Later Jin, faced four Ming columns marching on his capital. Concentrating his banners against each in turn, he destroyed three of them in five days around Sarhū. Two years later he took Liaoyang and Shenyang, and the Manchu conquest of the northeast had begun.

In late August 1619 an English privateer, the White Lion, put in at Point Comfort and traded 'twenty and odd Negroes,' taken from a Portuguese slave ship bound from Angola to Veracruz, for provisions. They were the first Africans recorded in English North America. That same summer the first representative assembly in English America, the House of Burgesses, met at Jamestown.

t: The Battle of the White Mountain
x: On 8 November 1620 the Catholic League under Tilly and the imperial army routed the army of the Bohemian estates on the White Mountain outside Prague in less than two hours. Frederick, the Winter King, fled. Twenty-seven leaders of the revolt were executed in the Old Town Square, the Protestant nobility was dispossessed, and Bohemia was brought back to the Catholic faith by force.

The Mayflower, carrying 102 passengers, among them Separatists who had fled England for Leiden, made landfall at Cape Cod in November 1620, and before going ashore the men signed the Mayflower Compact, binding themselves into a 'civil body politic.' At Plymouth half of them died in the first winter, but with the help of Squanto and the Wampanoag sachem Massasoit the colony endured.

t: The Conquest of the Banda Islands
x: Determined to hold the world's only source of nutmeg and mace, Coen landed on the Banda Islands with some two thousand men and Japanese mercenaries. Of perhaps fifteen thousand Bandanese only about a thousand remained after war, massacre, starvation, and deportation as slaves to Batavia, and the Company parceled the islands among Dutch planters worked by slaves.

Sent by her brother, the ngola of Ndongo, to treat with the Portuguese governor João Correia de Sousa, Nzinga found no chair set for her and sat upon a kneeling servant to meet him as an equal. She was baptized Ana in Luanda; as queen of Ndongo and then Matamba from 1624 until her death in 1663, she fought the Portuguese for thirty years and allied herself with the Dutch.

For a century the Portuguese fortress on the island of Hormuz had commanded the mouth of the Persian Gulf. In 1622 the army of Shah Abbas, carried and supported by ships of the English East India Company, besieged and took it. Its trade moved to the mainland port that Abbas named Bandar Abbas, and Portuguese power in the Gulf was broken.

In the summer of 1627 Barbary corsairs from Salé and Algiers, among them the Dutch renegade Jan Janszoon, called Murat Reis, sailed as far as Iceland. At Grindavík, in the eastern fjords, and in the Westman Islands they slew dozens and carried off nearly four hundred people to the slave markets of Algiers and Salé. Few were ever ransomed home; Icelanders remember it as the Turkish Abductions.

Sultan Agung of Mataram, master of nearly all Java, sent his armies against the Dutch at Batavia in 1628 and again in 1629. The Javanese dug siegeworks and dammed the river, but the Dutch burned their rice stores along the coast, and famine and disease wasted the besiegers. Coen died of sickness during the second siege, yet Batavia held.

The Company ship Batavia ran onto the reefs of the Houtman Abrolhos in June 1629. While the commander Francisco Pelsaert sailed for Java to fetch help, the undermerchant Jeronimus Cornelisz led a band of mutineers who murdered more than a hundred of the survivors. Pelsaert returned, hanged the ringleaders, and marooned two men on the mainland.

On 20 May 1631 the imperial army of Tilly and Pappenheim stormed Magdeburg, the Protestant city that had defied the emperor. Fire swept the town and soldiers butchered its people; of perhaps 25,000 inhabitants some 20,000 perished, and little but the cathedral stood. Magdeburg quarter became the cry of Protestant soldiers who would give no mercy.

Algerian corsairs under Murat Reis landed at the village of Baltimore in County Cork before dawn on 20 June 1631 and carried off over a hundred English settlers and Irish villagers, men, women, and children. Most lived out their lives as slaves in Algiers, the women in harems and the men at the oars of the galleys; only two or three ever saw home again.

Victor at Breitenfeld the year before, Gustavus Adolphus met Wallenstein's army near Lützen on 16 November 1632, in fog and gunsmoke. Leading a cavalry charge, the king was lost in the mist and shot dead. His men fought on and drove Wallenstein from the field, but the Protestant cause had lost its champion, and Sweden passed to his daughter Christina, not yet six.

When his empress Mumtaz Mahal died bearing their fourteenth child in 1631, Shah Jahan began on the Yamuna at Agra a tomb of white marble inlaid with precious stones. Some twenty thousand workmen laboured on it for two decades, and the domed mausoleum in its garden became the crown of Mughal architecture.

Hong Taiji, son of Nurhaci, having won the imperial seal of the Yuan from the heirs of Ligdan Khan of the Chahar, renamed his people Manchu and his dynasty Qing, the Pure, and took the title of emperor at Mukden. That winter his armies overran Joseon, and King Injo knelt to him at Samjeondo. The Ming now faced a rival empire beyond the wall.

Having expelled the Jesuits, whose Latin rites his father Susenyos had imposed at the cost of civil war, the emperor Fasilides ended the wandering of the royal camp and founded a fixed capital at Gondar, north of Lake Tana. There he and his heirs raised castles of stone with battlements and towers and dozens of churches; Gondar remained the capital for more than two centuries.

In 1597 the Zaydi imam al-Qasim ibn Muhammad raised the northern tribes against the Ottoman governors of Yemen, and his son al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad drove the last Turkish garrisons from the Tihama and out by the port of Mocha in 1636. The Qasimid imams ruled all Yemen and grew rich on the coffee that Mocha shipped to Cairo, Constantinople, and Europe.

Living quietly in the Dutch Republic, the French philosopher René Descartes published at Leiden in 1637 his Discourse on Method, resolving to doubt all that could be doubted and finding certainty in the thinking self: 'I think, therefore I am.' With it he published his geometry, joining algebra to the figures of Euclid.

Crushed by taxes and persecuted for their faith, the peasants and masterless samurai of Shimabara and Amakusa, most of them Christians, rose under the youth Amakusa Shirō and held the ruined castle of Hara against a shogunal army of over a hundred thousand. When it fell, the defenders were slaughtered almost to a man. The shogunate expelled the Portuguese and closed Japan to the world.

Murad IV, a sultan of iron severity, retook Baghdad from the Persians in December 1638 after a siege of forty days. The next May the two empires made peace at Zuhab near Qasr-e Shirin: Mesopotamia remained Ottoman, the Caucasus was divided, and the frontier drawn along the Zagros endures in substance as the border of Iran with Turkey and Iraq.

After a siege of five months, in which plague and hunger wasted the defenders, the Dutch East India Company, with the help of Johor, took Malacca from the Portuguese on 14 January 1641. The city that had been the emporium of the East sank into a quiet Dutch outpost, its trade drawn away to Batavia.

Abel Tasman, sent from Batavia by Anthony van Diemen to find the Great South Land, sighted Tasmania in November 1642 and named it Van Diemen's Land. In December he raised the mountains of the South Island of New Zealand; at Golden Bay Maori canoes rammed his ship's boat and killed four seamen, and Tasman sailed away without landing.

t: Güshi Khan Crowns the Great Fifth
x: Güshi Khan of the Khoshut Mongols, called in by the Gelug church, overthrew the Tsangpa king Karma Tenkyong at Shigatse and laid the rule of all Tibet at the feet of the Fifth Dalai Lama. The Great Fifth made Lhasa his capital, and in 1645 began the Potala Palace on the Red Hill, the seat of the Dalai Lamas for three centuries.

t: The Duke of Enghien at Rocroi
x: On 19 May 1643, five days after the death of Louis XIII, the twenty-one-year-old Duke of Enghien, later the Great Condé, met the Spanish army of Flanders before Rocroi. His cavalry swept the field, and the famed Spanish infantry, the tercios, were broken by French guns and charges. The long ascendancy of Spanish arms was over.

The rebel Li Zicheng broke into Beijing, and the Chongzhen Emperor, last of the Ming, hanged himself on Coal Hill behind the palace. The Ming general Wu Sangui, guarding the Shanhai Pass, opened the gate of the Great Wall to the Manchus, and together they routed Li Zicheng. The regent Dorgon entered Beijing and set the boy Shunzhi Emperor on the throne of China.

After five years of negotiation at Münster and Osnabrück, the treaties signed in October 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War, which had cost Germany perhaps a fifth to a third of its people. Calvinists won recognition, and the princes of the Empire their sovereignty in all but name; Sweden and France took German lands, and the independence of the Dutch and the Swiss was confirmed. A new order of sovereign states began.

Bohdan Khmelnytsky, a Cossack officer wronged by a Polish noble, allied with the Crimean Tatars and in May 1648 destroyed the Commonwealth's armies at Zhovti Vody and Korsun, taking both hetmans captive. Ukraine rose in a war of great savagery against Polish lords, Catholic priests, and Jews, many thousands of whom were slain. In 1654 at Pereyaslav the Cossacks swore allegiance to the tsar.

Beaten at Naseby and handed over by the Scots, Charles I was tried by a High Court of Justice of Parliament's making and condemned as a tyrant, traitor, and murderer. On 30 January 1649 he stepped from a window of the Banqueting House onto a scaffold in Whitehall and died with dignity, and a groan went up from the crowd. England was declared a Commonwealth.

The Dutch West India Company had held the sugar coast of Pernambuco since 1630, but the Portuguese planters rose against it in 1645, and on the hills of Guararapes south of Recife their army of Portuguese, Indians under Felipe Camarão, and black soldiers under Henrique Dias twice routed the Dutch, in 1648 and 1649. Besieged in Recife, the Dutch surrendered in January 1654.

The Ya'rubi imam Sultan ibn Saif, heir to his kinsman Nasir ibn Murshid's war to unite the tribes of Oman, drove the Portuguese from Muscat in January 1650. The Omanis built a fleet of their own and carried the war down the coast of East Africa, where in 1698 they took Fort Jesus at Mombasa after a siege of nearly three years and founded an Omani empire on the Swahili coast.

Jan van Riebeeck landed below Table Mountain with some ninety men of the Dutch East India Company to build a fort and garden to provision the fleets bound for the Indies. Free burghers soon took land along the Liesbeek River, slaves were brought from Angola, Madagascar, India, and the Indies, and after two wars with the Khoikhoi and the smallpox of 1713 the colony spread inland.

After a siege of seven months the Dutch East India Company, allied with King Rajasinha II of Kandy, took Colombo from the Portuguese in May 1656, and by 1658 had driven them from Jaffna and the whole island. The king of Kandy, who had hoped to recover the coast, kept only the highlands, and the Company held the cinnamon lands for nearly a century and a half.

Bijapur sent its general Afzal Khan to crush Shivaji, a young Maratha chief who had been seizing its hill forts. The two met alone beneath the fort of Pratapgad; by the Maratha account Afzal Khan clasped Shivaji in an embrace and struck, and Shivaji, wearing mail beneath his coat and steel claws on his hand, tore him open. The Bijapuri army was then ambushed and destroyed.

Zheng Chenggong, called Koxinga, son of a Fujianese merchant-pirate and a Japanese mother and the last great champion of the Ming, failed before Nanjing in 1659 and turned to Taiwan. After a nine-month siege the Dutch governor Frederick Coyett surrendered Fort Zeelandia. Koxinga died months later, but his house ruled the island until 1683.

Four English frigates under Colonel Richard Nicolls appeared off New Amsterdam in August 1664, sent by James, Duke of York, to whom his brother Charles II had granted the lands between the Connecticut and the Delaware. Peter Stuyvesant, peg-legged and defiant, wished to fight, but the burghers would not, and the town surrendered without a shot and took the duke's name.

King António I of Kongo, resolved to check the Portuguese on his borders, met an army of Portuguese musketeers and their African auxiliaries at Mbwila. He was killed and beheaded, and his head was carried to Luanda and buried in the chapel of Our Lady of Nazareth. Kongo dissolved into decades of civil war among rival claimants; its capital, São Salvador, sacked in 1678, lay deserted until 1709.

Starting in a baker's shop in Pudding Lane in the early hours of 2 September 1666, a fire driven by an east wind burned for four days, consuming some 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches, and St. Paul's Cathedral. From the ashes Christopher Wren raised a new St. Paul's and fifty-one city churches.

Sabbatai Zevi of Smyrna, hailed by Jewish communities from Yemen to Amsterdam as the Messiah, sailed for Constantinople in 1666 and was arrested. Brought before the court of Mehmed IV at Edirne in September and given the choice of death or Islam, he put on the turban and took the name Aziz Mehmed Efendi. The movement collapsed in grief and shame, though a remnant, the Dönme, followed him.

For half a century Arakanese and Portuguese corsairs sailing from Chittagong had raided the rivers of Bengal, carrying off its peasants by the thousand to be sold as slaves or set to work in the rice fields of Arakan. Shaista Khan, Mughal governor of Bengal, built a war fleet, won over the Portuguese, and in 1666 took Chittagong from the king of Mrauk U.

The sultanate of Gowa at Makassar, a cosmopolitan Muslim port that defied the Dutch spice monopoly, fell to the Company admiral Cornelis Speelman and his Bugis ally Arung Palakka of Bone. By the treaty signed at Bongaya Sultan Hasanuddin, the Rooster of the East, yielded his forts and his trade; the great brick fortress of Somba Opu fell to storm in 1669.

The Jesuit Diego Luis de San Vitores landed on Guam in 1668 and began the mission to the Chamorro people. He was killed in 1672 by the chief Mata'pang, whose infant daughter he had baptized, and Spanish soldiers then waged a long war on the islands. War and the diseases of Europe cut the Chamorros from tens of thousands to fewer than four thousand by 1710.

In 1669 Aurangzeb ordered his governors to demolish the schools and temples of the infidels. That year the Vishvanath temple of Benares was pulled down and a mosque raised on its plinth, and in 1670 the great Keshava Deva temple of Mathura. In 1679 he reimposed the jizya, the poll tax on non-Muslims that Akbar had abolished.

When a Mughal army and fleet under Raja Ram Singh came up the Brahmaputra to reconquer Guwahati, the Ahom general Lachit Borphukan, gravely ill, had himself carried into a boat to lead the attack. In the narrows at Saraighat the Ahom boats broke the Mughal fleet, and the Mughals never again pushed far up the valley of Assam.

Ismail ibn Sharif, second sultan of the Alawite dynasty, made Meknes his capital from 1672 and spent his fifty-five-year reign building palaces, granaries, and stables behind miles of walls. The work was done by Christian captives taken by the corsairs of Salé and by the black slave army, the Abid al-Bukhari, which he raised to rule Morocco without depending on the tribes.

t: The Revolt of the Three Feudatories
x: When the young Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish their princedoms, Wu Sangui, the general who had let the Manchus through the wall, rose in Yunnan, joined by the feudatories of Fujian and Guangdong. For eight years the south was at war. Wu proclaimed himself emperor before he died in 1678, and by 1681 Kangxi had crushed the revolt and was master of all China.

On 6 June 1674, at his mountain capital of Raigad, Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati, lord of the royal umbrella, by the Brahmin Gaga Bhatt of Benares, weighed against gold, and enthroned as a sovereign Hindu king. He went on to conquer the Carnatic as far as Gingee and left at his death in 1680 a kingdom the Mughals could never subdue.

t: The Martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur
x: Guru Tegh Bahadur, ninth of the Sikh Gurus, took up the cause of the Kashmiri Brahmins who were being pressed to convert, and was arrested and beheaded at Chandni Chowk in Delhi on Aurangzeb's orders when he refused to embrace Islam. The gurdwara of Sis Ganj marks the spot. His son Gobind was not yet nine years old.

Popé, a Tewa medicine man flogged by the Spaniards for sorcery, sent runners bearing knotted cords to the pueblos, and on 10 August 1680 the Pueblo peoples rose together, killing some four hundred settlers and twenty-one Franciscan friars and burning the churches. They besieged Santa Fe and drove the survivors south to El Paso; the Spaniards did not return until Diego de Vargas's reconquest of 1692.

On 6 May 1682 Louis XIV made Versailles, his father's hunting lodge transformed by Le Vau, Le Brun, Le Nôtre, and Hardouin-Mansart into the grandest palace in Europe, the seat of his court and government. Thousands of nobles lived there under the king's eye, bound by an etiquette that turned the warrior aristocracy of France into courtiers.

René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, having come down from the Illinois country by canoe with a small party of Frenchmen and Indians, reached the Gulf of Mexico on 9 April 1682, raised a column with the arms of France, and claimed the whole basin of the Mississippi for Louis XIV under the name of Louisiana. New France now arched from the St. Lawrence to the Gulf.

On 18 October 1685 Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, ordering Protestant churches pulled down and pastors banished, after years of dragonnades in which soldiers were quartered on Huguenot families until they converted. Some two hundred thousand Huguenots fled, defying the law, to England, Holland, Prussia, and the Cape, carrying their skills and their grievance with them.

On 2 September 1686, after a siege of eleven weeks, the armies of the Holy League under Charles of Lorraine stormed Buda, held by the Turks for 145 years. Its defender, Abdurrahman Abdi Pasha, fell on the walls. Within thirteen years all Hungary save the Banat of Temesvár had been won back for the Habsburgs.

In July 1687 the Royal Society published, at Edmond Halley's expense, Isaac Newton's Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. From three laws of motion and a single law of universal gravitation the Cambridge professor deduced the orbits of the planets, the paths of comets, and the tides of the sea. The heavens and the earth obeyed one law, and the Age of Reason took the book as its model.

Having taken Bijapur in 1686, Aurangzeb laid siege to Golconda, the last of the Deccan sultanates. Its walls held for eight months against mines and assaults, until a bribed officer opened a postern gate by night. Abul Hasan Qutb Shah was carried off to captivity at Daulatabad, and the Mughal Empire reached its widest bounds.

t: William of Orange Lands at Torbay
x: Invited by seven leading Englishmen who dreaded a Catholic dynasty after the birth of a son to James II, William of Orange, the king's nephew and son-in-law, landed at Torbay on 5 November 1688 with a Dutch army. James's army melted away and he fled to France. Parliament gave the crown to William and Mary with a Bill of Rights, and the Glorious Revolution made Parliament supreme.

King Narai of Ayutthaya had welcomed French embassies and Jesuits and raised the Greek adventurer Constantine Phaulkon to be his chief minister, while French troops held Bangkok and Mergui. As Narai lay dying at Lopburi, the Master of the Elephants, Phetracha, seized power, had Phaulkon beheaded, and besieged the French until they sailed away.

After Qing armies twice besieged the Russian fort of Albazin on the Amur, the envoys of Kangxi and of the Tsars met at Nerchinsk, the Jesuits Thomas Pereira and Jean-François Gerbillon interpreting in Latin. Russia gave up the Amur valley, and the frontier was fixed along the Argun and the Stanovoy mountains: the first treaty China made with a European power.

Sambhaji, Shivaji's son and successor, was surprised and captured by Mughal troops at Sangameshwar. Brought before Aurangzeb, he refused to yield his forts or embrace Islam, and after weeks of torture he was hacked to death at Tulapur. His brother Rajaram escaped to Gingee in the far south, and the Marathas fought on without a capital.

On 24 August 1690 Job Charnock, agent of the East India Company, landed at Sutanuti on the Hooghly and set up a factory among three villages, Sutanuti, Kalikata, and Gobindapur. Fortified as Fort William a few years later, Calcutta grew into the capital of British India and the second city of the British Empire.

On 1 July 1690 William III forced the crossing of the Boyne against his father-in-law James II and his Irish and French army. James fled to France, and William entered Dublin. The Treaty of Limerick the following year ended the war and left Ireland under a Protestant ascendancy for two centuries.

Bandeirantes from São Paulo, ranging the interior for slaves and treasure, struck gold in the streams of the highlands that came to be called Minas Gerais, the General Mines. A rush of Portuguese and of African slaves followed; for much of the eighteenth century Brazil was the greatest gold producer on earth, and Vila Rica, now Ouro Preto, rose in baroque splendor with churches carved by the sculptor Aleijadinho.

For most of the seventeenth century runaway slaves held Palmares, a league of fortified villages in the hills of Alagoas that numbered many thousands and beat off expedition after expedition. In 1694 bandeirantes under Domingos Jorge Velho stormed its citadel on the Serra da Barriga; its last war leader, Zumbi, was betrayed and killed on 20 November 1695, and his head was displayed in Recife.

The Dzungar khan Galdan had overrun the Khalkha Mongols, who fled to the protection of the Qing. The Kangxi Emperor led three armies across the Gobi in person, and at Jao Modo, near the Tuul River, his general Fiyanggū routed Galdan's army with cannon; Galdan's wife fell in the battle. Galdan died a fugitive the next year, and Outer Mongolia passed under the Qing.

For more than a century and a half after the conquest of Yucatán, the Itza Maya held their island capital of Nojpetén in Lake Petén Itzá, keeping their books and gods and turning away the friars. On 13 March 1697 Martín de Urzúa y Arizmendi attacked by water with a galley built on the lake and took the city; the king Kan Ek' was captured, and the last independent Maya kingdom was no more.

On 11 September 1697 Prince Eugene of Savoy caught the army of Sultan Mustafa II in the act of crossing the Tisza at Zenta and attacked at once, though the day was late. Some 25,000 Turks were killed or drowned, the Grand Vizier among them, for the loss of a few hundred imperial troops. At Karlowitz in 1699 the sultan yielded Hungary and Transylvania.

After a siege of thirty-three months, in which plague and hunger reduced the Portuguese garrison to a handful, the Arabs of Oman under the imam Saif ibn Sultan stormed Fort Jesus, the great bastion the Portuguese had built at Mombasa in 1593. Portuguese power north of Mozambique was broken, and the Swahili coast passed under the lordship of Oman.

t: Nguyen Huu Canh Organizes Gia Dinh
x: The Nguyen lord Nguyen Phuc Chu sent his general Nguyen Huu Canh to bring order to the Mekong lands, where Vietnamese settlers and Chinese refugees loyal to the Ming had long been moving among the Khmer. Canh set up the prefecture of Gia Dinh about the Khmer town of Prey Nokor, the future Saigon, and the delta passed step by step from Cambodia to Vietnam.

After the defeat before Vienna and sixteen years of war with the Holy League, ending in Prince Eugene's victory at Zenta, the Ottomans signed peace at Karlowitz on 26 January 1699. Hungary and Transylvania went to Austria, the Morea to Venice, and Podolia to Poland. For the first time the empire of the sultans yielded great provinces by treaty, and its long retreat from Europe began.

At the spring festival of Baisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh asked before a great assembly at Anandpur who would give his head for the faith. Five men stepped forward, and with them he founded the Khalsa, the order of the pure, baptized with sweetened water stirred by a double-edged sword, bound to keep the five Ks and to bear arms.

Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Johor, last of the line of Malacca, was a youth of savage cruelty who, the chronicles say, had the pregnant wife of the noble Megat Sri Rama cut open for eating a jackfruit from the royal garden. Megat Sri Rama stabbed the sultan as he was borne to Friday prayers, and the bendahara Abdul Jalil took the throne.
