On 30 November 1700 Charles XII of Sweden, eighteen years old, attacked Peter the Great's army besieging Narva with some 10,000 men against more than three times as many. Under cover of a blinding snowstorm the Swedes broke through the Russian lines, and the Russian army dissolved. Peter learned his lesson and rebuilt his army; Charles turned to Poland.

Osei Tutu, king of Kumasi, united the Akan chiefdoms of the forest and broke their overlords of Denkyira at the battle of Feyiase. Tradition tells that his priest Okomfo Anokye called down from the sky a stool of gold that held the soul of the Asante nation; the union grew into an empire that sold gold and captives to the Europeans on the coast for two centuries.

On 18 January 1701 Frederick III, Elector of Brandenburg, crowned himself at Königsberg as Frederick I, King in Prussia, with the consent of the emperor, bought by the promise of troops for the coming war with France. Prussia, a duchy outside the Empire, gave the Hohenzollerns the royal title on which they would build a great power.

On 27 May 1703, on land newly taken from Sweden at the mouth of the Neva, Peter the Great laid the foundations of the fortress of St. Peter and St. Paul on Hare Island. Built in the marshes by conscripted laborers, thousands of whom died, the new city became Russia's capital in 1712, its window on Europe.

On 13 August 1704 the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene, having marched from the Netherlands to the Danube, fell on the French and Bavarian army at Blenheim. Marshal Tallard was taken, and some 30,000 of his men were killed, wounded, or captured. Vienna was saved, Bavaria knocked out of the war, and the legend of Louis XIV's invincible armies broken.

t: The Union of England and Scotland
x: On 16 January 1707 the Scottish Parliament ratified the Treaty of Union, amid the riots of the Edinburgh mob, many members swayed by compensation for the losses of the Darien scheme. On 1 May the kingdom of Great Britain came into being, with one Parliament at Westminster, while Scotland kept its own Church and its own law.

Aurangzeb died at Ahmadnagar in his eighty-ninth year, after a quarter century of war in the Deccan against the Marathas, leaving the treasury drained and the empire seething with revolt. His sons fought for the throne, and within a generation the governors of Bengal, Awadh, and the Deccan were masters in all but name. He was buried in a plain grave near Ellora.

Sourigna Vongsa, the great king of Lan Xang, had put his only son to death for adultery and died without an heir in 1694. Rival princes split the realm into the kingdoms of Luang Prabang and Vientiane in 1707, and Champasak broke away in 1713. Divided, the Lao fell under Siam, whose general Chakri took Vientiane and its Emerald Buddha in 1779.

Charles XII, marching on Moscow, had turned south into Ukraine to join the Cossack hetman Ivan Mazepa. On 8 July 1709, wounded and carried in a litter, he flung his winter-wasted and hungry army against Peter's redoubts at Poltava. The Swedes were destroyed, the survivors surrendered at Perevolochna, and Charles fled to the Turks. Russia had replaced Sweden as the power of the North.

Mirwais Hotak, chief of the Ghilzai Pashtuns, chafed under the Georgian prince Gurgin Khan, whom the Safavid shah had set over Kandahar. In April 1709, while the governor's troops were away, he had him slain at a feast outside the city and seized Kandahar. The Persian armies sent to recover it were beaten, and his son Mahmud would carry the war to Isfahan itself.

The treaties signed at Utrecht in April 1713 ended the War of the Spanish Succession. Louis XIV's grandson kept Spain and the Indies as Philip V, on condition that the French and Spanish crowns never unite; Austria would take the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, and Naples; Britain won Gibraltar, Minorca, and the slave-trading contract to Spanish America; and Savoy received Sicily with a royal crown.

In 1717 a Dzungar army had stormed Lhasa, killed the Khoshut king Lha-bzang Khan, and plundered the monasteries. Three years later two Qing armies drove them out and escorted the young Seventh Dalai Lama, Kelzang Gyatso, to the Potala. The Kangxi Emperor left a garrison in Lhasa, and from 1727 two imperial residents, the ambans, watched over Tibet for the Qing.

Each December fleets of praus from Makassar rode the northwest monsoon to the coast of Arnhem Land, which they called Marege, to gather and cure the sea cucumber prized in China. For nearly two centuries they traded cloth, metal, and tobacco with the Yolngu and their neighbors, leaving tamarind trees and Macassan words behind, until Australian law shut them out in 1907.

The Norwegian Lutheran pastor Hans Egede sailed to Greenland in 1721 to seek the descendants of the old Norse colonists and bring them the Reformation, but found only the Inuit, to whom he preached instead. In 1728 he founded Godthåb, now Nuuk; his mission and the Danish trading posts that followed made Greenland a colony of Denmark-Norway.

Mahmud Hotak with some twenty thousand Afghans routed a far larger Persian army at Gulnabad on 8 March 1722 and laid siege to Isfahan. Through the summer the capital starved; its people ate dogs, rats, and at last the dead. On 23 October Shah Sultan Husayn came out and set the royal plume on Mahmud's turban. The Safavid order was destroyed, and Russia and the Ottomans fell upon Persia's provinces.

t: The Years of the Barefoot Flight
x: In the spring of 1723 the Dzungar Oirats, Buddhist Mongols of the Ili valley, fell upon the Kazakh hordes and drove them in panic from their pastures, taking Turkestan and Tashkent. The Kazakhs remember it as the Years of the Great Disaster and of the Barefoot Flight. In the 1730s the khans of the Junior and Middle Hordes sought the protection of the Russian empress.

King Agaja of Dahomey, having conquered Allada in 1724, fell upon Savi and the port of Ouidah and drove King Huffon of Hueda into the lagoons. Dahomey now held a coast on the Bight of Benin, and its kings, with their famed regiments of women soldiers, became for a century and more great sellers of captives to the Atlantic slave ships.

The cavalry of the Oyo empire, greatest power of the Yoruba, had ridden into Dahomey again and again since 1726, laying waste the country while its people hid in the bush. In 1730 Agaja bought peace with an annual tribute, and Dahomey remained Oyo's tributary for nearly a century, until King Gezo threw off the yoke in the 1820s.

t: Nader Shah Crowned on the Mughan Plain
x: Nader Qoli, an Afshar Turkmen of Khorasan who had driven the Afghans from Persia and the Ottomans from the Caucasus in the name of the Safavids, summoned the notables of the realm to the Mughan plain and in March 1736 had himself proclaimed shah. Three years later he sacked Delhi and carried home the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.

t: Baji Rao Humbles the Nizam at Bhopal
x: Baji Rao I, the Peshwa who had led the Maratha horse from the Deccan to the gates of Delhi in 1737, surrounded the army of the Nizam of Hyderabad at Bhopal and starved it into terms. By the convention of Doraha the Nizam pledged to win from the emperor the cession of Malwa to the Marathas, who now made and unmade the powers of northern India.

Nadir Shah of Persia routed the Mughal army at Karnal and entered Delhi as the guest of the emperor Muhammad Shah. When a riot killed some of his soldiers, he drew his sword in the Sunehri mosque and gave the order; in a single day some twenty thousand or more of the people were slaughtered. He left with the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor, and the hoarded wealth of the Mughals.

Seven months after coming to the throne, Frederick II of Prussia marched into the Habsburg province of Silesia in December 1740, as the young Maria Theresa struggled to secure her inheritance. His victory at Mollwitz the next spring kept it. The rich province gave Prussia the weight of a great power and began the long rivalry of Hohenzollern and Habsburg for Germany.

t: The Massacre of the Chinese at Batavia
x: Fearing a rising of the Chinese sugar workers in the countryside, whom the Company had threatened with deportation to Ceylon, Governor-General Adriaan Valckenier let soldiers and townsfolk loose on the Chinese quarter of Batavia in October 1740. Some ten thousand were slaughtered. The survivors joined a war across Java that drew in Mataram and ended in the Company's greater mastery.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, a preacher from Uyayna who condemned the veneration of saints and tombs as idolatry, was received in 1744 by Muhammad ibn Saud, emir of the oasis of Diriyah. Each swore to uphold the other: the emir would wage holy war for the reformer's doctrine, and the reformer would sanctify the emir's rule. The alliance of the two houses still governs Arabia.

t: The Last Battle of the Jacobites
x: Charles Edward Stuart, the Young Pretender, had raised the Highland clans in 1745, taken Edinburgh, and marched as far as Derby. Retreating, his tired and hungry army was destroyed on Culloden Moor on 16 April 1746 by the Duke of Cumberland's guns and bayonets. Many wounded were killed where they lay, and the clan system of the Highlands was broken by law.

After Nadir Shah was murdered in his tent, the Afghan chiefs met in council near Kandahar and chose Ahmad Khan Abdali, commander of Nadir's Afghan cavalry and not yet thirty, as their king. Taking the title Durr-i-Durran, pearl of pearls, he built the Durrani Empire from Khurasan to Kashmir and the Punjab, and is honoured as the father of Afghanistan.

In 1751 Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert published at Paris the first volume of the Encyclopédie, a reasoned dictionary of the sciences, arts, and trades. Its seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates, written by Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu, and a host of others, carried the reasoning and the skepticism of the Enlightenment across Europe in spite of royal and papal bans.

When the Mon of the restored kingdom of Pegu sacked Ava and ended the Toungoo dynasty, Aung Zeya, headman of the village of Moksobo, refused to submit, raised the Burmans of the upper country, and took the royal name Alaungpaya, the future Buddha. Within eight years he had reconquered Burma, destroyed Pegu, and renamed the delta village of Dagon as Yangon, the End of Strife; his Konbaung dynasty ruled until the British came.

After years of war over the succession of Mataram, the Dutch Company divided the realm of Sultan Agung by the Treaty of Giyanti. Pakubuwono III kept Surakarta, while his uncle and rival Mangkubumi became Sultan Hamengkubuwono I of Yogyakarta. The two courts, rivals in ceremony and dance, remained the guardians of Javanese high culture.

Robert Clive, with some three thousand men, a third of them European, met the army of Siraj ud-Daulah, nawab of Bengal, fifty thousand strong, in a mango grove at Plassey. Rain soaked the nawab's powder while the British kept theirs dry, and Mir Jafar, the nawab's commander bought by the Company, held his troops aloof. Siraj fled and was murdered; the East India Company became master of Bengal.

The Qianlong Emperor, called in by the Dzungar prince Amursana, conquered the Dzungar Khanate in 1755, and when Amursana rose against him he ordered the nation destroyed. Qing soldiers, smallpox, and famine killed the greater part of the Dzungar people, and by 1759 the Qing held the oases of the Tarim as well. The new conquests came to be called Xinjiang, the New Frontier.

A month after routing the French at Rossbach, Frederick II faced an Austrian army nearly twice his size at Leuthen on 5 December 1757. Screened by low hills, his columns marched across the Austrian front and fell on its left flank in oblique order, rolling up the whole line. That night the Prussian army sang the hymn 'Now thank we all our God.'

In the night of 12 to 13 September 1759, General James Wolfe's army climbed a goat path up the cliffs above the St. Lawrence and formed on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec. The Marquis de Montcalm attacked, and in a quarter of an hour the British volleys broke the French line; both generals were mortally wounded, Quebec surrendered, and the Treaty of Paris of 1763 gave Canada to Britain.

The Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau, marching north to defend Delhi, was penned at Panipat by Ahmad Shah Durrani and starved for weeks. On 14 January 1761 it attacked and was destroyed; the Peshwa's son Vishwasrao and the Bhau fell, and tens of thousands of soldiers and camp followers were slaughtered or carried into slavery in the pursuit. The Maratha drive to rule all India was broken.

In the Seven Years' War a British fleet from Madras under Admiral Samuel Cornish and General William Draper stormed Manila in October 1762. Archbishop Manuel Rojo, the acting governor, surrendered the city, but Simon de Anda withdrew to Bacolor in Pampanga and kept up the war in the provinces. Confined to Manila, the British handed it back in 1764.

On 9 July 1762 the guards regiments of St. Petersburg, led by the Orlov brothers, proclaimed Peter III's German-born wife Catherine empress; the unloved tsar, who had made peace with Frederick the Great, abdicated and within days was dead at Ropsha. Catherine the Great reigned thirty-four years and added the Crimea, the Black Sea coast, and the larger share of Poland to the empire.

t: Ahmad Shah Blows Up the Harmandir
x: Returning to the Punjab, Ahmad Shah Durrani caught the Sikh fighters and their families near Kup in February 1762 and slew many thousands in a single day, remembered as the Vadda Ghallughara, the Great Massacre. He then blew up the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar with gunpowder and filled its sacred pool with refuse. The Sikhs rebuilt it within a few years.

Mir Qasim, the deposed nawab of Bengal, joined Shuja ud-Daula of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II against the Company. At Buxar on the Ganges Major Hector Munro, with about seven thousand men, routed their forty thousand. The emperor came over to the British, and the next year at Allahabad granted the Company the diwani, the right to collect the revenue of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

Karim Khan, a chief of the Zand tribe of the Zagros, emerged from the wars after Nader Shah's murder as master of all Persia but Khorasan. Refusing the title of shah, he ruled as vakil, the regent, from Shiraz, where he built a citadel, a bazaar, and a great mosque. His reign was remembered as the gentlest that Persia knew in the eighteenth century.

After a siege of fourteen months, the armies of Hsinbyushin of Burma stormed Ayutthaya on 7 April 1767. The city of four centuries was burned, its temples stripped of their gold, its king Ekkathat dead, and tens of thousands carried off to Burma. Yet within months a general of Chinese descent, Taksin, had gathered an army in the southeast to win Siam back.

Samuel Wallis in HMS Dolphin, the first European to reach Tahiti, anchored in Matavai Bay in June 1767 after a battle with the islanders' canoes. Bougainville followed in 1768 and called the island New Cythera, and in 1769 James Cook observed the transit of Venus from its shore; Tahiti became in European eyes the image of an earthly paradise.

t: The Jesuits Expelled from the Missions
x: By order of Charles III the Society of Jesus was expelled from all the Spanish dominions in 1767, and the next year the last Jesuits left the thirty Guaraní missions of the Paraná and Uruguay rivers, where for a century and a half the fathers had gathered some hundred thousand Indians into towns of stone churches, workshops, and choirs, and armed them against the slave raiders of São Paulo. Without them the missions decayed.

Prithvi Narayan Shah, king of the hill state of Gorkha, had blockaded the rich Malla kingdoms of the Kathmandu valley for years. During the festival of Indra Jatra in 1768 his troops entered Kathmandu, and Patan and Bhaktapur fell soon after. He made Kathmandu the capital of a united Nepal, which he called a yam between two boulders, China and the Company.

Four times between 1765 and 1769 the Qianlong Emperor sent armies into Burma, and four times they were broken in the hills and fevers of the frontier; the commander Mingrui perished in 1768. At Kaungton the Burmese general Maha Thiha Thura trapped the last host and, against the wishes of his king, let it go home under a truce.

After the rains failed in 1769, famine swept Bengal and Bihar. The Company's servants, newly masters of the revenue, kept up their collections, and hoarders of grain made fortunes. Warren Hastings reckoned that a third of the people perished, perhaps ten million souls, and great stretches of the delta fell back into jungle.

Cook, having charted New Zealand, came upon the unknown east coast of Australia and anchored in April 1770 in a bay Joseph Banks found so rich in plants that it was named Botany Bay. Sailing north, Cook nearly lost his ship on the Great Barrier Reef, and on Possession Island in August claimed the whole eastern coast for George III.

Three brothers of Tay Son village, Nguyen Nhac, Nguyen Hue, and Nguyen Lu, rose against the corrupt regent of the Nguyen lords, promising to take from the rich and give to the poor. They seized Quy Nhon in 1773, and when the Trinh invaded from the north the Nguyen house was crushed between them; by 1777 only the youth Nguyen Anh survived.

On 5 August 1772 Russia, Prussia, and Austria signed at St. Petersburg a treaty taking nearly a third of the lands of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, whose liberum veto and foreign intrigues had left it defenseless. Frederick the Great took West Prussia, joining his scattered domains; of Maria Theresa he said that she wept, but she took.

After crushing defeats on land and sea, Sultan Abdul Hamid I made peace with Catherine the Great at Küçük Kaynarca on 21 July 1774. The Crimean Khanate, Muslim and an Ottoman vassal for three centuries, was declared independent, Russia gained ports on the Black Sea, and the empress won a right to speak for the Orthodox Christians of the sultan's realm. Russia annexed the Crimea in 1783.

Meeting in the State House at Philadelphia, the Second Continental Congress voted on 2 July 1776 that the thirteen colonies were free and independent states, and on 4 July adopted the Declaration drafted by Thomas Jefferson, which held that all men are created equal and endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights. It founded the first great modern republic, and its words echoed through every revolution that followed.

Cook, who had come upon the Hawaiian Islands in 1778, returned to Kealakekua Bay during the Makahiki festival and was received with the highest honors. Forced back weeks later by a broken mast, his men quarreled with the islanders over a stolen boat, and on 14 February 1779 Cook was killed on the shore while trying to take the chief Kalaniopuu hostage.

t: The Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II
x: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a mestizo cacique and muleteer descended from the last Inca, took the name Túpac Amaru II, seized and hanged the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga at Tinta in November 1780, and raised the southern Andes against the forced sale of goods and the mita. Captured in 1781, he was made to watch the execution of his wife Micaela Bastidas and was then torn by horses and beheaded in the square of Cusco.

With the French fleet of the Comte de Grasse holding the Chesapeake and the armies of Washington and Rochambeau entrenched around him, Lord Cornwallis surrendered some eight thousand men at Yorktown on 19 October 1781, his band playing, it is said, 'The World Turned Upside Down.' The war was all but over; by the Treaty of Paris of 1783 Britain recognized the independence of the United States.

Taksin, who had driven out the Burmese and reigned from Thonburi, was deposed amid charges of madness and put to death. His general Chao Phraya Chakri took the throne as Rama I and moved the capital across the river to Bangkok, where he raised a Grand Palace and the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in the image of lost Ayutthaya. His Chakri dynasty reigns still.

On 19 April 1783 Catherine the Great proclaimed the annexation of the Crimean Khanate, last heir of the Golden Horde, whose horsemen had for three centuries carried off Russian, Ukrainian, and Polish captives to the slave markets of the Black Sea. Prince Potemkin founded the naval base of Sevastopol, and the Black Sea fleet was born.

The Al Khalifa, a clan of the Utub who had settled at Zubarah on the Qatar peninsula, crossed to Bahrain in 1783 with their allies and drove out its governor, who held the islands for Persia. Their house has ruled Bahrain ever since, growing rich on the pearl banks of the Gulf and later on oil.

t: Tipu's Captivity of the Mangalore Christians
x: Tipu Sultan of Mysore, believing the Catholics of Kanara had aided the British, had them seized on Ash Wednesday 1784, perhaps sixty thousand men, women, and children, and marched them over the Ghats to Seringapatam. Thousands died on the road; many of the men were circumcised and forced into Islam, and the churches of the coast were destroyed. Only a remnant returned in 1799.

King Bodawpaya sent his armies over the Arakan Yoma, took Mrauk U on 2 January 1785, and carried off the Mahamuni, the most sacred image of the Arakanese, to his capital at Amarapura. Thousands of Arakanese fled into British Bengal, and their raids back across the frontier set Burma on the road to war with Britain.

Francis Light, a country trader, persuaded the Sultan of Kedah to lease Penang to the East India Company in hope of help against Siam, and on 11 August 1786 raised the British flag there. He named the settlement George Town and the island Prince of Wales Island; the promised help never came, and Penang became the first British foothold on the Malay Peninsula.

t: The Constitution of the United States
x: Fifty-five delegates of twelve states met in the Pennsylvania State House through the summer of 1787, with George Washington presiding, and by the Great Compromise and long debate led by James Madison framed a federal government of three branches checking one another. Signed on 17 September and ratified the next year, it remains the oldest written national constitution in force.

t: The First Fleet at Sydney Cove
x: Eleven ships under Captain Arthur Phillip, carrying some fifteen hundred souls, more than half of them convicts, found Botany Bay unfit and moved to Port Jackson, where on 26 January 1788 the British flag was raised at Sydney Cove. The penal colony of New South Wales was the seed of Australia.

Three weeks after the Third Estate swore in a tennis court at Versailles to give France a constitution, with troops gathering around Paris and the popular minister Necker dismissed, crowds seeking powder stormed the Bastille, the royal fortress-prison of the city, on 14 July 1789. Its governor, de Launay, was murdered and his head paraded on a pike. Louis XVI yielded, and the French Revolution had begun.

t: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
x: In the night of 4 August 1789 the National Assembly abolished the feudal privileges of nobles, clergy, and provinces. On 26 August it adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen: men are born and remain free and equal in rights, and sovereignty resides in the nation. In October a crowd of Parisian women marched to Versailles and brought the royal family back to Paris.

t: Quang Trung Routs the Qing at Dong Da
x: When a Qing army under Sun Shiyi marched into Thang Long to restore the fugitive Le emperor, Nguyen Hue proclaimed himself Emperor Quang Trung and drove his army north by forced marches. On the fifth day of the lunar New Year of 1789 his troops, some behind shields of wet straw, stormed the Qing forts at Ngoc Hoi and Dong Da and sent the invaders flying back to China.

In the richest colony on earth, where half a million slaves produced much of Europe's sugar and coffee, the houngan Dutty Boukman gathered conspirators by night in the Bois Caïman in August 1791. Within days the northern plain was in flames, its plantations burned by the hundred and their masters slain; among the rebel leaders rose a freed coachman named Toussaint, later called Louverture.

t: The Constitution of the Third of May
x: On 3 May 1791 the Great Sejm, meeting in the Royal Castle of Warsaw while Russia was at war with the Turks, adopted a written constitution, the first in Europe, abolishing the liberum veto, making the throne hereditary, and dividing the powers of government. Catherine the Great answered with invasion, and two more partitions erased the Commonwealth by 1795.

On 20 September 1792 the Prussian army, marching on Paris to rescue Louis XVI, came upon the French under Dumouriez and Kellermann at Valmy. The French line held under a long cannonade to cries of 'Long live the nation!', and the Duke of Brunswick withdrew. The next day the Convention abolished the monarchy. Goethe, present with the Prussians, wrote that a new epoch of world history began there.

Some eleven hundred black Loyalists, who had won their freedom fighting for the Crown in the American war and been settled in Nova Scotia, sailed in fifteen ships under John Clarkson and founded Freetown on the Sierra Leone estuary. After Parliament abolished the slave trade in 1807, Freetown became a Crown colony and the base of the West Africa Squadron, where liberated Africans were landed by the thousand.

Tried by the National Convention and condemned by a narrow majority, Louis Capet, once Louis XVI, was guillotined in the Place de la Révolution on 21 January 1793. Britain, Holland, and Spain joined the war against France, the Vendée rose in March, and the Convention made terror the order of the day. Queen Marie Antoinette followed her husband to the scaffold in October.

George III sent Lord Macartney with telescopes, a planetarium, and a request for open ports and a resident minister. The aged Qianlong Emperor received him at his summer palace at Jehol, accepted the gifts as tribute, and replied that the Celestial Empire possessed all things in abundance and had no need of the manufactures of outer barbarians.

In the summer of 1794, as the Terror reached its height with more than a thousand heads falling in Paris in seven weeks, the Convention turned on Maximilien Robespierre. On 9 Thermidor, 27 July, he was outlawed, his jaw shattered by a pistol shot at the Hôtel de Ville, and the next day he was guillotined with twenty-one of his followers. The Terror was over.

Tadeusz Kościuszko, veteran of the American war, proclaimed a national insurrection in the market square of Kraków on 24 March 1794, and at Racławice his peasant scythemen captured Russian guns. But in November Suvorov stormed Praga across the river from Warsaw, massacring its people, and in 1795 the last partition erased Poland from the map.

Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, a eunuch prince who had made himself master of Persia, demanded that King Heraclius II of Georgia renounce his Russian protection. When the aged king refused, the Persians routed his small army at Krtsanisi on 11 September 1795 and stormed Tbilisi. The city was burned and some fifteen thousand of its people carried off as slaves; Russia, which had promised aid, sent none in time.

Kamehameha, chief of the island of Hawaii, armed with European muskets and cannon and aided by the seamen John Young and Isaac Davis, landed on Oahu and drove the army of Kalanikupule up the Nuuanu valley, where many were forced over the cliffs of the Pali. By 1810, when Kauai submitted, he ruled all the Hawaiian Islands as king.

After Bonaparte's victories over the Austrians at Arcole and Rivoli, and under his threats, the Great Council of Venice voted itself out of existence on 12 May 1797, and Doge Ludovico Manin laid down the ducal cap. French troops entered the city and carried off the bronze horses of St. Mark. By the Treaty of Campo Formio the thousand-year Republic was handed to Austria.

Napoleon Bonaparte landed in Egypt with some thirty-five thousand men and a commission of scholars. On 21 July 1798 at Embabeh on the Nile, in sight of the pyramids, his squares broke the charges of Murad Bey's Mamluk cavalry, and Cairo was taken. Eleven days later Nelson destroyed the French fleet in Aboukir Bay, and the army was marooned in Egypt.

Returning secretly from Egypt, Napoleon Bonaparte joined the Director Sieyès in a plot against the discredited Directory. On 18 and 19 Brumaire, 9 and 10 November 1799, the councils were moved to Saint-Cloud, where grenadiers cleared the hall of the Five Hundred. Bonaparte became First Consul, and the Revolution had found its master.

In the Fourth Mysore War the Company's armies under General Harris besieged Tipu Sultan in his island fortress on the Kaveri. On 4 May 1799 the British stormed the breach in the heat of the afternoon, and Tipu, fighting at a gateway, fell among the dead. The Wodeyar dynasty was restored to a reduced Mysore, and the last great rival of the British in the south was gone.

Ranjit Singh, an eighteen-year-old Sikh chief who had lost an eye to smallpox, rode into Lahore in July 1799, and in 1801 was proclaimed Maharaja of the Punjab. With an army later drilled by French and Italian veterans of Napoleon, he united the Sikh confederacies, took Multan, Kashmir, and Peshawar from the Afghans, and made the Koh-i-Noor the jewel of his treasury.

t: The Dutch East India Company Dissolved
x: Ruined by corruption, war with Britain, and the debts of its Asian trade, the Dutch East India Company, once the richest corporation in the world, saw its charter lapse on 31 December 1799. Its possessions passed to the Batavian Republic, and the Indies became a colony of the Dutch state, soon to be shaken by the wars of Napoleon.

On 14 June 1800 the First Consul, who had crossed the Great St. Bernard with his reserve army in May, was all but beaten on the plain of Marengo by the Austrian general Melas, until Desaix came up in the afternoon and the younger Kellermann's cavalry charge broke the Austrian column. Desaix fell in the counterstroke. Melas signed away Piedmont and Lombardy, and Bonaparte's consulship was secured.

In a letter of March 1800 to Sir Joseph Banks of the Royal Society, Alessandro Volta of Pavia described a column of zinc and copper discs separated by brine-soaked card, which gave a steady current of electricity. It was the first battery, and within weeks William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle in London had used one to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

On 15 July 1801 Bonaparte's envoys and Cardinal Consalvi signed the Concordat, which recognized the Catholic faith as the religion of the great majority of Frenchmen and closed the schism of the Revolution. Pius VII accepted the loss of the Church's lands, the First Consul gained the naming of bishops, and the restored worship was celebrated with a Te Deum at Notre-Dame on Easter Sunday 1802.

On the night of 23 March 1801 a band of guards officers led by Count Pahlen and General Bennigsen broke into the new Mikhailovsky Castle and strangled the erratic Emperor Paul I, who had broken with Britain and sent Cossacks marching toward India. His son Alexander I, who had known of the plot to depose him, came to the throne and made peace with London.

t: The Union of Great Britain and Ireland
x: On 1 January 1801 the Act of Union, carried through the Dublin parliament by Pitt and Castlereagh with patronage and peerages after the rising of 1798, joined the two kingdoms as the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Ireland sent a hundred members to Westminster; the Catholic emancipation Pitt had promised was refused by George III, and Pitt resigned.

Nguyen Phuc Anh, heir of the Nguyen lords, who had fought the Tay Son for twenty-five years with Siamese, French, and Chinese help, took Phu Xuan in 1801 and Thang Long in 1802. Reigning as Emperor Gia Long from Hue, he ruled from the Chinese border to the Gulf of Siam, and in 1804 the Qing court recognized the country under the name Viet Nam.

In the Second Anglo-Maratha War Major General Arthur Wellesley, with fewer than ten thousand men, attacked the combined armies of Daulat Rao Scindia and the Raja of Berar, several times as numerous, across the Kaitna river at Assaye. The Maratha gunners died at their pieces, but Wellesley carried the day, and as Duke of Wellington he called it the bloodiest for the numbers that he ever saw.

Napoleon, his army lost in Saint-Domingue and war with Britain at hand, sold the whole of Louisiana, some 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi and the Rocky Mountains, to the envoys of President Jefferson for fifteen million dollars. On 20 December 1803 the American flag rose over New Orleans; the United States had doubled in size at a stroke.

After the janissary chiefs, the dahije, murdered the leading Serbian knezes of the pashalik of Belgrade in the winter of 1804, the elders gathered at Orašac in February and chose the livestock trader Karađorđe Petrović as their leader. The rising against the janissaries became a war against the Ottoman Porte itself, and by the beginning of 1807 the rebels held Belgrade.

t: The Civil Code of the French
x: Promulgated on 21 March 1804 after debates over which the First Consul himself often presided, the Civil Code gathered the customs of the old provinces and the reforms of the Revolution into 2,281 articles on persons, property, and contract. Equality before the law, civil marriage, and the end of feudal tenure traveled with the French armies, and the Code, much amended, still governs France and Belgium and shaped the law of much of the world.

In Notre-Dame on 2 December 1804, with Pope Pius VII come from Rome to anoint him, Napoleon took the crown from the altar and set it on his own head, then crowned Joséphine kneeling before him. The Senate and a plebiscite had made the First Consul hereditary Emperor of the French that spring; Beethoven, hearing the news, had torn the dedication to Bonaparte from his Third Symphony.

Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar who preached against the laxity of the Hausa kings, withdrew from Gobir with his followers in 1804, as the Prophet had withdrawn to Medina, and was proclaimed Commander of the Faithful. His holy war overthrew the Hausa states, and from Sokoto, founded in 1809, his son Muhammad Bello and their heirs ruled the largest state in West Africa, a great slaving power, until the British came in 1903.

Napoleon sent his brother-in-law General Leclerc with twenty thousand veterans to restore slavery in Saint-Domingue; Toussaint Louverture was seized and died in a French fortress, but yellow fever and the armies of Jean-Jacques Dessalines destroyed the French, who surrendered after Vertières in November 1803. At Gonaïves on 1 January 1804 Dessalines proclaimed Haiti, the first nation founded by former slaves, and that spring had the remaining French colonists put to death.

Off Cape Trafalgar on 21 October 1805, Vice-Admiral Lord Nelson led twenty-seven ships of the line in two columns straight through the Franco-Spanish fleet of Admiral Villeneuve, taking or destroying twenty-two of thirty-three without losing one. A sharpshooter's ball from the Redoutable killed Nelson on the Victory's quarterdeck; Britain's command of the seas went unchallenged for a century.

On 2 December 1805, the first anniversary of his coronation, Napoleon drew the Russian and Austrian armies of Alexander I and Francis II down from the Pratzen Heights against his weakened right, then struck their abandoned center out of the morning mist. The allied army was broken in a day. Austria made peace at Pressburg, ceding Venetia and the Tyrol, and the Third Coalition dissolved.

t: Muhammad Ali Made Pasha of Egypt
x: Muhammad Ali, an Albanian officer from Kavala who had come to Egypt with the Ottoman force sent against the French, won over the ulema and people of Cairo and was named pasha by the sultan in 1805. On 1 March 1811 he invited the Mamluk beys to a feast in the Citadel and had them shot down in a narrow lane as they left. He made Egypt the strongest power in the Muslim world.

t: The End of the Holy Roman Empire
x: In July 1806 sixteen German princes left the Empire to form the Confederation of the Rhine under Napoleon's protection. On 6 August, threatened with war, Francis II laid down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire, which had stood since Otto the Great, and released its estates; he reigned on as Francis I, Emperor of Austria, a title he had taken in 1804.

On 14 October 1806 Napoleon routed Prince Hohenlohe on the plateau above Jena, while a dozen miles north at Auerstedt Marshal Davout's single corps defeated the main Prussian army under the King and the Duke of Brunswick, who was mortally wounded. The army of Frederick the Great dissolved in the pursuit; Napoleon stood at Frederick's tomb in Potsdam and entered Berlin on 27 October.

t: Two Emperors on a Raft at Tilsit
x: After beating Bennigsen's Russians at Friedland on 14 June 1807, Napoleon met Alexander I on 25 June on a raft moored in the Niemen at Tilsit. The treaties that followed bound Russia to join his blockade of British trade and stripped Prussia of half its lands, from which he carved the Kingdom of Westphalia for his brother Jérôme and the Duchy of Warsaw.

On 25 March 1807, after twenty years of agitation by William Wilberforce, Thomas Clarkson, and the evangelicals of Clapham, the Act for the Abolition of the Slave Trade received the royal assent, forbidding British subjects to carry slaves. The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron, formed the next year, spent half a century hunting slavers and freed about 150,000 Africans at sea.

t: The Second of May in Madrid
x: When Murat's troops moved to carry the last of the Spanish royal family off to Bayonne, the people of Madrid rose on 2 May 1808 and fought the Mamelukes and grenadiers in the Puerta del Sol. Murat had prisoners shot through the night, as Goya later painted. Napoleon made his brother Joseph King of Spain, and the Peninsular War began.

t: The Portuguese Court Comes to Rio
x: As Junot's French army closed on Lisbon in November 1807, the Prince Regent John, his mad mother Queen Maria, and some ten thousand courtiers sailed for Brazil under British escort, reaching Rio de Janeiro in March 1808. Rio became the capital of the Portuguese monarchy, the ports of Brazil were opened to the world, and in 1815 Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal with Portugal.

Crossing the Danube below Vienna in May 1809, Napoleon was thrown back at Aspern and Essling by Archduke Charles, his first defeat in the field in ten years. Six weeks later he crossed again in force, and on 5 and 6 July defeated Charles on the Marchfeld at Wagram in a battle of some 300,000 men. By the Peace of Schönbrunn Austria lost Salzburg, western Galicia, and Illyria.

Conquered by Russia in the war of 1808 and 1809, Finland was torn from Sweden after six centuries. At the Diet of Porvoo in March 1809 Alexander I swore to uphold the Lutheran faith and the fundamental laws of the land, and the four estates swore allegiance to him as Grand Duke; Finland kept its own laws and Senate under the Russian crown until 1917.

At dawn on 16 September 1810 the parish priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla rang the bell of his church at Dolores and called his Indian and mestizo parishioners to rise against the Spanish-born rulers of New Spain, beneath the banner of Our Lady of Guadalupe. His host of tens of thousands sacked Guanajuato but was routed at the Bridge of Calderón; Hidalgo was captured and shot in 1811.

News that the French had overrun Andalusia and the Supreme Central Junta of Seville had fallen led the cabildo of Buenos Aires, pressed by crowds in the plaza, to depose the viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros on 25 May 1810. A junta under Cornelio Saavedra took power in the name of the captive Ferdinand VII; Buenos Aires never again obeyed Spain.

With Holland annexed to Napoleon's empire, an army from British India under Sir Samuel Auchmuty landed near Batavia and stormed the Franco-Dutch lines at Meester Cornelis in August 1811. Thomas Stamford Raffles ruled Java as lieutenant-governor for five years, sacked the court of Yogyakarta, and began a land tax, before the island was handed back to the Netherlands in 1816.

On 5 July 1811 a congress at Caracas, urged on by Francisco de Miranda and the young Simón Bolívar, declared Venezuela the first independent republic of Spanish America. It fell the next year, after the earthquake of Holy Thursday 1812 leveled Caracas and the royalist clergy proclaimed it the judgment of God; Miranda was handed to the Spaniards and died in a prison at Cádiz.

Some seventy-five miles west of Moscow on 7 September 1812, Field Marshal Kutuzov stood to fight, and the Grande Armée stormed the Raevsky redoubt and the Bagration flèches in the bloodiest single day of the age, some seventy thousand men falling. Bagration was mortally wounded. Napoleon would not commit his Guard; Kutuzov withdrew in good order, and the French entered an abandoned Moscow a week later.

As the French entered Moscow on 14 September 1812, fires broke out across the city, set by agents of the governor, Count Rostopchin, and in four days some two thirds of it burned. Alexander would not treat; on 19 October Napoleon began his retreat, and frost, hunger, and Cossacks destroyed the greater part of an army that had crossed the Niemen in June more than 400,000 strong.

For four days in October 1813 the armies of Russia, Prussia, Austria, and Sweden closed upon Napoleon around Leipzig in the greatest battle Europe had yet seen, more than half a million men in all. The Saxons went over to the allies in the field; on 19 October a sapper blew the Elster bridge too soon, drowning Marshal Poniatowski and trapping the rearguard. Napoleon's German empire collapsed.

t: The Prince of Orange Lands at Scheveningen
x: As the French withdrew in November 1813, a triumvirate of Dutch notables led by Gijsbert Karel van Hogendorp called back the heir of the stadholders. William Frederick of Orange landed on the beach at Scheveningen from a British warship on 30 November, accepted sovereignty as William I, and in 1815 was made king of a United Netherlands that took in Belgium.

With the allies in Paris and his marshals refusing to march, Napoleon abdicated unconditionally at Fontainebleau on 6 April 1814. On 20 April he bade farewell to the Old Guard in the Court of the White Horse and left for Elba, a sovereign island of some twelve thousand people, while Louis XVIII returned to the throne of his fathers.

Ceded by Denmark to Sweden at Kiel in January 1814, the Norwegians refused the bargain; 112 delegates met at the manor of Eidsvoll and on 17 May signed a liberal constitution, electing the Danish prince Christian Frederick king. A short war with Bernadotte followed, and Norway accepted the Swedish king that autumn, but it kept its constitution, which remains in force today.

When Fulani jihadists sacked Ngazargamu, capital of Bornu for three centuries, in 1808, the scholar and warrior Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi rallied the old Sayfawa kingdom and threw them back. In 1814 he built a new capital at Kukawa near Lake Chad, and he and his son Umar became the true masters of Bornu, the Sayfawa kings their shadows until the line ended in 1846.

t: The Final Act of the Congress of Vienna
x: After nine months of negotiation, balls, and intrigue led by Metternich, Castlereagh, Talleyrand, Hardenberg, and Tsar Alexander I, the powers signed the Final Act on 9 June 1815, nine days before Waterloo. Russia took most of Poland, Prussia three fifths of Saxony's land and the Rhineland, Austria Lombardy and Venetia; a German Confederation replaced the Empire, and the balance struck at Vienna kept Europe from general war for a century.

The chiefs of Kandy, the last independent kingdom of Lanka, turned against their cruel king Sri Vikrama Rajasinha and opened the way to a British force. By the Kandyan Convention of March 1815 they ceded the kingdom to the British crown, which pledged to protect the Buddhist faith. For the first time the whole of Ceylon lay under one government.

In April 1815 Mount Tambora on Sumbawa blew itself apart in the greatest eruption of recorded history, its roar heard in Sumatra, more than a thousand miles away. The little kingdoms of Tambora and Sanggar vanished, and tens of thousands died by fire and famine. The veil it cast around the earth brought the Year Without a Summer of 1816, with frost and hunger in Europe and New England.

Landing at Golfe-Juan with about a thousand men on 1 March 1815, Napoleon marched over the Alps by Grenoble; at Laffrey the Fifth Line Regiment, sent to stop him, went over to him with cries of Vive l'Empereur. Marshal Ney, who had promised to bring him back in an iron cage, joined him; Louis XVIII fled, and on 20 March the Emperor was back in the Tuileries.

To end the enslavement of Christians by the Barbary states, a British and Dutch fleet under Lord Exmouth bombarded Algiers for nine hours on 27 August 1816, burning its fleet and much of the harbor town. The dey, Omar Agha, released more than a thousand Christian slaves and promised to end the practice. The corsairs were broken, though not ended, until the French came in 1830.

José de San Martín led the Army of the Andes, some five thousand men with mules and cannon, over passes higher than twelve thousand feet from Mendoza into Chile in January 1817, and with Bernardo O'Higgins routed the royalists at Chacabuco on 12 February. A year later the victory of Maipú made Chile free, and San Martín turned north by sea against the Spanish citadel of Peru.

At the sultan's command Muhammad Ali sent his son Ibrahim Pasha into Arabia to destroy the Wahhabi state. After a march across the peninsula Ibrahim besieged Diriyah for six months and took it in September 1818. The town was razed, and the emir Abdullah ibn Saud was sent to Constantinople, paraded through the streets, and beheaded. Within six years the Saudis had raised a new capital at Riyadh.

On New Year's Day 1818 some eight hundred Company troops, many of them Mahar sepoys, held the village of Koregaon on the Bhima for twelve hours against the Peshwa's army of more than twenty thousand. Within months Baji Rao II surrendered and was pensioned off to Bithur near Cawnpore, and the Maratha Empire came to an end.

Seeking a British port to break the Dutch hold on the Straits, Raffles landed on the island of Singapore on 29 January 1819, then home to perhaps a thousand Malays, Orang Laut, and Chinese under the Temenggong. Playing on a disputed succession, he recognized Hussein as Sultan of Johor and won the right to a trading post. Free of duties, Singapore grew within years into the emporium of the East.

Shaka, chief of the small Zulu clan since 1816, drilled his regiments to close with the short stabbing spear behind the great cowhide shield, in the horns-of-the-buffalo formation. After he defeated Zwide of the Ndwandwe on the Mhlatuze River in 1819, he ruled the land between the Phongolo and the Thukela, and the wars of the age, the Mfecane, set peoples in flight across half of southern Africa.

Simón Bolívar, the Caracas aristocrat who had sworn on Rome's Monte Sacro to free his country, marched his army across the flooded llanos and over the frozen páramo of Pisba in the rainy season to fall upon New Granada. At the bridge of Boyacá on 7 August 1819 he destroyed the royalist army; three days later he entered Bogotá, and in December the Republic of Colombia was proclaimed.

On 16 August 1819 some sixty thousand people gathered on St. Peter's Field in Manchester to hear Henry Hunt speak for parliamentary reform. The magistrates sent in the yeomanry and then the Fifteenth Hussars with drawn sabers; some fifteen were killed and hundreds wounded. The radicals named it Peterloo in mockery of Waterloo, and the government answered with the Six Acts.

t: The Army of the Three Guarantees
x: Agustín de Iturbide, a royalist colonel who had spent years hunting insurgents, changed sides, joined the rebel Vicente Guerrero under the Plan of Iguala, which promised independence, the Catholic faith, and the union of Spaniards and Mexicans, and entered Mexico City in triumph on 27 September 1821. The next year he had himself crowned Emperor Agustín I; he was overthrown in 1823 and shot in 1824.

When the Greeks of the Morea rose in 1821 and slaughtered the Muslims and Jews of Tripolitsa, the sultan's vengeance fell elsewhere. In April 1822, after a band of Samians raised revolt on the rich island of Chios, an Ottoman fleet landed troops who killed perhaps twenty thousand Christians and sold some forty-five thousand into slavery. Delacroix's painting of the massacre roused all Europe for the Greek cause.

Ordered by the Cortes at Lisbon to return to Portugal while Brazil was reduced again to a colony, the Prince Regent Pedro, left behind by his father John VI, refused. On 7 September 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo, he tore the Portuguese colors from his uniform and cried 'Independence or death!'; in December he was crowned Emperor Pedro I of Brazil.

Burma's conquests of Arakan, Manipur, and Assam brought it to the borders of British Bengal. In May 1824 a British fleet seized Rangoon, and after two years of war, in which the great general Maha Bandula was killed by a shell at Danubyu, King Bagyidaw signed the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826, giving up Assam, Manipur, Arakan, and Tenasserim and paying a million pounds.

By the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of London in March 1824 the Netherlands gave up Malacca and all claims on the Malay Peninsula and Singapore, and Britain gave up Bencoolen and its claims in Sumatra. A line drawn through the Straits of Malacca split the Malay world in two, a division that survives in the frontier between Malaysia and Indonesia.

On the high plain of Ayacucho on 9 December 1824, the patriot army of Antonio José de Sucre, some six thousand Colombians and Peruvians, met the last royal army of the viceroy José de la Serna. In a few hours the viceroy was wounded and taken and his army surrendered; Spanish rule in South America was at an end, save for a few holdouts that fell by early 1826.

t: Locomotion on the Stockton and Darlington
x: On 27 September 1825 George Stephenson drove his engine Locomotion along the new Stockton and Darlington Railway, drawing coal wagons and a coach full of shareholders, on the first public railway to use steam locomotives. Five years later his Rocket ran on the Liverpool and Manchester, and within a generation iron rails had remade the commerce and the warfare of Europe.

Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta, a mystic who saw himself as the destined just king of the Javanese, rose in July 1825 when the Dutch drove a road across his family's lands at Tegalrejo. His holy war set central Java aflame for five years and cost some two hundred thousand Javanese lives. Lured to a parley at Magelang in 1830, he was seized and exiled.

In the confusion after Alexander I's death, guards officers of the secret societies led some three thousand soldiers onto Senate Square on 26 December 1825 to refuse the oath to Nicholas I and demand a constitution. Nicholas waited, then brought up cannon and scattered them with grapeshot. Five leaders, Pestel and the poet Ryleyev among them, were hanged, and over a hundred sent to Siberia.

An assembly at Chuquisaca declared Upper Peru independent on 6 August 1825, the anniversary of the battle of Junín, and named the new republic Bolivia for the Liberator, whose constitution, with a president for life, it adopted the next year. Antonio José de Sucre, victor of Ayacucho, became its first constitutional president; the city itself later took his name.

When the Janissaries, long since a hereditary rabble that made and unmade sultans, overturned their soup kettles in revolt against a new drilled army in June 1826, Mahmud II was ready. The sacred banner of the Prophet was unfurled, his loyal gunners shelled their barracks, and thousands were killed in the flames and the executions that followed. The Ottomans called it the Auspicious Event.

Chao Anouvong, king of Vientiane and vassal of Siam, marched on Bangkok in 1827, believing a false rumor that Britain was at war with Siam. Turned back at Khorat, where legend credits Thao Suranari with rallying the captives against him, he was pursued to Vientiane. The Siamese razed his city and carried its people across the Mekong, and Anouvong died a prisoner in Bangkok.

After Russian armies under Paskevich took Erivan and Tabriz, Fath-Ali Shah made peace at the village of Turkmenchay on 21 February 1828. Persia gave up the khanates of Erivan and Nakhichevan, paid an indemnity of twenty million roubles, and granted Russian subjects extraterritorial rights. The Caucasus north of the Araxes was lost for good, and Armenians from Persia were resettled in the ceded lands.

t: The Black War in Van Diemen's Land
x: As settlers and their flocks spread over the island, the Aboriginal Tasmanians fought back, and Lieutenant-Governor George Arthur declared martial law in November 1828. A line of armed men drawn across the island in 1830 caught almost no one, but war and disease had done their work; George Augustus Robinson led the few hundred survivors into exile on Flinders Island.

Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata had fought since 1825 over the Banda Oriental, the land east of the Uruguay River where José Artigas had once led the gauchos against them both. Through the mediation of Britain, eager for a buffer between the two and an open river trade, the peace of August 1828 made it an independent state, the Oriental Republic of Uruguay.

Lord William Bentinck, governor-general, encouraged by the reformer Ram Mohan Roy, outlawed sati, the burning of widows on their husbands' pyres, in Bengal in December 1829. Hundreds of widows had been burned each year in the Bengal presidency alone. Orthodox Hindus appealed against the law to the Privy Council in London and lost.

When Charles X and his minister Polignac issued ordinances in July 1830 muzzling the press and dissolving the new Chamber, Paris rose behind barricades for three days, 27 to 29 July, and the royal troops gave way. The old king abdicated and sailed for England; the liberal deputies, with Lafayette's blessing, gave the crown to his cousin Louis Philippe, Duke of Orléans, as King of the French.

On 25 August 1830 a performance of Auber's La Muette de Portici at the Théâtre de la Monnaie, with its duet Amour sacré de la patrie, sent the Brussels audience into the streets. The riot became a revolt against William I's Dutch rule; Dutch troops were driven out of the city in September, a national congress declared independence, and the powers in London recognized a neutral Belgium.

On the night of 29 November 1830 cadets of the infantry school attacked the Belweder Palace, residence of the Grand Duke Constantine, and Warsaw rose against Russian rule. In January the Sejm dethroned Nicholas I as King of Poland. The Polish army fought well at Olszynka Grochowska, but Field Marshal Paskevich stormed Warsaw in September 1831, and the Great Emigration carried the Polish cause to Paris.

Provoked by the blow of a fly-whisk that the dey Hussein struck the French consul in 1827, Charles X sent an expedition that landed at Sidi Ferruch in June 1830. Algiers capitulated on 5 July, and the dey sailed into exile. The last of the corsair regencies fell, and France began a conquest, resisted for fifteen years by the emir Abd al-Qadir, and a rule that endured for 132 years.

To pay for the Java War and the revolt of Belgium, Governor-General Johannes van den Bosch required Javanese villages to set aside a fifth of their land, or sixty-six days' labor a year, to grow coffee, sugar, and indigo for the government at fixed prices. The system filled the Dutch treasury for forty years and paid for its railways, but brought famine to Cirebon and Demak in the 1840s.

The last Cham principality, Panduranga about Phan Rang, had lived for more than a century as a vassal of the Nguyen. In 1832 Emperor Minh Mang abolished it and made its lands Vietnamese provinces; the Cham revolt that followed was put down without mercy, and the kingdom that had held the coast since the second century passed into history.

t: Slavery Abolished in the British Empire
x: The Slavery Abolition Act, passed in August 1833 a few weeks after Wilberforce's death, freed some 800,000 slaves in the British West Indies, the Cape, and Mauritius from 1 August 1834, though most were bound as apprentices until 1838. Parliament voted twenty million pounds, about two fifths of the government's yearly spending, to compensate the slaveholders.

Emperor Minh Mang, a stern Confucian who saw the Christian religion as a solvent of loyalty, ordered the churches destroyed and the missionaries hunted down; in 1833 the French priest Francois-Isidore Gagelin was strangled near Hue. Vietnamese Catholics were made to trample the cross, and many of the 117 martyrs canonized in 1988 died under him and his successors.

On 1 January 1834 the Zollverein came into force, joining Prussia, Bavaria, Württemberg, Saxony, and most of the smaller German states in a single customs territory of some twenty-three million people; at midnight the barriers between them were lifted. Austria stood outside. The union bound the German economy to Berlin a generation before Bismarck bound its politics.

t: Emancipation in the British West Indies
x: Spurred by the great Jamaican slave rising of Christmas 1831, led by the Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe, Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act, and on 1 August 1834 some eight hundred thousand slaves in the British colonies were declared free, subject to an apprenticeship that ended in 1838. The planters received twenty million pounds in compensation; the freed people received nothing.

t: Ranavalona I Forbids the Christian Faith
x: Queen Ranavalona I, who had come to the Merina throne in 1828 and set herself against the foreign ways admitted by her predecessor Radama I, outlawed the Christian religion in 1835. The missionaries of the London Missionary Society were driven out, and Malagasy converts who kept their faith were speared, burned, or flung from the cliffs of Antananarivo; Rasalama, killed in 1837, was the first of the martyrs.

The settlers of Texas, chiefly Americans, rose against Santa Anna's centralist rule; in March 1836 his army stormed the mission of the Alamo at San Antonio and killed all its defenders, among them Davy Crockett and James Bowie. Six weeks later, on 21 April, Sam Houston's army surprised the Mexicans at San Jacinto in eighteen minutes of fighting and captured Santa Anna, who signed away Texas.

The Padri War began among the Minangkabau when reformers, inspired by pilgrims who had seen the Wahhabi rule of Mecca, waged war on the customary chiefs to impose a stricter Islam. The Dutch took the chiefs' side in 1821, and after long campaigns stormed the Padri stronghold of Bonjol in August 1837. Its leader, Tuanku Imam Bonjol, died in exile.

After Dingane had the Voortrekker leader Piet Retief and his party slain at uMgungundlovu in February, some 470 Boers under Andries Pretorius drew sixty-four wagons into a laager beside the Ncome River. On 16 December more than ten thousand Zulu warriors hurled themselves upon it; some three thousand fell, while not one Boer was killed. The trekkers kept the day ever after as a covenant with God.

Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and a treaty signed at New Echota by a minority faction, the Cherokee Nation, with its own constitution, alphabet, and newspaper, was ordered west of the Mississippi. In 1838 federal troops rounded up some sixteen thousand Cherokee into stockades and marched them to the Indian Territory; some four thousand died of cold, hunger, and disease on the way.

On 3 November 1839, in the rose garden of the Topkapı Palace, the foreign minister Mustafa Reşid Pasha read before the ambassadors of Europe the decree of the young Sultan Abdulmejid promising security of life, honor, and property to all subjects, Muslim and non-Muslim alike, with fair taxation and regular conscription. It opened the era of reforms called the Tanzimat.

Sent to Canton by the Daoguang Emperor to stamp out the opium trade, the commissioner Lin Zexu blockaded the foreign factories until the British merchants surrendered over twenty thousand chests of the drug. At Humen his men dissolved it in trenches of lime and salt water and flushed it into the sea. Britain answered with gunboats, and the First Opium War began.

By the Treaty of London of 19 April 1839, William I of the Netherlands at last recognized Belgian independence, and Britain, France, Austria, Prussia, and Russia guaranteed Belgium as a perpetually neutral state; Luxembourg and Limburg were divided. Seventy-five years later the German chancellor would call the treaty a scrap of paper, and Britain went to war to uphold it.

After the plunder of a wrecked Indian ship, troops of the East India Company from Bombay stormed Aden on 19 January 1839, the first conquest of Queen Victoria's reign. The ancient port, then a village of some six hundred souls, became a coaling station on the steamer route to India and grew into one of the busiest harbors in the world.

On 6 February 1840 Captain William Hobson and some forty chiefs signed a treaty on the lawn at Waitangi, later carried about the islands until more than five hundred had set their names to it. In the English text the chiefs ceded sovereignty to Queen Victoria; in the Maori, they granted governance while keeping their chieftainship, a difference that has shaped New Zealand ever since.

Sayyid Said, sultan of Oman, who had broken the Mazrui of Mombasa and won back the Swahili coast, moved his court from Muscat to Zanzibar, where he had planted the island with cloves worked by slaves. Zanzibar became the chief market of the East African trade in slaves and ivory, and Arab and Swahili caravans pushed inland to the Great Lakes and the Congo.

James Brooke, an English adventurer in his own armed schooner, helped the Brunei prince Pengiran Muda Hashim put down a revolt of Malays and Dayaks in Sarawak and was rewarded with its government. Proclaimed rajah in 1841, he hunted down Iban and Malay pirates with the Royal Navy, and his family, the White Rajahs, ruled Sarawak for a hundred years.

With British warships beneath the walls of Nanjing after the fall of Zhenjiang had cut the Grand Canal, the Qing signed the Treaty of Nanking aboard HMS Cornwallis. China ceded Hong Kong Island, opened five ports to trade, abolished the Canton merchant monopoly, and paid an indemnity of twenty-one million dollars.

The British army that had set Shah Shuja on the throne of Kabul was besieged in its cantonments by the Afghan chiefs. In January 1842 some 4,500 soldiers and 12,000 camp followers set out for Jalalabad through snow-choked passes under constant fire. The last stand was made at Gandamak, and of the Europeans only Dr. William Brydon rode into Jalalabad, on a wounded pony.

After Queen Pomare IV, guided by English Protestant missionaries, expelled two French Catholic priests, Admiral Abel Dupetit-Thouars arrived with his warships and forced her in 1842 to accept a French protectorate. The Tahitians fought the French from 1844 to 1847 and lost; France annexed the islands outright in 1880.

Sir Charles Napier, with some 2,800 men, broke the army of the Talpur Mirs of Sind, many times as numerous, at Miani in February 1843, and annexed the country. Punch credited him with a one-word dispatch, Peccavi, I have sinned; the pun was in fact the invention of an English schoolgirl who sent it to the magazine.

The potato blight that first struck in 1845 destroyed nearly the whole crop of 1846, and the Irish poor, who lived on little else, began to starve. Relief works and soup kitchens were overwhelmed, and Skibbereen in County Cork became a byword for horror. By 1851 about a million had died of hunger and fever and another million had emigrated.

On the night of 14 September 1846 the leading nobles of Nepal, summoned to the Kot, the palace armoury courtyard in Kathmandu, were cut down by the soldiers and brothers of the young general Jang Bahadur Kunwar. As prime minister he founded the Rana dynasty, which ruled Nepal in the king's name for over a century, until 1951.

Founded in 1822 by the American Colonization Society as a home for freed slaves from the United States, the settlement at Cape Mesurado had grown into a string of colonies along the Pepper Coast. On 26 July 1847 its settlers proclaimed the Republic of Liberia, with a constitution modeled on the American, and chose the Virginia-born Joseph Jenkins Roberts as first president.

After the annexation of Texas, President James K. Polk went to war with Mexico, and General Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz and fought his way inland. On 13 September 1847 his troops stormed the castle of Chapultepec, defended by the cadets remembered as the Niños Héroes, and entered Mexico City; by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Mexico ceded California and the Southwest, half its territory.

When the government banned a reform banquet, Paris rose on 22 February 1848; troops fired on a crowd on the Boulevard des Capucines, and within two days Louis Philippe had abdicated and a provisional government, with the poet Lamartine as its leading voice, proclaimed the Second Republic. The news ran across Europe like fire: within a month Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Venice, and Pest were in revolution.

Elected across the German Confederation, more than five hundred deputies, most of them professors, lawyers, and officials, filed into St. Paul's Church in Frankfurt on 18 May 1848 to make a united Germany. They wrote fundamental rights and a constitution, and in March 1849 elected Frederick William IV of Prussia emperor; he refused a crown from the gutter, and the rump of the Parliament was dispersed by soldiers at Stuttgart in June.

Commissioned by the Communist League at its congress in London, the Manifesto of the Communist Party by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels was printed in German in Bishopsgate in February 1848, days before the Paris rising. Its twenty-three pages declared all history the history of class struggles and ended in a call to the workers of all countries to unite.

On 24 January 1848 James Marshall, building a sawmill for John Sutter on the American River, found flakes of gold in the tailrace. By the end of 1849 some ninety thousand forty-niners had poured into California by sea and overland, San Francisco had grown from a village to a city, and California entered the Union as a free state in 1850.

On 13 March 1848 students and workers stormed the Diet of Lower Austria in Vienna, troops fired, and the court let fall the man who had directed its foreign policy since 1809. Prince Metternich fled to England, it was said in a laundry cart. Ferdinand I promised a constitution; in December he abdicated in favor of his eighteen-year-old nephew, Francis Joseph.

Driven from Milan by the Five Days of March, the eighty-one-year-old Field Marshal Radetzky held the Quadrilateral fortresses, and on 25 July 1848 broke the Piedmontese army of Charles Albert at Custoza. The Austrians reentered Milan in August; when Charles Albert tried again in 1849 he was beaten at Novara and abdicated that night in favor of his son Victor Emmanuel II.

For generations the Iranun and Balangingi Samal, fed by the slave markets of Sulu, had raided the Christian coasts of the Philippines and the Indies, carrying off many thousands of men, women, and children to toil and be sold. In 1848 Governor Narciso Claveria sent steam gunboats against Balangingi, stormed its forts, and freed hundreds of captives.

Hungary declared its independence at Debrecen in April 1849, and Kossuth's honvéd armies drove the Austrians from most of the kingdom, until Nicholas I sent some 200,000 Russians over the Carpathians to aid Francis Joseph. On 13 August General Görgei laid down his arms to the Russians at Világos; in October thirteen Hungarian commanders, twelve of them generals, were hanged or shot at Arad, and Kossuth fled to Turkey.

Ten years after Ranjit Singh's death his kingdom was torn by palace murders and two wars with the British. After the bloody drawn battle of Chillianwala, Lord Gough crushed the Sikh army at Gujrat in February 1849, and Lord Dalhousie annexed the Punjab. The boy Maharaja Duleep Singh gave up the Koh-i-Noor, which was sent to Queen Victoria.

The duchies of Schleswig and Holstein rose against Denmark in March 1848 with Prussian and federal German help. Once Prussia made peace, the army of the Schleswig-Holstein provisional government stood alone, and on 25 July 1850 the Danes defeated it at Idstedt, the largest battle yet fought in Scandinavia. The London Protocol of 1852 left the duchies to the Danish crown.

t: The Coup of the Second of December
x: Barred by the constitution from a second term, President Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte struck on 2 December 1851, the anniversary of Austerlitz: troops occupied Paris, the leading deputies were arrested, and resistance on the boulevards was shot down; Victor Hugo, who had tried to raise the barricades, fled into exile. A plebiscite approved the coup, and a year later to the day he was proclaimed Napoleon III.

On 1 May 1851 Queen Victoria opened the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations in Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace, a greenhouse of iron and nearly a million square feet of glass raised in Hyde Park in months. Six million visitors came by the new railways to see locomotives, looms, and the Koh-i-Noor; Prince Albert's profits founded the museums of South Kensington.

Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate who after feverish visions proclaimed himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, a heresy abhorrent to the missionaries, declared the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace at Jintian in Guangxi. His God Worshippers swept north, took Nanjing in 1853, and made it their Heavenly Capital. The civil war that followed cost at least twenty million lives.

Commodore Matthew Perry steamed into Edo Bay with four black ships, their guns run out, and delivered a letter from President Fillmore asking that Japan open its ports. He returned the next year with a larger squadron, and the shogunate signed the Treaty of Kanagawa. Two centuries of seclusion were over, and the authority of the shogun began to crumble.

On 16 April 1853 a train of fourteen carriages drawn by three locomotives, Sultan, Sindh, and Sahib, ran thirty-four kilometres from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane with four hundred guests aboard, to a salute of twenty-one guns. Within half a century India had one of the largest railway systems on earth, binding the subcontinent together.

t: The Charge of the Light Brigade
x: Britain and France had gone to war in 1854 to save the Ottoman Empire from Russia, and landed in the Crimea to take Sevastopol. On 25 October, at Balaclava, a misread order sent Lord Cardigan's Light Brigade of about 670 sabers down a valley commanded by Russian guns on three sides; it reached the battery and came back with fewer than two hundred mounted men.

Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria in 1851 brought a flood of diggers from every land. At Ballarat, angered by costly licenses and brutal police, miners under the Irishman Peter Lalor swore by the Southern Cross flag and built a stockade; on 3 December 1854 troops stormed it, killing more than twenty. Within a year the miners' cause had triumphed in court and in law.

King Mongkut, a monk for twenty-seven years who read Latin and English, chose to bend before the West rather than break. With Sir John Bowring, governor of Hong Kong, he signed a treaty opening Siam to free trade at a duty of three percent and granting British subjects their own courts. Like treaties with other powers followed, and Siam kept its independence.

After a siege of eleven months, in which cholera and the winter killed more allied soldiers than Russian guns, General MacMahon's French stormed the Malakoff redoubt on 8 September 1855, declaring J'y suis, j'y reste. The Russians blew up their works, sank their remaining ships, and abandoned the south side of the city. The Peace of Paris in 1856 neutralized the Black Sea.

On 10 May 1857, after eighty-five troopers had been fettered for refusing cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, the sepoys at Meerut rose, shot their officers, and rode for Delhi. There they proclaimed the aged Bahadur Shah II emperor of Hindustan. Rebellion spread across the north, and the British needed more than a year to put it down.

Nana Sahib, adopted son of the last Peshwa, besieged the British entrenchment at Cawnpore for three weeks and then offered safe passage downriver. At the Satichaura ghat the boats were fired upon and most of the men killed. The surviving women and children, some two hundred, were held in the Bibighar and hacked to death as a relieving column drew near. British vengeance was merciless.

King Mindon, who had seized the throne after the British took Lower Burma in 1852, founded a new royal city at the foot of Mandalay Hill, where the Buddha was said to have foretold a great city. A devout and gentle ruler, he held the Fifth Buddhist Council there in 1871 and had the whole Pali canon carved on 729 marble slabs at the Kuthodaw pagoda.

The Government of India Act ended the rule of the East India Company, and on 1 November 1858 Lord Canning read at Allahabad Queen Victoria's proclamation promising religious toleration and equal law to her Indian subjects. Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal emperor, was tried and exiled to Rangoon, and the British Raj began.

Between February and July 1858 Bernadette Soubirous, the fourteen-year-old daughter of a ruined miller, saw eighteen times in the grotto of Massabielle by the river Gave a lady who named herself the Immaculate Conception. A spring rose where Bernadette dug at her bidding. The bishop of Tarbes approved the devotion in 1862, and Lourdes became the greatest place of pilgrimage in modern Europe.

Lakshmibai, the widowed rani of Jhansi, whose state had been seized under the doctrine of lapse, fought the British in the saddle at the head of her troops. After Jhansi fell she joined Tantia Tope in seizing Gwalior, and there in June 1858 she was killed in a cavalry fight. Her foe Sir Hugh Rose called her the bravest and best military leader of the rebels.

On 24 June 1859 the armies of Napoleon III and Victor Emmanuel II met Francis Joseph's Austrians south of Lake Garda in a battle of some 300,000 men, the last in Europe in which three monarchs commanded in person. Austria lost Lombardy. The Genevan Henri Dunant, who tended the wounded at Castiglione, wrote a book on the carnage that led to the founding of the Red Cross in 1863.

More than twenty years after the voyage of the Beagle, and spurred by a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace in the Moluccas setting out the same theory, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species on 24 November 1859. Its argument that species arise by natural selection sold out the first printing of 1,250 copies to the booksellers at once and began a controversy that outlived him.

Rigault de Genouilly sailed south from Tourane and on 17 February 1859 stormed the citadel of Saigon. Defeated again at Ky Hoa in 1861, the court of Tu Duc yielded three eastern provinces of the Mekong delta by the Treaty of Saigon in 1862, and Admiral de la Grandiere seized the western three in 1867, forming the French colony of Cochinchina.

Sailing from Quarto near Genoa in two steamers, Giuseppe Garibaldi landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 with about a thousand red-shirted volunteers to aid the Sicilian rising. He beat the Bourbon troops at Calatafimi, took Palermo, crossed to the mainland, and entered Naples in September. At Teano on 26 October he hailed Victor Emmanuel II as King of Italy and handed him half a kingdom.

Civil war between Druze and Maronites in Mount Lebanon in the spring of 1860 left thousands of Christians dead, and in July the mob of Damascus fell upon the Christian quarter, burning churches and killing thousands while Ottoman troops looked on or joined in. The exiled Algerian emir Abd al-Qadir and his men sheltered many in his house. France landed an army, and Mount Lebanon received a Christian governor.

t: The Burning of the Summer Palace
x: In the Second Opium War an Anglo-French army marched on Beijing, and the Xianfeng Emperor fled to Jehol. When envoys seized under a flag of truce died under torture, Lord Elgin ordered the burning of the Yuanmingyuan, the vast garden palace of the Qing emperors, with its European pavilions built by the Jesuits. The fires burned for three days.

Eduard Douwes Dekker, a former colonial official in Java, published in 1860 under the pen name Multatuli his novel Max Havelaar, an indictment of the Cultivation System by which the Javanese were made to grow coffee and sugar for the treasury at The Hague. It shamed Dutch opinion, and the forced cultivation of the system was dismantled over the following decades.

On 17 March 1861 the first Italian parliament, meeting in Turin, proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II King of Italy, uniting Piedmont, Lombardy, the central duchies, the Romagna, and the Two Sicilies. Cavour, the minister who had made it, died in June. Venice was won in 1866 and Rome in 1870, and the capital moved to Florence in 1865 and to Rome in 1871.

By the manifesto of 3 March 1861, Alexander II freed some twenty-three million privately owned serfs from bondage to their landlords, a reform he had said was better made from above than from below. The peasants received land, but less than they had tilled, burdened with redemption payments for forty-nine years, and held in common by the village commune.

After Abraham Lincoln's election on a platform against the spread of slavery, seven states of the Deep South seceded and formed the Confederate States of America under Jefferson Davis. When Lincoln moved to resupply Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor, Confederate batteries under General P. G. T. Beauregard opened fire on 12 April 1861; the fort surrendered the next day, and the Civil War began.

El Hadj Umar Tall, a Tukulor scholar of the Tijaniyya brotherhood who had made the pilgrimage to Mecca and armed his host with trade muskets, captured Ségou, capital of the Bambara kingdom, in March 1861. The next year he overthrew the Muslim state of Massina as well, but rebellion trapped him in the cliffs of Bandiagara, where he perished in 1864.

Taking the occasion of the Union's narrow victory at Antietam, Lincoln proclaimed that on 1 January 1863 all slaves in the states in rebellion would be 'then, thenceforward, and forever free.' The proclamation made the war a war against slavery, opened the Union armies to black soldiers, of whom some 180,000 served, and led to the Thirteenth Amendment of 1865.

Robert E. Lee's second invasion of the North met George Meade's Army of the Potomac at Gettysburg in the first three days of July 1863. After two days of savage fighting at Little Round Top and Culp's Hill, Pickett's charge against the Union center failed; the two armies lost some fifty thousand men killed, wounded, or captured, and Lee never again invaded the North. The next day Vicksburg surrendered to Grant.
