When the Russian authorities tried to break the patriotic movement by conscripting its young men into the army, the Poles rose on 22 January 1863 under a secret National Government. With no army, the insurgents fought a guerrilla war in the forests for over a year. Romuald Traugutt, the last dictator, was hanged on the slope of the Warsaw Citadel in August 1864.

King Norodom, ruling a shrunken kingdom under the joint shadow of Siam and Vietnam, accepted a French protectorate in August 1863 at the urging of the naval officer Doudart de Lagree. Crowned the next year in the presence of both French and Siamese envoys, he moved his court from Oudong to Phnom Penh in 1866.

Russia's long war for the western Caucasus ended in May 1864 with a victory parade at Kbaada above Sochi. The Circassian tribes who would not move to the plains were driven to the Black Sea shore and shipped to Ottoman lands; hundreds of thousands were expelled, and tens of thousands died of hunger and typhus in the ports and on the voyage. Their descendants live from Turkey to Jordan.

t: The Fall of the Heavenly Capital
x: After a siege of two years the Hunan Army of Zeng Guofan, led by his brother Zeng Guoquan, blew a breach in the walls of Nanjing and stormed the Taiping capital. Hong Xiuquan had died weeks before, and his followers were slaughtered in their tens of thousands. The provincial armies that had saved the dynasty became the power behind it.

When Christian IX signed a constitution binding Schleswig to Denmark, Prussia and Austria invaded the duchies in February 1864. On 18 April Prussian infantry stormed the Danish redoubts at Dybbøl after a long siege and bombardment. Denmark lost Schleswig, Holstein, and Lauenburg at the Peace of Vienna, and the spoils led within two years to war between the victors.

In the Waikato War, waged to break the Maori King movement and open its lands, some three hundred men and women under Rewi Maniapoto held a hastily built pa at Orakau against fifteen hundred British troops for three days. Called on to surrender, they answered that they would fight on forever, then broke out through the cordon; about half of them were killed.

With Richmond fallen and his starving army cut off in its retreat west, Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of the McLean house at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865. The war that had cost some 620,000 lives preserved the Union and ended slavery in the United States; five days later Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre.

In February and March 1865 Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar of the abbey of St. Thomas at Brünn, read to the local natural history society the results of eight years of crossing garden peas, showing that inherited characters pass in fixed ratios as discrete units. His paper lay almost unread for thirty-five years until botanists rediscovered it in 1900, founding the science of genetics.

On 3 July 1866 three Prussian armies, moved by railway and directed by telegraph by General von Moltke, converged on Benedek's Austrian army at Königgrätz in Bohemia; the Crown Prince's arrival on the Austrian flank in the afternoon decided the day. The war lasted seven weeks. Austria was shut out of Germany, and Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, and Frankfurt.

Beaten by Prussia, Francis Joseph made his peace with Hungary in the Compromise of 1867 worked out by Ferenc Deák and Count Gyula Andrássy. On 8 June he and Empress Elisabeth were crowned King and Queen of Hungary in the Matthias Church at Buda with the Holy Crown of St. Stephen. The empire became the Dual Monarchy, two states sharing a sovereign, an army, a foreign policy, and the finances to pay for them.

Napoleon III had sent a French army to Mexico, beaten at Puebla on 5 May 1862 but victorious the next year, and set the Austrian archduke Maximilian on a Mexican throne in 1864. When the French withdrew under American pressure, Benito Juárez's republicans besieged Maximilian at Querétaro; he was taken and shot with his generals Miramón and Mejía on the Hill of Bells on 19 June 1867.

By the British North America Act, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick were joined on 1 July 1867 into a federal Dominion of Canada, with its capital at Ottawa and John A. Macdonald as its first prime minister. The new nation bought Rupert's Land from the Hudson's Bay Company, won British Columbia with the promise of a railway to the Pacific, and stretched from sea to sea by 1871.

Young samurai of Satsuma and Chōshū, resolved that Japan should not share China's humiliation, forced the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, to give up his power, and proclaimed the rule of the boy Emperor Meiji. Within a generation they abolished the domains and the samurai class, built railways, factories, and a conscript army, and made Japan the first industrial power of Asia.

Tewodros II, who had risen from a frontier chief to end the Era of the Princes and reunite Ethiopia, imprisoned the British consul and a band of missionaries in a fit of wrath. Sir Robert Napier landed with some 13,000 troops and elephants to carry the guns, marched four hundred miles into the highlands, and stormed the mountain fortress of Magdala; Tewodros died by his own hand rather than be taken.

General Konstantin von Kaufman, first governor-general of Russian Turkestan, defeated the army of the emir of Bukhara and took Samarkand, Timur's capital, in May 1868, and Bukhara became a Russian protectorate. Khiva submitted in 1873, Kokand was annexed in 1876, and at Geok Tepe in 1881 the Turkmen were crushed with great slaughter. By 1885 all western Central Asia was Russian.

Ferdinand de Lesseps had begun digging at Port Said in 1859 under a concession from the viceroy Said, and tens of thousands of Egyptian peasants were drafted to the work. On 17 November 1869, before the Empress Eugénie and the princes of Europe, the khedive Isma'il opened the canal from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The voyage from London to Bombay was shortened by some four thousand miles.

The Central Pacific, built east from Sacramento over the Sierra Nevada largely by Chinese laborers, and the Union Pacific, built west from Omaha by Irish laborers, veterans, and freedmen, met at Promontory Summit on 10 May 1869, where Leland Stanford drove a ceremonial spike of gold. A journey across the continent that had taken months now took a week.

Goaded by Bismarck's edited Ems dispatch, France declared war on Prussia in July 1870, and within six weeks its field armies were beaten. On 1 September Moltke's armies ringed Marshal MacMahon's army in the valley of the Meuse at Sedan, and the next day Napoleon III gave up his sword and over eighty thousand men. Paris proclaimed the Third Republic on 4 September.

Francisco Solano López had drawn Paraguay in 1864 into war against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay together. For five years his people fought on with desperate courage, boys and women in the ranks at the last, until Brazilian cavalry ran him down at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870. Paraguay had lost perhaps half its people, and the greater part of its men.

When the French garrison was withdrawn for the war against Prussia, Italian troops under General Cadorna breached the Aurelian wall beside the Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, and Rome, ruled by the popes for over a thousand years, became the capital of Italy. Pius IX, who had proclaimed papal infallibility at the Vatican Council that July, withdrew into the Vatican as its prisoner.

t: The German Empire Proclaimed at Versailles
x: With Paris under siege, the German princes gathered in the Hall of Mirrors of Louis XIV's palace on 18 January 1871, and King William I of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor. Bismarck had made the empire by three short wars. France ceded Alsace and northern Lorraine with Metz and paid five billion francs, and the new power at the heart of Europe changed the balance of the continent.

t: The Bloody Week of the Commune
x: When Thiers tried to seize the cannon of the National Guard on Montmartre on 18 March 1871, Paris rose and elected a revolutionary Commune. In the Bloody Week of 21 to 28 May the Versailles army retook the city street by street; the Communards shot hostages, among them Archbishop Darboy, and burned the Tuileries, and the army shot thousands, the last against a wall in Père Lachaise.

Diamonds found on the farm of the De Beer brothers drew diggers from every land to the 'New Rush,' where the Big Hole was dug by hand, and Britain annexed Griqualand West to make it hers. Out of the scramble rose Cecil Rhodes, whose De Beers company had swallowed the whole field by 1888 and gave him the fortune to dream of an Africa British from the Cape to Cairo.

Henry Morton Stanley, sent by the New York Herald to find the Scottish missionary and explorer David Livingstone, of whom nothing had been heard for years, marched inland from Bagamoyo and found him, sick and destitute, at Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika in November 1871. Livingstone refused to go home, and died in 1873 at Chitambo, still seeking the sources of the Nile.

After a mutiny of native soldiers at the Cavite arsenal in January 1872, the Spanish authorities garroted three Filipino priests, Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos, and Jacinto Zamora, who had championed the rights of the native clergy. Their innocence was widely believed, and their deaths awakened the patriotism of the generation of Jose Rizal, who dedicated his second novel to them.

The Dutch, left free by Britain to act in northern Sumatra, declared war on the Sultanate of Aceh in 1873; their first expedition failed and its general Kohler was shot before the Great Mosque. A second took the capital in 1874, but the Acehnese, led by their ulama in a holy war, fought on for thirty years, and the last sultan surrendered only in 1903.

Ratu Seru Cakobau, who had styled himself King of Fiji and accepted Christianity in 1854, could neither pay his debts nor govern the planters and adventurers of Levuka. On 10 October 1874 he and the other high chiefs ceded the islands to Queen Victoria. The next year measles killed perhaps a third of the Fijians, and from 1879 laborers were brought from India.

To end the civil wars of the Perak chiefs and of the Chinese tin miners' secret societies, Governor Sir Andrew Clarke recognized Raja Abdullah as Sultan of Perak in January 1874, on condition that he accept a British Resident whose advice he must follow in all but religion and Malay custom. The killing of the first Resident, J. W. W. Birch, in 1875 brought troops and full British control.

George Tupou I, the Methodist warrior king who had united Tonga by 1845, freed the commoners from forced service to the chiefs and in 1875 gave his kingdom a written constitution, with a parliament, courts, and land guaranteed to every Tongan man. Tonga became a British protected state in 1900 but was never colonized, the only Pacific kingdom to keep its crown.

When gold was found in the Black Hills, sacred to the Lakota and guaranteed to them by treaty, the army moved to drive the free bands onto reservations. On 25 June 1876 Lieutenant Colonel George Custer attacked a vast encampment of Lakota and Cheyenne under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse on the Little Bighorn; he and all five companies with him, some 210 men, were killed.

After the Ottoman suppression of the Bulgarian April Rising of 1876, in which thousands of Christians were massacred at Batak and elsewhere, Russia went to war with Turkey. Osman Pasha's entrenched garrison at Plevna threw back three Russian and Romanian assaults; starved out, it surrendered on 10 December 1877, and the Russians were soon at the gates of Constantinople.

Saigō Takamori, the great hero of the Restoration, led the disaffected samurai of Satsuma against the government that had taken their swords and stipends. They besieged Kumamoto castle in vain; the new conscript army of peasants relieved it, drove them back, and cornered the last of them on the hill of Shiroyama above Kagoshima, where Saigō fell. The age of the samurai ended with him.

During the Muslim risings of the 1860s the Kokandi adventurer Yakub Beg had made himself master of Kashgar and the Tarim, courted by Britain and Russia alike. The Qing general Zuo Zongtang, marching west across the deserts with an army that grew its own grain along the way, crushed his state in 1877. Xinjiang was made a province of China in 1884.

Alarmed by the Treaty of San Stefano and its great Russian-sponsored Bulgaria, the powers met in Berlin in June and July 1878 under Bismarck, the honest broker. Romania, Serbia, and Montenegro became independent; Bulgaria was cut to about a third and left under the Sultan's suzerainty; Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Disraeli brought home Cyprus and peace with honor.

In June 1878 the Kanak of central New Caledonia, pressed by the spread of French settlers and their cattle, rose under the high chief Atai and killed some two hundred colonists. The French, with Kanak auxiliaries from rival clans, crushed the revolt over the following months; Atai was killed, and perhaps a thousand Kanak died.

Lord Chelmsford invaded Zululand to break the power of King Cetshwayo and left his camp beneath the crag of Isandlwana lightly guarded. On 22 January some 20,000 Zulu warriors overran it and killed more than 1,300 of its defenders, Britain's most humiliating defeat of the Victorian age; that night some 150 men held the mission station at Rorke's Drift against thousands.

When Bolivia raised its tax on the Chilean company working the nitrate beds of its Atacama coast, Chile seized Antofagasta in February 1879, and Peru, bound to Bolivia by a secret treaty, was drawn in. Chile's navy won command of the sea at Angamos, its army occupied Lima in 1881, and the peace left Chile the nitrate provinces and Bolivia without a coast.

On 13 March 1881, as Alexander II drove beside the Catherine Canal after a parade, a bomb thrown by a member of the People's Will shattered his carriage; when he stepped out to see the wounded, Ignacy Hryniewiecki threw a second bomb at his feet. He died that afternoon in the Winter Palace, on the day he had approved a plan for consultative reform. His son Alexander III buried it.

Colonel Ahmed Urabi led a movement of Egyptian officers against the khedive Tewfik and the European controllers of Egypt's debts. After riots in Alexandria, the British bombarded the city, landed an army on the Suez Canal, and on 13 September 1882 stormed Urabi's lines at Tel el-Kebir after a night march. Britain occupied Egypt for seventy-four years.

On 27 August 1883 the volcano of Krakatoa in the Sunda Strait destroyed itself in four tremendous explosions, the last heard on Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean, three thousand miles away. Its waves, more than thirty meters high, swept away 165 villages on the coasts of Java and Sumatra and some 36,000 people; the telegraph carried the news around the world within hours.

From November 1884 to February 1885 the delegates of fourteen powers met in Bismarck's residence on the Wilhelmstrasse to settle the rules for claiming Africa. The General Act required effective occupation of coasts claimed, declared free trade on the Congo and the Niger, and in effect recognized King Leopold II's International Association as the Congo Free State, the King's personal domain.

Seventy-two delegates, lawyers, journalists, and teachers from every province, gathered at Gokuldas Tejpal College in Bombay in December 1885 at the call of the retired civil servant Allan Octavian Hume, and founded the Indian National Congress. Moderate and loyal at first, it became the vehicle of the movement that won India its independence.

t: Ham Nghi and the Can Vuong
x: The treaties of 1883 and 1884 made Annam and Tonkin French protectorates. In July 1885 the regent Ton That Thuyet attacked the French garrison at Hue and fled to the hills with the boy emperor Ham Nghi, who called on the scholars to rise in the Can Vuong, Aid the King. Bands of the movement slaughtered thousands of Vietnamese Catholics before Ham Nghi was betrayed in 1888.

King Thibaw's court fined a British timber company and sought friendship with France. In November 1885 a British force steamed up the Irrawaddy and took Mandalay almost without a fight, and Thibaw and Queen Supayalat were carried off to exile in India. On 1 January 1886 Upper Burma was annexed and joined to British India, and a long guerrilla war followed.

Muhammad Ahmad, a Dongolawi holy man who had proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the redeemer awaited by Muslims, raised the Sudan against its Egyptian masters and destroyed every army sent against him. After a siege of ten months his ansar stormed Khartoum on 26 January 1885 and slew General Charles Gordon at the governor's palace, two days before British relief steamers came in sight.

When Bulgaria absorbed Eastern Rumelia in September 1885 against the will of the powers, King Milan of Serbia invaded to claim compensation. Prince Alexander of Battenberg rushed his young army west from the Turkish frontier, and from 17 to 19 November beat the Serbs at Slivnitsa and drove them over the border to Pirot. Austria-Hungary halted his advance; the union stood.

George Harrison, an Australian prospector, struck the main gold reef on the farm Langlaagte, and within months a camp named Johannesburg spread across the high veld of Paul Kruger's South African Republic. The Rand proved the richest goldfield on earth, and the quarrel between Kruger and its foreign miners, the uitlanders, and their mining magnates led on to the Boer War.

On 29 January 1886 the Mannheim engineer Karl Benz applied for patent number 37435 for a three-wheeled vehicle driven by a petrol engine of his own design. In August 1888 his wife Bertha drove it with their two sons some sixty-five miles to her mother's house in Pforzheim, the first long journey by automobile, buying fuel from apothecaries on the way.

Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda, enraged that his Christian pages refused his commands for the sake of their faith, had them seized, and on 3 June 1886 more than thirty were burned alive at Namugongo, among them the young Catholic Charles Lwanga and Anglican converts beside him. Their deaths, honored by both churches, made Uganda one of the strongest Christian lands of Africa.

In June 1887 bands of Haw, Chinese freebooters of the Black Flag kind, under the White Tai chief Deo Van Tri, sacked and burned the royal city of Luang Prabang. The French vice-consul Auguste Pavie carried the aged King Oun Kham to safety down the Mekong, and the gratitude of the Lao court opened the way to the French protectorate over Laos.

Brazil, which had received nearly five million enslaved Africans, more than any other land, was the last nation of the Americas to abolish slavery. On 13 May 1888, with her father Pedro II abroad, the Princess Imperial Isabel signed the Golden Law freeing the last seven hundred thousand slaves without compensation; the embittered planters helped overthrow the monarchy the next year.

The young William II, who had come to the throne in the Year of the Three Emperors, would not share power with the old chancellor who had made the Reich. Forced to resign on 18 March 1890, Bismarck retired to Friedrichsruh to write his memoirs and criticize his successors. The Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapsed that June, and Russia turned to France.

On 31 May 1891 the Tsarevich Nicholas, returning from a journey to Japan where a policeman had slashed him with a sword, turned the first earth for the Ussuri line at Vladivostok. Driven by Sergei Witte, the Trans-Siberian Railway reached across nearly six thousand miles of steppe and taiga to the Pacific, bound Siberia to Russia, and drew the empire into Manchuria and war with Japan.

Colonel Alfred-Amédée Dodds, a Senegal-born officer of mixed descent, led a French column up the Ouémé River against King Béhanzin, whose women warriors fought with famous courage in battle after battle. Béhanzin set fire to his capital of Abomey before abandoning it in November 1892; he surrendered in 1894 and died in exile in Algeria.

Sir Mortimer Durand, foreign secretary of British India, agreed with the Amir Abdur Rahman Khan at Kabul on a boundary between Afghanistan and the Raj running some 2,600 kilometres through the Pashtun and Baluch hills. It split the Pashtun tribes between two states, and no Afghan government has since accepted it as the border with Pakistan.

Pressing claims to the lands east of the Mekong, France sent two gunboats past the forts at Paknam at the river mouth on 13 July 1893, and they anchored before the Grand Palace. Facing blockade, King Chulalongkorn yielded all Laos east of the Mekong. Siam survived as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina, but at the price of its outer provinces.

t: Votes for Women in New Zealand
x: After petitions bearing some thirty-two thousand signatures, gathered by Kate Sheppard and the Women's Christian Temperance Union, the Electoral Act became law on 19 September 1893. New Zealand thus became the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the vote, and that November nearly two-thirds of its adult women went to the polls.

When Queen Liliuokalani sought a new constitution to restore royal power, a Committee of Safety of American and European sugar men, backed by marines landed from the USS Boston, deposed her on 17 January 1893. The Republic of Hawaii under Sanford Dole crushed a royalist rising in 1895, and in 1898 the United States annexed the islands.

After the Armenians of Sasun resisted Kurdish tribute-takers in 1894 and were butchered by troops and irregulars, a wave of massacres swept the Armenian towns of Anatolia in 1895 and 1896, at Trebizond, Erzurum, Diyarbakır, Urfa, and Constantinople itself, under the rule of Abdul Hamid II. At least a hundred thousand Armenians perished; in the cathedral of Urfa some three thousand were burned alive.

Japan's modern army and navy had shattered the Qing forces in Korea and at sea off the Yalu, and taken Port Arthur and Weihaiwei. At Shimonoseki Li Hongzhang, wounded by a Japanese assassin during the talks, signed away Taiwan and the Penghu islands, recognized the independence of Korea, and agreed to an indemnity of two hundred million taels.

Queen Min, consort of King Gojong, who had turned to Russia to check Japanese power, was cut down in her quarters in the Gyeongbok Palace by Japanese swordsmen sent by the minister Miura Gorō, and her body was burned. The king fled to the Russian legation, and in 1897 proclaimed himself Emperor of Korea.

A French expeditionary force of some 15,000 landed at Majunga and toiled for months through fever-ridden country, losing thousands to disease and few to battle, before shelling the royal palace of Antananarivo on 30 September 1895. Queen Ranavalona III submitted; the island was annexed the next year, and in 1897 General Joseph Gallieni abolished the Merina monarchy and sent her into exile.

Andres Bonifacio, a warehouse clerk, had founded the secret Katipunan to win independence by arms. Discovered by the Spanish, its members tore up their cedulas, the tax certificates of Spanish rule, in the hills north of Manila in late August 1896 and rose in revolt. In Cavite the young Emilio Aguinaldo won the first victories and soon eclipsed Bonifacio, whom his rivals put to death in 1897.

Jose Rizal, physician, poet, and author of the novels Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo, which laid bare the abuses of friars and officials, had never joined the revolution. The Spanish nonetheless tried him for rebellion and shot him at Bagumbayan field on 30 December 1896. His farewell poem, written in his cell, made him the martyr of the Filipino nation.

When Italy claimed, under a disputed clause of the Treaty of Wuchale, a protectorate over Ethiopia, Emperor Menelik II summoned the lords of the empire, and the Empress Taytu marched beside him. On 1 March 1896 his host of some 100,000 crushed General Baratieri's army of 17,000 among the mountains of Adwa, killing some 7,000; Italy recognized Ethiopia's independence, and it alone of the old African kingdoms escaped the partition.

In the winter of 1895 to 1896 the Amir Abdur Rahman sent his armies into the Hindu Kush valleys of Kafiristan, whose people had kept their ancient gods and wooden effigies of the dead while all around them turned to Islam. They were conquered and converted by force, their shrines burned, and the land renamed Nuristan, the Land of Light.

After men of Oba Ovonramwen killed a British party under Acting Consul-General James Phillips, which had insisted on entering the kingdom during a sacred festival, a punitive expedition of some 1,200 marines and sailors took Benin City in February 1897. The city burned, the oba was exiled to Calabar, and thousands of bronzes and ivories were carried off and sold to museums and collectors.

Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer of the General Staff, was condemned in 1894 for betraying secrets to Germany on flimsy evidence and a secret file, and sent to Devil's Island. When a court-martial acquitted the real traitor, Major Esterhazy, Émile Zola published in L'Aurore on 13 January 1898 an open letter to the President headed J'accuse. The Affair split France for a decade; Dreyfus was exonerated in 1906.

A week after war broke out between Spain and the United States, Commodore George Dewey's squadron entered Manila Bay by night and on the morning of 1 May 1898 destroyed the Spanish fleet off Cavite without losing a man to enemy fire. On 12 June Aguinaldo proclaimed Philippine independence from his house at Kawit, but in December Spain ceded the islands to the United States for twenty million dollars.

General Herbert Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army, brought south by a railway laid across the Nubian desert, met the Khalifa Abdallahi's host of some 50,000 on the plain of Kerreri outside Omdurman on 2 September 1898. Maxim guns, artillery, and gunboats on the Nile cut down some ten thousand of the Khalifa's men for fewer than fifty of their own; the young Winston Churchill rode in the charge of the 21st Lancers.

Three years into the Cuban war of independence, the battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbor in February 1898, and the United States declared war on Spain. At Santiago, Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders and the regulars stormed the San Juan Heights on 1 July, and two days later the American fleet destroyed Admiral Cervera's squadron; Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.

The Boxers, peasant bands who believed their rites made them proof against bullets, swept across the north killing missionaries and Chinese Christians by the thousands. In June the Empress Dowager Cixi declared war on the powers, and the legations of Beijing were besieged for fifty-five days until an army of eight nations relieved them and sacked the city.

When the British governor Sir Frederic Hodgson demanded to sit upon the Golden Stool, the soul of the nation, Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, shamed the Asante chiefs into war and besieged the British in the fort at Kumasi. The siege was relieved and the rising broken; she died in exile in the Seychelles, but the Golden Stool was never surrendered.

On 1 January 1901 the six colonies of Australia united as a federal Commonwealth, proclaimed before a vast crowd in Sydney's Centennial Park, with Edmund Barton as first prime minister. One of the new Parliament's first acts was the Immigration Restriction Act, foundation of the White Australia policy. A new capital, Canberra, was laid out in the bush from 1913.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, a young exile living with his family in Kuwait, rode into Najd with some forty companions. Before dawn on 15 January 1902 his men surprised the Rashidi governor Ajlan outside the Masmak fort in Riyadh and killed him. The town rallied to the house of Saud, and from it Ibn Saud built the kingdom that would bear his family's name.

The war Britain had expected to end by Christmas of 1899 lasted two years and seven months. Boer commandos fought on long after Pretoria fell, and Lord Kitchener answered with blockhouses, burned farms, and concentration camps in which some 26,000 Boer women and children and many thousands of black Africans died. In May 1902 the two republics accepted British sovereignty.

t: The First Flight at Kitty Hawk
x: On the windswept dunes of Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, on 17 December 1903, Orville Wright lifted the brothers' gasoline-engined Flyer into the air for twelve seconds and 120 feet, the first controlled and sustained flight of a powered machine heavier than air. Wilbur's fourth flight that day lasted fifty-nine seconds; within forty years the airplane had transformed war, commerce, and travel.

Stirred by a blood libel printed in the local newspaper, mobs attacked the Jews of Kishinev, capital of Bessarabia, over Easter on 19 and 20 April 1903, while the police stood by. Forty-nine were killed and hundreds of houses and shops sacked. The pogrom horrified Europe and America and hastened both the emigration of Russian Jews and the Zionist movement.

Six years after their confrontation at Fashoda, Britain and France signed on 8 April 1904 a set of agreements settling their colonial quarrels: France recognized British control of Egypt, and Britain gave France a free hand in Morocco, with lesser bargains over Newfoundland, Siam, and the New Hebrides. Lansdowne and Paul Cambon had ended centuries of rivalry, and the entente hardened against Germany.

The Herero of German South West Africa, stripped of land and cattle by settlers, rose under Samuel Maharero in January 1904. After the battle at the Waterberg in August, General Lothar von Trotha drove the survivors into the waterless Omaheke and decreed that every Herero found within German borders be shot; with the Nama rising that followed, perhaps four in five of the Herero perished.

Fearing Russian influence in Tibet, Lord Curzon sent Colonel Francis Younghusband over the Himalayas with a British and Indian force. At Chumik Shenko its machine guns cut down several hundred Tibetans armed with matchlocks and swords; Gyantse was stormed, and the British entered Lhasa, from which the Thirteenth Dalai Lama had fled to Mongolia.

After a voyage of eighteen thousand miles from the Baltic, the Russian fleet of Admiral Rozhestvensky met Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō in the Tsushima Strait. In two days the Japanese sank or captured nearly all of it, losing only three torpedo boats. With Port Arthur fallen and Mukden lost, Russia made peace, and for the first time in modern history an Asian power had beaten a European one.

On Sunday, 22 January 1905, the priest Georgy Gapon led tens of thousands of workers carrying icons and portraits of the Tsar toward the Winter Palace with a petition for an eight-hour day and a constituent assembly. Troops fired on the columns at several points, and well over a hundred were killed. The revolution of 1905 followed, ended only by the October Manifesto and a Duma.

In 1905 a twenty-six-year-old technical examiner at the Swiss patent office in Bern, Albert Einstein, published four papers in Annalen der Physik: on light as quanta, on the motion of particles suspended in liquid, on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, which set out special relativity, and on the equivalence of mass and energy. Physics was not the same again.

When Oscar II refused to sanction a separate Norwegian consular service, Christian Michelsen's government resigned, and on 7 June 1905 the Storting declared the union with Sweden dissolved, as the King had ceased to function as king of Norway. A plebiscite approved by 368,208 votes to 184; Sweden yielded at Karlstad, and Prince Carl of Denmark became King Haakon VII.

In the summer of 1906 some fourteen thousand merchants, clerics, and craftsmen took sanctuary in the gardens of the British legation at Tehran, demanding a house of justice. The ailing Mozaffar al-Din Shah yielded; the first Majlis met in October and drew up a constitution, which he signed just before his death. His son Mohammad Ali Shah shelled the Majlis in 1908 but was deposed the next year.

When a Dutch expedition marched on Denpasar to enforce the claims of the Indies government, the Raja of Badung, dressed in white and decked with his jewels, led his court, priests, women, and children out against the troops on 20 September 1906 in a puputan, a fight to the end. Rifles and artillery cut down hundreds; Klungkung met the same fate in 1908.

On 17 December 1907 an assembly of lamas, officials, and chiefs at Punakha chose Ugyen Wangchuck, penlop of Trongsa, who had made himself master of the country and aided the British mission to Lhasa, as the first hereditary king of Bhutan. His house, the Wangchucks, reigns still.

Officers of the Committee of Union and Progress in the Third Army in Macedonia, among them Enver Bey, took to the hills in July 1908 and threatened to march on the capital. Abdul Hamid II restored the constitution of 1876 on 24 July, and the empire rejoiced in a brief brotherhood of creeds. When a counter-revolution failed in 1909, the sultan was deposed and sent to Salonica.

After seven years of fruitless drilling under William Knox D'Arcy's concession, a British crew struck oil at Masjed Soleyman in the Zagros foothills on 26 May 1908, the first great oil field of the Middle East. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company was formed the next year, and in 1914 the British government, turning its navy from coal to oil, bought a controlling share.

King Leopold II had ruled the Congo Free State as his private domain since 1885, and his agents and concession companies drove its people to gather wild rubber by terror, with the taking of hostages and the severing of hands. After the reports of Roger Casement and the agitation of E. D. Morel, Belgium annexed the territory in 1908 as the Belgian Congo; the toll in lives had been immense.

Using the Young Turk revolution as pretext, Austria-Hungary, steered by its foreign minister Aehrenthal, proclaimed on 6 October 1908 the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, occupied since 1878, a day after Bulgaria declared its independence at Tarnovo. Serbia raged, and Russia, unready, backed down before a German ultimatum in March 1909; the humiliation was not forgotten in St. Petersburg.

Having made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and forced Emperor Gojong to abdicate, Japan annexed the country outright, and the last emperor, Sunjong, yielded his throne. For thirty-five years Korea was ruled by Japanese governors-general from Keijō, its land surveyed and taken, its schools taught in Japanese, and its patriots hunted.

A bomb that went off by accident in a revolutionary hideout in Hankou forced the hand of the plotters in the New Army at Wuchang, who rose on the night of 10 October and seized the city. Province after province declared for the revolution, and on 12 February 1912 the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor, Puyi, abdicated. More than two thousand years of imperial rule had ended.

As the Qing fell, the princes of Outer Mongolia declared their independence and enthroned the Jebtsundamba Khutughtu, the highest lama of the Mongols, as Bogd Khan, the Holy Emperor, at Urga. The new state turned to Russia for protection, and China would grant it only autonomy, but Mongolia was never again ruled from Beijing for long.

Francisco Madero, a wealthy landowner jailed for daring to run against the aged dictator Porfirio Díaz, called the nation to arms in November 1910. In May 1911 the irregulars of Pascual Orozco and Pancho Villa took Ciudad Juárez, and Díaz, after some thirty-five years in power, sailed for exile; a decade of revolution followed in which perhaps a million Mexicans died.

t: The First Bombs from the Air
x: Italy declared war on the Ottoman Empire in September 1911 to take Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, the last African provinces ruled directly by the Sultan. On 1 November Lieutenant Giulio Gavotti, flying an Etrich monoplane over the Turkish camp at Ain Zara near Tripoli, dropped four small bombs by hand, the first bombing from an aeroplane. By the Treaty of Ouchy in 1912 Libya passed to Italy.

Italy declared war on the Ottoman Empire in September 1911 and landed troops at Tripoli and Benghazi to seize the last Ottoman provinces in Africa. On 1 November Lieutenant Giulio Gavotti dropped small bombs from his aeroplane on a Turkish camp near Tripoli, the first bombing from the air in war. The Ottomans ceded Libya in 1912, but the Sanusi tribes of Cyrenaica fought on for twenty years.

In October 1912 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, and Montenegro fell upon the Ottoman Empire. The Serbs routed the Ottoman army of the Vardar at Kumanovo on 23 and 24 October, the Bulgarians drove to the Chatalja lines before Constantinople, and the Greeks entered Salonica. Within weeks five centuries of Ottoman rule in Europe were reduced to Thrace, and the victors fell to quarreling over Macedonia.

With Serbian, Montenegrin, and Greek armies overrunning the Ottoman Balkans, Albanian delegates met at Valona on 28 November 1912, and Ismail Qemali raised the black double-headed eagle of Skanderbeg over a free Albania. The Conference of Ambassadors in London recognized the new state and gave it a German prince, William of Wied, who stayed six months.

t: The Founding of the African National Congress
x: Chiefs, clergymen, and lawyers from every province of the new Union met at Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912 and founded the South African Native National Congress, with John Dube as president and Sol Plaatje as secretary, to defend the rights of black South Africans. The Natives Land Act of the next year, confining Africans to a small fraction of the land, gave it its first great cause.

At his Highland Park plant Henry Ford installed in 1913 the moving assembly line, cutting the time to build a Model T chassis from more than twelve hours to about an hour and a half. The next year he doubled his workers' pay to five dollars a day; the motorcar became the possession of the common man, and mass production the method of the century.

At the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées on 29 May 1913, Diaghilev's Russian Ballet gave the first performance of Igor Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, danced to Nijinsky's choreography of pagan Russia. Its pounding rhythms and dissonance brought jeering, catcalls, and fights in the audience, and the music, more than the riot, marked a turning in the art of the century.

Following the Schlieffen plan to defeat France by a wheel through the Low Countries, German armies crossed the Belgian frontier on 4 August 1914, and Britain, guarantor of Belgian neutrality, declared war that night. The forts of Liège held for twelve days until crushed by Krupp and Škoda siege howitzers, and at Louvain on 25 August the Germans burned the university library.

Russia invaded East Prussia sooner than Germany expected. Recalled from retirement, General Paul von Hindenburg, with Erich Ludendorff as chief of staff, fell on Samsonov's Second Army in the forests and lakes of Masuria from 26 to 30 August 1914, encircling it and taking some 92,000 prisoners. Samsonov shot himself; the victory was named for the field where the Teutonic Knights had fallen in 1410.

With the German right wing wheeling east of Paris, General Joffre turned his retreating armies on 6 September 1914 and struck its exposed flank along the Marne, while General Gallieni sent reinforcements from Paris in requisitioned taxicabs. A gap opened between the German First and Second Armies; on 9 September Moltke's staff ordered retreat to the Aisne, and the war of movement in the west ended in trenches.

After the French under Ferdinand de Lesseps had failed at the cost of some twenty thousand lives, the United States, which had backed Panama's secession from Colombia in 1903, built the canal in ten years, conquering yellow fever and malaria under William Gorgas and cutting through the Culebra divide. The SS Ancon made the first official passage on 15 August 1914, joining the Atlantic and the Pacific.

To force the Dardanelles and knock Turkey out of the war, as Winston Churchill urged, British, French, Australian, and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April 1915. The Turks, with Mustafa Kemal commanding above Anzac Cove, held the heights there and at Cape Helles; after eight months and over a quarter of a million casualties on each side, the allies withdrew in January 1916.

On the night of 24 April 1915 the Young Turk government arrested the Armenian leaders of Constantinople, and in the months that followed Armenian men across Anatolia were massacred and the women, children, and old driven on death marches into the Syrian desert toward Deir ez-Zor. Assyrian and Greek Christians suffered a like fate. Most historians reckon the Armenian dead at a million or more.

On 21 February 1916 General von Falkenhayn opened the attack on the fortress of Verdun with a bombardment of over a thousand guns, meaning to bleed the French army white where it could not retreat. General Pétain fed troops up the single road, the Sacred Way, and the forts of Douaumont and Vaux fell and were retaken. By December some 700,000 men on both sides had been killed, wounded, or taken.

On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, some 1,200 Irish Volunteers and Citizen Army men seized the General Post Office and other strongpoints in Dublin, and Patrick Pearse read the proclamation of an Irish Republic from its steps. British artillery shelled them into surrender within six days. The execution of fifteen leaders in May, Pearse and James Connolly among them, turned Irish opinion toward the rebels.

On 31 May 1916 the British Grand Fleet under Jellicoe and Beatty met Admiral Scheer's High Seas Fleet in the North Sea off Jutland, some 250 ships in all. Three British battlecruisers blew up, and Britain lost fourteen ships and over six thousand men to Germany's eleven ships and some 2,500 men. But Scheer slipped home in the night, and the German battle fleet never again risked a general action.

t: The First Day of the Somme
x: After a week's bombardment that was meant to leave no German alive, the British Fourth Army went over the top along the Somme at 7:30 on the morning of 1 July 1916. The wire was uncut and the machine-gunners had survived in deep dugouts; by nightfall the British had suffered 57,470 casualties, 19,240 of them dead, the worst day in the history of their army.

Encouraged by British promises of an independent Arab kingdom, Sharif Hussein ibn Ali of Mecca proclaimed revolt against the Ottomans in June 1916. His sons Faisal and Abdullah, with British officers such as T. E. Lawrence, raided the Hejaz Railway, took Aqaba in July 1917, and rode north with Allenby. Meanwhile Britain and France had secretly divided the Arab lands in the Sykes-Picot agreement.

On the night of 7 November 1917, the October Revolution by the Russian calendar, the Red Guards and soldiers of the Military Revolutionary Committee directed by Trotsky occupied the bridges, stations, and telegraph of Petrograd and took the Winter Palace, arresting Kerensky's ministers. Lenin proclaimed Soviet power, peace, and land to the peasants, and founded the first communist state.

Bread riots and strikes in Petrograd in March 1917, the February Revolution by the Russian calendar, became revolution when the garrison mutinied and joined the crowds. Halted by his generals in his train at Pskov, Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March for himself and his son; his brother Michael declined the crown the next day, and three centuries of Romanov rule ended.

On 6 December 1917 the Finnish parliament approved the declaration of independence presented by Pehr Evind Svinhufvud's Senate, and Lenin's government recognized it on the last day of the year. Civil war followed between the socialist Reds and the government's Whites under General Mannerheim, who stormed Tampere in April 1918 and with German help won by May, at a cost of some 36,000 Finnish lives.

General Sir Edmund Allenby broke the Ottoman line at Beersheba and Gaza and on 11 December 1917 entered Jerusalem on foot through the Jaffa Gate, in reverence for the Holy City. Five weeks before, the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour had declared that the government viewed with favor a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, without prejudice to the rights of its non-Jewish communities.

After eleven Italian offensives on the Isonzo, Austro-Hungarian and German divisions, the young Erwin Rommel among them, broke through at Caporetto on 24 October 1917 with gas and infiltration tactics. The Italian Second Army collapsed; Cadorna's armies fell back some seventy miles to the Piave, leaving about 265,000 prisoners, and there held with British and French help.

From May to October 1917 three shepherd children of Fátima, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, saw a lady from heaven who came to them month after month and asked for prayer and penance. On 13 October a crowd of tens of thousands, gathered in the rain, beheld the miracle of the sun, and Fátima became one of the great shrines of Christendom.

To keep the revolution alive, Lenin forced on his comrades a separate peace with Germany and its allies, signed in the fortress of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918 after the Germans had resumed their advance. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland, and Ukraine, a third of its population and most of its coal and iron; Germany's defeat in November annulled the treaty.

With its allies collapsing, its navy in mutiny, and revolution in Berlin, where the Kaiser's abdication was announced and a republic proclaimed on 9 November 1918, Germany sent envoys to Marshal Foch's railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne. They signed at five in the morning of 11 November, and at eleven o'clock the guns fell silent on the Western Front.

In October 1918 the Habsburg monarchy dissolved into its nations: the Czechs proclaimed their state in Prague on the 28th, the South Slavs in Zagreb on the 29th, and Hungary broke away. On 11 November, in the palace of Schönbrunn, Emperor Charles I renounced all part in the affairs of state, and the next day German Austria was declared a republic.

Released from the German fortress of Magdeburg, Józef Piłsudski arrived in Warsaw on 10 November 1918; the next day the Regency Council handed him command of the army, and the German garrison was disarmed. After 123 years of partition Poland was a state again, though its frontiers would be fought for against Ukrainians, Lithuanians, Czechs, and Bolsheviks for three more years.

In the cellar of the merchant Ipatiev's house in Ekaterinburg, in the early hours of 17 July 1918, a Bolshevik firing squad under Yakov Yurovsky shot the deposed Nicholas II, the Empress Alexandra, their son Alexei, their four daughters, and four servants, finishing the wounded with bayonets, as Czech and White forces approached the city. The bodies were burned and buried in the forest.

In November 1918 the steamer Talune, allowed to land at Apia by the New Zealand administration, brought the Spanish influenza to Western Samoa. Within weeks some 8,500 people, more than a fifth of the population, were dead, among them many of the chiefs. American Samoa, which had shut its harbor, lost no one, and Samoan anger fed the Mau movement for self-rule.

In the Hall of Mirrors where the German Empire had been proclaimed, the German delegates signed on 28 June 1919, five years to the day after Sarajevo, the treaty dictated by Clemenceau, Lloyd George, and Wilson. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine, its colonies, and much of its eastern provinces to Poland, accepted responsibility for the war, and was disarmed and burdened with reparations; the Covenant of the League of Nations stood at its head.

Thirty-three religious leaders, Christians, Cheondogyo believers, and Buddhists, signed a declaration of Korean independence, which was read aloud in Tapgol Park in Seoul. Peaceful demonstrations spread to every province, and the Japanese police and army answered with rifles and fire, killing thousands. A Provisional Government of Korea was founded in Shanghai.

When the Paris Peace Conference gave Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan instead of returning them to China, three thousand students of Peking University and other colleges marched to Tiananmen and burned the house of a pro-Japanese minister. Strikes and boycotts spread to Shanghai, and the movement grew into a revolt against Confucian tradition in the name of science and democracy.

On 13 April 1919, the festival of Baisakhi, General Reginald Dyer marched troops into the Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden at Amritsar where thousands had gathered in defiance of a ban on meetings, and without warning fired until the ammunition was spent. The official count was 379 dead, Indian estimates far higher. Gandhi, Tagore, and millions of moderate Indians turned against the Raj.

Amanullah Khan, newly emir after his father's murder, declared Afghanistan wholly independent and sent his troops across the frontier in May 1919. The Third Anglo-Afghan War lasted a month; British aircraft bombed Kabul and Jalalabad, but the war-weary British conceded at Rawalpindi in August that Afghanistan should conduct its own foreign affairs. Afghans keep 19 August as their day of independence.

Fleeing the street fighting of Berlin, the German National Assembly met in Goethe's city of Weimar from February 1919, elected Friedrich Ebert president, and adopted on 31 July a democratic constitution with universal suffrage for men and women, proportional representation, and a strong president with emergency powers under its Article 48. The republic took its name from the town.

In August 1920 Tukhachevsky's Red Army stood before Warsaw, meaning to carry revolution over Poland's corpse into Germany. While the line held at Radzymin, Piłsudski struck on 16 August from the Wieprz river into the Soviet flank and rear; the Red armies broke and fled, leaving tens of thousands of prisoners. The Peace of Riga in 1921 fixed Poland's eastern frontier.

Signed on 4 June 1920 in the Grand Trianon palace at Versailles, the peace with Hungary stripped the old kingdom of St. Stephen of over two thirds of its territory and a third of its Magyar people, who found themselves under Romanian, Czechoslovak, and Yugoslav rule. Flags in Budapest flew at half-mast, and the revision of Trianon became the creed of Hungarian politics.

In September 1920 the Red Army under Mikhail Frunze stormed Bukhara after four days of bombardment, and the last emir, Alim Khan, fled to Afghanistan. A Bukharan People's Soviet Republic was set up, and for a decade the Basmachi rebels fought the Soviets in the hills. In 1924 Moscow redrew Central Asia into national republics, Uzbek and Turkmen first, then Tajik, Kazakh, and Kyrgyz.

t: The Communist Party of China Founded
x: Thirteen delegates, among them a young schoolteacher from Hunan named Mao Zedong, met with two agents of the Communist International in a house in the French Concession of Shanghai; when a stranger came to the door, they finished their congress on a pleasure boat on South Lake at Jiaxing. The party then had some fifty members.

In March 1921 the sailors of the island fortress of Kronstadt, once the pride of the revolution, rose for free soviets without Bolshevik domination, free speech, and an end to grain requisitions. Trotsky and Tukhachevsky sent troops across the ice to storm the fortress on 17 and 18 March, and the Tenth Party Congress meeting that month adopted Lenin's New Economic Policy.

The White Russian baron Roman von Ungern-Sternberg had driven the Chinese from Urga and restored the Bogd Khan, ruling the city by terror. Mongolian partisans under Damdin Sükhbaatar, with the Red Army behind them, defeated him and entered Urga in July. When the Bogd Khan died in 1924 the Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed, the second communist state in the world.

On 1 November 1922 the Grand National Assembly at Ankara, led by Mustafa Kemal, abolished the Ottoman sultanate, and on 17 November Mehmed VI, last of the thirty-six sultans of the house of Osman, left Constantinople on a British warship. His cousin Abdulmejid was left as caliph alone, until the caliphate itself was abolished in March 1924. Six centuries of Ottoman rule were at an end.

The Anglo-Irish Treaty signed in London in December 1921 by Michael Collins and Arthur Griffith made twenty-six counties a self-governing dominion, and on 16 January 1922 Collins took over Dublin Castle from the last Lord Lieutenant. De Valera rejected the oath to the Crown; civil war followed, Collins was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth in August, and the Free State won by May 1923.

As some thirty thousand Fascist blackshirts converged on Rome in the rain on 28 October 1922, King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign his government's decree of martial law. The next day he summoned Benito Mussolini, who came down from Milan by sleeping car and on 30 October became, at thirty-nine, the youngest prime minister Italy had yet had.

t: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
x: On 30 December 1922 the First Congress of Soviets of the USSR, meeting in the Bolshoi Theater in Moscow, approved the treaty uniting the Russian, Ukrainian, Belorussian, and Transcaucasian soviet republics in a federal union. Its republics had the right on paper to secede; in fact all answered to the Communist Party, whose general secretary since April was Joseph Stalin.

The Greek army that had marched deep into Anatolia was broken at Dumlupınar in August 1922 and fled to the coast. Turkish troops entered Smyrna on 9 September; the Greek and Armenian quarters were looted and burned, and tens of thousands of Christians perished while Allied warships looked on. By the Treaty of Lausanne some 1.2 million Greek Orthodox and 400,000 Muslims were exchanged between Turkey and Greece.

The Treaty of Lausanne, signed in July 1923, recognized a Turkish state in Anatolia and eastern Thrace. On 29 October 1923 the assembly proclaimed the Republic of Turkey with Ankara as its capital and Mustafa Kemal as president. In the years that followed he closed the Sufi lodges, replaced the sharia with European codes, gave women the vote, and put Turkish into the Latin alphabet.

In the year of the French occupation of the Ruhr, when a dollar came to buy four trillion marks, Adolf Hitler burst into the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich on 8 November 1923 and proclaimed a national revolution. The next day police fired on his march with Ludendorff at the Feldherrnhalle; fourteen of his followers and four policemen died. In Landsberg prison he dictated Mein Kampf.

Just before noon on 1 September an earthquake struck beneath Sagami Bay, and the fires that swept Tokyo and Yokohama, fanned by the winds of a passing typhoon, killed over a hundred thousand people. In the panic that followed, mobs and vigilantes murdered thousands of Koreans falsely accused of poisoning wells and setting fires.

Paralyzed by strokes, Lenin died at Gorki outside Moscow on 21 January 1924, leaving a testament that warned against Stalin's rudeness and power. Over his widow's protests his body was embalmed and laid in a mausoleum on Red Square, Petrograd was renamed Leningrad, and within five years Stalin had outmaneuvered Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev, and Bukharin for the succession.

t: Reza Khan Takes the Peacock Throne
x: Reza Khan, an officer of the Persian Cossack Brigade who had seized Tehran in a coup in February 1921, made himself war minister and then prime minister. In October 1925 the Majlis deposed the absent Ahmad Shah, last of the Qajars, and in December a constituent assembly gave the crown to Reza Shah Pahlavi. He drove Persia toward modernity by force, and in 1935 bade the world call it Iran.

Chiang Kai-shek, whose Northern Expedition had swept from Canton to the Yangtze in alliance with the Communists, turned on them as his armies reached Shanghai. With the help of the Green Gang he had the unions disarmed and hundreds of Communists and workers shot in the streets. The united front was broken, and the long civil war between Nationalists and Communists began.

Twenty years after the medical students of Budi Utomo founded the first modern Indonesian association, delegates of the youth congress in Batavia swore on 28 October 1928 to one motherland, one nation, and one language: Indonesia. The song Indonesia Raya was first played there on the violin of W. R. Supratman; a year before, Sukarno had founded the Indonesian Nationalist Party at Bandung.

After years of speculation on borrowed money, the New York stock market broke in October 1929; on Black Tuesday, the 29th, some sixteen million shares changed hands as prices collapsed. The crash opened the Great Depression: by 1933 a quarter of American workers were idle and thousands of banks had failed, and the slump, spreading round the world, helped carry Hitler to power.

On 11 February 1929 Cardinal Gasparri for Pius XI and Mussolini for the King signed in the Lateran Palace the treaty and concordat that settled the Roman Question opened in 1870. The Holy See recognized the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital; Italy recognized the sovereign State of the Vatican City and made Catholicism the religion of the state.

Mohandas Gandhi set out from his ashram at Sabarmati with seventy-eight followers and walked 385 kilometres in twenty-four days to the sea at Dandi. There on 6 April 1930 he picked up a lump of natural salt in defiance of the government monopoly. Across India tens of thousands followed his example and went to prison, and the world watched.

In February 1930 the Vietnamese Nationalist Party of Nguyen Thai Hoc led native soldiers of the garrison at Yen Bai in a rising against the French. It was crushed within a day, and Nguyen Thai Hoc and twelve comrades went to the guillotine that June. Leadership of the struggle passed to the Indochinese Communist Party founded that year by Nguyen Ai Quoc, the future Ho Chi Minh.

The Imperial Conference of 1926 under Arthur Balfour declared Britain and the dominions autonomous communities, equal in status and united by allegiance to the Crown. The Statute of Westminster of 11 December 1931 made it law: Canada, South Africa, and the Irish Free State were freed at once from legislation by Westminster, Australia and New Zealand when they adopted it in the 1940s, and the British Commonwealth of Nations took shape.

Officers of Japan's Kwantung Army set off a small charge on the South Manchuria Railway outside Mukden and blamed Chinese soldiers. Without orders from Tokyo they seized the city and within months all Manchuria, where in 1932 they set up the puppet state of Manchukuo under Puyi, the last Qing emperor. When the League of Nations condemned it, Japan walked out.

When the republicans swept the cities in the municipal elections of 12 April 1931, crowds filled the Puerta del Sol, and on the 14th the Republic was proclaimed. Alfonso XIII left Spain without abdicating. Within weeks churches and convents were burned in Madrid and the south; the new constitution separated church and state, and the Republic was torn between left and right from the first.

Stalin's forced collectivization of the peasants and impossible grain quotas brought famine to the Soviet countryside in 1932 and 1933. In Ukraine, where it is remembered as the Holodomor, villages were stripped of food, blacklisted, and sealed, and peasants were forbidden to leave in search of bread; some four million Ukrainians starved, and over a million more died in Kazakhstan.

Ibn Saud's Ikhwan warriors had won him the Hejaz and Mecca in 1924 and 1925, but would not stop at his frontiers; he broke them at Sabilla in 1929. On 23 September 1932 he united his realms by decree as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It was a poor desert kingdom living on the pilgrimage, but in 1933 he granted an oil concession to Standard Oil of California.

At dawn on 24 June 1932 the People's Party, a band of officers and officials schooled in Europe and led by Pridi Banomyong and Phraya Phahon, seized key points in Bangkok while King Prajadhipok was at Hua Hin. The king accepted a constitution and the end of absolute monarchy. Quarrels with the new men followed, and in 1935 he abdicated in England.

Bolivia, which had lost its coast to Chile, and Paraguay went to war over the arid Gran Chaco, believed to hold oil. After Paraguay's victory at Fortín Boquerón in September 1932, its soldiers, at home in the thorn scrub, drove the Bolivian army back toward the foothills of the Andes; some ninety thousand men died before the truce of 1935, many of them of thirst.

On 30 January 1933 President Hindenburg, persuaded by Franz von Papen that the conservatives could hold him in check, appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor at the head of a coalition cabinet. Within two months the Reichstag fire had served as pretext to suspend civil liberties, and the Enabling Act of 23 March gave Hitler power to make laws without parliament. By summer every other party was gone.

A year after Iraq's admission to the League of Nations, Iraqi troops under General Bakr Sidqi and tribal irregulars fell upon the Assyrian Christian villages of the north in August 1933. At Simele and scores of other villages Assyrian men, women, and children were slaughtered, by differing counts from six hundred to three thousand. The killings shaped Raphael Lemkin's thinking toward the crime he later named genocide.

Encircled by Chiang Kai-shek's blockhouses, some eighty-six thousand men of the Red Army broke out of the Jiangxi soviet at Ruijin. Over a year of marching through the mountains of the southwest, across the chains of the Luding bridge and the grasslands of the Tibetan borderlands, they lost all but a few thousand. At Zunyi Mao Zedong won the leadership, and in Shaanxi the survivors made their new base.

t: The Generals Rise against the Republic
x: After the murder of the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo by Republican police, the army garrisons rose on 17 July 1936, beginning at Melilla in Morocco. General Francisco Franco flew from the Canaries to command the Army of Africa, which German and Italian aircraft ferried across the Strait. The rising failed in Madrid and Barcelona, and Spain was split in a civil war of three years.

Chiang Kai-shek flew to Xi'an to press the Manchurian marshal Zhang Xueliang to destroy the Communists. Instead Zhang's men seized Chiang at the hot springs of Huaqing, where he had fled up the hillside in his nightshirt, and held him until he agreed to end the civil war and unite against Japan. Zhang went with him to Nanjing and spent the next half century under arrest.

Mussolini's armies invaded Ethiopia from Eritrea and Somaliland in October 1935, bombing Haile Selassie's armies and villages and spraying them with mustard gas. Marshal Badoglio entered Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, the emperor having gone into exile to plead in vain before the League of Nations; five years to the day later, British and Ethiopian forces brought him home.

After the show trial of Zinoviev and Kamenev in 1936, the purge directed by Stalin and his commissar Nikolai Yezhov swept the party, the army, and the people. Marshal Tukhachevsky and most of the high command were shot in 1937, Bukharin after the third Moscow trial in 1938; by the NKVD's own figures some 680,000 were executed in those two years, and hundreds of thousands more sent to the camps.

On the night of 7 July a Japanese unit on manoeuvres near the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beiping reported a soldier missing and demanded to search the walled town of Wanping. Shots were exchanged, neither side would yield, and the skirmish grew into full war between Japan and China, the beginning, in Asia, of the Second World War.

After three months of bitter fighting at Shanghai, the Japanese army took the Nationalist capital at Nanjing in December. For six weeks its soldiers murdered prisoners and civilians, raped tens of thousands of women, and burned and looted the city, while a few Western residents, among them the German businessman John Rabe, sheltered some two hundred thousand in a safety zone. The Tokyo tribunal put the dead at over two hundred thousand.

On the market-day afternoon of 26 April 1937 the German Condor Legion and Italian aircraft bombed the old Basque town of Guernica, seat of the oak beneath which the lords of Biscay swore to keep the Basque liberties. The town was burned out, and scores, perhaps hundreds, were killed. Picasso painted his Guernica for the Paris Exposition that summer.

When Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg called a plebiscite on Austrian independence, Hitler forced his resignation, and on 12 March 1938 the German army marched into Austria unopposed. Three days later Hitler, Austrian-born, announced to a vast crowd on the Heldenplatz in Vienna the entry of his homeland into the German Reich. The persecution of Vienna's Jews began in the streets at once.

In the early hours of 30 September 1938 Neville Chamberlain, Édouard Daladier, Mussolini, and Hitler signed at Munich the cession of the Sudetenland to Germany, with no Czechoslovak at the table. Chamberlain flew home waving a paper and promising peace for our time. Stripped of its frontier fortifications, the rest of Czechoslovakia was occupied by Germany in March 1939.

Taking the murder of a diplomat in Paris by a young Polish Jew as pretext, the SA and party men burned synagogues and smashed Jewish shops and homes across Germany and Austria on the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, while police looked on. Some hundred Jews were killed and about 30,000 men sent to Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen, and the Jews were fined a billion marks for the damage.

After years of dry holes on the Dammam dome near the Gulf coast, the American geologists of Standard Oil of California brought in Dammam Well No. 7 in March 1938, flowing over 1,500 barrels a day. Beneath the sands of eastern Arabia lay the greatest reserves of oil in the world, and the destiny of the kingdom and of the world's economy was changed.

At dawn on 1 September 1939 the old battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte in Danzig harbor, and German armies crossed the Polish frontier from three sides. Britain and France declared war on 3 September. On the 17th the Red Army invaded from the east; Warsaw surrendered on the 28th, and Poland was partitioned between the two dictators.

On the night of 23 August 1939 the foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov signed in the Kremlin, with Stalin looking on, a treaty of non-aggression between Germany and the Soviet Union. A secret protocol divided Poland, the Baltic states, Finland, and Bessarabia into spheres of interest. Hitler was free to attack Poland, and the war began nine days later.

When Finland refused to cede territory, the Soviet Union attacked on 30 November 1939. In the frozen forests round Suomussalmi, Finnish ski troops cut two Soviet divisions into pockets and destroyed them by January. Mannerheim's line on the Karelian Isthmus held until February; by the peace of March 1940 Finland lost Karelia and Viipuri but kept its independence.

A frontier quarrel on the Khalkhin Gol between Mongolia and Manchukuo drew in the armies of the Soviet Union and Japan. In August General Georgy Zhukov struck with tanks and aircraft and encircled the Japanese force. The defeat turned Japan's ambitions away from Siberia and toward the south, and the two powers kept peace with each other until August 1945.

In April and May 1940, on an order signed by Stalin and the Politburo, the NKVD shot some 22,000 Polish prisoners, army officers, police, landowners, and professional men, in the Katyn forest near Smolensk, at Kalinin, at Kharkov, and other places. The Germans found the graves at Katyn in 1943; Moscow blamed them for the crime until 1990.

The German armor broke through the Ardennes at Sedan in May 1940 and reached the Channel in ten days, cutting off the British Expeditionary Force and the French northern armies. From 26 May to 4 June destroyers, ferries, and hundreds of small boats brought some 338,000 men off the beaches and mole of Dunkirk, while the French rearguard held the perimeter.

Through the summer of 1940 Göring's Luftwaffe tried to destroy the Royal Air Force as the prelude to invasion. Guided by radar and the operations rooms of Dowding's Fighter Command, the Hurricanes and Spitfires held; on 15 September the great daylight raids on London were beaten off, and Hitler postponed the invasion. The night Blitz on British cities went on until May 1941.

At its session in Lahore in March 1940 the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, resolved that the Muslim-majority regions of the northwest and east of India should form independent states. The resolution did not use the word, but the press at once called it the Pakistan Resolution, and within seven years Pakistan was a fact.

On 9 April 1940 German forces seized Denmark in a morning and landed at Oslo, Bergen, Trondheim, and Narvik; the old fortress of Oscarsborg sank the cruiser Blücher in the Oslofjord, giving King Haakon time to escape. British destroyers sank ten German destroyers at Narvik, and allied troops took the port in May, but the fall of France forced them out in June.

t: The British Fire on the French Fleet
x: Fearing that the French fleet would fall to Germany after the armistice of 22 June 1940, signed in the same railway carriage at Compiègne as in 1918, Churchill sent Admiral Somerville's Force H to Mers-el-Kébir. When Admiral Gensoul refused the British terms on 3 July, the British opened fire, sinking the battleship Bretagne and killing nearly 1,300 French sailors.

t: The Greeks Throw Back the Italians
x: Before dawn on 28 October 1940 Mussolini's envoy demanded passage for Italian troops, and General Metaxas answered with a refusal the Greeks remember as Ochi, No. The Greek army stopped the invasion in the Pindus mountains and drove the Italians deep into Albania, taking Koritsa in November. Hitler came to his ally's rescue in April 1941, and on the 27th the swastika flew over the Acropolis.

Félix Éboué, governor of Chad and a descendant of slaves from French Guiana, declared on 26 August 1940 for General de Gaulle's Free French against the Vichy regime, the first French colony in Africa to do so. French Equatorial Africa followed, Brazzaville became the capital of Free France, and from Chad Colonel Leclerc's column struck across the Sahara to take Kufra in 1941.

Before dawn on 22 June 1941 more than three million German soldiers in three army groups, with their allies, crossed the Soviet frontier from the Baltic to the Black Sea. The garrison of the Brest fortress fought on for weeks, but the Red Army lost millions in vast encirclements at Białystok, Minsk, Smolensk, and Kiev. By December the Germans stood before Moscow and Leningrad.

Facing an American embargo on oil, Japan struck first. On the morning of 7 December, aircraft from six carriers under Admiral Nagumo Chūichi, carrying out the plan of Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku, sank or crippled eight American battleships at Pearl Harbor and killed over 2,400 Americans. Within hours Japan fell upon Malaya, Hong Kong, and the Philippines, and the war became a world war in full.

Ten days after the Germans took Kiev, the Jews of the city were ordered to assemble with their belongings on 29 September 1941. They were marched to the ravine of Babi Yar on the outskirts, stripped, and shot by Einsatzgruppe C and its auxiliaries over two days: 33,771 men, women, and children, by the killers' own report. It was among the largest single massacres of the Holocaust.

On 8 September 1941 the Germans took Shlisselburg and cut the last land link to Leningrad. For 872 days, until January 1944, the city of three million was besieged and shelled; in the first winter people burned furniture and ate glue, and the only supply line was the Road of Life over the ice of Lake Ladoga. Perhaps a million civilians died, most of hunger.

In October 1941 the Germans broke through at Vyazma and Bryansk, and Moscow lay in panic; on 7 November Stalin held the revolution parade on Red Square, the troops marching straight to the front. As the frosts deepened, Zhukov struck on 5 December with fresh divisions from Siberia and the Far East and drove the frozen Germans back a hundred miles and more from the capital.

t: The Japanese Land at Kota Bharu
x: Shortly after midnight on 8 December 1941, more than an hour before the attack on Pearl Harbor, Japanese troops stormed ashore at Kota Bharu on the northeast coast of Malaya, while others landed at Singora and Patani in Siam. Two days later Japanese aircraft sank the British battleships Prince of Wales and Repulse off Kuantan.

After a campaign of seventy days down the length of Malaya, General Yamashita's army crossed the Johor Strait, and on 15 February 1942 General Arthur Percival surrendered Singapore with some eighty thousand British, Australian, and Indian troops, the greatest capitulation in British history. The belief in European invincibility in Asia died with it, and tens of thousands of Chinese were massacred in the purge that followed.

On 20 January 1942, in a lakeside villa at Wannsee, Reinhard Heydrich of the SS chaired a meeting of fourteen senior officials of the ministries and the party, minuted by Adolf Eichmann, to coordinate the final solution of the Jewish question: the deportation of Europe's eleven million Jews to the east for death. The killing centers at Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka opened that year.

Rommel's Afrika Korps had been stopped some sixty miles short of Alexandria in July 1942. On 23 October General Bernard Montgomery's Eighth Army opened the second battle of El Alamein with a barrage of nearly a thousand guns, and after twelve days of attrition broke through on 4 November. The Axis armies began the long retreat to Tunisia; Churchill had church bells rung across England.

Six months after Pearl Harbor, Yamamoto sought to draw the remaining American carriers into a decisive battle off Midway atoll. But American codebreakers had read his plans, and in a few minutes on the morning of 4 June dive bombers from the Enterprise and Yorktown set three Japanese carriers ablaze; a fourth was struck that afternoon and sank the next morning. Japan never again took the offensive in the Pacific.

After MacArthur left for Australia, vowing to return, some seventy-six thousand American and Filipino troops on the Bataan peninsula surrendered on 9 April 1942. Driven on foot under the tropical sun for more than a hundred kilometers to Camp O'Donnell, beaten, starved, and bayoneted when they fell, thousands died on the road; Corregidor surrendered on 6 May.

Japanese troops landed near Buna in July 1942 and pushed over the Owen Stanley Range toward Port Moresby along the Kokoda Track, a muddy footpath through mountain jungle. Outnumbered Australian militia and then veterans of the Middle East fought them back step by step, carried when wounded by Papuan bearers, and by November the Japanese had been driven back over the mountains.

On 7 August 1942 American Marines landed on Guadalcanal and seized the airfield the Japanese were building, which they named Henderson Field. For six months land, sea, and air battles raged about it, the waters off the shore so full of sunken ships they were called Iron Bottom Sound. In February 1943 the Japanese withdrew, and the tide of the Pacific war had turned.

On 8 November 1942 American and British troops under General Eisenhower landed at Casablanca, Oran, and Algiers in Vichy French North Africa. After brief resistance Admiral Darlan, who happened to be in Algiers, ordered a ceasefire; Germany answered by occupying the rest of France and rushing troops to Tunisia, where the Axis armies in Africa surrendered in May 1943, some 250,000 strong.

On 19 February 1942 some 240 aircraft, many from the carriers that had struck Pearl Harbor, attacked Darwin in two raids, sinking ships in the harbor, wrecking the town and airfield, and killing about 235 people. It was the first and heaviest of nearly a hundred raids on northern Australia, and the nation knew the war had come to its own shores.

Through the autumn of 1942 the German Sixth Army fought for Stalingrad street by street and factory by factory on the Volga. On 19 November Zhukov and Vasilevsky's Operation Uranus broke the Romanian armies on its flanks and closed the ring. Forbidden to break out, the newly made Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus surrendered on 31 January 1943; some 91,000 starving men went into captivity, and few came home.

Of some 400,000 Jews penned in the Warsaw ghetto, more than a quarter of a million had been sent to the gas chambers of Treblinka in the summer of 1942. When the SS came on 19 April 1943 to clear the rest, the young fighters of Mordechai Anielewicz met them with pistols and petrol bombs. SS General Stroop needed four weeks and the burning of the ghetto block by block to crush them.

On 5 July 1943 the Germans attacked the great Kursk salient from north and south with new Tiger and Panther tanks, against defenses dug in depth through the spring. At Prokhorovka on 12 July the Soviet Fifth Guards Tank Army met the SS panzer corps in one of the largest tank battles of the war. The offensive failed, and the Red Army held the initiative all the way to Berlin.

Two weeks after the allies landed in Sicily, the Fascist Grand Council voted against Mussolini on the night of 24 July 1943, and the next day the King had him arrested at the Villa Savoia. Marshal Badoglio's government signed an armistice that was announced on 8 September; the Germans seized Rome and northern Italy, and SS commandos freed Mussolini from his prison on the Gran Sasso.

With Burma lost to Japan and its rice cut off, a cyclone wrecking the crop, and the governments in Delhi and London giving war needs first call on grain and shipping, famine fell on Bengal. Prices soared beyond the reach of the poor, who streamed into Calcutta to die in its streets. Some three million perished.

To supply their army in Burma the Japanese drove a railway 415 kilometers through jungle and mountain from Ban Pong in Siam to Thanbyuzayat in Burma, finished in October 1943. Some sixty thousand Allied prisoners and perhaps two hundred thousand Asian laborers toiled on it; about twelve thousand of the prisoners and as many as ninety thousand of the Asians died of beatings, cholera, and hunger.

In an Iran occupied by British and Soviet troops since 1941, Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill met together for the first time from 28 November to 1 December 1943, at the Soviet embassy in Tehran. They agreed on an Anglo-American landing in France in May 1944; Stalin promised to enter the war against Japan after Germany's defeat, and Poland's frontiers were to be moved west.

On 6 June 1944, after a night drop of three airborne divisions, American, British, and Canadian troops under General Eisenhower landed on five beaches of Normandy from nearly seven thousand vessels; by midnight some 156,000 men were ashore. Prefabricated Mulberry harbors were towed across the Channel. After eleven weeks of fighting in the hedgerows the Germans were routed in the Falaise pocket.

As the Red Army reached the Vistula, the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw on 1 August 1944 to free the capital before the Soviets came.
