The Red Army halted across the river, and Stalin refused allied aircraft landing rights. After sixty-three days General Bór-Komorowski surrendered; some 150,000 civilians had died, and Hitler ordered the city razed.

On 20 October 1944 General Douglas MacArthur waded ashore at Palo on Leyte, fulfilling his vow to return to the Philippines. Days later the Japanese navy threw its last strength at the landings in the battle of Leyte Gulf, the greatest naval battle in history, and lost four carriers and three battleships, while its pilots made the first organized kamikaze attacks.

Delegates of forty-four Allied nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in July 1944 and, led by John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White, founded the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. They tied the world's currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce, an order that underlay the postwar boom until Nixon closed the gold window in 1971.

On 22 June 1944, three years to the day after Barbarossa, four Soviet fronts struck Army Group Center in Belorussia. In five weeks the Red Army destroyed some twenty-eight German divisions, retook Minsk on 3 July, and advanced over three hundred miles to the Vistula; in Moscow 57,000 German prisoners were marched through the streets.

With the Red Army fighting through the ruins of Berlin, Hitler shot himself in his bunker on 30 April 1945, and two days later the city's garrison surrendered. Grand Admiral Dönitz's envoys signed an unconditional surrender at Reims on 7 May, ratified before Marshal Zhukov at Karlshorst late on 8 May. The war in Europe was over; it had cost some forty million European lives.

On 6 August an American B-29 dropped a single uranium bomb on Hiroshima, destroying the city and killing some seventy thousand people at once, with tens of thousands more dying by the year's end. Three days later a second bomb fell on Nagasaki, and the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito broadcast the surrender, and on 2 September it was signed in Tokyo Bay.

At 5:29 in the morning of 16 July 1945, in the desert of the Jornada del Muerto, the scientists of the Manhattan Project under J. Robert Oppenheimer exploded the first atomic bomb, with the force of some twenty thousand tons of TNT. Oppenheimer recalled the words of the Bhagavad Gita, 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'; within a month the bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

On 27 January 1945 soldiers of the Soviet 60th Army entered Auschwitz and found some seven thousand sick and dying prisoners left behind when the SS drove the rest west on death marches. About 1.1 million people had been murdered there, nearly a million of them Jews, most gassed at Birkenau on arrival; the Nazis murdered some six million Jews in all.

From 4 to 11 February 1945, in the Tsar's white palace at Livadia above Yalta, a dying Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin agreed on the occupation of Germany in zones, the United Nations, and Soviet entry into the Pacific war. Poland was to lose its east to the Soviet Union and gain German lands; Stalin's promise of free elections there was never kept.

At the Cecilienhof palace from 17 July to 2 August 1945, Truman, Stalin, and Churchill, replaced midway by Clement Attlee after his election victory, settled the occupation of Germany and set Poland's western frontier on the Oder and Neisse. They approved the transfer of the German populations of Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary; some twelve million Germans fled or were expelled.

For eighty-two days American soldiers and marines fought their way across Okinawa against Japanese troops dug into caves and ridges, while kamikaze pilots struck the fleet offshore and the great battleship Yamato was sunk on a one-way sortie. Some hundred thousand Japanese soldiers died, and perhaps as many Okinawan civilians, some driven to suicide by their own army.

When American troops entered Manila in February 1945, Japanese naval troops under Admiral Iwabuchi chose to fight for the city street by street. For a month they massacred civilians while American artillery leveled the old walled city of Intramuros; some hundred thousand Filipinos died, and Manila was left among the most devastated cities of the war.

Two days after Japan's surrender, pressed by radical youths who had briefly carried them off, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta read a short proclamation of independence before Sukarno's house at 56 Pegangsaan Timur on the morning of 17 August 1945. The Republic of Indonesia was born, with Sukarno as president, and the Dutch, returning behind British troops, faced four years of war.

t: Ho Chi Minh at Ba Dinh Square
x: In the August Revolution the Viet Minh seized Hanoi, and Emperor Bao Dai abdicated at Hue. On 2 September 1945 Ho Chi Minh read the declaration of independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam before a vast crowd in Ba Dinh Square, opening with the words of the American Declaration. A famine in the north that year had killed a million people or more.

Of some 2,400 Australian and British prisoners held at Sandakan in North Borneo, those still alive in 1945 were driven on foot through jungle and swamp to Ranau, more than two hundred kilometers inland, and the rest were left to die in the camp. Only six survived the war, every one of them an escaper hidden by the people of Borneo.

After the British brigadier Mallaby was killed in a skirmish, British and Indian troops with tanks, warships, and aircraft attacked Surabaya on 10 November 1945, and Indonesian fighters defended the city street by street for three weeks. Thousands died. The battle, honored in Indonesia as Heroes' Day, persuaded the British that the Republic could not be crushed and must be bargained with.

When the officers who ruled Argentina arrested their labor minister, Colonel Juan Perón, hundreds of thousands of workers, the descamisados or 'shirtless ones,' filled the Plaza de Mayo on 17 October 1945 until he was freed. Elected president in 1946 with his wife Eva at his side, Perón built a movement of unions and welfare that dominated Argentine politics for the rest of the century.

Before an International Military Tribunal of American, British, French, and Soviet judges, twenty-one leaders of the Third Reich, Göring, Ribbentrop, Keitel, and Speer among them, stood trial at Nuremberg from November 1945 for aggressive war, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. On 1 October 1946 twelve were condemned to death; Göring took poison the night before the hangings.

On 4 July 1946, as Congress had promised in 1934, the American flag was lowered at the Luneta in Manila and Manuel Roxas took office as first president of the Republic of the Philippines. The new state, its capital in ruins, granted American bases and trade privileges, and soon faced the Communist Huk rebellion in central Luzon, broken by Ramon Magsaysay.

At midnight on 14 August 1947 British rule ended and two dominions were born, Pakistan and India, divided by lines Sir Cyril Radcliffe had drawn in five weeks through the Punjab and Bengal. Nehru told the Constituent Assembly that India awoke to life and freedom. Some fifteen million people fled across the new borders, and perhaps a million were killed in the massacres.

When Pashtun tribesmen invaded Kashmir from Pakistan in October 1947, its Hindu maharaja Hari Singh signed the instrument of accession to India, and Indian troops were flown into Srinagar. The fighting ended with a ceasefire on the first day of 1949 that left the valley with India and Gilgit and the western strip with Pakistan. Kashmir remains divided and disputed.

Aung San, the young general who had led the Burma Independence Army beside Japan and then turned against it, won from Britain a promise of independence and from the hill peoples the Panglong Agreement. On 19 July 1947 gunmen of his rival U Saw burst into the Secretariat and killed him and eight others, six of them ministers. Burma became independent without him on 4 January 1948.

On 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate expired, David Ben-Gurion read the declaration of independence of the State of Israel in the Tel Aviv museum. The next day the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon invaded. By the armistices of 1949 Israel held more than three-quarters of Mandatory Palestine; Jordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt the Gaza Strip.

Offered by the American Secretary of State George Marshall at Harvard in June 1947 and refused by Stalin for the Soviet bloc, the European Recovery Program was administered from April 1948 through the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation in Paris. In four years some thirteen billion dollars in food, fuel, and machinery flowed to sixteen nations of western Europe and the western zones of Germany.

When the western powers introduced the new Deutsche Mark, Stalin cut the land routes to West Berlin on 24 June 1948. For over ten months American and British aircraft flew food, coal, and medicine to two million Berliners, landing at Tempelhof at times every few minutes, some 2.3 million tons in all. The Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949.

In the fighting of 1947 to 1949 some seven hundred thousand Arabs of Palestine fled or were driven from their homes, among them the tens of thousands of Lydda and Ramla, expelled by Israeli troops in July 1948. Israel barred their return, and hundreds of villages were emptied. The Palestinians call it al-Nakba, the catastrophe, and the refugees and their descendants remain a central grievance of the Middle East.

On 30 January 1948, as he walked to his evening prayer meeting at Birla House in New Delhi, Mahatma Gandhi was shot three times at close range by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for the partition and for concessions to Pakistan. Nehru told the nation that the light had gone out of their lives.

On 16 June 1948 Communist guerrillas killed three European planters near Sungai Siput, and the British declared an emergency. Chin Peng's army, mostly Chinese, fought from the jungle for twelve years. General Gerald Templer and his predecessors resettled half a million squatters in guarded New Villages and promised independence, which cut the ground from under the rebels.

Daniel François Malan's National Party, campaigning on the program of apartheid, 'separateness,' won a majority of seats, though not of votes, in the election of May 1948. In the years that followed it classified every South African by race, forbade marriage across the color line, assigned each race its own residential areas, and set out to strip the black majority of all rights outside tribal homelands.

When the non-communist ministers resigned in February 1948 over the packing of the police, Klement Gottwald brought armed workers' militias into the streets, and President Beneš, ill and fearing civil war, accepted a communist government on 25 February. Two weeks later the foreign minister Jan Masaryk, son of the republic's founder, was found dead below his window in the Czernin Palace.

Tito's Yugoslavia, which had won its liberation with little help from the Red Army, would not take orders from Moscow. On 28 June 1948, the feast of St. Vitus, the Cominform expelled the Yugoslav party; Stalin is said to have boasted that he had only to shake his little finger and there would be no more Tito. Yugoslavia held, took Western aid, and went its own way between the blocs.

In the plains around Xuzhou the Communist armies under Chen Yi, Liu Bocheng, and Deng Xiaoping, supplied by hundreds of thousands of peasant carriers with wheelbarrows, encircled and destroyed the best of the Nationalist field armies over two winter months. With Manchuria already lost and Beiping soon to fall, Chiang Kai-shek's cause on the mainland was lost.

On 4 February 1948 Ceylon became an independent dominion within the Commonwealth under D. S. Senanayake, without a shot fired. Within the year the new state passed a citizenship law that left stateless most of the Tamils of Indian origin, whose forebears the British had brought from South India to work the tea estates of the hills.

On 1 October, from the Gate of Heavenly Peace, Mao Zedong proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic of China. The Communists had won the civil war in three years of campaigns; within months they held the whole mainland and began to remake it through land reform, the destruction of the landlord class, and campaigns that cost millions of lives.

On 4 April 1949 the foreign ministers of the United States, Canada, Britain, France, the Benelux states, Italy, Portugal, Norway, Denmark, and Iceland signed in Washington a treaty declaring that an armed attack against one of them in Europe or North America would be considered an attack against them all. West Germany joined in 1955, and the Soviet bloc answered with the Warsaw Pact.

On 23 May 1949 the Basic Law of the Federal Republic of Germany was proclaimed at Bonn, the small Rhineland university town chosen as a provisional capital, and in September Konrad Adenauer became chancellor by a single vote, his own. In the Soviet zone the German Democratic Republic was founded on 7 October, and Germany stayed divided for forty-one years.

Chiang Kai-shek's government, its armies broken on the mainland, withdrew across the strait to Taiwan with some two million soldiers and refugees, the gold of the treasury, and the treasures of the Palace Museum. Under martial law, which lasted until 1987, the Republic of China held the island, and the Taiwan Strait became one of the frontiers of the Cold War.

The second of two Dutch 'police actions' took the Republic's capital at Yogyakarta in December 1948 and captured Sukarno and Hatta, but guerrilla war and American pressure forced the Netherlands to the Round Table Conference at The Hague. On 27 December 1949 sovereignty passed to the United States of Indonesia, and the red and white flag rose over the palace in Jakarta.

When India resolved to become a republic, the Commonwealth prime ministers met in London in April 1949 and declared that India would remain a full member, accepting King George VI as the symbol of the free association of its independent nations and as Head of the Commonwealth. The word British was dropped, and a republic could belong.

In the Salon de l'Horloge of the French foreign ministry on 9 May 1950, Robert Schuman proposed, on a plan drafted by Jean Monnet, to pool the coal and steel of France and Germany under a common High Authority, making war between them materially impossible. Italy and the Benelux states joined; the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951 was the first of the European Communities.

At dawn on 25 June, with Stalin's consent, Kim Il Sung's army crossed the 38th parallel behind Soviet tanks and took Seoul in three days. The United Nations sent forces under General MacArthur, whose landing at Incheon in September broke the invaders; when the Americans pressed on to the Yalu, some three hundred thousand Chinese soldiers fell upon them in the winter mountains.

On 26 January 1950 the Constitution of India, drafted under the chairmanship of B. R. Ambedkar, came into force, and India became a sovereign republic with Rajendra Prasad as its first president. With 395 articles it was the longest written constitution of any nation, and it granted the vote to every adult at a stroke.

t: The Exodus of the Iraqi Jews
x: Ten years after the Farhud, the Baghdad pogrom of 1941 in which some 180 Jews were killed, Iraq allowed its Jews to leave on condition of giving up their citizenship. Some 120,000, nearly the whole of a community that traced itself to the Babylonian exile, were airlifted to Israel in 1950 and 1951, their property frozen by the state. The Jewries of Yemen, Libya, Egypt, and Morocco were likewise emptied in the same years and the decades that followed.

On 24 December 1951 Sayyid Idris al-Sanusi, head of the Sanusi Sufi order and leader of the long resistance to Italy, proclaimed in Benghazi the independence of the United Kingdom of Libya, the first state to gain its independence through the United Nations. It was then among the poorest countries on earth, until oil was found in 1959.

On the night of 23 July 1952 the Free Officers, a secret society of young army officers with General Muhammad Naguib as their figurehead, seized Cairo without bloodshed. King Farouk sailed into exile from Alexandria three days later. The monarchy was abolished in 1953, and Gamal Abdel Nasser, the movement's true leader, pushed Naguib aside and ruled Egypt until his death in 1970.

Kikuyu fighters bound by secret oaths to drive the white settlers from the highlands waged a forest war from the slopes of Mount Kenya and the Aberdares, and Governor Sir Evelyn Baring declared an emergency in October 1952. By 1956, when Dedan Kimathi was captured, more than 11,000 rebels had been killed and tens of thousands of Kikuyu held in camps; the rebels had slain 32 European settlers and far more loyalist Africans.

When the government of Pakistan declared that Urdu alone would be the national language, the students of Dacca University marched for Bengali. On 21 February 1952 police opened fire and killed several of them. The day became the rallying point of Bengali nationalism and is kept by UNESCO as International Mother Language Day.

Struck down by a stroke at his dacha at Kuntsevo, Stalin lay for hours before his frightened guards called doctors, and he died on 5 March 1953. Beria, Malenkov, and Khrushchev divided his power; Beria was arrested in June and shot. In East Berlin that June a workers' rising against raised work quotas was crushed by Soviet tanks.

Mohammad Mossadegh, the elderly prime minister who nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951 to the acclaim of the Majlis and the crowds, defied the British embargo and the young Shah alike. In August 1953 a coup organized by the American and British intelligence services, with royalist officers and paid mobs, overthrew him. The Shah returned from Rome to rule with a firmer hand.

After two years of stalemate along the old frontier, and of talks over the fate of prisoners who refused to go home, the commanders of the United Nations, the Chinese volunteers, and North Korea signed an armistice at Panmunjom. No peace treaty followed. Some three million Koreans had died, and the peninsula remained divided by a demilitarized zone four kilometres wide.

King Norodom Sihanouk, whom the French had crowned in 1941 as a pliant youth of eighteen, went abroad in 1953 to shame Paris into granting independence and withdrew to the countryside in a royal crusade. France, mired in war with the Viet Minh, yielded, and on 9 November 1953 Cambodia became independent. Sihanouk abdicated in 1955 to rule as prince and politician.

t: The Fall of Dien Bien Phu
x: To draw the Viet Minh into a pitched battle, the French dropped paratroops into the valley of Dien Bien Phu in upper Tonkin. General Giap's men hauled artillery onto the surrounding hills by hand and opened their siege in March 1954; after fifty-six days the garrison of General de Castries was overrun on 7 May. At Geneva in July France gave up Indochina.

On 1 November 1954 the National Liberation Front set off bombs and raids across Algeria, most of them in the Aurès mountains, beginning a war that would last nearly eight years. Algeria was French soil in law and home to a million European settlers; the war brought massacre and terror on both sides, torture by the army, and in 1958 the fall of the Fourth Republic.

The people of Bikini had been moved from their atoll in 1946 so that the United States might test atomic bombs there. On 1 March 1954 the hydrogen bomb Castle Bravo, the largest the Americans ever fired, exploded with a force of fifteen megatons, far beyond its makers' reckoning; its fallout poisoned the islanders of Rongelap and the crew of the Japanese tuna boat Lucky Dragon.

In April 1955 Sukarno welcomed to Bandung the leaders of twenty-nine Asian and African nations, Nehru, Zhou Enlai, and Nasser among them, to declare the solidarity of the newly independent nations. Its ten principles of peaceful coexistence and its refusal to choose between the blocs of the Cold War foreshadowed the Non-Aligned Movement.

On 15 May 1955, the day after the Soviet bloc signed its Warsaw Pact, the foreign ministers of the four occupying powers signed in the Belvedere palace the treaty restoring a sovereign Austria. Foreign Minister Leopold Figl showed it to the cheering crowd from the balcony. The last occupation troops left in October, and Austria declared its permanent neutrality.

At a closed session on the last day of the Twentieth Party Congress, 25 February 1956, Nikita Khrushchev spoke for four hours on the crimes of Stalin: the cult of personality, the torture and murder of loyal communists, and the blunders of 1941. The text reached the West within weeks, shaking communist parties everywhere and emboldening Poland and Hungary.

On 23 October 1956 Budapest students marching in sympathy with Poland pulled down the giant statue of Stalin, and the revolution spread across Hungary in days. Imre Nagy formed a government and on 1 November declared Hungary neutral and out of the Warsaw Pact. On 4 November Soviet tanks returned; some 2,500 Hungarians were killed, 200,000 fled west, and Nagy was hanged in 1958.

When America withdrew its offer to fund the Aswan High Dam, Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company in July 1956. By secret agreement Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October, and British and French paratroops landed at Port Said on 5 November. Under American and Soviet pressure they withdrew. Nasser, beaten in the field, emerged the hero of the Arab world, and British power in the region was broken.

On 25 March 1957, in the Hall of the Horatii and Curiatii on the Capitoline hill, the six members of the Coal and Steel Community, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg, signed treaties founding the European Economic Community, a common market with a customs union, and the European Atomic Energy Community. Both came into force on 1 January 1958.

On 4 October 1957 an R-7 rocket designed by Sergei Korolev, whose name was a state secret, lifted from the steppe of Kazakhstan and put into orbit the first artificial satellite, a polished sphere of 83 kilograms whose radio beeped round the world every ninety-six minutes. The space age began with a Soviet triumph, and on 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin flew the first man round the earth.

On 31 August 1957, in the new Merdeka Stadium, Tunku Abdul Rahman read the proclamation of independence of the Federation of Malaya and led the crowd in seven cries of Merdeka, Freedom. The Alliance of Malay, Chinese, and Indian parties that he headed had won independence by negotiation, and the nine Malay rulers were to take turns as king.

At midnight on 6 March 1957 Kwame Nkrumah, who had gone from a colonial prison to the head of the government in 1951, told the crowds at the Old Polo Ground that 'Ghana, your beloved country, is free forever.' The Gold Coast, renamed for the medieval empire, was the first of Britain's black African colonies to become independent, and most of the others followed within a decade.

t: De Gaulle and the Fifth Republic
x: When the army and the settlers of Algiers rose on 13 May 1958 against a government they feared would abandon Algeria, and paratroops landed in Corsica, the Fourth Republic turned to General de Gaulle. Invested as premier on 1 June, he gave France a constitution with a strong president, approved by referendum on 28 September, and became its first president in January 1959.

On 14 July 1958 the troops of Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim seized Baghdad. The young King Faisal II, the former regent Abd al-Ilah, and other members of the royal family were shot in the palace courtyard, and the veteran statesman Nuri al-Said was caught in a woman's cloak and killed the next day. The Hashemite monarchy and the British alliance were swept away.

Mao Zedong ordered China to overtake Britain in steel within fifteen years. The peasants were herded into vast people's communes, set to melting their pots in backyard furnaces, and made to deliver grain quotas that boastful cadres had inflated. The famine that followed, worst in provinces such as Henan and Anhui, killed tens of millions, the deadliest in recorded history.

When de Gaulle offered France's African colonies a choice between a French Community and immediate independence, Ahmed Sékou Touré told him, 'We prefer poverty in liberty to riches in slavery.' Guinea alone voted no in the referendum of 28 September 1958; the French left within weeks, carrying off files, equipment, and even telephones.

Nine years after the People's Liberation Army had marched into eastern Tibet and broken the Tibetan army at Chamdo, crowds surrounded the Norbulingka palace in Lhasa to keep the Fourteenth Dalai Lama from Chinese hands. On the night of 17 March he slipped away disguised as a soldier and made for India. The rising was crushed by artillery, and the old Tibetan government was dissolved.

Fidel Castro, a lawyer who had landed from the yacht Granma in 1956 with eighty-two men, waged guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra until the dictator Fulgencio Batista fled on New Year's Day 1959. Castro entered Havana in triumph on 8 January, shot hundreds of Batista's men, seized American property, and by 1961 had declared Cuba a socialist state allied with Moscow.

In the Year of Africa, when seventeen African nations became independent, the Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960, and Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba answered King Baudouin's speech with an attack on Belgian rule. Within days the army mutinied and Katanga seceded under Moise Tshombe; Lumumba was deposed, delivered to his enemies, and shot in Katanga in January 1961.

On 21 March 1960 a crowd of several thousand gathered outside the police station of Sharpeville, near Vereeniging, at the call of the Pan Africanist Congress to protest the pass laws. The police opened fire and killed 69 people, many of them shot in the back. The government declared an emergency and banned the ANC and the PAC, which turned from protest to sabotage and armed struggle.

President Juscelino Kubitschek, promising 'fifty years of progress in five,' built a new capital on the empty plateau of Goiás to draw Brazil's people into the interior. Laid out by Lúcio Costa in the shape of an airplane, with palaces and a cathedral by Oscar Niemeyer, Brasília was inaugurated on 21 April 1960, after forty-one months of building.

Addressing the South African parliament in Cape Town on 3 February 1960, the British prime minister Harold Macmillan told his hosts that the wind of change was blowing through the continent and that national consciousness was a political fact. In that year seventeen African states became independent, most of them former French colonies, and by 1968 Britain had let go almost all of its African empire.

Senegal and the French Sudan joined as the Mali Federation and won independence from France on 20 June 1960. Within two months the union broke apart; on the night of 19 August Senegal seceded and sent the Sudanese leader Modibo Keïta home to Bamako on a sealed train. The French Sudan declared itself the Republic of Mali on 22 September, as Niger and Mauritania also became independent that year.

By 1961 some three million East Germans had fled to the West, most through Berlin. In the early hours of 13 August soldiers and workers' militia of the German Democratic Republic strung barbed wire along the sector border, soon replaced by a concrete wall of guard towers and a death strip. At least 140 people died at the Wall before 1989, most of them shot while trying to cross.

After the failure of the American-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, Khrushchev secretly sent nuclear missiles to Cuba, and on 14 October 1962 a U-2 photographed their launch sites near San Cristóbal. President Kennedy proclaimed a naval quarantine of the island, and for thirteen days the world stood nearer to nuclear war than ever before or since, until Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles.

After the failed generals' putsch of April 1961 and the bombs of the settlers' Secret Army Organization, de Gaulle's ministers and the provisional Algerian government signed a ceasefire at Évian on 18 March 1962. Algeria voted for independence and became independent on 5 July. Some 800,000 Europeans fled to France within months, and tens of thousands of Muslim harkis who had fought for France were massacred.

Summoned by Pope John XXIII to open the windows of the Church, some 2,500 bishops from every continent gathered in St. Peter's on 11 October 1962 for the twenty-first ecumenical council. Over four sessions to 1965, under John and then Paul VI, it renewed the liturgy, permitted the Mass in the vernacular, and defined the Church's relation to the modern world and to other faiths.

The war that the National Liberation Front began on 1 November 1954 was waged with terror on both sides and cost hundreds of thousands of Algerian lives. By the Évian Accords of March 1962 de Gaulle conceded independence, proclaimed on 5 July. Nearly a million European settlers fled to France within months, and tens of thousands of harkis, the Muslims who had fought for France, were slaughtered by the victors.

In October 1962 Chinese armies struck across the disputed frontier in Ladakh and the North-East Frontier Agency, overrunning Indian posts and taking Tawang. After a month China declared a ceasefire, withdrew in the east, and kept Aksai Chin in the west. The defeat humbled the Indian army and shattered Nehru's faith in Chinese friendship.

On 2 March 1962 General Ne Win overthrew the elected government of U Nu, who had been preparing to grant the minority states more freedom. His Revolutionary Council proclaimed the Burmese Way to Socialism, nationalized trade and industry, drove out some three hundred thousand Indians, and shut the country off from the world, and one of the richest lands of Asia sank into poverty.

The Netherlands kept western New Guinea after 1949 and prepared its Papuans for self-rule, while Sukarno's Indonesia claimed the territory and landed infiltrators. Pressed by Washington, the Dutch signed the New York Agreement of 15 August 1962; a United Nations authority took over in October and ruled for seven months, and Indonesia took over in May 1963.

Divided between Germany and the United States in 1899 and ruled by New Zealand from 1914, Western Samoa had long resisted through the Mau movement, whose leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III was shot down by New Zealand police on a day of peaceful protest in 1929. On 1 January 1962 it became the first Pacific island nation to win back its independence.

On 8 December 1962 the armed wing of A. M. Azahari's Brunei People's Party, which opposed joining Malaysia and sought a greater state of northern Borneo, rose against the sultan and seized the oil town of Seria. Gurkhas and Highlanders flown from Singapore crushed the revolt within days; Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III kept Brunei out of Malaysia and ruled thereafter by decree.

On 16 September 1963 Malaya joined with Singapore, Sarawak, and North Borneo, now called Sabah, to form Malaysia; Brunei, wary of sharing its oil, stayed out. Sukarno denounced the federation as a British plot and launched the Confrontation, a war of raids across the Borneo frontier fought against British, Gurkha, and Malaysian troops until his fall.

t: The Fall of Ngo Dinh Diem
x: Ngo Dinh Diem, the Catholic president of South Vietnam, and his brother Nhu answered the Buddhist protests of 1963 with raids on the pagodas and mass arrests of monks. With Washington's assent, generals led by Duong Van Minh overthrew the regime on 1 November; Diem and Nhu, captured the next morning, were murdered in an armored car.

The heads of thirty-two independent African states met in Haile Selassie's capital in May 1963 and signed the charter of the Organization of African Unity, pledging to defend their sovereignty, to respect the borders inherited from the colonial powers, and to free the continent's remaining colonies. In 2002 it gave way to the African Union.

On 28 August 1963 some 250,000 people marched on Washington for jobs and freedom, and from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial the Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. told them of his dream that his four children would one day 'not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.' The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 followed.

As his open limousine passed through Dealey Plaza on 22 November 1963, President John F. Kennedy was shot and killed by rifle fire from the Texas School Book Depository, where Lee Harvey Oswald, a former Marine who had defected to the Soviet Union, was employed. Lyndon Johnson took the oath aboard Air Force One; two days later Oswald himself was shot dead by Jack Ruby.

p: Gulf of Tonkin, off Thanh Hoa, Vietnam
x: On 2 August 1964 North Vietnamese torpedo boats attacked the destroyer USS Maddox in the Gulf of Tonkin; a second attack reported two nights later most likely never took place. Congress nonetheless passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, giving President Johnson power to wage war in Vietnam, and by 1968 more than half a million American troops were in the country.

From 1964 to 1973, to cut the Ho Chi Minh Trail and support General Vang Pao's Hmong army against the Pathet Lao, American aircraft flew some 580,000 bombing missions over Laos, dropping more than two million tons of bombs. Laos became, for the number of its people, the most heavily bombed country in history, and millions of unexploded bomblets still lie in its fields.

Nineteen years after the firebombing of Tokyo, Japan opened the first Olympic Games held in Asia, the flame lit by a runner born in Hiroshima prefecture on the day of the bomb. Days before, the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, the first high-speed railway in the world, had begun running between Tokyo and Osaka, and the economy was growing by some ten percent a year.

Four years after the Soviet Union withdrew its advisers, Chinese scientists exploded a uranium bomb of twenty-two kilotons on a tower at the Lop Nur test site in the Xinjiang desert. China became the fifth nuclear power, and less than three years later it tested its first hydrogen bomb.

In the night of 30 September 1965 a band of officers kidnapped and killed six generals and threw their bodies into a well at Lubang Buaya. General Suharto crushed the movement and blamed the Communist Party, and in the months that followed army units and civilian militias slaughtered at least half a million suspected Communists. Suharto took power from Sukarno in March 1966.

Race riots and quarrels between Lee Kuan Yew's People's Action Party and the Malay leaders of Kuala Lumpur ended Singapore's place in Malaysia. On 9 August 1965 Lee, near tears on television, announced the island's separation. Without hinterland or water of its own, the city-state made itself under his long rule one of the richest nations on earth.

Rather than accept majority rule, Ian Smith's government of white Rhodesians declared independence unilaterally on 11 November 1965, the first such break with the Crown since 1776. Britain and the United Nations imposed sanctions, and the guerrilla war of Robert Mugabe's and Joshua Nkomo's movements ended only with the Lancaster House settlement and Zimbabwe's independence in April 1980.

To destroy his rivals and renew the revolution, Mao Zedong called on the young to rise against the Four Olds and against officials taking the capitalist road. Millions of Red Guards rallied before him in Tiananmen Square, then turned on teachers, writers, and temples; the head of state Liu Shaoqi died in prison. Ten years of terror cost, by most reckonings, more than a million lives.

After Nasser expelled the United Nations force from Sinai and closed the Straits of Tiran, Israel struck first on 5 June 1967, destroying the Egyptian air force on the ground. In six days it took Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. Israeli soldiers prayed at the Western Wall for the first time since 1948.

After the massacres of Igbo in northern Nigeria in 1966, Lieutenant Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu proclaimed the Eastern Region the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967. The federal government of General Yakubu Gowon ground it down by blockade, and between half a million and two million people, most of them children, died of hunger before Biafra surrendered in January 1970.

Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, the Argentine physician who had been Castro's comrade in the Sierra Maestra, tried to kindle a continental revolution from the Bolivian wilderness, but the peasants would not follow him. Wounded and captured by Bolivian Rangers trained by the Americans, he was shot in the schoolhouse of La Higuera on 9 October 1967.

t: The End of the Prague Spring
x: Under Alexander Dubček, first secretary from January 1968, Czechoslovakia lifted censorship and promised socialism with a human face. On the night of 20 August some quarter of a million troops of the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary, and Bulgaria invaded. Dubček was taken to Moscow and forced to submit; in January 1969 the student Jan Palach burned himself to death in Wenceslas Square in protest.

In the lunar New Year truce of January 1968 some eighty thousand Communist troops struck more than a hundred towns of South Vietnam, and commandos broke into the American embassy compound in Saigon. At Hue the fighting lasted a month, and the occupiers massacred some three thousand civilians. A military defeat for Hanoi, the offensive broke the will of Washington.

On 16 July 1969 a Saturn V rocket lifted Apollo 11 from Cape Kennedy, and on 20 July Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin set the lunar module Eagle down on the Sea of Tranquillity while Michael Collins circled above. Armstrong stepped onto the surface with the words 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind,' fulfilling the pledge Kennedy had made in 1961.

On 1 September 1969, while King Idris was taking the waters in Turkey, junior officers led by the twenty-seven-year-old Captain Muammar Gaddafi seized power without resistance. Gaddafi expelled the American and British bases and the Italian settlers, nationalized the oil, and in 1977 proclaimed the Jamahiriya, a state of the masses, which he ruled as Guide of the Revolution for forty-two years.

The Dutch had kept western New Guinea out of the transfer of 1949, but American pressure brought it under Indonesian rule in 1963 on the promise of a vote. In 1969 Indonesia gathered 1,025 hand-picked elders, who declared unanimously for union with Indonesia. The Papuan resistance born of that day has never wholly died.

Built with Soviet loans and engineers from 1960, the High Dam at Aswan was completed in July 1970, holding back the Nile in Lake Nasser, more than three hundred miles long. It ended the yearly flood that had governed Egyptian life since the Pharaohs and gave the country electric power, but it drowned Nubia, whose people were resettled; the temples of Abu Simbel were cut apart and raised to higher ground.

On the night of 12 November 1970 a cyclone drove a storm surge over the low islands of the Bay of Bengal in East Pakistan, drowning between three hundred thousand and half a million people, the deadliest tropical storm on record. The government's slow relief inflamed Bengali anger, and a month later the Awami League swept the East in the national elections.

In Warsaw to sign the treaty by which West Germany recognized the Oder-Neisse line as Poland's frontier, Chancellor Willy Brandt laid a wreath at the memorial to the ghetto uprising on 7 December 1970 and then sank silently to his knees. His Ostpolitik of treaties with Moscow and Warsaw brought him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971, and the Basic Treaty with East Germany followed in 1972.

In July 1970, with British help, the young Sultan Qaboos deposed his father Said ibn Taimur, who had kept Oman shut against the modern world from his palace at Salalah. Qaboos defeated the Marxist rebellion in Dhofar with British, Iranian, and Jordanian aid by 1976, and spent his oil revenues on roads, schools, and hospitals in a country that had had three schools.

When the army of West Pakistan launched Operation Searchlight against the Bengalis on 25 March 1971, killing students, intellectuals, and Hindus by the thousand, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's followers proclaimed independence. Ten million refugees fled to India. In December India intervened, and on 16 December General Niazi surrendered with some ninety thousand men at Dacca. Bangladesh was free.

As Britain withdrew from east of Suez, six of the Trucial sheikhdoms joined on 2 December 1971 as the United Arab Emirates, with Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi as president and Sheikh Rashid of Dubai as vice president; Ras al-Khaimah joined in February 1972. Oil turned fishing and pearling villages into some of the richest cities on earth.

Three years after Soviet and Chinese soldiers had fought on the frozen Ussuri, President Richard Nixon flew to Beijing, met Mao Zedong in his study, and with Zhou Enlai issued the Shanghai Communiqué. The United States acknowledged that the Chinese on both sides of the strait held there to be but one China, and the opening of China to the West began.

The Troubles of Northern Ireland, in which the IRA, loyalist gunmen, and the security forces killed over 3,500 people between 1969 and 1998, reached a turning on 30 January 1972, when soldiers of the Parachute Regiment fired on a civil rights march in the Bogside of Derry, killing thirteen. Stormont was suspended that March, and London ruled the province directly.

Meeting in Kuwait on 17 October 1973, the Arab oil ministers agreed to cut production month by month and soon embargoed shipments to the United States and the Netherlands for their support of Israel. The price of oil quadrupled within months. The age of cheap energy ended, the West fell into recession, and the Gulf states gained wealth and power beyond all precedent.

On 6 October 1973, the Jewish Day of Atonement, the Egyptian army crossed the Suez Canal and stormed the Bar Lev line, while Syria attacked on the Golan Heights. Israel, taken by surprise, held and then struck back, crossing the canal and encircling an Egyptian army before a ceasefire took hold. Sadat's crossing restored Arab pride and opened the road to his visit to Jerusalem in 1977 and peace with Israel.

While King Zahir Shah was in Italy, his cousin and former prime minister Mohammed Daoud Khan seized power in a nearly bloodless coup on 17 July 1973 and proclaimed Afghanistan a republic. The kingdom founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747 was no more, and a generation of coups, invasion, and war lay ahead.

Salvador Allende, the first Marxist elected president of a Latin American nation, had nationalized the copper mines and the banks amid strikes, shortages, and inflation of several hundred per cent. On 11 September 1973 the armed forces under General Augusto Pinochet rose; jets bombed the La Moneda palace, and Allende died by his own hand within it. Pinochet ruled for seventeen years.

Wearied by thirteen years of colonial war in Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea, junior officers of the Armed Forces Movement overthrew Marcelo Caetano's Estado Novo, the dictatorship founded by Salazar, on 25 April 1974, and Lisbon crowds put carnations in the soldiers' rifles. By November 1975 Portugal had granted independence to all its African colonies, ending five centuries of empire in Africa.

Famine in Wollo, concealed by the court, and mutinies in the army undermined the aged emperor, and in September 1974 a committee of officers, the Derg, deposed Haile Selassie, last emperor of the Solomonic line, who died in custody the next year. Under Mengistu Haile Mariam the Derg turned Marxist and in the Red Terror of 1977 and 1978 killed tens of thousands.

Seven years after the colonels' coup of April 1967, the Greek junta's chief, Brigadier Ioannidis, backed a coup against President Makarios of Cyprus on 15 July 1974. Turkey invaded the island five days later and has held its north ever since. The junta collapsed, and Konstantinos Karamanlis flew home from Paris on 24 July to restore democracy; a referendum that December abolished the monarchy.

Two years after the last American combat troops left, North Vietnam's spring offensive of 1975 swept down the coast. As helicopters lifted the last Americans and thousands of Vietnamese from the city, a North Vietnamese tank broke through the gates of the Independence Palace on 30 April, and General Duong Van Minh surrendered. Vietnam was united under Communist rule the next year.

Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975 after thirty-six years in power, and two days later Juan Carlos de Borbón, grandson of Alfonso XIII and the successor Franco had named, was proclaimed king. With Adolfo Suárez as prime minister he dismantled the regime by its own laws; a democratic constitution was approved in 1978, and the King faced down an attempted coup in the Cortes in February 1981.

On 13 April 1975, after gunmen fired on a church in the Ain al-Rummaneh quarter of Beirut, Phalangist militiamen ambushed a bus carrying Palestinians and killed some two dozen. Lebanon's delicate balance of Christian and Muslim sects collapsed into a civil war of militias, massacres, and foreign armies that lasted fifteen years and killed some 150,000 people, until the Taif Agreement of 1989.

t: The Khmer Rouge Take Phnom Penh
x: On 17 April 1975 the black-clad soldiers of the Khmer Rouge entered Phnom Penh and drove its two million people into the countryside. Under Pol Pot, Democratic Kampuchea abolished money, markets, schools, and religion and turned the land into a vast labor camp. Before Vietnamese troops ended the regime in January 1979, some 1.7 million Cambodians had died of execution, starvation, and disease.

On 16 September 1975 the Australian flag was lowered at Port Moresby, and Papua New Guinea became an independent state under Prime Minister Michael Somare. Its nearly three million people spoke more than eight hundred languages; many highland valleys had first been entered by outsiders only in the 1930s, when gold prospectors found there a million people unknown to the world.

Portugal's revolution of 1974 left its colony in Timor to civil war, and Fretilin declared independence on 28 November 1975. Nine days later Indonesian paratroops dropped on Dili. Annexed as Indonesia's twenty-seventh province, East Timor resisted for twenty-four years, during which war, hunger, and killing took more than a hundred thousand lives.

After the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon overthrew the Estado Novo, Portugal abandoned its African empire, and some 300,000 Portuguese settlers fled Angola. On 11 November 1975 Agostinho Neto's Marxist MPLA, aided by Cuban troops and Soviet arms, proclaimed independence in Luanda, while UNITA and the FNLA, backed by South Africa and the United States, fought on in a civil war that lasted until 2002.

As Spain prepared to leave the Western Sahara, King Hassan II of Morocco sent some 350,000 unarmed Moroccans across the border on 6 November 1975, bearing Qurans and flags. Spain handed over the administration of the territory to Morocco and Mauritania, but the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic and took up arms; Mauritania withdrew in 1979, and the dispute endures.

On 16 June 1976 thousands of black schoolchildren in Soweto marched against a decree that half their lessons be taught in Afrikaans; the police opened fire, and among the first to die was Hector Pieterson, aged twelve. The unrest spread across the country, hundreds were killed, and a generation of young South Africans went into exile to join the armed struggle.

In the small hours of 28 July an earthquake levelled the industrial city of Tangshan, killing at least 242,000 people by the official count, and the government refused foreign help. That September Mao Zedong died, and within a month his widow Jiang Qing and her allies, the Gang of Four, were arrested. Many Chinese believed the earthquake had foretold the end of an era.

On 16 October 1978 the cardinals elected Karol Wojtyła, Archbishop of Kraków, the first non-Italian pope in more than four and a half centuries, who took the name John Paul II. When he returned to Poland in June 1979, millions came to his Masses, and in Warsaw's Victory Square he prayed that the Spirit would renew the face of the earth, the face of this land. A year later Solidarity was born.

In the winter of 1978 eighteen farmers of the hungry village of Xiaogang secretly divided the collective fields into family plots, pressing their thumbprints on the pact. A few weeks later the party's Third Plenum confirmed Deng Xiaoping's ascendancy and turned the state toward reform and opening. The communes were dissolved within five years, and a generation of growth followed.

Persecution of the ethnic Chinese and of all who had served the South drove hundreds of thousands to flee Vietnam by sea in leaking boats, prey to storms and to pirates of the Gulf of Thailand. The little island of Pulau Bidong off Malaysia held forty thousand refugees at the height of the exodus; in all some eight hundred thousand reached other lands by boat.

After a year of mass demonstrations, Mohammad Reza Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, and on 1 February the Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from fifteen years of exile to a welcome of millions. The monarchy fell within days, and by referendum Iran became an Islamic Republic under the guardianship of the jurist. In November student militants seized the American embassy and held fifty-two hostages for 444 days.

On 24 December 1979 Soviet airborne troops began landing at Kabul, and on the 27th special forces stormed the Tajbeg Palace, killed the communist ruler Hafizullah Amin, and installed Babrak Karmal. Some hundred thousand Soviet troops fought for nine years against the mujahideen, armed by America, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia; about a million Afghans died and five million fled abroad.

Provoked by Khmer Rouge massacres in its border provinces, Vietnam invaded Cambodia at Christmas 1978 and took Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979, setting up a government under Heng Samrin. The world now saw the mass graves and the prison of Tuol Sleng, where some fourteen thousand had been tortured and killed. Pol Pot's army withdrew to the Thai border to fight on.

The Somoza family had ruled Nicaragua since 1936; when the opposition editor Pedro Joaquín Chamorro was murdered in 1978, the country rose behind the Sandinista guerrillas. Anastasio Somoza Debayle fled on 17 July 1979; the Sandinistas under Daniel Ortega governed, through a decade of war with the American-backed Contras, until the voters chose Chamorro's widow Violeta in 1990.

Striking over the dismissal of a crane operator, Anna Walentynowicz, the workers of the Lenin Shipyard at Gdańsk were led from August 1980 by the electrician Lech Wałęsa; on 31 August the government signed an agreement allowing free trade unions. Solidarity grew to some ten million members before General Jaruzelski declared martial law on 13 December 1981 and interned its leaders.

Saddam Hussein, seeing revolutionary Iran in disarray, invaded on 22 September 1980 and took Khorramshahr after weeks of street fighting. Iran recovered the city in 1982 and carried the war into Iraq with human-wave assaults of young volunteers, and Iraq answered with poison gas. When a ceasefire came in August 1988 the frontier was unchanged, and perhaps half a million had died.

After the assassination of President Park Chung-hee, the general Chun Doo-hwan seized power and extended martial law. In Gwangju paratroopers beat and shot student demonstrators, and the citizens armed themselves and drove the soldiers out. After ten days the army retook the city; by official count some two hundred people died. Gwangju became the rallying cry of Korean democracy, won in 1987.

As the New Hebrides moved to independence under the Anglican priest Walter Lini, the Nagriamel movement of Jimmy Stevens, backed by French planters and American adventurers, proclaimed Espiritu Santo the free state of Vemerana. Vanuatu became independent on 30 July 1980, and troops from Papua New Guinea put down the secession within weeks.

In 1981 the military government of Mauritania decreed the abolition of slavery, the last country in the world to do so. Among the Moors of the Saharan republic the bondage of the black Haratin to Arab-Berber masters had survived French rule and independence alike. Slaveholding was made a crime only in 2007, and hereditary servitude lingers in the desert camps.

When the Argentine junta seized the Falkland Islands, a British colony since 1833, on 2 April 1982, Margaret Thatcher sent a task force eight thousand miles across the Atlantic. After the sinking of the cruiser General Belgrano and the loss of British ships to air attack, troops landed at San Carlos and marched on Port Stanley, where the Argentines surrendered on 14 June.

After the Tamil Tigers ambushed and killed thirteen soldiers near Jaffna, Sinhalese mobs in Colombo and across the island hunted Tamils through July 1983, burning their homes and shops and murdering hundreds, while some police and soldiers looked on. Thousands of young Tamils joined the separatist militants, and the civil war began that would last twenty-six years.

In June 1984 the Indian army stormed the Golden Temple at Amritsar to dislodge the armed Sikh militant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and his followers, who had fortified the shrine. The militants and hundreds of pilgrims died, and the Akal Takht was wrecked. On 31 October two of Indira Gandhi's Sikh bodyguards shot her dead, and mobs in Delhi slaughtered thousands of Sikhs in reprisal.

On the night of 2 to 3 December 1984 some forty tonnes of methyl isocyanate gas escaped from the Union Carbide pesticide plant at Bhopal and drifted over the sleeping slums around it. Thousands died within days, and many thousands more in the years after, in the worst industrial disaster in history.

On 11 March 1985, after the deaths of three ailing leaders in three years, the Politburo chose Mikhail Gorbachev, at fifty-four its youngest member, as general secretary. He preached glasnost and perestroika, openness and restructuring, to save the Soviet system, withdrew from Afghanistan, and at summits with Ronald Reagan agreed to scrap intermediate-range nuclear missiles.

In the early hours of 26 April 1986, during a botched safety test, reactor number four of the Chernobyl power station north of Kiev exploded and burned, throwing radioactive dust across Ukraine, Belorussia, and Europe. The town of Pripyat was evacuated only after thirty-six hours, and a zone of some thirty kilometers around the plant was emptied of its people.

The murder of the opposition leader Benigno Aquino on the airport tarmac in 1983 turned the Philippines against Ferdinand Marcos, who had ruled under martial law from 1972. When Marcos proclaimed himself the victor of the snap election of February 1986 over Aquino's widow Corazon, army rebels mutinied, Cardinal Sin called the faithful into the streets, and a million unarmed people shielded them; Marcos fled to Hawaii.

With inflation running at hundreds of percent and its people hungry, the Communist Party of Vietnam at its Sixth Congress in December 1986 chose Nguyen Van Linh to lead and proclaimed Doi Moi, Renovation. Collective farming was abandoned and private trade and foreign investment welcomed, and within a few years Vietnam turned from importing rice to being one of the world's great rice exporters.

On 14 May 1987 Lieutenant-Colonel Sitiveni Rabuka led soldiers into the Fijian parliament and overthrew the newly elected government of Timoci Bavadra, which drew most of its support from Indo-Fijians. A second coup in September was followed by a republic in October and the departure of Fiji from the Commonwealth; tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians emigrated.

Captain Thomas Sankara, who seized power in Upper Volta in 1983 and renamed it Burkina Faso, 'the land of upright men,' warred on corruption, planted millions of trees, and vaccinated the nation's children. On 15 October 1987 he was shot dead with twelve of his aides in a coup that brought his comrade Blaise Compaoré to power for twenty-seven years.

On 16 March 1988, in the last months of the war with Iran, Iraqi aircraft dropped mustard gas and nerve agents on the Kurdish town of Halabja, which Iranian troops and Kurdish fighters had just taken. About five thousand civilians died in a day. It was the worst blow of the Anfal campaign, in which Saddam Hussein's regime destroyed thousands of Kurdish villages and killed tens of thousands of their people.

Students and monks led a nationwide rising against the ruin wrought by Ne Win's socialism, reaching its height in a general strike on 8 August 1988. Aung San Suu Kyi, daughter of the national hero, addressed half a million people at the Shwedagon. On 18 September the army seized power outright and shot down the protesters, killing perhaps three thousand.

In the largest conventional battle on African soil since the Second World War, South African forces fighting beside UNITA besieged the Angolan army and its Cuban allies at Cuito Cuanavale from late 1987 into March 1988 without taking the town. The stalemate led to the New York accords of December 1988, by which Cuba withdrew from Angola and South Africa let Namibia go free in 1990.

t: The Fall of the Berlin Wall
x: After a summer of flight through Hungary and an autumn of mass demonstrations in Leipzig, the East German party spokesman Günter Schabowski announced on the evening of 9 November 1989, by mistake, that citizens might cross the border at once. Crowds massed at the checkpoints; at Bornholmer Strasse the guards opened the gate before midnight, and Berliners danced on the Wall.

When riot police beat a student march in Prague on 17 November 1989, the city rose in nightly demonstrations of hundreds of thousands in Wenceslas Square, where Dubček reappeared beside the playwright Václav Havel of Civic Forum. A general strike on 27 November ended communist rule without a shot, and on 29 December the Federal Assembly elected Havel president.

The attempted arrest of the Hungarian pastor László Tőkés at Timișoara set off a rising in mid-December 1989 that the Securitate met with gunfire. On 21 December Nicolae Ceaușescu was jeered by the crowd he had summoned in Bucharest, and he fled by helicopter the next day. Captured, he and his wife Elena were tried by a drumhead court at Târgoviște and shot on Christmas Day.

After the death of the reformer Hu Yaobang, students occupied Tiananmen Square for seven weeks, raising a white Goddess of Democracy to face Mao's portrait. On the night of 3 to 4 June the army cleared the streets of Beijing with tanks and rifle fire, killing hundreds, perhaps thousands. The party chose economic reform without political freedom.

On 15 February 1989 General Boris Gromov, the last Soviet commander, walked across the Friendship Bridge over the Amu Darya from Hairatan into Soviet Uzbekistan, ending nine years of war that had cost the Soviet army some fifteen thousand dead. The defeat hastened the fall of the Soviet Union; Najibullah's government held out three more years.

On 23 August 1989, the fiftieth anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, some two million Estonians, Latvians, and Lithuanians joined hands in a human chain of over four hundred miles from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius, demanding the independence the pact had cost them. Within months Moscow admitted the existence of the secret protocol.

The Round Table talks between the government and Solidarity, held from February to April 1989, allowed partly free elections on 4 June. Solidarity won all 161 freely contested seats in the Sejm and ninety-nine of the hundred seats of the new Senate. In August Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the first non-communist prime minister in the Soviet bloc since the 1940s.

t: The Wa Rise Against the Burmese Communists
x: In April 1989 Wa soldiers of the Communist Party of Burma, led by Kyauk Ni Lai and Bao Youxiang, mutinied against their aged Burman leaders, seized the party's headquarters at Panghsang, and drove the leadership into China. They founded the United Wa State Army, made a ceasefire with the junta within weeks, and ruled the Wa Hills thereafter as a state of their own.

After the East German elections of March 1990 and a currency union in July, the Treaty on the Final Settlement signed in Moscow in September by the two German states and the four wartime allies restored full sovereignty to a united Germany. At midnight on 3 October 1990 the black, red, and gold flag rose before the Reichstag, and the five eastern states joined the Federal Republic.

Accusing Kuwait of stealing its oil and driving down prices, Saddam Hussein sent his army over the border on 2 August 1990 and overran the emirate in a day; the emir fled to Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait was declared Iraq's nineteenth province. Fearing for the Saudi oil fields, the United States assembled a coalition of some thirty-five nations and over half a million American troops in the desert.

President F. W. de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC and on 11 February 1990 released Nelson Mandela after twenty-seven years in prison; that evening Mandela spoke to a vast crowd from the balcony of Cape Town's City Hall. Four years of negotiation, shadowed by bloody strife in Natal and the townships, brought apartheid to an end.

Through the winter of 1989 to 1990 young Mongolians gathered in the bitter cold of Sükhbaatar Square to demand free elections, and some went on hunger strike. In March the Politburo of the ruling party resigned, and in July Mongolia held its first multiparty elections, the first communist state in Asia to give up one-party rule in peace.

At the end of 1989 the Nikkei index stood near 39,000, and the land under the Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. As the Bank of Japan raised interest rates, shares lost nearly half their value within the year and land prices began a long fall. The banks were left with bad loans, and Japan entered its Lost Decade.

t: The End of the Soviet Union
x: On 8 December 1991, at a hunting lodge in the Belovezha Forest, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus declared that the USSR had ceased to exist and founded a Commonwealth of Independent States. Gorbachev resigned on Christmas Day; that evening the red flag came down over the Kremlin, and fifteen republics stood as independent states.

On 19 August 1991, the day before a new union treaty was to be signed, hardliners of the State Committee for the State of Emergency confined Gorbachev at his dacha in the Crimea and sent tanks into Moscow. Boris Yeltsin, president of Russia, climbed onto a tank before the parliament building to denounce them; the troops would not fire on the crowds, and the coup collapsed in three days.

Ukraine's parliament declared independence on 24 August 1991, in the days after the failed coup in Moscow, and on 1 December more than ninety percent of voters approved it, a majority in every region including the Crimea. Leonid Kravchuk was elected president that day. Without Ukraine, the second republic of the Union, the Soviet state could not survive.

On 17 January 1991 coalition aircraft began five weeks of bombing of Baghdad and the Iraqi army. The ground offensive launched on 24 February freed Kuwait in a hundred hours, while the retreating Iraqis set some seven hundred oil wells ablaze. Saddam survived, crushing risings of the Shi'a in the south and the Kurds in the north, and Iraq spent the next twelve years under sanctions.

Facing a crisis of payments with reserves enough for only a few weeks of imports, the government of P. V. Narasimha Rao and his finance minister Manmohan Singh devalued the rupee, cut tariffs, and dismantled the licence raj that had governed Indian industry since independence. Growth quickened, and India began its rise as one of the great economies of the world.

Slovenia and Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991; Slovenia won its freedom in a ten-day war, but in Croatia the Serb minority rose with the Yugoslav army behind it. The Danube town of Vukovar was besieged and shelled for eighty-seven days until it fell on 18 November; some two hundred of the wounded taken from its hospital were shot at Ovčara.

On 16 December 1991, last of the Soviet republics to do so, Kazakhstan declared its independence under Nursultan Nazarbayev. It inherited the Soviet nuclear test ground at Semipalatinsk, closed that year after over four hundred and fifty explosions, and some fourteen hundred warheads, which it gave up by 1995. In 1997 the capital moved north to Akmola, soon renamed Astana.

After five centuries asleep, Mount Pinatubo on Luzon erupted on 15 June 1991, the second greatest eruption of the century, as a typhoon soaked the falling ash into a wet cement that crushed roofs across the plain. Timely warning saved tens of thousands, though some eight hundred died; the Americans abandoned Clark Air Base, and the earth cooled by half a degree.

Months after Siad Barre fled Mogadishu, the Somali National Movement and the elders of the northern clans met at Burao and on 18 May 1991 proclaimed the former British Somaliland independent of Somalia. Its capital Hargeisa had been bombed to ruins by Barre's air force in 1988. With its own elections, currency, and army, Somaliland has kept the peace while the south fell to war, yet no state has recognized it.

Signed on 7 February 1992 by the twelve members of the European Communities, the Treaty of Maastricht founded the European Union, with European citizenship, a common foreign and security policy, and a plan for economic and monetary union with a single currency. Danish voters rejected it at first and the French barely approved it; it came into force in November 1993.

When Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence in the spring of 1992, the Bosnian Serb forces of Radovan Karadžić ringed Sarajevo with artillery and snipers on the hills. The siege lasted nearly four years, the longest of a capital in modern war; some eleven thousand people were killed, among them sixty-eight in the Markale market by a single shell in February 1994.

The Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh, an autonomous region of Soviet Azerbaijan, voted in 1988 to join Armenia, and the dispute became open war as the Soviet Union fell. On the night of 25 to 26 February 1992 Armenian forces took the town of Khojaly and killed hundreds of fleeing Azerbaijani civilians. By the ceasefire of 1994 the Armenians held Karabakh and seven surrounding districts.

t: The Demolition of the Babri Mosque
x: On 6 December 1992 a crowd of Hindu volunteers broke into the compound at Ayodhya and tore down the mosque built in 1528 in the name of Babur, on the site Hindus revere as the birthplace of Rama. Riots across India and in Bombay killed some two thousand. A temple to Rama was consecrated on the site in January 2024.

On 3 June 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled in the case brought by Eddie Mabo and other Meriam people of Murray Island that the doctrine of terra nullius, by which the continent had been treated as no man's land in 1788, was false, and that the native title of its first peoples had survived. Mabo had died a few months before the judgment.

After thirty years of war against Ethiopian rule, the Eritrean People's Liberation Front under Isaias Afwerki took Asmara in May 1991, in the same week that Mengistu fled Addis Ababa. In April 1993 Eritreans voted almost unanimously for independence; but a quarrel over the border village of Badme brought war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 that killed tens of thousands.

With Somalia fallen into clan war and famine after the overthrow of Siad Barre in 1991, American troops came to guard the relief convoys and then to hunt the warlord Mohamed Farrah Aidid. On 3 and 4 October 1993 two Black Hawk helicopters were shot down over Mogadishu; eighteen Americans and hundreds of Somalis died in the fighting, and the United States withdrew.

When the aircraft of President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down over Kigali on 6 April 1994, Hutu extremists of the army and the Interahamwe militia began the systematic slaughter of the Tutsi minority and of the Hutu who opposed them, with machetes and with lists prepared in advance. In about a hundred days some 800,000 were killed, until Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front took Kigali in July.

In April 1994 South Africans of every race voted together for the first time, standing for hours in lines that stretched across the veld. The ANC won nearly two-thirds of the votes, and on 10 May Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as president at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, with Thabo Mbeki and F. W. de Klerk as his deputies.

Chechnya under Dzhokhar Dudayev had declared independence in 1991. In December 1994 Yeltsin sent the army in; the storm of Grozny on New Year's Eve ended in the slaughter of the Russian columns, and the city was pounded to ruin before it fell. The war ended in humiliation for Moscow in 1996, but a second war from 1999 under Putin crushed the republic.

In July 1995 the Bosnian Serb army of General Ratko Mladić overran Srebrenica, a United Nations safe area guarded by a few hundred Dutch peacekeepers. Over the following days it separated the Muslim men and boys from the women and murdered some eight thousand of them in fields and warehouses, the worst massacre in Europe since the Second World War, judged genocide by the international courts.

t: Operation Storm and the Dayton Peace
x: In August 1995 the Croatian army retook Knin and the Krajina in four days, and some 200,000 Serbs fled. NATO bombed the Bosnian Serbs after Srebrenica and a second Markale shelling. At Dayton, Ohio, in November, Milošević, Tuđman, and Izetbegović agreed to a Bosnia of two entities under a High Representative, and the agreement was signed in Paris on 14 December.

Fifteen years after a first referendum on sovereignty had failed by a wide margin, the Parti Québécois government of Jacques Parizeau put the question again on 30 October 1995. Quebecers voted to remain in Canada by 50.6 per cent to 49.4, a margin of some 54,000 votes; Parizeau blamed 'money and the ethnic vote' and resigned the next day.

The Taliban, student militias raised among the refugees and religious schools of the Pashtun south, had taken Kandahar in 1994 with Pakistani backing. In September 1996 they entered Kabul, dragged the former president Najibullah from the United Nations compound, and hanged him. Under Mullah Omar they barred girls from school, banned music and television, and sheltered Osama bin Laden.

At midnight on 30 June 1997, in a convention center on Hong Kong's harbor, the Union Jack was lowered and the colony taken by Britain in the Opium War passed to the People's Republic of China under the formula of one country, two systems. The Prince of Wales and the last governor, Chris Patten, sailed away on the royal yacht Britannia; the empire's last great colony was gone.

On 2 July 1997 Thailand, its reserves drained in defense against speculators, let the baht float, and it soon lost half its value. Panic ran through the borrowed prosperity of the Asian tigers: the rupiah fell by four-fifths, banks and builders failed from Seoul to Jakarta, and the International Monetary Fund imposed its remedies. In Indonesia the crash brought down Suharto within a year.

Rwanda and Uganda, pursuing the Hutu killers who had fled into eastern Zaire, armed a rebellion under the veteran guerrilla Laurent-Désiré Kabila that marched across the country in seven months. Mobutu Sese Seko, who had ruled and plundered Zaire for thirty-two years, fled in May 1997; the Second Congo War that followed drew in nine African nations, and millions died of war, hunger, and disease.

In May 1998 India exploded five nuclear devices beneath the desert at Pokhran, and two weeks later Pakistan answered with five of its own and then a sixth, beneath the Ras Koh hills of Chagai in Balochistan. Both nations declared themselves nuclear powers, and the old quarrel over Kashmir took on a new and terrible weight.

As prices soared, students occupied the parliament in Jakarta, and riots in May 1998 burned the Chinese quarters of the capital, killing more than a thousand. Abandoned by his ministers and the army, Suharto resigned on 21 May after thirty-two years in power. His successor B. J. Habibie freed the press, called elections, and allowed East Timor its vote.

After the ceasefires of 1994 and talks chaired by the American senator George Mitchell, the British and Irish governments and most of Northern Ireland's parties agreed at Stormont on Good Friday, 10 April 1998, to a power-sharing assembly, cross-border bodies, and the principle that the province's status could change only by the consent of its people. Voters north and south approved it in May.

When Serbian forces under Milošević drove hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes, NATO bombed Yugoslavia for seventy-eight days from 24 March 1999 until Belgrade withdrew its army in June and the province passed under United Nations rule. Milošević fell to a popular rising in October 2000 and died in 2006 while on trial at The Hague.

On 30 August 1999, under the eyes of the United Nations, 78.5 percent of the East Timorese voted for independence. Militias armed by the Indonesian army then burned Dili and much of the country and drove a quarter of a million people into West Timor, until an Australian-led force landed on 20 September. East Timor became independent on 20 May 2002.

On the morning of 11 September 2001, nineteen Islamist hijackers of al-Qaeda seized four American airliners, flew two into the towers of the World Trade Center, which collapsed, and one into the Pentagon; the fourth crashed in Pennsylvania as its passengers fought back. Nearly three thousand died. The United States invaded Afghanistan within a month and Iraq in 2003, beginning a twenty-year war on terror.

In March 2001 the Taliban, deaf to appeals from across the world and from Muslim scholars, declared the giant Buddhas of Bamiyan idols and destroyed them with artillery and explosives over several weeks. The empty niches, some fifty-five and thirty-eight metres high, still gape in the cliff where the statues had stood for fourteen centuries.

After the attacks of 11 September 2001, planned by al-Qaeda from its Afghan bases, the United States and Britain began bombing in October, and the Northern Alliance, whose leader Ahmad Shah Massoud had been murdered two days before the attacks, swept into Kabul on 13 November. In December the Bonn conference named Hamid Karzai to lead a new government.

t: China Joins the World Trade Organization
x: After fifteen years of negotiation, China entered the World Trade Organization on 11 December. Tariffs fell, foreign capital poured into the factories of the coast, and within a decade China had become the world's greatest exporter and its second largest economy, the workshop of the world.

Created as the currency of eleven states on 1 January 1999 and managed by the European Central Bank at Frankfurt, the euro became money in the hand on 1 January 2002, when notes and coins replaced the mark, the franc, the lira, the guilder, the peseta, the drachma, and the other national currencies of twelve nations. The deutschmark, emblem of German recovery, passed away.

On 12 October 2002 bombs planted by Jemaah Islamiyah, a jihadist network linked to al-Qaeda that sought an Islamic state across Southeast Asia, tore through two crowded nightclubs at Kuta on Bali. Two hundred and two people were killed, eighty-eight of them Australians. Indonesia's police, with foreign help, hunted the network down over the following decade.

On 20 March 2003 American and British forces invaded Iraq to destroy weapons of mass destruction that were never found. Baghdad fell on 9 April, when Marines helped a crowd pull down Saddam Hussein's statue in Firdos Square. Saddam was found hiding in a hole near Tikrit that December and hanged in 2006, while Iraq sank into insurgency and a civil war between Sunni and Shi'ite.

When rebels of the Fur, Masalit, and Zaghawa peoples attacked the airfield at El Fasher in April 2003, Omar al-Bashir's government loosed the Arab Janjaweed militias upon their villages. By the reckoning of the United Nations some 300,000 people died of the massacres, hunger, and disease that followed, and two million were driven from their homes; in 2009 the International Criminal Court issued a warrant for Bashir's arrest.

t: The Regional Mission to Solomon Islands
x: Fighting between militias of Guadalcanal and of Malaita, which drove some twenty thousand settlers from their homes and brought a coup in Honiara in 2000, left the Solomon Islands near collapse. In July 2003 an Australian-led Regional Assistance Mission of soldiers and police from across the Pacific landed, disarmed the militias, and stayed fourteen years.

On 1 May 2004 ten states joined the European Union: Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, and Cyprus, welcomed at a ceremony in Dublin under the Irish presidency. Most had entered NATO in 1999 or that March. Romania and Bulgaria followed in 2007 and Croatia in 2013, and the Union counted twenty-eight members.

On 26 December 2004 an earthquake of magnitude 9.1 beneath the sea off Sumatra loosed waves that struck the coasts of the Indian Ocean from Thailand to Somalia. Aceh suffered worst: some 170,000 died there, many in Banda Aceh. Amid the ruin, the Free Aceh Movement and Jakarta made peace at Helsinki in 2005, ending thirty years of war.

When the Kremlin's candidate Viktor Yanukovych was declared winner of Ukraine's presidential run-off in November 2004 amid open fraud, hundreds of thousands camped in the frost on Independence Square in Kyiv wearing the orange of Viktor Yushchenko, who had been poisoned with dioxin that autumn. The Supreme Court ordered the vote rerun, and Yushchenko won in December.

After fourteen years of civil war, which began with Charles Taylor's invasion at Christmas 1989 and ended with his flight into exile in 2003, Liberians in November 2005 elected Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, a Harvard-trained economist, over the footballer George Weah. Inaugurated in January 2006, she was the first woman elected head of state in Africa; Taylor was later convicted at The Hague for his crimes in Sierra Leone.

The regime of Kim Jong Il, which had outlived a famine in the 1990s that killed hundreds of thousands, exploded its first nuclear device in a tunnel beneath Mount Mantap at Punggye-ri. Five more tests followed by 2017, the last far more powerful, and North Korea built missiles to carry its weapons across the Pacific.

On 2 May 2008 Cyclone Nargis drove a wall of seawater across the low rice lands of the Irrawaddy delta, and some 138,000 people died.
