The ruling generals, who had crushed the monk-led Saffron Revolution the year before, at first barred foreign relief workers and pressed on a week later with a referendum on their new constitution.

The bursting of the American housing bubble, swollen by loans to borrowers who could not repay and by the securities built upon them, brought down the investment bank Lehman Brothers on 15 September 2008, the largest bankruptcy in American history. Credit froze around the world, governments poured vast sums into their banks, and the Great Recession that followed was the worst since the 1930s.

On the night of 7 to 8 August 2008 Georgian troops attacked Tskhinvali, chief town of the breakaway region of South Ossetia, after days of skirmishing. Russia sent its armies through the Roki Tunnel and across Abkhazia, routed the Georgians in five days, and occupied Gori. Moscow then recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states, and its troops remain there.

On 12 May an earthquake beneath Wenchuan county shook the mountains of western Sichuan, killing some seventy thousand people. Thousands of children died in the ruins of badly built schools, and parents who protested were silenced. Three months later Beijing opened the Summer Olympic Games.

t: The End of the Nepalese Monarchy
x: Seven years after Crown Prince Dipendra shot dead King Birendra and much of the royal family at a palace dinner, and after a decade of Maoist insurgency that cost some seventeen thousand lives, Nepal's elected Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy on 28 May 2008. King Gyanendra left the Narayanhiti palace, and the last Hindu kingdom became a federal republic.

t: The Defeat of the Tamil Tigers
x: After twenty-six years of civil war the Sri Lankan army drove the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam into a strip of coast near Mullaitivu, where tens of thousands of civilians were trapped with them. On 18 May 2009 the Tiger leader Velupillai Prabhakaran was killed near the Nanthi Kadal lagoon, and the war was over.

On 17 December 2010 Mohamed Bouazizi, a young fruit seller in the Tunisian town of Sidi Bouzid whose cart had been confiscated by officials, set himself on fire before the governor's office. His death in January set off protests across Tunisia, and on 14 January 2011 President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia after twenty-three years in power. The Arab Spring had begun.

On 12 January 2010 an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 struck near Léogâne, some sixteen miles from Port-au-Prince, and in less than a minute leveled much of the capital, among its ruins the National Palace and the cathedral. Estimates of the dead ranged from a hundred thousand to more than three hundred thousand, making it one of the deadliest earthquakes ever recorded; cholera followed.

Inspired by Tunisia, crowds filled Cairo's Tahrir Square on 25 January 2011 and held it for eighteen days against police, hired thugs on camels, and the regime's propaganda. On 11 February Hosni Mubarak resigned after thirty years. The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the presidency in 2012, but in July 2013 the army under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi removed him and killed hundreds of his supporters at the Rabaa sit-in.

In March 2011 security men in Daraa arrested and tortured schoolboys who had written slogans against the regime on a wall, and the protests that followed were met with gunfire. The uprising spread across Syria and became a civil war of many sides, in which Russia and Iran upheld Bashar al-Assad, and which by 2024 had killed perhaps half a million and driven half the nation from their homes.

On 11 March the strongest earthquake ever measured in Japan struck off the coast of Tōhoku, and a tsunami up to forty metres high swept over the shore, killing some eighteen thousand people. At the Fukushima Daiichi plant the waves cut the power to the cooling systems, three reactors melted down, and over a hundred thousand people were evacuated.

Two civil wars between the Arab and Muslim north of Sudan and the African, largely Christian and animist south, the second of them costing some two million lives between 1983 and 2005, ended in a peace that promised the south a vote. In January 2011 nearly ninety-nine per cent voted to separate, and on 9 July South Sudan became the newest nation on earth under Salva Kiir.

The rising that began in Benghazi in February 2011 was saved from Gaddafi's columns by NATO air strikes, and in August the rebels took Tripoli. Gaddafi fled to his home town of Sirte, where on 20 October he was dragged from a drainage pipe and killed. Libya broke into rival governments and militias, and from 2014 into a second civil war between east and west.

A Tuareg rebellion in northern Mali in 2012, swelled by fighters and weapons from Gaddafi's fallen army, was soon taken over by jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda. They imposed their law on Timbuktu, flogging and amputating, and took pickaxes to the tombs of its Sufi saints. French troops drove them from the northern towns in January 2013, but the insurgency spread across the Sahel.

On 8 November 2013 Typhoon Haiyan, called Yolanda in the Philippines and among the strongest storms ever to make landfall, struck the central islands with winds near 300 kilometers an hour. Its storm surge drowned much of Tacloban, the city near which MacArthur had landed, and more than six thousand people died.

When President Yanukovych, under pressure from Moscow, refused in November 2013 to sign an association agreement with the European Union, protesters occupied Independence Square in Kyiv for three winter months. Between 18 and 20 February 2014 snipers and riot police killed about a hundred of them, remembered as the Heavenly Hundred; Yanukovych fled the capital on the night of the 21st, and on 22 February parliament removed him.

Days after Yanukovych's fall, Russian soldiers without insignia seized the Crimean parliament and the airports of the peninsula. A referendum held under occupation on 16 March 2014 was followed on the 18th by Russia's annexation of the Crimea, which the United Nations General Assembly declared invalid. In April Russian-led militias seized towns in the Donbas, and war began in eastern Ukraine.

In June 2014 a few thousand fighters of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria routed the Iraqi army and seized Mosul. From the pulpit of its Great Mosque Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi proclaimed himself caliph. Mosul's Christians, their houses marked with the Arabic letter nun, were given the choice of conversion, tribute, or the sword and fled, leaving the city without a Christian community for the first time in many centuries.

On 17 July 2014 Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, flying from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur, was shot down over the Donbas by a Buk missile brought from Russia, killing all 298 aboard, 196 of them Dutch. The international investigators traced the launcher to the Russian 53rd Anti-Aircraft Missile Brigade, and a Dutch court in 2022 convicted three men of murder in absentia.

In August 2014 the Islamic State overran Sinjar, homeland of the Yazidis, an ancient faith the jihadists reviled as devil worship. Men and older women were massacred in their thousands, and some six thousand women and children were carried off to be sold as slaves in Raqqa and Mosul. Tens of thousands fled to Mount Sinjar, until Kurdish fighters opened a corridor to safety.

The Zaydi Houthi movement of Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, aided by soldiers still loyal to the deposed president Ali Abdullah Saleh, marched down from the northern highlands and took the capital on 21 September 2014 almost without a fight. In January 2015 they confined President Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi in his residence; he escaped to Aden, and the war for Yemen began.

The Houthis, a Zaydi revivalist movement from the mountains of Sa'da, seized Sana'a in September 2014 and drove President Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi south to Aden. On 26 March 2015 Saudi Arabia and its allies began a campaign of air strikes and blockade on his behalf. The war that followed brought famine and cholera to the poorest country in Arabia.

In a referendum called by David Cameron on 23 June 2016, the British people voted by 51.9 percent to 48.1 percent to leave the European Union they had joined in 1973. Cameron resigned; after three years of parliamentary deadlock under Theresa May, Boris Johnson won an election on the promise to get Brexit done, and the United Kingdom left on 31 January 2020.

On 12 July 2016 a tribunal sitting at The Hague under the Law of the Sea Convention, in a case brought by the Philippines, ruled that China's claim to historic rights within its nine-dash line had no basis in law. China rejected the award and went on fortifying the artificial islands with airstrips and harbors that it had raised on the reefs of the Spratlys.

After more than half a century of war between the Colombian state and the Marxist guerrillas of the FARC, which cost hundreds of thousands of lives, President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC commander Rodrigo Londoño signed a peace accord at Cartagena in September 2016. Voters narrowly rejected it in October; a revised accord was ratified by Congress in November, and Santos received the Nobel Peace Prize.

After Rohingya militants attacked police posts in northern Rakhine on 25 August 2017, the Burmese army burned hundreds of villages of the Muslim Rohingya, whom the state had long denied citizenship. More than seven hundred thousand fled across the Naf River into Bangladesh, and investigators of the United Nations accused the generals of genocidal intent.

On 23 May 2017 fighters of the Maute group and Abu Sayyaf, sworn to the Islamic State, seized Marawi, the chief Muslim city of Mindanao, took Christian hostages, among them a priest, and set fire to the cathedral. Five months of fighting left the city center in ruins and more than eleven hundred dead, most of them militants, before the army retook it in October.

In December doctors in Wuhan began to see a cluster of pneumonia cases caused by a new coronavirus, and the authorities silenced those who raised the alarm. In January 2020 the city of eleven million was sealed off, but the disease had already spread. The COVID-19 pandemic killed some seven million people by official counts across the world and halted much of its economy.

Two decades after a civil war over the vast Panguna copper mine had taken some fifteen to twenty thousand lives between 1988 and 1998, the people of Bougainville voted in a referendum in late 2019. Nearly 98 percent chose independence from Papua New Guinea, though the vote did not bind the national parliament.

On 4 April 2019 Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, master of the east and the oil ports, sent his Libyan National Army against Tripoli and the United Nations-recognized government of Fayez al-Sarraj. Wagner mercenaries and Emirati drones fought for him, Turkish troops and drones for Tripoli; in June 2020 his forces fell back to Sirte, and Libya remained divided between two governments.

When Alexander Lukashenko, ruler of Belarus since 1994, claimed eighty percent of the vote in the election of 9 August 2020 against Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, hundreds of thousands marched in Minsk under the white-red-white flag. The police beat and jailed them by the thousand, Tsikhanouskaya was driven into exile, and Lukashenko survived with Moscow's support.

As the last American troops withdrew under a bargain struck with the Taliban, the Afghan army collapsed province by province, and on 15 August 2021 President Ashraf Ghani fled and the Taliban entered Kabul. Thousands besieged the airport, some clinging to departing aircraft. The Islamic Emirate was restored, and girls were again barred from secondary school.

On 1 February 2021, as the newly elected parliament was to meet, General Min Aung Hlaing arrested Aung San Suu Kyi and seized power, alleging fraud in the vote her party had won. Mass protests were met with gunfire; the deposed lawmakers formed a National Unity Government, and its People's Defence Forces joined the ethnic armies in a civil war across the country.

Before dawn on 24 February 2022 Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine from Russia, Belarus, and the Crimea, the largest war in Europe since 1945. Russian airborne troops landed at Hostomel airfield and columns drove on Kyiv, but President Zelensky stayed in his capital and the Ukrainians stopped the assault; by early April the Russians had withdrawn from the north.

When Russian troops withdrew from the Kyiv suburb of Bucha at the end of March 2022, Ukrainian soldiers and reporters found the bodies of civilians in the streets, some with hands bound, and a mass grave behind a church. Over four hundred people had been killed during the month-long occupation. In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued a warrant for Putin's arrest over the deportation of Ukrainian children.

Encircled in the first days of March 2022, the port of Mariupol on the Sea of Azov was shelled for nearly three months. On 16 March a Russian bomb struck the drama theater where hundreds of civilians sheltered beneath the word children painted on the ground outside. The last defenders, holding the Azovstal steelworks, surrendered on 20 May; thousands of townspeople had died.

In September 2022 Ukrainian forces broke through south of Kharkiv and in days recovered Izium, Kupiansk, and most of the province, finding mass graves at Izium. Putin answered by mobilizing three hundred thousand reservists and proclaiming the annexation of four Ukrainian provinces he did not wholly hold. On 11 November the Russians abandoned Kherson, the only provincial capital they had taken in the invasion.

Abe Shinzō, the longest-serving prime minister in Japan's history, who had sought to revive the economy and to free the armed forces from the limits of the postwar constitution, was shot dead while giving a campaign speech outside a railway station in Nara, by a man who bore a grudge against a religious sect.

General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's army and the Rapid Support Forces of Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, called Hemedti, had overthrown Omar al-Bashir together in 2019 and the civilian government in 2021. On 15 April 2023 they turned on each other in the streets of Khartoum. The war drove over ten million people from their homes, the greatest displacement in the world, and the RSF renewed the massacres of Darfur.

On 7 October 2023 Hamas fighters broke through the fence around Gaza and attacked Israeli villages, army posts, and a music festival near Re'im, killing about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and carrying some 250 hostages into Gaza. Israel answered with a war of bombardment and invasion that by the end of 2024 had killed over forty thousand people in Gaza by its health ministry's count and laid much of the strip in ruins.

On 27 October 2023 three ethnic armies of northern Shan State, the Three Brotherhood Alliance, opened a joint offensive against the junta, overrunning hundreds of outposts and taking the border town of Laukkai in January 2024. In August 2024 the Kokang army captured Lashio, seat of the army's Northeastern Command, one of the gravest defeats the Burmese military had ever suffered.

The invasion of Ukraine ended the long neutrality of Finland and Sweden. Finland, which shares a frontier of over eight hundred miles with Russia, joined the North Atlantic alliance on 4 April 2023, and Sweden, neutral since the Napoleonic wars, followed on 7 March 2024 after Turkey and Hungary had at last ratified its entry.

Azerbaijan, rearmed with Turkish and Israeli drones, retook the districts around Karabakh and the town of Shusha in a forty-four-day war in the autumn of 2020. After a blockade of nine months, its army attacked on 19 September 2023, and the Armenian authorities surrendered the next day. Within a week over a hundred thousand Armenians, nearly the whole population, had fled to Armenia.

On 26 July 2023 the presidential guard under General Abdourahamane Tchiani detained Niger's elected president, Mohamed Bazoum, in his residence. Following the juntas of Mali and Burkina Faso, the new rulers expelled the French troops, turned to Russia, and with their neighbors formed an Alliance of Sahel States, breaking with the West African bloc.

On 23 August 2023 the lander Vikram of the Chandrayaan-3 mission, launched from Sriharikota on the Bay of Bengal, touched down near the south pole of the Moon, the first craft to land so far south. India became the fourth nation to make a soft landing on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States, and China.

On 27 October 2023 the Three Brotherhood Alliance, the Kokang, Ta'ang, and Arakan armies, fell upon the junta's posts in northern Shan State along the roads to China. Town after town fell, and on 4 January 2024 the garrison of Laukkai, capital of the Kokang region, surrendered: some 2,100 soldiers and six brigadier generals. It was the army's worst defeat in decades, and the resistance took heart across the country.

At the end of November 2024 the rebels of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, led by Ahmed al-Sharaa, called Abu Mohammad al-Jolani, swept out of Idlib and took Aleppo in days, while the regime's army melted away. Hama and Homs fell, and on 8 December Bashar al-Assad fled to Moscow as the rebels entered Damascus. Fifty-four years of rule by the Assad family were over.

On 6 August 2024 Ukrainian brigades crossed the frontier into Russia's Kursk province and took the town of Sudzha and some hundreds of square miles, the first foreign occupation of Russian soil since the Second World War. Moscow brought in reinforcements, among them thousands of North Korean soldiers sent by Kim Jong Un that autumn.

Student protests in Bangladesh against quotas in government jobs swelled in July 2024 into a revolt across the country, and many hundreds were killed as police and party cadres fired on the crowds. On 5 August Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who had ruled for fifteen years, fled by helicopter to India, and the Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus came home to lead an interim government.

On 17 August 2024 President Joko Widodo held the Independence Day ceremonies at Nusantara, the new capital rising in the forests of East Kalimantan to relieve crowded and sinking Jakarta. Its palace, built in the shape of the mythical bird Garuda, stood amid unfinished ministries as he handed power to Prabowo Subianto in October.

On 3 August 2024 the Kokang army of the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance took Lashio, the largest town of northern Shan State, with the headquarters of the junta's Northeastern Command. It was the first of the army's regional commands ever to fall, and with the Arakan Army sweeping through Rakhine the junta held little more than the heartland of the Irrawaddy valley.

By the end of 2023 the Rapid Support Forces of Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo held four of the five state capitals of Darfur, and at El Geneina they and allied Arab militias had slaughtered the Masalit by the thousand. In May 2024 they closed upon El Fasher, the army's last stronghold in Darfur, crowded with refugees, and laid it under a siege of shelling and hunger.
